Volume Seventeen
The Book of Quranic Exegesis
Part Four
Commentary on Sūrat al-Ikhlās and the Two Surahs of Refuge

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy. All praise belongs to Allah alone, and may blessings and peace be upon him after whom there is no prophet.

Sūrat al-Ikhlās

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah be pleased with him—was asked:

Concerning the report that the surah “Say, ‘He is Allah, the One’” is equivalent to one-third of the Quran, and similar reports concerning the surahs (The Earthquake), “Say, ‘O disbelievers’” and (The Opening): Are these reports of equivalence established for all these surahs or only some of them? Who narrated them, and which of them are authentic? What does this equivalence mean, given that Allah’s speech is one in relation to Him, Mighty and Majestic? And does this difference in merit—assuming

it is established—extend to the names and attributes, or not? Is it permissible to regard some eternal attributes and eternal names as superior to others, even though they are eternal? Who has held this view, and in which of his books did he state it? What grounds support the preferred view, with whatever rational and transmitted evidence can be provided?

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

All praise belongs to Allah. The compilers of the authentic collections, such as al-Bukhārī and Muslim, recorded reports concerning the excellence of “Say, ‘He is Allah, the One.’” It is reported that al-Dāraqutnī said: “No surah has more authentic reports concerning its excellence than this one.”

They likewise recorded reports concerning the excellence of the Opening of the Book. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said of it:

“Nothing like it has been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, or the Quran.”

He did not state that it was equivalent to a portion of the Quran, as he said of “Say, ‘He is Allah, the One’” that it was equivalent to one-third of the Quran.

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, al-Dahhāk al-Mashriqī narrated from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to his Companions, ‘Is any one of you unable to recite one-third of the Quran in a night?’ They found this difficult and said, ‘Which of us could manage that, O Messenger of Allah?’ He said, ‘“Allah, the One, the Eternal Refuge” is one-third of the Quran.’”

In Sahīh Muslim, Ma‘dān ibn Abī Talhah narrated from Abū al-Dardā’:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Is any one of you unable to recite one-third of the Quran in a night?’

translated_text:
They asked, ‘How can one recite one-third of the Quran?’ He replied, ‘“Say: He is Allah, the One” is equivalent to one-third of the Quran.’”

Muslim also narrated from Abū al-Dardā’ that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah divided the Quran into three parts and made ‘Say: He is Allah, the One’ one of those parts.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn Abī Sa‘sa‘ah narrated from Abū Sa‘īd:

“A man heard another man repeatedly reciting ‘Say: He is Allah, the One.’ In the morning, he went to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and mentioned this to him, regarding that recitation as little. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, it is indeed equivalent to one-third of the Quran.’”

Al-Bukhārī also recorded from Abū Sa‘īd, who said: “My brother Qatādah ibn al-Nu‘mān informed me that a man stood in prayer during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reciting ‘Say: He is Allah, the One’ before dawn, without reciting anything else…” The rest of the hadith follows in similar wording.

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Gather together, for I shall recite to you one-third of the Quran.’ So people gathered. Then the Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came out, recited ‘Say: He is Allah, the One,’ and went back inside. We said to one another, ‘I think some news has come to him from heaven, and that is what made him go inside.’ Then the Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came out and said, ‘I told you that I would recite to you one-third of the Quran. Indeed, it is equivalent to one-third of the Quran.’”

In another wording recorded by Muslim, he said: “The Messenger of Allah came out to us

, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘I shall recite to you one-third of the Quran.’ He then recited, ‘Say: He is Allah, the One; Allah, the Eternal Refuge,’ continuing to the end of the surah.”

As for the hadith concerning “The Earthquake” and “Say: O disbelievers,” al-Tirmidhī narrated from Anas ibn Mālik, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Whoever recites “When the earth is shaken,” it is equivalent for him to half the Quran. Whoever recites “Say: O disbelievers,” it is equivalent for him to one-quarter of the Quran.’”

Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘“When the earth is shaken” is equivalent to half the Quran, and “Say: O disbelievers” is equivalent to one-quarter of the Quran.’”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated both reports and described each as singular.

As for the hadith concerning al-Fātihah, al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh from Abū Sa‘īd ibn al-Mu‘allā, who said:

“I was praying in the mosque when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called me, but I did not answer him. I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, I was praying.’ He said, ‘Has Allah not said, “Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you”?’ Then he said, ‘I shall surely teach you a surah that is the greatest surah in the Quran.’ He said, ‘“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds” is the seven oft-repeated verses and the glorious Quran.’”

In the Sunan and Musnad collections, al-‘Alā’ ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān narrated from his father, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Ubayy ibn Ka‘b:

“Shall I teach you a surah the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Criterion?” He said, “I hope

that you will not leave through this door before you have learned it.” The report also states: “He asked, ‘How do you recite in prayer?’ I recited the Mother of the Quran to him, and he said, ‘By Him in Whose hand is my soul, nothing like it has been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Quran. It is the seven oft-repeated verses and the glorious Quran that I have been given.’” Mālik also narrated it in al-Muwatta’, from al-‘Alā’ ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān, from Abū Sa‘īd, the freedman of ‘Āmir ibn Kurayz, with an interrupted chain of transmission.

In Sahīh Muslim, ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Have you not considered the verses revealed tonight, the like of which has never been seen: “Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak” and “Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind”?’”

Another wording reads:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to me, ‘Verses have been revealed to me, the like of which has never been seen: the two surahs of refuge.’”

In this authentic hadith, he stated that nothing like the two surahs of refuge had ever been seen, just as he stated that nothing like al-Fātihah had been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Quran. This demonstrates that some portions of the Quran are superior to others.

Section

As for the question about the meaning of this equivalence, given that all of it is equally the speech of Allah, this question encompasses two matters:

First: Are some portions of Allah’s speech superior to others, or not?

Second: What does it mean that “Say: He is Allah, the One” is equivalent to one-third of the Quran? And what is the reason for that?

translated_text:
We say in response:

As for the first, it is “a major question” over which there is widespread disagreement. Some groups maintain that certain portions of Allah’s speech are superior to others, as the prophetic texts explicitly state. The Prophet said that nothing like al-Fātihah had been revealed in the three scriptures, and that Sūrat al-Ikhlās is equivalent to one-third of the Quran. Its equivalence to one-third of the Quran precludes its being equal in merit to other passages containing the same number of letters.

He also declared Āyat al-Kursī to be the greatest verse in the Quran, as is established in the Sahīh. It is likewise established in Sahīh Muslim that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Ubayy ibn Ka‘b:

“Abū al-Mundhir, do you know which of the verses of Allah’s Book that you know is the greatest?”

He said: “I replied, ‘Allah and His Messenger know best.’ He said, ‘Abū al-Mundhir, do you know which verse in Allah’s Book is the greatest?’ I replied, ‘Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all.’ He then struck my chest and said, ‘May your knowledge bring you joy, Abū al-Mundhir!’”

Ibn Abī Shaybah also narrated it in his Musnad through Muslim’s chain of transmission, adding:

“By Him in Whose hand is my soul, this verse has a tongue and two lips with which it glorifies the Sovereign at the foot of the Throne.”

It has also been reported that it is “the foremost of the verses of the Quran.” Concerning the two surahs of refuge, he said:

“The like of them has never been seen.”

Allah Most High has said:

“Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it.”

He thus states that He brings one better than it or similar to it. This is Allah’s declaration that He may sometimes bring a verse similar to that one, and at other times one better than it. This indicates that

the verses are sometimes equal in merit and at other times differ in merit. Moreover, the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran are all Allah’s speech, yet Muslims know that the Quran is the best of the three books.

Allah Most High says:

“And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming the Scripture that came before it and as a guardian over it.”

He also says:

“Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will preserve it.”

And He says:

“Say: If mankind and jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like, even if they supported one another.”

And He says:

“Allah has sent down the finest discourse—a Book consistent in its parts and oft-repeated—at which the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver; then their skins and hearts soften at the remembrance of Allah.”

He thus declares it to be the finest discourse, indicating that it is better than all other discourse, whether revealed by Allah or not.

Allah Most High also says:

“And We have certainly given you the seven oft-repeated verses and the magnificent Quran.”

Whether this refers to al-Fātihah or to the Quran in its entirety, it indicates that the magnificent Quran is distinguished by this description above what does not share it. Allah has also described the entire Quran as glorious, noble, and mighty.

He has challenged creation to produce its like, or the like of ten of its surahs, or the like of a single surah of it. He says:

“Then let them produce a discourse like it, if they are truthful.”

And He says:

“Then produce ten fabricated surahs like it.”

And He says:

“Then produce a surah like it.”

He has further distinguished it in that nothing but it is to be recited in prayer. No one may recite anything else, whether alongside it or without it, nor may one pray without reciting the Quran. Thus, nothing else can take

its place when one is able to recite it. Likewise, Muslims agree that no other passage can take the place of al-Fātihah in every respect, whether it is considered an obligation whose omission requires the prayer to be repeated, a duty whose omission is sinful but does not require repetition, or a sunnah. No one has said that reciting another passage is equal in every respect to reciting it.

The Quran is also distinguished by the requirement that only someone in a state of purity may touch a written copy of it. This is established from the Companions—such as Saʿd, Salmān, and Ibn ʿUmar—and from the vast majority of earlier and later scholars, including the four imams of jurisprudence and others. This was also prescribed in the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the letter he wrote to ʿAmr ibn Hazm, which he undoubtedly wrote to him. Allah’s Book also indicates this. Likewise, according to the vast majority of scholars, including the four imams of jurisprudence and others, someone in a state of janābah (major ritual impurity) may not recite the Quran, as the Sunnah indicates.

Distinguishing one of two discourses through rulings that confer honor upon it indicates that it is intrinsically superior, even if this were to amount to preferring one of two identical things without any grounds for preference. This is contrary to what is known of the way of the Lord Most High in His legislation, and indeed in His creation, and contrary to what both rational and scriptural evidence indicate.

Furthermore, Allah Most High says:

“And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord.”

And He says:

“So give good tidings to My servants who listen to what is said and follow the best of it.”

And He says:

“Hold firmly to them, and command your people to follow the best of them.”

“Al-Hasan al-Basrī said: ‘Allah sent down one hundred and four books from heaven and placed their knowledge within four of them: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and al-Furqān (the Criterion). He then placed the knowledge of these four within al-Furqān, then the knowledge of the Quran within al-Mufassal, then the knowledge of al-Mufassal within the Opening of the Book. Whoever knows its interpretation is therefore like one who knows the interpretation of all Allah’s revealed books, and whoever recites it is as though he has recited the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Quran.’

“As for the substantive consideration, Allah set it alongside the entire Quran, saying:

‘We have certainly given you seven oft-repeated verses and the glorious Quran.’

“This is a distinction in which no other surah comes close to it.”

I say: This follows the interpretation of those who identify it as the seven oft-repeated verses and understand ‘the glorious Quran’ to mean the entire Quran.

He said: “Furthermore, it is called ‘the Mother of the Quran’; the mother of a thing is its source and substance. Thus Allah called Mecca ‘the Mother of Cities’ because of its superiority over them. Moreover, it is the seven oft-repeated verses, and it contains what no other surah contains: praise and glorification of the Lord Most High, and the servant’s seeking His help and refuge and offering supplication, as in the well-known hadith in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said that Allah Most High says: ‘I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant.’”

He said: “Furthermore, He has revealed nothing like it in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or any of the revealed books. Evidence of this is that its recitation has been made easy for everyone in a way that is not the case with other parts of the Quran.

translated_text:
And it is used as a proverbial comparison; thus people say, ‘So-and-so knows something by heart as well as he knows al-Fātiha.’ Since it holds this position, no other surah equals it in this respect, and it therefore enjoys a unique distinction. Moreover, it is the seven oft-repeated verses. The Quran commentators said that this means its recitation is repeated in every unit of prayer. Some said, ‘It was revealed to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, twice.’”

I say: There are other interpretations as well.

He said: “As for the legal ruling, its recitation is recommended in every unit of prayer, and omitting it is disliked. Were it not superior, it would not have been singled out in this way. Supporting this is the position of those who disagree—meaning the followers of Abū Hanīfa—that whoever omits its recitation must perform the prostrations of forgetfulness.

“We therefore say: Either it is a pillar of prayer or it is not. If it is a pillar, its omission cannot be made up for by prostration; if it is not a pillar, prostration should not be obligatory for omitting it.”

I say: He means that prostration is required only for omitting an act that is obligatory when one is acting deliberately; if one forgets it, prostration becomes obligatory. If an act is obligatory, deliberately omitting it must invalidate one’s prayer, because one has not done what one was commanded to do. This differs from forgetting some obligatory acts, since their omission can be made up for by the prostrations of forgetfulness.

The position of Mālik, Ahmad, and Abū Hanīfa is that the prostrations of forgetfulness are obligatory, because they hold that some obligatory acts may be omitted forgetfully without invalidating the prayer. Likewise, according to the scholars’ consensus, the prayer is not invalidated by a forgetful addition, whereas a deliberate addition would invalidate it.

However, according to the well-known position reported from Mālik and Ahmad, they say:

“Deliberately omitting an obligatory act invalidates one’s prayer. If it is omitted forgetfully, some such omissions invalidate the prayer, while others can be made up for by the prostrations of forgetfulness. Thus, omitting bowing, prostration, or recitation invalidates the prayer in either case. According to both of them, deliberately omitting the first tashahhud invalidates the prayer, whereas forgetting it requires the prostrations of forgetfulness.”

Abū Hanīfa, however, says: “If someone omits an obligatory act (wājib) that is not a strict obligation (fard)—such as reciting al-Fātiha—he has acted wrongly, but his prayer is not invalidated.” Al-Shāfi‘ī makes no distinction in prayer between a pillar and an obligatory act, although he and all the other imams distinguish between them in Hajj. The purpose here is to mention some of those who said that al-Fātiha is more excellent than other surahs.

Abū Umar ibn Abd al-Barr said:

“As for the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to Ubayy:

‘Do you know a surah the like of which Allah has not revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Quran?’

“The meaning is that none equals it in encompassing the meanings of goodness. It praises Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as He deserves, with the praise that truly belongs to Him alone, for every blessing and every good comes from Him and no other. He is the Creator, the Provider. He continued:

“It has also been said that this means prayer is valid through its recitation, but not through that of another surah, and that no other surah can take its place. This interpretation, however, is not unanimously accepted.”

I say:

He means that scholars disagree over this point—namely, that prayer is valid only with its recitation. This indicates that scholars agree on the first description: that it is the most excellent surah.

The same applies to what the Quran and Sunnah state concerning the Quran’s superiority to the rest of Allah’s speech—the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other scriptures. All the early Muslim generations acknowledged this. None of them said, “It is all Allah’s speech,” and therefore refused to regard the Quran as superior to the others. Allah Most High says:

“Allah has sent down the best discourse: a Book consistent in its parts, repeating its teachings.”

He thus declares that it is the best discourse. He also says:

“We relate to you the best of narratives through Our revelation to you of this Quran, although before it you were among the unaware.”

Regarding “the best of narratives,” some have said that it is a verbal noun, while others have said that it is a direct object.

According to the first interpretation, the meaning is: “We narrate to you in the finest manner,” just as one might say, “We speak to you in the finest manner,” or, “We explain to you in the clearest manner.”

Al-Zajjāj said:

“We explain to you in the clearest manner. A narrator is someone who relates a story as it truly happened.”

He explained that His words,

“through Our revelation to you of this Quran,”

mean, “by Our revealing this Quran to you.” Whoever holds this view says, “through Our revelation to you of this Quran.” According to this interpretation, it is like saying, “We recite

to you in the finest manner, and recite to you in the finest way.”

The second interpretation is that the meaning is: “We relate to you the best of what can be related”—that is, the finest accounts and narratives—as He says in another surah:

“Allah has sent down the best discourse.”

He also says:

“And who is more truthful than Allah in speech?”

This is supported by His words in the account of Moses:

“When he came to him and related his story,”

and His words:

“There was certainly a lesson in their narratives for people of understanding.”

What is meant is their accounts, reports, and stories, not merely the act of narration. The two interpretations necessarily imply one another in meaning, as we shall explain. Thus, this accusative expression may combine the sense of a verbal noun with that of a direct object, since it contains both meanings. This differs from cases in which the action is distinct from its object: there, construing the accusative in one sense precludes the other.

The grammarians who preferred the first interpretation—such as al-Zajjāj and others—said that qasas is a verbal noun. One says, qassa atharahu, yaqussuhu qasasan, meaning that he traced someone’s footsteps. Hence the words of Allah Most High:

“So they turned back, retracing their footsteps.”

The expressions iqtassa atharahu and taqassasa have the same meaning. One also says, iqtasastu al-hadītha, meaning, “I related the account as it actually happened,” and iqtassa ‘alayhi al-khabara qasasan, meaning, “He related the news to him.”

Qasas, with an a, is not the plural of qissah, as some ordinary people suppose. Rather, the plural is qisas, with an i, and its singular is qissah. A qissah is an event or account that is related; it follows the pattern fi‘lah with a passive meaning. Its plural is qisas, with an i.

In His words,

“We relate to you the best of narratives,”

the word is qasas, with an a. He did not say qisas, with an i. Yet

some people thought that what was meant was “the best of stories”—qisas, with an i—and that the story in question was that of Joseph. A number of Quran commentators mentioned this.

They then asked: Why was it called the best of narratives? One answer was that no other story in the Quran contains as many lessons, wise teachings, and subtle insights as this story. Another was that a long period of time separates its beginning from its end. Another was the excellence of the dialogue between Joseph and his brothers, his patience in bearing their mistreatment, his refraining from mentioning what they had done when they met again, and his generous forgiveness.

Another explanation was that it mentions prophets, righteous people, angels, devils, humans, jinn, livestock, and birds; the lives of kings, slaves, merchants, scholars, the ignorant, men, and women; and women’s scheming and stratagems. It also discusses Allah’s oneness, jurisprudence, history, dream interpretation, governance, social relations, and the management of one’s livelihood. It is therefore the best of narratives because of the meanings and benefits it contains that serve both religious and worldly life. Another explanation was that it mentions the lover and the beloved. Yet another was that “best” means “most remarkable.”

Among those who regard Joseph’s story as the best of narratives are some who know that qasas, with an a, means an account or report, and who say that it is the finest of all accounts and reports. Many of them, however, think that what is meant is “the best of stories”—qisas, with an i. These people are ignorant of Arabic. Both views are mistaken. His words, “the best of narratives,” do not refer to Joseph’s story alone. Rather, it is one of the accounts Allah has related and is included among the best of narratives.

and for this reason Allah Most High says at the end of the surah:

“We sent before you only men from the towns, to whom We revealed. Have they not travelled through the land and seen what became of those before them? The home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Will you not then use reason?”

“Until, when the messengers had lost hope and their people thought they had been lied to, Our help came to them, and those We willed were saved. Our punishment cannot be averted from the criminal people.”

“There is certainly a lesson in their accounts for people of understanding. This is no fabricated tale, but a confirmation of what came before it, a detailed explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy for people who believe.”

Thus He explains that the lesson lies in the accounts of the messengers. He commands us to consider the fate of those who rejected them, and how the messengers themselves ultimately attained victory. It is well known that the story of Moses, including what happened between him and Pharaoh and others, is far, far greater and nobler than the story of Joseph. It is therefore the greatest of the accounts of the prophets related in the Quran. Allah repeats it more often than any other and recounts it at greater length and in greater detail. Indeed, the accounts of the other prophets—such as Noah, Hūd, Sālih, Shuʿayb, and the other messengers—are greater than the story of Joseph. For this reason, Allah repeats those accounts in the Quran but does not repeat the story of Joseph.

This is because those who opposed Joseph did not oppose him on account of religion. Rather, their hostility arose from worldly concerns: they envied him for his father’s love and wronged him, but he remained patient and feared Allah. He—may Allah’s blessings be upon him—was tested both by those who wronged him and by someone who invited him to sexual immorality. In both trials, he remained patient and feared Allah. He was also tested with sovereignty, and thus underwent trials in prosperity as well as adversity. In both circumstances, he remained patient and feared Allah. Yet none of those not mentioned in the Quran equalled Joseph in fearing Allah and remaining patient, nor did any of them attain, like Joseph, the finest outcome in this world and the Hereafter. Likewise, the accounts of the People of the Cave and of Dhū al-Qarnayn are each superior to others of their kind. The account of Dhū al-Qarnayn is the finest account of kings, and that of the People of the Cave is the finest account of Allah’s close servants who lived during the interval between messengers.

Thus, the words of Allah Most High:

embrace everything He has related in His Book: it is better than what He has not related. They do not mean that the story of Joseph is the best account related in the Quran. How can what happened to Joseph compare with what happened to Moses, Noah, Abraham, and the other messengers? How can the hostility Joseph faced compare with the hostility they faced? How can Joseph’s standing before Allah compare with their distinction and lofty ranks—may Allah’s blessings be upon them all? And how can the victory granted to Joseph compare with that granted to them?

For Joseph’s case was as Allah Most High says:

“Thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle wherever he wished. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

Allah humbled those who had wronged him, and they then repented. Thus, among the lessons of this story is that when someone who is wronged and envied remains patient and fears Allah, the final outcome will be in his favour, and that the envious wrongdoer

may have his repentance accepted and be pardoned by Allah, and that one who has been wronged should pardon his oppressor when he has power over him.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, drew upon this lesson on the day of the conquest of Mecca. Standing at the door of the Kaaba, after Allah had humbled before him those who had opposed and fought him—the men he set free—he asked, “What do you have to say?”

They replied, “We say: you are a noble brother and a noble cousin.”

He said, “I say to you what Joseph said to his brothers: ‘No blame will there be upon you today. May Allah forgive you, for He is the Most Merciful of the merciful.’”

Likewise, when ʿĀʾishah was wronged and falsely accused, and was told, “If you have committed a sin, seek Allah’s forgiveness and repent to Him,” she said in her response, “I say as Joseph’s father said: ‘So patience is most fitting, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe.’”

Thus, Joseph’s story contains many kinds of lessons for those who are wronged, those who are envied, those tested by temptations to immorality and sin, and others. But how does it compare with the accounts of Noah, Abraham, Moses, the Messiah, and others like them, whose stories tell how they called people to worship Allah alone, without any partner, only for their people to reject them, harm them, and harm those who believed in them?

These men suffered harm because they chose to worship Allah. They faced hostility and harm for freely choosing to love and worship Him. Had they not believed and called people to worship Allah, they would not have been harmed. This is unlike someone who suffers harm without having chosen it, as Joseph was taken from his father against his will. greater in their significance for his faith, his standing before Allah, and his reward than his patient endurance of his brothers’ wrongdoing toward him. Thus, Joseph is more greatly honoured for the former than for the latter. This is why Allah Most High said of him:

“Thus it was, so that We might turn evil and immorality away from him. Indeed, he was one of Our chosen servants.”

This is like comparing steadfast restraint from sin with patient endurance of calamities: the former is greater, and it is the patience of the God-fearing allies of Allah.

Sahl ibn Abd Allāh al-Tustarī said: “Both the righteous and the wicked perform good deeds, but only one of unwavering truthfulness remains steadfast in refraining from sin.” Joseph, may Allah’s blessings be upon him, was a man of unwavering truthfulness and a prophet. As for those who suffer wrongdoing against their will and endure it patiently, they are many. Whoever does not endure with the patience of the noble will eventually forget his grief as beasts do.

Likewise, when someone who has been wronged gains power and overcomes his oppressor, and the oppressor repents and submits to him, pardoning him is a fine and virtuous act. Yet many religious people and worldly people of sound judgment do this. For the forbearance of kings and governors better consolidates their rule, secures people’s obedience, and wins their hearts. Mu‘āwiyah was among the most forbearing of people. Al-Ma’mūn was also forbearing, to the point that he would say: “If people knew how much I love to pardon, they would seek my favour by committing offences.” Thus, when he gained power over the man who had contested his rule—his uncle Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mahdī—he pardoned him.

But steadfastly resisting desires and overpowering passions for Allah’s sake—not out of hope for anything from a created being or fear of one—despite the many inducements to commit an indecent act, and choosing prolonged imprisonment over it, as Joseph said:

“My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to”—

such conduct is found only among the finest of Allah’s righteous servants and His allies

who fear Him, as the Most High said:

“Thus it was, so that We might turn evil and immorality away from him. Indeed, he was one of Our chosen servants.”

He was thus among Allah’s chosen servants, of whom Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, you have no authority over My servants.”

For this reason, Joseph, the man of unwavering truthfulness, committed no sin whatsoever. Even the inclination he felt was recorded for him as a good deed when he abandoned it for Allah’s sake. This is why Allah, glorified be He, did not mention any repentance or seeking of forgiveness on his part, as He mentioned the repentance of prophets such as Adam, David, Noah, and others. Yet He did not mention any indecent act on the part of those prophets either—all praise belongs to Allah. Rather, they repented of other matters that would count as good deeds in the case of others.

Thus, no one is known to have equalled Joseph in the inducements to immorality with which he was tested, or in his fear of Allah and steadfastness amid that trial. What is known of others falls short of this, as in the report in the two Sahīh collections, in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Seven will be shaded by Allah beneath the shade of His Throne on the Day when there is no shade but His: a just ruler; a young man who grew up worshipping Allah; a man whose heart remains attached to the mosque from the time he leaves it until he returns; two men who love one another for Allah’s sake, meeting and parting upon that love; a man whom a woman of rank and beauty invites to herself, but who says, ‘I fear Allah’; a man who remembers Allah in solitude and whose eyes overflow with tears; and a man who gives charity so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends.”

If his patient endurance of harm in order not to commit an indecent act was greater than his patient endurance of his brothers’ wrongdoing, then what of the messengers’ patient endurance of the harm inflicted by those who rejected them, so as not to abandon their appointed task of calling them to worship Allah alone, enjoining what is right upon them, and forbidding them from

what is wrong? Such patience is a form of jihad in Allah’s cause, for the purpose of jihad is that Allah’s word should reign supreme and that all worship should be devoted to Allah alone. Jihad and patient endurance in it are therefore the finest deeds, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is prayer, and its pinnacle is jihad in Allah’s cause.”

This is an authentic hadith, related by Imam Ahmad and by al-Tirmidhī, who graded it authentic. It forms part of the lengthy hadith of Muʿādh ibn Jabal. Jihad is also the deed most beloved to Allah.

Thus, patient restraint from that sin is the patience of an emigrant who abandons what he has been forbidden, and of one who wages jihad, striving against his own soul for Allah’s sake and against Allah’s enemies, both outward and inward. The emigrant who patiently refrains from sin has striven only against his own soul and his devil. He then strives against Allah’s outward enemy so that Allah’s word may reign supreme and all worship may be devoted to Allah alone.

The patience of someone wronged is the patience of someone afflicted by calamity. Yet someone struck by a heaven-sent calamity can endure what someone wronged by other people cannot. The former is conscious that Allah is the One who has brought this upon him, so he gives up all hope of warding it off, exacting punishment, or taking revenge. By contrast, someone wronged by others feels that he can repel his oppressor, punish him, and take revenge upon him. Patient endurance of this calamity is therefore more meritorious and greater, as was the patience of Joseph, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him.

Such patience arises because the person knows that Allah has decreed what happened, so he bears it patiently, just as he would a heaven-sent calamity. It may also arise from his desire to attain the reward of those who restrain their anger and pardon

others—and Allah loves those who do good—and to keep his heart free of rancor toward people. In both cases, the person is conscious that this has befallen him because of his sins and that Allah expiates his misdeeds through it, so he seeks forgiveness and repents. He also recognizes that patience is obligatory upon him and that giving way to anguish is something for which he may be punished.

If he rises to the level of contentment, he recognizes that contentment is the paradise of this world, the resting place of worshippers, and the greatest gateway to Allah. If he sees his affliction as a blessing because it sets his heart and religion aright, brings him closer to Allah, expiates his misdeeds, and protects him from sins to which the devils among humans and jinn entice him, he thanks Allah for these blessings.

Heaven-sent afflictions and those inflicted by people share these features. People’s awareness and understanding of these matters are part of Allah’s bounty, which He bestows upon whomever He wills among His servants. This is why people’s responses to afflictions and other circumstances differ so greatly.

When the servant recognizes the divine decree—that this is something Allah has ordained and decreed, and that He is its Creator—he combines patience with submission to the all-powerful Lord, the Sovereign who does whatever He wills. This is the state of the patient person.

He may also submit to the Lord who does good to him and manages his affairs by choosing what is best for him, who

“never decrees anything for the believer except that it is good for him: if prosperity comes to him, he gives thanks, and that is good for him; if adversity befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him.”

see this as a blessing, his submission is that of one who is content but not grateful.

He may also submit to Allah, besides whom there is no god, who deserves to be worshipped for His own sake and is praised for everything He does. He is All-Knowing, All-Wise, Most Merciful; He does nothing without wisdom and deserves to be loved, worshipped, and praised for everything He has created. This is the submission of a servant who worships and praises Him. Such a person belongs among those who praise Allah, who will be the first to be called to Paradise. Among them is the bearer of the Banner of Praise, beneath whose banner Adam and all those below him will stand.

For such a person, the divine decree is good and a blessing from Allah. Yet his praise of Allah and contentment with His decree arise from knowing Allah, loving Him, and worshipping Him because He alone, without partner, deserves worship. His patience, contentment, and praise are thus acts of worship arising from this knowledge and testimony. He bears witness in his heart that there is no god but Allah, understanding a god to be one who deserves worship.

This differs from someone who recognizes only His lordship, will, and power, or only His kindness and blessings. These are two incomplete and limited perspectives. Only those whose knowledge of Allah and of His religion—with which He sent His messengers and revealed His Books—is deficient confine themselves to them. Such are the people of innovation among the Jahmiyyah, the Qadariyyah Jabriyyah, and the Qadariyyah Mu‘tazilah: the first perspective is that of the former groups, and the second is that of the latter.

Recognizing His lordship, power, and will, together with His mercy, kindness, and bounty, while also recognizing His divinity, His love and good pleasure, and the praise, commendation, and glory that are His—this is the perspective of the people of knowledge and faith among the people of the Sunnah and the community, who faithfully follow

the first and foremost among the Emigrants and the Helpers. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere. The point here is that a believer may adopt this attitude toward calamities in general. When they result from the actions of believers, he can restrain his anger and pardon people. Joseph the truthful—may Allah’s blessings be upon him—displayed this, as well as something greater: patiently resisting immorality despite the powerful urge to commit it. This patience is greater than the former kind, indeed greater even than perseverance in obedience.

Thus Allah, glorified is He, says, describing the God-fearing for whom He has prepared Paradise:

“And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Paradise as vast as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing.”

“Those who spend in ease and hardship, who restrain their anger and pardon people—and Allah loves those who do good.”

“And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins—and who forgives sins except Allah?—and do not knowingly persist in what they have done.”

“Their reward is forgiveness from their Lord and gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever. How excellent is the reward of those who strive!”

He thus describes them as generous and forbearing, spending, restraining their anger, and pardoning people. Then, when it comes to forbidden desires, He describes them as repenting of them, saying: “And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins—and who

forgives sins except Allah?—and do not persist in what they have done.” He thus describes them as repenting of these sins and not persisting in them, rather than abstaining from them altogether. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“Each son of Adam has his share of sexual sin decreed for him, which he will inevitably encounter. The eyes commit sexual sin, and their sin is looking; the ear commits sexual sin, and its sin is listening; the tongue commits sexual sin, and its sin is speaking; the hand commits sexual sin, and its sin is grasping; the foot commits sexual sin, and its sin is walking. The heart wishes and desires, and the private parts confirm this or deny it.”

Another hadith states:

“All the children of Adam frequently sin, and the best of those who sin are those who repeatedly repent.”

A person inevitably engages in some of the preliminaries to a major sin, and many people commit the major sin itself. They are therefore commanded to repent and instructed not to persist in a minor sin, for no sin remains minor when persisted in, and no sin remains major when forgiveness is sought.

Joseph, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, patiently refrained from sin altogether. Nothing arose in him beyond an inclination that he abandoned for Allah’s sake, for which Allah recorded a good deed for him. Some Quran commentators have mentioned that he engaged in certain preliminaries, such as unfastening his trousers, sitting in the posture of a circumciser, and the like. However, these accounts have not been transmitted in a manner that warrants believing them, for none of this has been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

When such Israelite reports have not been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, their truth is unknown. Hence, they may neither be affirmed nor denied without evidence. Allah Most High says in the Quran:

“Thus We averted from him evil and indecency.”

Thus the Quran indicates that He averted from him evil

and indecency altogether. Had he committed a minor sin, he would have repented of it, yet the Quran makes no mention of his repentance. If someone commits any kind of evil or indecency, it cannot be said that it was averted from him; rather, he committed it and Allah accepted his repentance for it. The Quran indicates the contrary here.

The women testified that they knew of no evil on his part. Had he engaged in these preliminaries, the woman would have seen them, and she was among the women who testified, saying, “We know of no evil on his part.” Moreover, she said:

“I did indeed try to seduce him, but he firmly resisted.”

She also said:

“I tried to seduce him, and he is indeed one of the truthful.”

The word “evil” is an indefinite noun in a negative construction, indicating that the woman had seen no evil on his part. She had no knowledge of the inclination within his heart. Even had she known of it, his abandoning it for Allah’s sake would have counted as a good deed. Had he simply abandoned it, it would have counted as neither a good deed nor a bad one, for such an inclination incurs no sin unless accompanied by speech or action.

As for the accounts of Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and others—may Allah bless them—their significance is greater, as is what took place on both sides. What these prophets did in calling people to Allah’s oneness, His worship, and His religion; making manifest His signs, commands, prohibitions, promises, and warnings; striving against those who denied them; and patiently enduring their abuse is greater in Allah’s sight. For this reason, they were superior to Joseph—may Allah bless them all. What they patiently endured, and what they patiently refrained from, was greater than what Joseph endured and refrained from. The correct view, however, is that al-qasas (“narrative”) functions as a direct object. The word kalām (“speech”) may denote the act expressed by kallamahu taklīman (“he spoke to him”), or it may denote the utterance itself. An utterance involves an act on the speaker’s part, which is what the verbal noun denotes, and the utterance arises from that act. Thus, an utterance is sometimes regarded as a kind of action, because it results from an activity, and sometimes as a separate category alongside action, as when one says, “speech and action.” The same distinction may apply to qasas (“narrative”), bayān (“explanation”), hadīth (“discourse”), khabar (“report”), and similar words.

When qasas and similar words are intended as verbal nouns denoting the act, that act necessarily entails an utterance, which follows from it. When they denote the speech or utterance itself, this necessarily entails an act and follows from that act.

Verbal nouns formed according to the regular patterns of their verbs denote the act, as in kallamtuhu taklīman (“I spoke to him”) and akhbartuhu ikhbāran (“I informed him”). By contrast, forms that do not follow the regular patterns of their verbs—such as kalām (“speech”), khabar (“report”), and the like—denote the utterance when used without qualification. The same may be said of qasas, since the regular verbal noun of its verb is qass, just as one says ‘addahu ‘addan (“he counted it”), maddahu maddan (“he extended it”), and likewise qassahu qassan (“he recounted it”).

Qasas, however, is not the regular verbal-noun form of a verb whose second and third root consonants are identical. The only evidence they have cited for its being a verbal noun is His statement:

“So they retraced their footsteps.”

Yet this does not establish that it is a verbal noun. Rather, it may be an action noun used in place of the verbal noun, as in His statement:

“And Allah has caused you to grow as a growth from the earth.”

Even if qasas is taken to be the verbal noun of qassa al-athar (“he followed the tracks”), it does not follow that it is the verbal noun of qassa al-hadīth (“he recounted the discourse”). For a discourse is a report and tidings; thus, qasas is like khabar (“report”), naba’ (“tidings”), and kalām (“speech”).

It is therefore clear that His words “the best of stories” are accusative as a direct object. Everything Allah recounts is the best of stories. You say, “I uttered good words” (qultu qawlan hasanan), and “I made him hear an utterance” (asma‘tuhu qawlan). He did not hear the act denoted by the verbal noun; rather, he heard the sound. the Sunnah who said that the Arabic Quran was not Allah’s speech, or who regarded what is recited as merely a meaning. Nor was there anyone among them who said that the servants’ voices—or their other distinctive attributes—were uncreated. Rather, they all agreed that the Quran recited is the Arabic Quran which the Holy Spirit brought down from Allah in truth, and that it is Allah’s speech, which He spoke.

They differed, however, concerning the servants’ recitation of it: is it the Quran itself, or the act by which one recites the Quran? The precise explanation is that the word “recitation” can mean either. Likewise, the word “Quran” can denote either the act of reciting or the speech itself. Allah Most High says:

“It is for Us to gather it and to recite it. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation. Then it is for Us to explain it.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said: “It is for Us to gather it in your heart and have you recite it with your tongue.”

The scholars of Arabic explain that both qirāʾah and qurʾān may serve as the verbal noun in the expression “I read the book.” This usage also occurs in Hassān’s verse:

They slaughtered a grey-haired man bearing the mark of prostration,
Who passed the night in glorification and recitation.

Allah Most High also says:

“So when you recite the Quran, seek refuge in Allah from Satan, the accursed.”

And He Most High says:

“When you recite the Quran, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier.”

And He Most High says:

“When the Quran is recited, listen to it and remain silent.”

What they listen to is the speech itself; they do not listen to

what the verbal noun denotes—namely, the act itself—for that cannot be heard. His saying,

“We relate to you the best of accounts,”

is of this kind: it means “We read to you the best of accounts” or “We recite to you the best of accounts,” as He Most High says:

“We recite to you in truth some of the account of Moses and Pharaoh.”

And He says:

“So when We have recited it”—Ibn ʿAbbās explained this as Gabriel’s recitation—“follow its recitation,”

meaning: listen to him until he has finished reciting.

The well-known grammatical analysis of His saying, “When you recite the Quran,” is that “the Quran” is in the accusative as the direct object. The same applies to “the best of accounts.” Yet both also carry the meaning of a verbal noun, as explained above. Thus, both the direct-object sense and the verbal-noun sense are present. Sometimes the verbal-noun sense predominates, as in His saying:

“It is for Us to gather it and to recite it.”

Here, what is intended is the very act denoted by the verbal noun. At other times, the other sense predominates, as in His saying:

“Listen to it and remain silent,”

and His saying:

“Say: If mankind and jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce its like,”

and His saying:

“Indeed, this Quran guides to that which is most upright.”

In most occurrences, the word “Quran” denotes the speech itself, not the act of uttering that speech, which is what the verbal noun denotes.

Such usage is common in language: two things are invariably or usually inseparable, so the same name is applied to both. Sometimes one sense predominates, and sometimes the other; the name may also refer to either one alone. Examples include “river,” “village,” “rainspout,” and similar terms involving something contained and its container. Thus, the name encompasses both the watercourse and the flowing water. Likewise, the word

“village” encompasses both the dwellings and their inhabitants. You say, “He dug the river,” meaning its channel, and “The river flowed,” meaning its water. You say, “The rainspout flowed,” meaning the water, and “He installed the rainspout,” meaning the wood. Allah Most High says:

“Allah sets forth the example of a village that was safe and secure, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place. Yet it denied Allah’s blessings, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger.”

What is meant is the inhabitants within that place. He Most High says:

“How many a village We destroyed! Our punishment came upon it by night or while they were resting at midday.”

He Most High says:

“Ask the village in which we were and the caravan with which we returned.”

He Most High says:

“And those villages—We destroyed them when they did wrong.”

He Most High says:

“Such is your Lord’s seizure when He seizes the villages while they are doing wrong.”

He Most High says:

“So that you may warn the Mother of Villages and those around it.”

He Most High says:

“How many a village We destroyed while it was doing wrong, leaving it fallen in upon its roofs; and how many an abandoned well and lofty palace!”

It is the place, not its inhabitants, that has fallen in upon its roofs. He Most High says:

“Or like the one who passed by a village that had fallen in upon its roofs.”

Since a village’s inhabitants are the focus of interest, it is more often they who are meant in the Book of Allah. Likewise, since water is the focus of interest in a river, it is more often what is meant, as in His saying:

“And We made rivers flow beneath them,”

and His saying:

“And We caused a river to flow between them.”

This usage is common—more common than saying, “We dug the river.” Likewise, the word “Quran” is applied more often to the speech itself than to the act of speaking. The same applies to the terms “speech,” “saying,” and “accounts,” and all other forms of

speech: these terms refer more often to the speech itself than to the speaker’s act. These matters can be discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that His saying, Most High:

“We relate to you the best of narratives,”

refers to the speech that constitutes the best of narratives. It encompasses everything Allah has related; He did not restrict it to Surah Yūsuf. Hence He said:

“Through Our revelation to you of this Quran,”

and did not say, “Through Our revelation to you of this surah.” All the reports transmitted from the early generations on this matter support this understanding. They also show that they believed the Quran to be superior to all other scriptures, which is the point at issue.

The intended conclusion holds whichever interpretation is adopted. Whether “the best of narratives” denotes the act of narration, what is narrated, or both, it indicates that the Quran and the narratives it contains are better than others. We have already explained that the two are inseparable: whichever is better, the other must also be better. Thus, His saying, Most High:

“The best of narratives,”

is like His saying:

“Allah has sent down the best of speech.”

The reports from the early generations support this.

The early generations acknowledged that the Quran is the best of speech and the best of narratives, just as it is the guardian over the heavenly scriptures that preceded it. How, then, can it be said that, throughout Allah’s speech, no part is superior to any other?

Ibn Abī Hātim narrated from al-Masʿūdī, on the authority of al-Qāsim:

“The Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, grew weary and said, ‘Speak to us, O Messenger of Allah.’ So Allah revealed:

‘We relate to you the best of narratives.’

Then they grew weary again and said, ‘Speak to us, O Messenger of Allah.’ Then the following was revealed:

‘Allah has sent down the best of speech.’

Then they grew weary once more and said, ‘Speak to us, O Messenger of Allah.’ So Allah revealed:

‘Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humbly submit to the remembrance of Allah and the truth that has been revealed?’”

Abū ʿUbayd also related a report from one of the Successors in Fadāʾil al-Qurʾān (The Virtues of the Quran). He said: Hajjāj narrated to us from al-Masʿūdī, from ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUtbah, who said:

“The Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, grew weary and said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, speak to us.’ So Allah Most High revealed:

‘Allah has sent down the best of speech.’”

He said: “Then He described it, saying:

‘A Book consistent in itself, with recurring passages, at which the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah,’

and so on to the end of the verse.”

He said: “Then they grew weary again and said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, tell us something above ordinary speech but below the Quran,’ meaning narratives. So Allah revealed:

‘Alif Lām Rā. These are the verses of the clear Book,’

through to His saying:

‘We relate to you the best of narratives through Our revelation to you of this Quran, though before it you were among those unaware.’”

He said: “If they wanted speech, He directed them to the best of speech; and if they wanted narratives, He directed them to the best of narratives.”

Ibn Abī Hātim also related it with a good chain of transmission, as a report traced back to the Prophet, through Musʿab ibn Saʿd, from Saʿd, who said:

“The Quran was revealed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he recited it to them for some time. Then they said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate narratives to us.’ So Allah Most High revealed:

‘Alif Lām Rā.’

‘These are the verses of the clear Book.’

‘We relate to you the best of narratives.’

He added that some linguists defined guardianship as overseeing something and caring for it. He cited the verse:

“Indeed, the best of people after their Prophet
Is their guardian, who follows him in good and ill.”

He means the one who oversees people and cares for them.

There are two views concerning the word muhaymin (guardian). According to one, its original form is mu’aymin, with the letter h replacing the hamzah; according to the other, the h is an original root letter.

Such is the Quran: it affirms what the earlier Scriptures contain of accounts concerning Allah and the Last Day, while providing further clarification and detail. It sets out the evidence and proofs for these matters, affirms the prophethood of all the Prophets and the missions of the Messengers, and confirms the universal laws with which all the Messengers were sent.

It argues against those who deny the Scriptures and the Messengers, using various arguments and proofs. It explains Allah’s punishments of them and His support for those who followed the Scriptures and adhered to them. It makes clear what has been distorted and altered in those Scriptures, and what the People of the Book have done to the earlier Scriptures. It also makes clear what they concealed of that which Allah commanded them to disclose, as well as everything brought by the prophetic revelations, through the finest laws and ways revealed in the Quran.

Thus, the Quran has guardianship over the Scriptures that preceded it in numerous respects. It bears witness to their truth and to the falsehood of what has been distorted in them. It judges by upholding what Allah has upheld and abrogating what He has abrogated. Thus, it is a witness in matters of fact and a judge in matters of command.

translated_text:
Likewise, “bearing witness” and “judging” entail affirming what Allah has affirmed as true and as remaining in force, and invalidating what He has declared false or abrogated. Neither the Gospel nor the Psalms occupy this position in relation to the Torah. Rather, they follow the Torah’s law, apart from the few provisions Allah abrogated through the Gospel. The Quran, however, is different.

Moreover, the Quran is itself miraculous: created beings cannot produce anything like it. It contains the Messenger’s call and is itself his sign and proof of his truthfulness and prophethood. It contains what the Messenger brought and is itself proof of what he brought. It also presents parables and explains signs demonstrating the superiority of what the Messenger brought, such that, were the knowledge of all scholars gathered together and compared with it, their knowledge would amount to only part of what the Quran contains.

Whoever reflects on what earlier and later generations have said concerning the foundations of religion, knowledge of divine matters, the Hereafter, prophethood, ethics, governance, worship, and everything else through which souls attain perfection, righteousness, happiness, and salvation will find that earlier and later generations—whether followers of prophetic revelation or proponents of reason, such as philosophers and others—possess only part of what the Quran has brought.

Thus, with its Messenger and its Book, this community has had no need of another prophet or another book, much less of anything else that cannot stand on its own—whether the knowledge of those granted inspired insight and those who receive inspiration, or the knowledge of those who engage in rational inquiry and analogy without also holding fast to a Book sent down from heaven. —may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in an authentic hadith:

“Among the nations before you were men granted inspired insight. If there is anyone of this kind in my community, it is Umar.”

He thus made their presence in his own community conditional, while affirming it decisively of earlier communities. This is because the communities before us needed people granted inspired insight, just as they needed one prophet after another. As for the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Allah has made their Messenger and their Book sufficient for them, leaving them in no need of anything else. Thus, even from someone among them granted inspired insight, such as Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, only what accords with the Book and the Sunnah is accepted. If something is conveyed to his heart, he may not accept it until he has tested it against the Book and the Sunnah. Nor may he accept it unless it accords with the Book and the Sunnah. This is an extensive subject concerning the merits of the Quran over everything else.

The point is to show that matters such as this were firmly established in the minds of the community’s earliest generations and those who followed them. No one among the early generations was ever known to reject such a thing or to say, “No part of Allah’s speech can be nobler than another, for all of it belongs to Allah’s attributes,” or anything similar. Such rejection arose only when the innovations of the Jahmiyyah appeared—those who differed concerning the Book and divided it into parts.

Among those who discussed “the intrinsic superiority of some parts of the Quran over others” were followers of al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others, including Shaykh Abū Hāmid al-Isfarāyīnī, Judge Abū al-Tayyib, Abū Ishāq al-Shīrāzī, and others; likewise, Judge Abū Ya‘lā, al-Halwānī the Elder and his son ‘Abd al-Rahmān, and Ibn ‘Aqīl. *al-Wādih fī Usūl al-Fiqh* (The Clear Exposition of the Principles of Jurisprudence), in his argument that the Quran cannot be abrogated by the Sunnah:

“One such proof is His saying:

‘Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or like it.’

The Sunnah is neither like the Quran nor better than it. Abrogation by the Sunnah is therefore ruled out, since it would entail an impossibility: His statement would not correspond to what it reports. That is impossible for Allah, and whatever entails it is likewise impossible.”

He said:

“If it is objected: ‘Your argument rests on the premise that “better” means superior in excellence. Yet that is not what is intended. Rather, the meaning is: “We bring one better than it for you.” For us, this amounts to one of two things: either an easier obligation, which is an immediate benefit, or a greater reward because the obligation is more burdensome and difficult, which brings benefit in the Hereafter and in the final outcome. Both may be brought about through the Sunnah.

‘Another possible meaning is: “We bring something better than it,” not as an abrogating replacement, but as an entirely new obligation that is better for you, even if it is conveyed neither through an abrogating Quranic passage nor through an abrogating Sunnah.’

They say: ‘These interpretations are supported by the fact that no part of the Quran itself is better than another. Thus, they must interpret the expression beyond its apparent meaning, so that “better” refers to the obligation rather than to the means by which it is conveyed.’”

In reply, he said:

“Their contention that ‘better’ refers to an ease or reward specific to us is unsound. Had He intended that, He would have said, ‘for you.’ His omission of those words therefore indicates the unrestricted meaning of the expression: that the abrogating passage is better both in itself, intrinsically, and in the benefit derived from it in this life and the Hereafter. Moreover, its apparent meaning requires

Thus, if someone says, ‘I never take a dinar from you without giving you something better than it,’ the unqualified statement can only be understood to mean a better dinar. Superiority is thus sought first within the same kind, and then in the benefit it offers. It cannot refer instead to a garment or some commodity other than a dinar.

The end of the verse also indicates that He intended the Quran, for He says:

‘Do you not know that Allah has power over all things?’

His description of Himself as powerful indicates that what He brings is something that belongs to Him alone, to the exclusion of others. Likewise, His words,

‘or like it,’

support what we have stated, because an unqualified comparison of likeness entails likeness in every respect. This is especially so since He uses a feminine pronoun referring to a verse. It is as though He said: ‘We bring a verse better than it, or a verse like it.’”

I say:

Furthermore, ‘better’ cannot mean that the prescribed action is easier, or that it is more difficult and carries a greater reward. These two descriptions apply to everything Allah commands, whether as an initial prescription or as an abrogating replacement. It is either easier than something else in this world, or more difficult and therefore greater in reward. Since this characteristic necessarily applies to all rulings, it would not be apt to say: ‘Whatever ruling We abrogate, We bring one better than it or like it.’ For, on this understanding, the abrogated ruling could likewise be better or equal. If they interpret ‘better’ as meaning easier, the abrogated ruling might be easier and thus better. If they interpret it as meaning greater in reward because of its difficulty, the abrogated ruling might also fit that description. Yet Allah has declared that He will necessarily bring something better than what He abrogates, or something like it; He does not bring something inferior to it.

Furthermore, on their interpretation, nothing would be better than anything else: if one thing were better in being easier, the other would be better in carrying a greater reward.

Ibn ʿAqīl said:

“As for their claim that the Quran itself admits no differences in excellence or superiority, and that ‘better’ therefore cannot mean superior, this is not so. The affirmation of Allah’s oneness in Sūrat al-Ikhlās, including its denial that He can be partitioned or divided, is superior to Sūrat Tabbat, which condemns Abū Lahab and his wife. You may consider this in terms of praise being superior to censure, or in terms of inimitability: reciting other verses whose eloquence and clarity are manifest is superior. The fact that the Speaker is one does not preclude differences in excellence on another level, for reasons pertaining to the speech itself. Likewise, the One who sent Jonah and Abraham is one, yet Abraham is superior to Jonah.”

He said:

“As for their claim that ‘We bring one better than it’ refers not to an abrogating replacement but to an independent prescription, this is incorrect. The verb occurs in the jussive as the consequence of a condition, which conveys substitution and reciprocity. This is like saying, ‘If you honour me, I will honour you,’ or ‘If you obey me, I will obey you.’ Such wording requires the consequence to be a corresponding response and replacement, not an independently initiated act.”

I say:

The purpose here is to mention the position he defended—that some parts of the Quran are, in themselves, better than others—not to discuss the question of abrogation. Others besides these scholars have also explicitly stated that some parts of the Quran may be better than others. Among those who mentioned this was Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī in his book Jawāhir al-Qurʾān (The Jewels of the Quran). He said:

“Perhaps you will say: ‘These observations of yours aim to establish the superiority of some Quranic verses over others. Yet all of it is Allah’s speech. How, then, can its verses differ from one another? How can some be nobler than others?’

“Know that if the light of insight does not guide you to the distinction between the Verse of the Throne and the verse on debts, or between Sūrat al-Ikhlās and Sūrat Tabbat, and your fainthearted soul, steeped in blind imitation, recoils from acknowledging such distinctions, then follow the bearer of the revealed Law—Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him. It was to him that the Quran was revealed, and he said:

‘Yā Sīn is the heart of the Quran.’

“The reports establish that some parts are nobler than others. He said:

‘The Opening of the Book is the best surah of the Quran.’

“He also said:

‘The Verse of the Throne is the foremost verse of the Quran.’

“And he said:

‘“Say: He is Allah, One” equals one-third of the Quran.’

“The reports concerning the merits of the Quran’s powerful passages, and the particular excellence of certain surahs and verses and the abundant reward for reciting them, are innumerable. Consult the books of hadith for them if you wish. We shall now draw your attention to the meaning of these four reports concerning the superiority of these surahs.”

I say:

Allah willing, we shall mention his explanation of the superiority of “Say: He is Allah, One.” Among those who discussed the scholars’ views on this subject and attributed this position to certain early scholars was al-Qādī ‘Iyād in his Commentary on Sahīh Muslim. “This provides evidence that some parts of the Quran are superior to others

and that the Quran is superior to Allah’s other Books, according to those who hold this view, including Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh and other scholars and theologians.”

He said:

“This refers to the great reward granted to those who recite these passages, and to the more abundant recompense for some parts than for others.”

He said:

“This is a matter on which the scholars have differed. Al-Ash‘arī, Ibn al-Bāqillānī, and a number of jurists and scholars rejected this, because superiority implies that the less excellent falls short of the more excellent, whereas Allah’s speech is indivisible. They said: ‘Where certain verses and surahs are described as “best” or “greatest,” the meaning is that they are excellent and great.’”

He said:

“It has also been said that the Verse of the Throne is the greatest because it encompasses the fundamental divine names and attributes: divinity, life, oneness, knowledge, dominion, power, and will. These seven, they said, are the foundations of the divine names and attributes.”

I say:

What concerns us here is his account of the scholars’ statements. As for the assertion that these seven are the foundations of the divine names, many theologians regard these seven as those known through reason, while maintaining that all others are known only through revelation. This, however, concerns how we come to know them, not an objective reality inherent in them. How, then, can this be so, when the majority hold that other attributes can also be known through reason, such as love, pleasure, commanding, and forbidding?

The position of Ibn Kullāb and most early scholars who affirmed the divine attributes is that Allah’s being above is among the attributes knowable through reason. This is also the position of Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī and al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī, as well as various groups of theologians, hadith scholars, and jurists. It was also the later of the two views held by al-Qādī

translated_text:
Abū Ya‘lā and Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī, among others, as well as the position of Ibn Karrām and his followers. It is also the view of the general body of leading scholars of hadith, jurisprudence, and Sufism.

Likewise, al-Qādī ‘Iyād’s explanation that those who affirm superiority mean a greater reward concerns something that al-Ash‘arī and Ibn al-Bāqillānī do not dispute. Reward is, after all, one of the things Allah Most High has created, and no one disputes that some of it is better than other parts. The disagreement concerns Allah’s speech itself, which is His speech. Thus, his account of the disagreement contradicts his explanation of the position of those who affirm superiority.

He has explained the reasoning of those who reject such superiority. Some deny any degrees of superiority among the attributes whatsoever, on the grounds that what is eternal admits no degrees of superiority, and the Quran is one of the attributes. Others single out the Quran on the grounds that, according to their fundamental premise, it is one indivisible whole: two distinct meanings cannot be conceived within it, let alone anything superior or inferior. This is the fundamental premise of Abū al-Hasan and those who agree with him, as we shall explain, if Allah Most High wills.

None of those whose statements we have cited affirming that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts holds that Allah’s speech is created, as is maintained by certain adherents of innovation, such as the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah. Rather, all of them say:

“Allah’s speech is uncreated.”

Were all those who held this view to be listed, they would be numerous, for this is the position of the vast majority of Muslims, earlier and later, both adherents of the Sunnah and adherents of innovation. As for the early generations—such as the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness—no disagreement among them is known concerning this principle. Rather, it is affirmed by mass-transmitted reports from them.

{نَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ مِنْهَا}
translated_text:
The denial that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts became widespread after the year 200 AH, when the Jahmiyyah openly proclaimed that the Quran was created. The leading scholars of the Sunnah and the vast majority of the Muslim community agreed in rejecting and refuting this claim. A large group—including Abū Muhammad ibn Kullāb and those who agreed with him—thought that this claim could only be refuted by maintaining that Allah has not spoken by His will and power; that He did not speak to Moses when Moses came to Him, nor say to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” after creating him; that He does not become angry with anyone after that person disbelieves in Him, nor become pleased with him after he obeys Him, nor love him after he draws near to Him through voluntary acts of worship; and that He does not utter one speech after another, such that His words would be without end—along with other things they thought must be denied of Allah.

They said that these people could only be opposed by maintaining that the Quran and all His other speech are inseparable from Allah Most High’s essence, and that He has always been, and will always be, uttering every utterance of His, such as:

“O Adam! O Noah!”

They divided into two groups. One group says that His speech is a single meaning subsisting in His essence. The other says that it consists of letters, or letters and sounds, conjoined with one another from all eternity and for all eternity, although they have an intrinsic sequence, not a sequence in which they come into existence. The various views concerning Allah’s speech have been explained elsewhere. According to the first group, Allah’s speech is a single thing with no parts, so there can be no question of some parts being superior to others.

The other group says:

“It is eternal and inseparable from His essence, and what is eternal admits no degrees of superiority.”

It is sometimes reported from some of the early generations, concerning the words of the Most High,

“We bring forth one better than it,”

أَنَّهُ قَالَ:

 وَحَدَّثَنَا أَبِي عَنْ جَدِّنَا أَبِي الْبَرَكَاتِ وَصَاحِبِهِ أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَبْدِ الْوَهَّابِ أَنَّهُمَا نَظَرَا فِيمَا ذَكَرَهُ بَعْضُ الْمُفَسِّرِينَ مِنْ الْأَقْوَالِ فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{نَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ مِنْهَا أَوْ مِثْلِهَا}
 وَأَظُنُّهُ كَانَ نَظَرَهُمْ فِي تَفْسِيرِ أَبِي عَبْدِ
translated_text:
that he said:

“Better for you than it, or more beneficial to you.”

Someone might therefore suppose that the person who said this agreed with those people. But that is not so. Rather, his purpose was to explain in what respect it is better: namely, that it is more beneficial to people. For speech that is more beneficial to people is also intrinsically superior, as explained elsewhere.

Those among the later followers of Ahmad, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī and others who followed the path of the Kullābiyyah came to think that affirming the superiority of some of Allah’s speech over other parts was possible only according to the position of the Mu‘tazilah and others like them who say that it is created. Those who say it is created regard the superiority of some parts over others as the superiority of one created thing over another; and no one denies that some created things are superior to others.

Thus, when those people supposed that affirming the superiority of some of Allah’s speech over other parts necessarily implied that the Quran was created, they recoiled from this affirmation and rejected it because of the necessary connection they imagined. Yet the matter is not as they supposed. Rather, the early generations of the Muslim community and its vast majority say:

“The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated; likewise, all the rest of Allah’s speech is uncreated.”

At the same time, they say:

“Some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts,”

as expressly stated in the Book, the Sunnah, and the reports from the Companions and their Successors, with no known disagreement among them concerning this.

My father related to us, on the authority of our grandfather Abū al-Barakāt and his companion Abū Abd Allāh ibn Abd al-Wahhāb, that they had examined the views mentioned by one of the Quran commentators concerning His words:

“We bring forth one better than it or similar to it.”

I believe they were consulting the Quran commentary of Abū Abd
