These people denied that Allah loves and approves of some things but not others. They said: “Love and approval have the same meaning as will. Allah wills everything He has created, so He approves of it and loves it.”

They claimed that the Quran’s denial that He loves or approves of disbelief and sins, as in His words:

“Allah does not love corruption,”

and:

“He does not approve of disbelief for His servants,”

refers only to those of His servants who have not committed such things, or means that He did not will them as a religion for which He would reward them. They also claimed that Allah does not love or approve of the acts of worship He has commanded unless they actually occur; then He wills them, just as He then wills whatever disbelief and sins have occurred. These and other views of theirs are discussed at length elsewhere.

Many later scholars suppose that this is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah, yet none of the early generations of this Muslim community or its leading scholars ever held it. Rather, all the early scholars who affirmed divine decree distinguished love and approval from will. Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī, however, followed Jahm in this regard.

Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī said:

“Among the matters concerning which the people of truth differed over whether the terms may or may not be applied are love and approval. The earlier scholars held that He, glorified be He, neither loves nor approves of disbelief, and likewise every sin.

“Our shaykh Abū al-Hasan said: ‘Love is will itself, as are approval and choosing. He, glorified be He, wills disbelief

and approves of it as reprehensible disbelief for which He exacts punishment.’”

The matter is as Abū al-Ma‘ālī stated: the earlier scholars of all Ahl al-Sunnah upheld what the Quran and Sunnah indicate—that He, glorified be He, neither approves of nor loves what He has forbidden. This was also the position of the early followers of the four imams—Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad—including Abū Bakr ‘Abd al-‘Azīz and others among their early followers. Some later scholars, however, equated all these meanings, as Abū al-Hasan did. This was originally Jahm’s position: he advocated compulsion in matters of divine decree and held views contrary to Ahl al-Sunnah. He denied Allah Most High’s mercy and would go out to people afflicted with leprosy and say:

“Would the Most Merciful of the merciful do this?”

Thus he denied that Allah is the Most Merciful of the merciful, whereas the truthful and trusted Messenger said:

“Allah is surely more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child.”

These are weighty matters, and this is not the place to discuss them at length.

The purpose here is simply to draw attention to the broad principles. Many people read works on the foundations of religion and the principles of jurisprudence—even commentaries on the Quran and hadith—without finding in them the position that accords with the Quran and Sunnah and was upheld by the early generations of this community and its leading scholars: the position consistent with authentic transmitted evidence and clear reason. Instead, they find views each containing some error and contradiction. They are consequently bewildered about what to believe concerning these matters, what the Messenger brought, and what is true and sound, since none of those views provides them with the answer. Guidance lies only in what the Messenger brought—the Messenger concerning whom Allah said:

“And indeed, you guide to a straight path—the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah do all matters return.”

Section

What does this mean? Is the reward for reciting it equal to the reward for reciting one-third of the Quran? Assuming that it is, what purpose does reciting the rest of the Quran serve?

What is required of Allah’s servants is both obligatory knowledge and obligatory action. The entire Muslim community agrees that the deeds Allah has prescribed are obligatory; no one has said that they are not. Since this is so, even supposing that a surah encompasses one-third of this knowledge, that would not constitute one-third of the Quran.

Second, we may say: When someone speaks of knowledge of His essence, knowledge of His names and attributes, and knowledge of His actions, if he means that His essence can be known without knowing any of His names or attributes, whether affirmative or negative, this is impossible. Even if he supposed this possible, or a servant imagined an essence abstracted from all negative and affirmative qualifications, that would certainly not constitute knowledge of Allah. Nor is the Lord of the worlds an essence abstracted from every negative or affirmative qualification.

Thus, no rational person has maintained this except the esotericist Qarmatians. They say: “Every affirmative and privative predicate is denied of Him. These people say:

Universal existence, divided into necessary and contingent existence, which the philosophers make the subject matter of metaphysics—also called “the highest wisdom” and “first philosophy”—is universal only in the mind, not in external reality. In external reality, there is never one and the same existence that is both necessary and contingent, nor one and the same existence that characterizes both the Necessary Being and a contingent being. Rather, the attributes of the Necessary Being are peculiar to Him, and those of a contingent being are peculiar to it. The existence of the Necessary Being is His alone, shared by no other; likewise, the existence of a contingent being is its alone, shared by no other.

Thus, every attribute with which the Lord has described Himself is peculiar to Him: it is impossible for anyone to share it with Him or resemble Him in it. His holy Essence resembles no other essence, and His attributes are peculiar to Him and resemble no other attributes. Rather, He—glorified be He—is One, the Self-Sufficient:

“He neither begets nor is born,”

“and there is none comparable to Him.”

His name al-Ahad (the One) indicates that none shares in His attributes or resembles Him, while His name al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient) indicates that He is entitled to every attribute of perfection. This has been explained at length in the extensive commentary devoted to this surah. All attributes declaring Him free of imperfection—indeed, all affirmative attributes as well—are encompassed by these two meanings.

Tawhīd (affirming Allah’s oneness) has been discussed at length, including its division into two kinds: one pertaining to knowledge and declaration, the other to practice and intention. Thus, Surah “Say, O disbelievers” explicitly sets forth tawhīd in practice and also indicates tawhīd in knowledge

by necessary implication. Surah “Say, He is Allah, One” explicitly sets forth tawhīd pertaining to knowledge and declaration, and indicates tawhīd in practice by necessary implication. For this reason, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—would recite these two surahs in the two units of prayer of Fajr, the two units of prayer associated with circumambulation, and on other occasions. It is also established that, in the two units of prayer of Fajr, he would recite the verse of faith from al-Baqarah in the first unit:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah,’”

and the verse of submission from Āl ‘Imrān:

“Say, ‘O People of the Scripture, come to a common word between us and you: that we worship none but Allah, associate nothing with Him, and do not take one another as lords besides Allah.’ But if they turn away, then say, ‘Bear witness that we are Muslims.’”

The point here is that the attributes declaring Him free of imperfection are encompassed by these two meanings mentioned in this surah.

The first is the denial of imperfections in Him. This necessarily follows from affirming the attributes of perfection: whoever possesses absolute perfection is free of the deficiency that contradicts it. Perfection is among the meanings conveyed by His name al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient).

The second is that nothing is like Him in the attributes of perfection affirmed of Him. This is among the meanings conveyed by His name al-Ahad (the One). These two magnificent names—al-Ahad and al-Samad—thus declare Him free of every deficiency and defect, and affirm that He has no equal in any of His attributes of perfection. The surah therefore encompasses everything that must be denied of Allah, as well as everything that must be affirmed of Him, in two ways: through His name al-Samad, and because denying that He has ancestors, offspring, or equals also entails affirming His attributes of perfection.

Every negation by which the Lord is praised must imply an affirmation. Indeed, the same applies to every negation by which any existing thing is praised: it must imply an affirmation. Otherwise, pure negation amounts to sheer nonexistence, and sheer nonexistence is nothing at all, let alone an attribute of perfection.

This is illustrated by what He, glorified be He, mentions in the Verse of the Throne, such as His words:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep.”

Denying that drowsiness or sleep overtakes Him necessarily implies the perfection of His life and His sustaining of all existence. Sleep is incompatible with sustaining all existence, and sleep is the brother of death. For this reason, the people of Paradise do not sleep.

Then He says:

“To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?”

Denying intercession without His permission necessarily implies the perfection of His sovereignty. For anyone who accepts an intercession made to him without his permission has been influenced by that intercessor: the intercession has affected him, prompting him to act after he had not done so. That intercessor would thus be a partner of the one petitioned in the matter sought through intercession, since the intercession took place without his permission. In particular, when a created being accepts an intercession made to him without his permission, he accepts it only out of hope or fear, whether from

the intercessor or someone else. Otherwise, if his own motivation were complete and he possessed the ability, he would have no need of intercession. Allah Most High is exalted above all of this, as He says in the divine hadith:

“O My servants, you can never confer any benefit upon Me, nor can you inflict any harm upon Me.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would instruct his Companions to intercede with him. When someone came to him seeking something, he would say:

“Intercede, and you will be rewarded; Allah will decree through the tongue of His Prophet whatever He wills.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded this in their Sahīh collections. His purpose was that they should be rewarded for interceding, while he himself would do only what Allah commanded him to do.

Likewise, He says:

“He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.”

He makes clear that they know nothing of His knowledge except what He has taught them, just as the angels said:

“We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.”

This negation thus affirms that His servants know only what He has taught them. It affirms that He is the One who taught them, and that they acquire knowledge only from Him. For He is:

“the One who created—created man from a clinging substance,”

and who

“taught by the pen—taught man that which he knew not.”

Then He says:

“His Kursī extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation does not burden Him.”

That is, it neither troubles Him nor weighs upon Him. This negation implies the perfection of His power: although He preserves the heavens and the earth, doing so does not weigh upon Him as it would upon someone whose strength is deficient.

This is like His saying, Most High:

“We certainly created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us.”

He thus declares Himself free from being touched by weariness. The lexicographers say:

“Weariness means exhaustion and fatigue.”

Likewise, He says:

“Vision does not encompass Him.”

According to the early generations and the majority, “encompassing” here means comprehending something in its entirety. Some have said that it means seeing, but this is a weak interpretation, because denying that He can be seen entails no praise: what does not exist cannot be seen either. Any description common to both existence and nonexistence entails no positive attribute and therefore offers no praise, since it is pure negation. By contrast, saying that He cannot be encompassed indicates the greatness of the Lord—majestic is His glory. Although His servants see Him, their vision does not encompass Him, just as, although they know Him, their knowledge does not encompass Him. Likewise, although they praise and extol Him, their praise cannot encompass Him. Rather, He is as He has praised His own holy Self.

For this reason, the best and most knowledgeable of creation said:

“I cannot enumerate Your praises; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

These matters are discussed at length elsewhere. The purpose here is to explain what it means for the surah “Say: He is Allah, the One” to equal one-third of the Quran, and to demonstrate that the first view is correct.

The third argument demonstrating the invalidity of the second view is as follows:

When someone speaks of “knowledge of His acts,” if he means knowledge of His signs that point to Him, this forms part of complete knowledge of Him. Yet he has left unmentioned knowledge of His promises and warnings and the accounts of believing and disbelieving nations—which constitute the second category of the Quran’s meanings—just as he has left unmentioned His commands and prohibitions. If, however, he includes these among the effects of His actions, then it is well known that the purpose of knowing the promises, warnings, and accounts is belief in the Last Day and the recompense of deeds

It is well known that even if such a person recited the Quran ten times, his reward would not equal that of a believer who fears Allah. Furthermore, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, declared that reciting it was equivalent to one-third of the Quran. He recited it to his Companions and told them that he had recited one-third of the Quran to them. His recitation of it was therefore equivalent to his own recitation of a third. The same applies to the man who kept repeating it. Likewise, when he told them that it was equivalent to one-third of the Quran, he meant a third as recited by them. He did not mean a third in the case of a hypocrite who recites it without believing in the meaning of:

“Say: He is Allah, One.”

Moreover, the interpretation that this refers to someone who recites a third without believing in this surah has no basis in the wording; rather, the wording indicates the opposite. This interpretation and others like it constitute the distortion of words from their proper places for which Allah condemned those among the People of the Book who did so. It is a form of deviation concerning the words of Allah and His Messenger.

This relates to the three categories we mentioned concerning the Quran’s essential subjects: knowledge of Allah, knowledge of the Hereafter, and knowledge of the straight path. These three kinds of knowledge are what matters most; the rest is subsidiary. Surah al-Ikhlās encompasses one of these three: knowledge of Allah, declaring Him free of imperfection, and affirming His oneness, with none sharing with Him in genus or species. This is what is meant by denying that He has any parent, offspring, or equal. Describing Him as al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient Master) indicates that He is the Master, the only one in existence to whom one turns for one’s needs. It does not, however, discuss the Hereafter or the straight path. That is why it is equivalent to one-third of the Quran—that is, one-third of the Quran’s fundamental subjects. This is like his statement:

“‘Hajj is Arafah.’

“That is, it is the essential part, while the rest is subsidiary.”

I say: The verses of the Quran are of two kinds: those concerned with knowledge and those concerned with practice. Some verses combine both. Abū Hāmid collected the verses concerned with knowledge relating to Allah’s essence, attributes, and actions, excluding those relating to

the Last Day and the narratives, and called them “The Jewels of the Quran.” He also collected the verses concerned with practice and called them “The Pearls of the Quran.” He placed the first half of al-Fātihah among the jewels and the second among the pearls. Verses combining both meanings he assigns to whichever category predominates in them. Together, the verses he included in these two categories constitute a quarter of the Quran’s verses—approximately fifteen hundred verses.

He divided the meanings of the Quran into six categories: three fundamental subjects and three subsidiary ones. He described the Quran as the all-encompassing ocean from which the knowledge of earlier and later generations branches out.

He said:

“The secret of the Quran, its purest essence, and its ultimate purpose is to call people to the Most High, the All-Compelling, Lord of this world and the Hereafter, Creator of the lofty heavens and the earths below.

“The three essential subjects are: making known the One to whom people are called; making known the straight path that must be followed in journeying to Him; and making known their condition upon reaching Him.

“As for the three remaining subjects, the first concerns the circumstances of those who respond to the call and the subtleties of Allah’s dealings with them. Its inner meaning and purpose are to inspire longing and desire. It also makes known the circumstances of those who turn aside and shrink from responding, and how Allah subdues them and makes an example of them. Its inner meaning and purpose are to provide a lesson and inspire fear.

“The second recounts the statements of those who deny the truth and exposes their shameful failings and ignorance through debate and argument in support of the truth. With regard to falsehood, its purpose and inner meaning are to lay it bare, warn against it, and make it repellent; with regard to truth, to clarify, confirm, and establish it.

“The third explains how to maintain the way stations along the path, and how to obtain provisions, a mount, and the equipment needed to prepare.”

I say: What he has stated—that the foundations of faith are three—is indeed true, just as he has said.

translated_text:
and all three are indispensable in every faith and religion, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabeans—whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—will have their reward with their Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

Something similar appears in Sūrat al-Mā’idah.

Thus, He mentions these three foundations: belief in Allah, belief in the Last Day, and righteous deeds. The other three, subsidiary subjects are included within these. The Quran’s accounts of the conditions of the blessed and the wretched in the Hereafter elaborate upon belief in the Last Day. Its discussion of maintaining the path falls under righteous deeds. Its debates and arguments complete its exposition of these three foundations: when it sets them forth, it presents the signs and proofs that establish them, mentions the specious arguments of those who deny them, and exposes their unsoundness.

Abū Hāmid himself mentioned this, saying:

“The section devoted to disputing and debating with the unbelievers, exposing their shameful failings through clear proof, and laying bare their falsehoods and illusory notions.

“Their falsehoods are of three kinds:

“First: speaking of Allah in ways unbefitting Him, claiming that the angels are His daughters, that He has a child as a partner, and that He is the third of three.

“Second: describing the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as a sorcerer, a soothsayer, and a poet, and denying his prophethood.

“Third: denying the Last Day and rejecting the resurrection, the rising of the dead, Paradise, and Hell, and denying the consequences of obedience and disobedience.”

As for its accounts of the circumstances of believers and unbelievers in this world—which is what Abū Hāmid meant by mentioning the circumstances of those who respond and those who turn aside—this forms part of

the full presentation of the proofs and signs. For this is something witnessed in this world: its effects have been seen, and reports of it have been transmitted through numerous independent sources. It is not among the events after death that remain unseen by Allah’s servants.

For this reason, He—glory be to Him—mentions such accounts as evidence and proof, alongside the admonition they contain, as in His words:

“Certainly, in their stories there is a lesson for people of understanding.”

“There was certainly a sign for you in the two armies that met: one fighting in the cause of Allah and the other disbelieving. They saw them with their own eyes as twice their number. Allah strengthens with His victory whom He wills. Indeed, in that is a lesson for those with insight.”

And His words:

“It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first gathering. You did not think they would leave, and they thought their fortresses would protect them against Allah. But Allah came upon them from where they had not expected and cast terror into their hearts. They destroyed their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take heed, O people of insight.”

And His words:

“Say: Travel through the land, then see what was the fate of those who denied the truth.”

And His words:

“How many a town We destroyed while it was doing wrong! It lies collapsed upon its roofs; how many an abandoned well and lofty palace!”

“Have they not travelled through the land so that they may have hearts with which to understand or ears with which to hear? For it is not the eyes that become blind, but the hearts within the breasts.”

And His words:

“Have they not travelled through the land and seen what was the fate of those before them? They were greater than them in strength, and they tilled the land and developed it more than these have developed it. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs”—and the following verses.

And His words, exalted is He, after mentioning the account of the people of Lot:

“We turned it upside down and rained upon them stones of baked clay.”

“Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern.”

“And indeed, it lies on an established road.”

One who discerns is someone who draws inferences from marks and distinguishing signs. The Most High says:

“If We willed, We could show them to you, and you would recognize them by their marks; and you will surely recognize them by the tenor of their speech.”

Recognizing the hypocrites by the tenor of their speech is thus affirmed by an oath, but this occurs when they speak. Recognizing them by their marks, however, depends upon Allah’s will, for that is more subtle.

In the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhī, who graded it sound, Abū Sa‘īd reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beware of the believer’s discernment, for he sees by the light of Allah.”

He then recited the words of the Most High:

“Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern.”

Mujāhid and Ibn Qutaybah explained this as referring to those endowed with perceptive insight. Ibn Qutaybah said: “One says, ‘I discerned goodness in so-and-so,’ meaning, ‘I perceived it.’” Al-Zajjāj said: “In Arabic, those who discern are observers who keep their gaze fixed until they recognize the true distinguishing mark of a thing. One says, ‘I discerned such-and-such in so-and-so,’ meaning, ‘I recognized it.’”

His words, “who keep their gaze fixed,” refer to looking with their eyes until they recognize the distinguishing marks, unlike those of whom it is said:

“How many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, yet turn away from it!”

Al-Dahhāk said: “Those who observe.” Ibn Zayd said: “Those who scrutinize.” Qatādah said: “Those who draw lessons.” All of this is correct, for one who discerns combines all these qualities.

Then the Most High said:

“And indeed, it lies on an established road.”

He then mentioned the account of the people of the thicket, and then said:

“And indeed, both lie on a clear highway.”

That is, on a road evident and clear to people.

Likewise, in another passage, He says:

“So We brought out whoever was there of the believers.

“But We found there only a single household of Muslims.

“And We left therein a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.”

And He says concerning Noah’s Ark:

“And We certainly left it as a sign. Is there, then, anyone who will take heed?”

He thus tells us that He left signs—that is, marks and proofs. This shows that the particular accounts of the believers and their good outcome in this world, and of the disbelievers and their evil outcome in this world, constitute signs and proofs from which evidence and lessons may be drawn, yielding both knowledge and admonition. They establish the truth of what the messengers conveyed and provide encouragement and warning. They also demonstrate that Allah is pleased with those who obey Him and honors them, and that He is angry with those who disobey Him and punishes them.

Similarly, His creation in general provides evidence of His power, for an act necessarily entails power on the part of its agent. The perfection of His acts provides evidence of His knowledge, for a perfectly executed act necessarily entails knowledge on the part of its agent. His determining things in their particulars provides evidence of His will, for such determination necessarily entails His willing it. Likewise, His choosing what leads to the most praiseworthy outcome provides evidence of His wisdom, for directing an act toward a praiseworthy outcome necessarily entails wisdom.

His singling out the prophets and their followers for victory and a good outcome, and singling out those who deny them for disgrace and an evil outcome, provides evidence that He commands, loves, and is pleased with what the prophets brought, and that He dislikes and is displeased with the ways of those who denied them. For singling out one of these two groups for honor, deliverance, a good name, and prayers on their behalf, while singling out the other for punishment, destruction, an evil name, and curses, necessarily entails His love for what the first group did and His hatred of what the second group did.

translated_text:
As for the will said to single out one of two equivalent things rather than the other without a reason, there is disagreement over whether Allah is to be described as possessing such a will.

If it is said that He is not, there is nothing further to discuss. If it is said that He is, it is nevertheless known that singling out the prophets—peace be upon them—for one treatment and their enemies for the other did not occur without a determining reason. Rather, it is known that He intended to single out the former for honor and the latter for punishment, and that the faith of the former was the reason for their treatment, while the disbelief of the latter was the reason for theirs. A fuller discussion of these matters belongs elsewhere. The point here, however, is that these three are included within the first three.

But Abū Hāmid identifies argumentation with the craft of speculative theology, maintaining the path with the science of jurisprudence, and accounts of the prophets with the science of narratives. He says that speculative theology and disputation do not establish any truth through evidence, but merely repel innovations by exposing their contradictions. He likens their practitioners to guards who protect pilgrims, and holds that the sole purpose of jurisprudence is worldly welfare. Most people have disputed his views on this and discussed them at a length that would be out of place here.

Likewise, they have criticized the philosophical ideas he presents in this book (Jawāhir al-Qur’ān, The Jewels of the Quran) and in his other books, which he regards as the Quran’s esoteric meaning. Muslim scholars have written more in refutation of this than in refutation of the foregoing, for it contains grave matters that contradict the Messenger’s intent. They have also criticized what he says about prophethood, which resembles the philosophers’ discourse on the subject.

The point is that what he says about “Say: He is Allah, One” is better than what many people have said about it, and closer to the view we cited from Ibn Surayj and defended. Yet that view is undoubtedly correct, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, stated that Allah divided the Quran into three parts, making “Say: He is Allah, One” one of those parts. This entails that the Quran as a whole consists of three parts, not six: three fundamental categories and three subsidiary ones.

Likewise, he stated that “Say: He is Allah, One” is equivalent to a third of the Quran. He did not say a third of its important content, of the greater part of it, or of its fundamental teachings. The entire Quran must therefore comprise three categories. According to Abū Hāmid’s account, however, it comprises six: three important categories and three supplementary ones, with this surah constituting one of the three important categories. This contradicts the hadith.

Moreover, dividing the Quran into three categories rests on a demonstrable basis: the Quran is speech, and speech is either informative or performative. Informative speech concerns either the Creator or creation. This is a clear division.

As for placing the science of jurisprudence outside the straight path and righteous action, and placing the science of proofs and arguments outside faith in and knowledge of Allah and the Last Day, this is rejected by the overwhelming majority of earlier and later scholars. Abū Hāmid only said this because he maintains that the meanings of these matters can be known solely through purification, not through prophetic reports or inferential reasoning.

Yet Abū Hāmid’s excuse is that, in what he knew of the methods of the philosophers and speculative theologians, he found nothing that clarified the truth concerning these matters. He knew of no other rational methods, and therefore denied that the truth could be known through rational inquiry.

As for methods based on prophetic reports, he lacked familiarity with the authentically transmitted words of the Messenger and with how those words convey his intended meanings. Sharing certain assumptions with some speculative theologians and philosophers, he supposed that the Messenger had not made his meaning clear through his words. Together, these two positions closed off the paths of reason and transmitted revelation. He thought that the desired end could be attained, not through purification and practice, so he pursued that course, but still failed to attain his objective. Thus, toward the end of his life, he returned to reading al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

Qādī ‘Iyād mentioned several explanations of how “Say: He is Allah, One” is equivalent to a third of the Quran, as did al-Māzirī before him. He reports the Imam—meaning Abū ‘Abd Allah al-Māzirī—as saying:

“It has been said that this means the Quran comprises three kinds of content: narratives, rulings, and descriptions of Allah—exalted is His power. ‘Say: He is Allah, One’ contains mention of His attributes, and thus constitutes a third in this respect.”

He said: “This interpretation may accord with the apparent meaning of the hadith which mentions that Allah divided the Quran into parts.”

I say: This is Ibn Surayj’s view—the one we have defended. Al-Māzirī mentioned it in his discussion of Ibn Battāl’s remarks, as will follow.

He said: “It has also been said that it means a third of the Quran for a person

in particular whom the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had in mind.”

Ibn Battāl also mentioned this. He said:

“It has also been said that Allah graciously multiplies the reward of whoever recites it, with this multiplication reaching an amount equal to one third of the reward he would merit for reciting the Quran without any multiplication of that reward.”

He said: “Some versions of this hadith report that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gathered the people and said, ‘I shall recite to you a third of the Quran.’ He then recited ‘Say: He is Allah, One.’”

Al-Māzirī said: “This version undermines the interpretation that makes this specific to a particular person.”

Qādī ‘Iyād said:

“Some have said: Allah Most High says, ‘Alif Lām Rā. Then He says, ‘Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bearer of good tidings.’ This is the section on prophethood. Then He says, ‘And seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then turn to Him in repentance.’ This is the section on religious obligation and the promises and warnings that follow it. This indicates that ‘Say: He is Allah, One’ encompasses the first section.”

I say:

This view too is weak, for it may be objected that commands and prohibitions are also part of what the Prophet brought, just as he brought promises and warnings.

It may also be said that the narratives attest to commands and prohibitions just as they attest to prophethood. They show that Allah honors those who obey Him and punishes those who disobey Him, thereby reinforcing commands and prohibitions, as explained earlier. Moreover, the purpose of prophethood is to convey what Allah has commanded and what He has made known. Whatever in the narratives establishes prophethood also establishes the truth of what the Prophet brought; and whatever establishes the truth of what the Prophet brought establishes the commands and prohibitions he brought. The two are thus inseparably connected.

Furthermore, matters concerning Allah are also part of what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. He explained the rational proofs for what can be known through reason and reported matters of the unseen wholly beyond the reach of reason. There is therefore no reason to include the narratives under prophethood but not matters concerning Allah. If what is meant is that the narratives attest to his prophethood, they do so because he reported them, just as he reported other matters of the unseen. Among his reports concerning Allah and future events are those that serve this purpose just as effectively as the narratives, and even more powerfully. If, however, what is meant is that the punishment of those who rejected the messengers attests to prophethood, then these narratives attest to prophethood in general and to

the prophethood of the one whose people He punished; they do not establish the prophethood of a later prophet unless what he reports is of the same kind as what the earlier prophet reported.

All these considerations, and more, apply to matters concerning Allah, for the Prophet reported concerning Him the same things that the prophets before him had reported. Allah has mentioned this in several places, as in His words:

“Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We appoint any gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?”

And His words:

“We never sent a messenger before you without revealing to him: There is no deity but Me, so worship Me.”

And His words:

“We certainly sent a messenger to every nation, saying: Worship Allah and shun false gods.”

Allah has also told us that the prophets whose accounts He related—such as Noah, Hūd, Sālih, and Shuayb, may Allah’s blessings be upon them all—each said to his people:

“My people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him.”

Indeed, each began his call with this. The Most High also stated that the prophets and their communities, from Noah to the disciples, were Muslims, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Furthermore, it is through matters concerning Allah, by which the Lord’s power, will, wisdom, and actions are known, that a true prophet is distinguished from a pretender and a prophet’s truthfulness is established. These matters therefore provide stronger evidence of a prophet’s truthfulness than the narratives alone. Whatever evidence the narratives contain of his truthfulness has force only in conjunction with matters concerning Allah; taken in isolation, it would establish nothing. Prophethood is thus more closely connected with matters concerning Allah than with anything else, and the prophets were sent only to call people to Allah

alone. They may describe the Hereafter both generally and in detail, while some of them may recount certain narratives only in general terms.

Matters concerning Allah, however, are the foundation. The command to worship Allah alone, to the exclusion of all others, must be explained in detail. Every prophet must therefore teach the three foundations: belief in Allah, belief in the Last Day, and righteous deeds. Allah mentions the universal foundations shared by the prophets in the Meccan surahs, such as al-Anʿām, al-Aʿrāf, the surahs beginning with “Alif Lām Rā,” “Tā Sīn Mīm,” and “Hā Mīm,” most of the Mufassal surahs, and others of this kind. The Medinan surahs include addresses to those who believe in messengers in general, from among the People of the Book, from among those who believe in the revealed laws with which the Seal of the Messengers was sent.

As for the claim that this concerns one particular individual, it is utterly untenable, both in wording and in meaning. Moreover, Allah singles out a particular case for a ruling peculiar to it only because of a consideration peculiar to that case. An example is what the Prophet said to Abū Burdah ibn Niyār. He had slaughtered his sacrifice on Eid before the prayer, before the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had prescribed for them that slaughtering should take place after the prayer. When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The first thing we do on this day of ours is pray; then we slaughter our sacrifices. Whoever slaughtered before the prayer must offer another sacrifice, for his animal was merely a sheep slaughtered for meat that he provided for his family,”

Abū Burdah told him that he had slaughtered before the prayer, not knowing that this was impermissible. He also told him that he had a young she-goat better than a jadhaʿah. He said:

“It will suffice for you, but it will not suffice for anyone after you.”

He singled him out for this ruling because he was excused for slaughtering before the prayer: he had done so before the ruling was instituted, so it was not

yet prohibited. Moreover, the only animal he had was of that age. As for his instruction to the wife of Abū Hudhayfah ibn ‘Utbah to breastfeed Sālim, her husband’s freedman, five times so that he would become a relative she was permanently forbidden to marry, the early generations differed over this: was the ruling exclusive to him, or did it also apply to others? If it is said that it applies to anyone who needs it—as she did—this reconciles the evidence.

In short, the Lawgiver is wise. He does not distinguish between two like cases unless one has a particular feature warranting that distinction, nor does He treat as equal things that differ and are unequal. Indeed, He—glory be to Him—has rebuked those who attribute this to Him and condemned those who judge in this way. He, Most High, says:

“Or should We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption on earth? Or should We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?”

He, Most High, also says:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, alike in their life and their death? How evil is their judgment!”

He, Most High, says:

“Shall We then treat those who submit to Us like the criminals?”

“What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”

He, Most High, says:

“Are your disbelievers better than those, or do you have immunity in the Scriptures?”

He, Most High, says:

“They destroy their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take heed, O people of insight.”

Such a lesson can only be drawn if like cases are treated alike. But if it is said, “That is not how things actually are,” then no lesson can be drawn. People have differed over this principle, namely, whether He singles someone out with a command

or prohibition without any cause or wisdom whatsoever, simply singling out one of two like cases rather than the other? Jahm ibn Safwān and those among the Jabriyyah (determinists) who agreed with him affirmed this, as did many speculative theologians who affirm divine decree.

The early generations, however, along with the leading scholars of jurisprudence, hadith, and Sufism, and most schools of speculative theology—both those who affirm divine decree, such as the Karrāmiyyah and others, and those who deny it, such as the Mu‘tazilah and others—do not accept this principle. Rather, they say that He—glory be to Him—makes particular distinctions in His creation and His commands for reasons and wisdom that He has in doing so. This principle has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Likewise, some say: “He multiplies its reciter’s reward to equal the unmultiplied reward given to someone who recites a third of the Quran.” This claim is supported neither by the hadith nor by reason, and there is no fitting rationale or wisdom in it. The text states that reciting it is equivalent to a third of the Quran, and that whoever recites it is as though he had recited a third of the Quran. If the reward is multiplied in one case, it is multiplied in the other; if it is not multiplied in one, neither is it multiplied in the other. To single out one of them for multiplication is therefore arbitrary.

Furthermore, assigning a multiplied reward equivalent to that of a third of the Quran can only be because of the surah’s distinctive merit. Its merit, then, accounts for this valuation, without any need to diminish the reward of the rest of the Quran. Moreover, this is sheer arbitrariness: no evidence supports it, no cause warrants it, and there is no wisdom in it.

Whoever knows that the Messenger is the most knowledgeable of all creation concerning the truth, the most eloquent in explaining it, and the most sincere in seeking the good of creation knows that he combines perfect knowledge of the truth, perfect ability to explain it, and perfect willingness to do so. When knowledge, ability, and willingness are all complete, the intended result must be achieved in the most perfect manner. It is therefore clear that his words explain the religious matters he addressed—concerning Allah and other subjects—with the utmost eloquence, completeness, and clarity.

Whoever takes this firmly to heart cannot distort the texts through interpretations such as these. Upon reflection, he will find that anyone who intended such meanings by those words would be far removed from the qualities that the Messenger must possess. He will also know that whoever follows this path does so only because of a deficiency in the knowledge and faith he has been given. Allah Most High has said:

“Allah will raise those who have believed among you and those who were given knowledge, by degrees.”

We therefore ask Allah to make us and our brothers among the people of knowledge and faith whose ranks He has raised.

Now that the weakness of these views has become clear—apart from the first view, which we defended, held by Ibn Surayj and others such as al-Muhallab, al-Asīlī, and others—we say:

It is known that differences in excellence within the Quran and the rest of Allah’s speech are not based on their attribution to the Speaker, for He—glory be to Him—is One. Rather, they are based on the meanings He expresses and on His words that convey those meanings.

Among the verses, he singled out the Verse of the Throne for superiority. In an authentic hadith, he said to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb:

“Do you know which verse in Allah’s Book that you know is the greatest?”

He replied: “Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence.”

He then struck him on the chest with his hand and said: “May your knowledge bring you joy, Abū al-Mundhir!”

No other single verse in the Quran contains all that the Verse of the Throne contains. What Allah mentions at the beginning of Sūrat al-Hadīd and the end of Sūrat al-Hashr extends over several verses, not just one.

We shall explain, if Allah wills, that even though “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” equals one-third of the Quran, it does not follow that it is superior to al-Fātihah, nor that reciting it three times suffices in place of reciting the Quran. Indeed, the early generations disapproved of reciting it more than once when reciting the entire Quran, just as it appears once in the written Quran. The Quran is to be recited as it is written in the written copy, without addition or omission.

The takbīr (declaration that Allah is the Greatest) transmitted from Ibn Kathīr is not traced through a chain of transmission to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. No one traced it through such a chain to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, except al-Bazzī, who thereby differed from everyone else who transmitted it. They transmitted it only as a practice chosen by someone below the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, whereas he alone traced it back to him. translated_text:
one scholar. The point is that the Sunnah is to recite the Quran as it appears in the written copies. However, when “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” is recited on its own, it may be recited three times or more. Whoever recites it receives a reward equivalent to one-third of the reward for reciting the Quran. Yet a thing’s equivalent—ʿadl, pronounced with a short a—is of a different kind from it, as we shall explain, if Allah wills.

Rewards are of different kinds, just as wealth is of different kinds: food, drink, clothing, housing, money, and so forth. If a man possesses, for example, a thousand dinars’ worth of one kind of wealth, it does not follow that he can dispense with all the other kinds. If his wealth consists of food, he still needs clothing, housing, and other things. Likewise, if it consists of some kind other than money, he needs other kinds; and if he possesses nothing but money, he needs all the various goods themselves and the benefits they provide.

Al-Fātihah contains benefits in the form of praise and supplication that people need, for which “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” cannot substitute, even though its reward is immense. A person benefits from that immense reward only alongside the reward of reciting the Opening of the Book. Thus, if he were to recite that surah alone in prayer, without al-Fātihah, his prayer would not be valid. Even if he were to recite the entire Quran except al-Fātihah, his prayer would not be valid, because the meanings of al-Fātihah encompass the fundamental needs that Allah’s servants cannot do without. and supplication—namely, the words:

“Guide us to the straight path.”

“The path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your anger, nor those who have gone astray.”

—constitute the finest, most binding, and most beneficial supplication a servant can address to his Lord. It encompasses all that benefits him in his religion, his worldly life, and the Hereafter. The servant constantly needs it, and nothing else can take its place. Even if he received the reward for reciting nine-tenths of the Quran—let alone one-third—but did not attain what this supplication seeks, that reward would neither replace it nor fulfil its purpose.

This is like a man who, hypothetically, gives immense sums in charity and undertakes great efforts in jihad, surpassing in merit repeated recitations of the Quran, yet has not performed the five prayers that day. The reward for these deeds would not take the place of those prayers. Likewise, a man might possess immense wealth in gold, silver, slaves, livestock, and real estate, yet have no food for his morning and evening meals. He would remain hungry, suffering, and in distress; all that immense wealth would not take the place of the food he needs. Hence Shaykh Abū Madyan, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

“The noblest knowledge is knowledge of Allah’s oneness;
the most beneficial knowledge is knowledge of the rulings governing His servants.”

Thus, what is superior and nobler is not necessarily what benefits a person at a particular time. Rather, what is most beneficial at any given time is what the servant needs then: doing what Allah has commanded and refraining from what He has forbidden. Hence it is said:

“What is generally less meritorious is, in its proper place and time, better than what is generally more meritorious.”

The merit of “Say: He is Allah, One” and other surahs should be understood accordingly. Reciting al-Fātihah at the beginning of prayer is better than reciting that surah; indeed, it is obligatory. That surah alone cannot suffice; rather, the prayer is invalid if one relies on it alone.

Thus, drawing near to Allah through obligatory deeds must precede drawing near through voluntary deeds. Voluntary deeds constitute a means of drawing near only when the obligatory deeds are performed. This contradicts what some proponents of union maintain, such as the author of al-Futūhāt al-Makkiyyah (The Meccan Revelations) and others like him: that nearness through obligatory deeds follows nearness through voluntary deeds, and that voluntary deeds make the Real his covering, whereas obligatory deeds make the Real his very self. This rests upon his corrupt doctrine of union, as explained.

It has also been explained that the hadith contradicts his doctrine in several respects. Al-Bukhārī narrated it in his Sahīh from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah says: ‘Whoever shows enmity towards a devoted servant of Mine has openly declared war against Me. My servant draws near to Me through nothing comparable to fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues drawing near to Me through voluntary deeds until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely grant him refuge.

translated_text:
and I have never hesitated over anything I am going to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he hates death, and I hate to distress him, yet he must inevitably face it.’”

This hadith makes clear that the one drawing near is not the One to whom he draws near; rather, he is distinct from Him. It also makes clear that His servant draws near to Him through nothing comparable to fulfilling the obligatory duties, and thereafter continues drawing near through voluntary deeds until he becomes beloved to Allah. He then hears through Him, sees through Him, grasps through Him, and walks through Him. Then He says:

“If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely grant him refuge.”

Thus He distinguishes between the one asking and the One being asked, and between the one seeking refuge and the One in whom refuge is sought. He describes the servant as asking his Lord and seeking refuge in Him. This is a noble hadith encompassing great purposes, which this is not the place to discuss. Our purpose here is to discuss “Say: He is Allah, One.”

We have explained that the best explanation is that the meanings of the Quran fall into three categories: affirmation of Allah’s oneness, narratives, and rulings. This surah describes the Most Merciful and contains only the affirmation of His oneness. This is because the Quran is Allah’s speech.

Speech is of two kinds: prescriptions and reports. Reports concern either the Creator or created beings. Prescriptions are rulings, such as commands and prohibitions. Reports concerning created beings are narratives, while reports concerning the Creator consist of the mention of His names and attributes. No surah in the Quran is devoted purely to describing the Most Merciful except this surah. In the two Sahīhs, ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah Most High be pleased with her, reported: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appointed a man to command a military detachment

and, when leading his companions in prayer, he would conclude his recitation with ‘Say: He is Allah, One.’ When they returned, they mentioned this to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said, ‘Ask him why he does that.’ They asked him, and he replied, ‘Because it describes the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Tell him that Allah loves him.’”

Al-Bukhārī also stated in the chapter “Combining Two Surahs in One Unit of Prayer”:

‘Ubayd Allāh reported from Thābit, from Anas:

“A man from the Ansār used to lead them in prayer in the mosque of Qubā’. Whenever he was about to recite a surah for them in prayer, he would first recite ‘Say: He is Allah, One’ in full, then recite another surah along with it. He did this in every unit of prayer. His companions spoke to him, saying, ‘You begin with this surah, but then you do not consider it sufficient without reciting another. Either recite it alone, or leave it and recite another.’

“He replied, ‘I will not give it up. If you would like me to lead you in prayer in this way, I will do so; but if you dislike it, I will stop leading you.’ They considered him one of the best among them and were reluctant to have anyone else lead them.

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came to them, they told him what had happened. He said, ‘So-and-so, what prevents you from doing what your companions ask of you, and what makes you adhere to this surah in every unit of prayer?’

“He replied, ‘I love it.’ He said, ‘Your love for it has admitted you to Paradise.’”

The Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “It is equivalent to one-third of the Quran,” is true, just as he said. For he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the truthful one whose truthfulness is confirmed, who does not speak from his own desire. Nothing but the truth ever passed his lips.

translated_text:
Those who find this statement problematic base their objections on two grounds:

The first is their denial that some of Allah’s speech is superior to other parts—a position whose weakness has already been demonstrated. The second is their belief that reward depends on the number of letters: the more letters a passage contains, the greater the reward for reciting it.

They argue that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever recites the Quran will have ten good deeds credited to him for every letter. I do not say that ‘Alif Lām Mīm’ is one letter; rather, alif is a letter, lām is a letter, and mīm is a letter.”

Al-Tirmidhī said, “An authentic hadith.” They argue, “It is well known that one-third of the Quran contains far more letters, so the good deeds credited for it must be more numerous.”

The response to them is:

This is true, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stated. Yet good deeds vary in magnitude: some are great and others small. The Prophet’s point, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was that Allah rewards His servant tenfold for every good deed, as He, Most High, says:

“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold.”

Thus, reciting a letter constitutes a good deed, and Allah grants the reciter ten times the value of that good deed. But he did not say that the good deeds credited for reciting different letters are equal in value. Likewise, someone who gives a dinar in charity receives ten times the reward for that good deed.

If someone who came after the earliest forerunners were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not equal a mudd given by any one of them, nor even half of it, as is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the two Sahīh collections. Thus, if that person gives a mudd, he receives ten times the reward for this good deed. But

that good deed is not equal in value to the good deed of one of the earliest Companions who gave a mudd. There are many similar examples. Likewise, the letters of the Quran differ in merit because their meanings differ in excellence, and for other reasons. For each letter of al-Fātihah, the reciter earns a good deed greater than those earned for letters of “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish.”

When one thing is equivalent to another, its ʿadl—with the vowel a—is its equal, even if it is of a different kind. As Allah, Most High, says:

“Or the equivalent of that in fasting.”

Fasting is not of the same kind as food or the compensatory offering, but it is equivalent to them in measure. Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah will accept from him neither sarf nor ʿadl.”

And Allah, Most High, says:

“Nor will any ransom be accepted from it.”

Here, ʿadl means a ransom: something equivalent to what is being redeemed, even if it is of a different kind.

“Yet those who disbelieve set up equals to their Lord.”

That is, they assign Him an equal—a rival in divinity—even though they know that it is not of the same kind as the Lord, glory be to Him.

If one man possessed various kinds of wealth, and another possessed gold of the same value, the wealth of the one would be equivalent to that of the other, even though they were of different kinds. Thus, a man may possess gold and other assets of immense value, yet if he needs medicine, a compound preparation, a dwelling, or something similar, and is unable to purchase it, that immense wealth will not benefit him.

People need the commands, prohibitions, and narratives contained in the Quran, even though the affirmation of Allah’s oneness is greater than these. If a person needs to know which actions He has commanded and which He has forbidden, or

needs the instruction and lessons conveyed by the narratives, promises, and warnings, nothing else can take their place. The affirmation of Allah’s oneness cannot replace these, nor can the narratives replace the commands and prohibitions, or the commands and prohibitions replace the narratives. Rather, people benefit from and need everything Allah has revealed.

When a person recites “Say: He is Allah, One,” he receives a reward equal in measure to the reward for a third of the Quran. Yet this reward need not be of the same kind as that obtained through the rest of the Quran. He may need the kind of reward obtained through its commands, prohibitions, and narratives, and “Say: He is Allah, One” neither replaces these nor serves in their stead.

Thus, if he does not recite “Say: He is Allah, One,” then, even if he receives a great reward, he does not obtain by reciting it the kind of reward obtained by reciting other parts of the Quran. Rather, he remains in need of the knowledge of commands, prohibitions, promises, and warnings through which his faith is perfected, even if he fulfills his obligations. The knowledge gained by reciting the rest of the Quran cannot be gained merely by reciting this surah.

In this respect, one who recites the entire Quran is better than one who recites this surah three times, because of the variety of rewards. Although someone who recites “Say: He is Allah, One” three times receives a reward equal in measure to that reward, it is of a single kind, lacking the various kinds that the servant needs. This is like one person possessing three thousand dinars, while another possesses food, clothing, dwellings, and money together worth three thousand dinars. The latter possesses what benefits him in all his affairs, whereas the former needs what the latter possesses, even though their possessions are equal in value. Likewise, if he possessed

food of the finest quality worth three thousand dinars, he would still need clothing, dwellings, and means of warding off harm, such as weapons, medicines, and other things that food alone cannot provide.

It should also be understood that the merit of recitation, remembrance of Allah, supplication, prayer, and other acts may vary according to a person’s condition. Recitation with reflection is better than recitation without reflection, and prayer with humility and an attentive heart is better than prayer without them. A report states:

“Two men may stand together in the same row, yet the difference between their prayers is as great as the distance between heaven and earth.”

One of the shaykhs used to recite “Say: He is Allah, One” for healing, and this brought great blessing. Others would recite it for healing without obtaining that result, so he would say: “Not everyone’s recitation of ‘Say: He is Allah, One’ benefits everyone.”

Once this is understood, one person’s glorification of Allah may be better than another’s recitation, and one person’s recitation of certain surahs may be better than another’s recitation of “Say: He is Allah, One” or other surahs. A single person’s condition also varies. He may perform an act of lesser merit in a perfect manner and thereby attain greater merit than through his other, more excellent deeds.

Allah forgave a prostitute for giving a dog water, as established in the two Sahīh collections. This was because of the acts of the heart and other factors that accompanied her deed. A man may spend many times as much yet not be forgiven, because the factors that purify a deed are absent. For Allah accepts only from those who are mindful of Him. فَصْلٌ:
وَأَصْلُ هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ أَنْ يَعْلَمَ أَنَّ التَّفَاضُلَ وَالتَّمَاثُلَ إنَّمَا يَقَعُ بَيْنَ شَيْئَيْنِ فَصَاعِدًا إذْ الْوَاحِدُ مِنْ كُلِّ وَجْهٍ لَا يُعْقَلُ فِيهِ شَيْءٌ أَفْضَلَ مِنْ شَيْءٍ فَالتَّفَاضُلُ فِي صِفَاتِهِ تَعَالَى إنَّمَا يُعْقَلُ إذَا أُثْبِتَ لَهُ صِفَاتٌ مُتَعَدِّدَةٌ كَالْعِلْمِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ وَالْإِرَادَةِ وَالْمَحَبَّةِ وَالْبُغْضِ وَالرِّضَا وَالْغَضَبِ. وَكَإِثْبَاتِ أَسْمَاءٍ لَهُ مُتَعَدِّدَةٍ تَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعَانٍ مُتَعَدِّدَةٍ وَأُثْبِتَ لَهُ كَلِمَاتٌ مُتَعَدِّدَةٌ
translated_text:
in an authentic hadith:

“Were any of you to spend as much gold as Mount Uhud, it would not equal one mudd (a measure) given by any one of them, nor even half of it.”

He said this concerning his earliest and foremost Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Thus, when it is said that the reward for “Say: He is Allah, One” equals the reward for one-third of the Quran, equality in all other respects must be taken into account. Otherwise, if reciting other passages with reflection and humility is compared with reciting this surah in heedlessness and ignorance, that equivalence does not hold.

Indeed, a servant’s saying:

“Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest,”

with an attentive heart imbued with these meanings may be better than reciting this surah in ignorance and heedlessness. People differ in their understanding of this surah and what it contains, just as they differ in their understanding of the rest of the Quran.

Section

The foundation of this issue is to understand that differences in excellence and equality can exist only between two or more things. Within that which is one in every respect, it is inconceivable that one thing should be better than another. Differences in excellence among His attributes, exalted is He, are therefore conceivable only if multiple attributes are affirmed for Him, such as knowledge, power, will, love, hatred, pleasure, and anger. that subsist in His Essence, so that one may ask: “Are some of them superior to others, or not?” Every position in this matter other than that of the early generations and the leading scholars is erroneous and self-contradictory. Whatever answer its proponent gives to this question will be erroneous; he cannot give a sound answer.

Thus, whoever says that He has no positive attributes, but only negative or relational attributes—as do the thoroughgoing Jahmiyyah among the philosophers and speculative theologians, the followers of Jahm ibn Safwān—cannot, on the basis of his false premise, give a sound answer when asked: “Which is superior: His relation to the heavens and the earth—namely, creating them—or His relation to a mosquito? Or which is superior: denying that He is ignorant of anything or incapable of anything, or denying that He is ignorant of universals?”

If he says, “Creating the heavens is equivalent to creating a mosquito,” this is an obstinate denial of both reason and revelation. Allah, Most High, says:

“The creation of the heavens and the earth is indeed greater than the creation of mankind, but most people do not know.”

But if he says, “Rather, the former is mightier and greater, as stated in the Quran,” he is told: “You acknowledge no two existing realities, one of which surpasses the other, since, according to you, creation is nothing beyond the created thing itself. Thus, nothing remains but sheer nonexistence. How, then, can one conceive of one of two things that are nonexistent in every respect being superior to the other, when there is no existent reality in which such a difference in excellence could occur?”

Likewise, to say that negating ignorance and inability with regard to some things is equivalent to negating them with regard to other things is an obstinate denial. translated_text:
follow from the negation of ignorance that knowledge of anything is affirmed, but rather both negations are pure nonexistence, how can differences in excellence be conceived in something that is identical in every respect? Such differences cannot be conceived in pure nonexistence and sheer negation, for that is nothing at all: it has no reality in existence and contains neither perfection nor anything praiseworthy. Differences in excellence arise only through attributes of perfection, and perfection must consist either in a self-subsisting existent or in an existing attribute subsisting in something else. Pure nonexistence contains no perfection whatsoever.”

This is why Allah describes Himself with attributes declaring His freedom from imperfection, not with merely negative attributes of nonexistence: they imply positive realities that constitute perfections by which He—glorified be He—praises Himself. This has been explained at length elsewhere. For example, He, Most High, says:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep.”

Negating these things implies the perfection of His life and of His self-subsistence and sustaining of all things. Likewise, His words:

“Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?”

imply the perfection of His sovereignty and lordship, and that these belong to Him alone. His exclusive possession of sovereignty, guidance, teaching, and all other attributes of perfection is itself an attribute of perfection. This is why the surah contains the two names al-Ahad (the One) and al-Samad, each of which indicates perfection. His word “Ahad” indicates that He has no equal, while His word “al-Samad,” with the definite article, indicates that the quality denoted by this name belongs exclusively to Him. This is why the definite article appears in His name al-Samad but not in Ahad: no one other than Him is described affirmatively as ahad, unlike samad, for the Arabs call a chief samad.

translated_text:
“al-Samad” indicates that the perfection denoted by this name belongs exclusively to Him.

We have already explained the meaning of al-Samad and how it encompasses every attribute of perfection, as the scholars transmitted from Ibn Abī Talha’s account of Ibn ʿAbbās’s explanation. Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Hātim, al-Bayhaqī and others cited it. Explaining His word “al-Samad,” he says:

“The Master whose mastery is perfect; the Noble One whose nobility is perfect; the Great One whose greatness is perfect; the Wise One whose wisdom is perfect; the All-Knowing One whose knowledge is perfect; and the Forbearing One whose forbearance is perfect. He is perfect in every aspect of nobility and mastery. Such is His description—glorified be He—and it befits Him alone. He has no equal, and there is nothing like Him. Glorified be He, the One, the All-Subduing.”

Likewise, it is established through the narration of al-Aʿmash from Abū Wāʾil, cited by al-Bukhārī in his Sahīh and transmitted by many scholars in their books, that he said:

“Al-Samad is the Master whose mastery has reached its utmost perfection.”

Several of the early generations, including Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and others, also said:

“Al-Samad is the One who has no hollow interior.”

Both explanations are true and accord with the Arabic language, as has been explained at length in its proper place. That al-samad means “the master” is well known; the other meaning is also recognized in the language. Al-Jawharī and others mentioned that al-samad is a variant of al-samt (that which is solid, without a hollow interior). This is not a case of substituting the letter t for d, as some have supposed; rather, the forms samada, yasmudu, samadan themselves indicate this meaning.

The point here is that attributes of perfection pertain only to things that exist

and negative attributes constitute perfection only when they imply positive realities. Thus, glorifying the Lord involves both declaring Him free of imperfection and magnifying Him. When a servant says, “Glory be to Allah,” this declares Allah’s freedom from all evil and imperfection. This meaning entails His intrinsic greatness; it is not mere negation devoid of any positive reality, for that would convey neither praise nor magnification.

The same applies to everything else from which the Lord is declared free, including partners, offspring and other things. Thus, He, Most High, says:

“Has your Lord, then, favoured you with sons and taken females from among the angels for Himself? You are indeed making an outrageous claim!”

—up to His words—

“Then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.”

“Glory be to Him! Exalted is He far above what they say!”

“The seven heavens, the earth, and all those within them glorify Him. There is nothing that does not glorify Him with praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing, All-Forgiving.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, far above what they ascribe to Him!”

“And peace be upon the messengers.”

There are other such passages. Negating faults and deficiencies necessarily entails affirming perfection, while denying partners entails oneness, which is part of complete perfection. For when something has a counterpart, the attributes and acts of perfection are divided between it and its counterpart, so it possesses some attributes of perfection, not all of them. Thus, the One who alone possesses every attribute of perfection is more perfect than one who has a partner sharing those attributes with him.

This is why those who affirm Allah’s oneness and devote themselves sincerely to Him love Allah more perfectly than the polytheists who love others besides Him—those who have taken rivals besides Him, loving them as they love Him. He says:

Most High:

“Among people are those who take rivals besides Allah, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

This has been discussed at length elsewhere, where it has been explained that this constitutes major polytheism, which Allah Most High does not forgive. In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Masʿūd reported:

“I asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, which sin is greatest?’ He replied, ‘To set up a rival to Allah when it is He who created you.’ I asked, ‘Then which?’ He replied, ‘To kill your child for fear that he will share your food.’ I asked, ‘Then which?’ He replied, ‘To commit adultery with your neighbour’s wife.’”

Allah Most High revealed confirmation of this:

“And those who do not invoke another god besides Allah, nor kill a soul whom Allah has forbidden to be killed except by right, nor commit adultery”—to the end of the verse.

Whoever sets up a rival to Allah, loving it as he loves Allah, is among those who invoke another god besides Allah. This constitutes major polytheism. The point here is that when something is divided and shared, the portion each receives is diminished; when all of it belongs to one, it is more complete. This is why the love for Allah of believers who affirm His oneness and devote themselves sincerely to Him is more perfect.

Likewise, refraining from the other major sins and indecencies they have been forbidden brings the positive realities of their worship, obedience, knowledge and love to perfection. This contributes to their purification and growth, just as removing weeds from a crop makes it flourish more fully and brings its positive attributes of perfection to greater fulfilment. Allah Most High says:

“Woe to the polytheists,”

“who do not give zakah.”

The foundation of zakah is affirming Allah’s oneness

This is the foundational principle of the outright Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, on which the Kullābiyyah and all others who affirm the divine attributes opposed them. They say: “He is pleased and becomes angry, but pleasure and anger do not subsist in Him; rather, they are created, and are His reward and punishment.” They say: “He is a speaker and speaks, but speech does not subsist in Him; rather, it is created and subsists in something other than Him.” They may also say: “He possesses will and wills.” Then they may say that will is not something existent; or they may say that it consists of created things and the created command. They may also say: “He brought into being a will that subsists in no subject.”

This false foundational principle, established by those who negate the attributes—the outright Jahmiyyah among the Muʿtazilah and others—is precisely the point on which all who affirm the attributes parted ways with them. These include the early generations, the imams, the scholars of jurisprudence, hadith, Sufism, and Quranic exegesis, and the various speculative thinkers who affirm the attributes: the Kullābiyyah and their followers among the Ashʿariyyah and others, as well as the Hishāmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and other groups of speculative thinkers who affirm the attributes. This is also the position of the recognized leading imams of the Muslims and the leading jurists among their followers—the adherents of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, Abū Hanīfah, and others.

Thus, the claim that the term ‘speech’ applies literally to the expression, while that expression is nevertheless created, contradicts the foundational principle distinguishing those who affirm the attributes from those who deny them—unless that to which an attribute relates is given the name of the attribute itself. Thus, what is commanded is called a ‘command’; that through which mercy is shown is called ‘mercy’; a created thing is called ‘creation’; what is decreed is called ‘power’; and what is known is called ‘knowledge’. But the reply to him is: “None of these is the literal meaning when the term is used without qualification.”
