translated_text:
Moreover, these things are entities that subsist in their own right. When they are ascribed to Allah, the ascription is understood to denote ownership, not an attribute. An expression, by contrast, does not subsist in its own right, just as a meaning does not. This is the fundamental distinction between ascribing attributes to Allah and ascribing created things to Him.

Those who negate and deny the attributes among the Sabians, philosophers, Muʿtazilah, and other Jahmiyyah, together with their followers—such as Ibn ʿAqīl and Ibn al-Jawzī in some of their writings, although elsewhere they state the opposite—say: “The texts merely ascribe these things to Allah. These are called texts concerning ascriptions, not texts concerning attributes.” They speak of “texts concerning ascriptions” and “hadiths concerning ascriptions,” rather than “verses concerning the attributes” and “hadiths concerning the attributes.”

An ascription may relate a created thing to Allah because it has a particular connection to Him in some respect, as with the House, the she-camel, and the spirit in His words:

“And purify My House,”

and His words:

“Allah’s she-camel,”

and His words:

“Then We sent to her Our Spirit, and he appeared to her as a well-proportioned man.”

The proponents of divine indwelling among the Christians, the extremist Shīʿah, and the Sufis, together with their followers who hold that the spirit—that is, the souls of human beings—has no beginning, and who claim affiliation with Muslim imams such as al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others—including a group from Jīlān and elsewhere—say: “Rather, ascribing the spirit to Allah is like ascribing speech and power to Him. Speech and power are His attributes, and so too is the spirit.”

They also say that His words:

“When I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit”

provide evidence that the human soul is a beginningless attribute of Allah.

The Christians said:

“Jesus is the Word of Allah, and Allah’s speech is uncreated; therefore Jesus is uncreated.”

The Sabians and the Jahmiyyah said:

“Jesus is the Word of Allah, and he is created. The Quran is Allah’s speech, so it too is created.”

These matters have confused many people. The imams, such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, discussed them, addressing the ascription of speech and spirit to Allah and debating the Jahmiyyah and the Christians.

I have been asked about this, sometimes in connection with the proponents of divine indwelling and sometimes in connection with those who negate the attributes. The questioners have sometimes been Muslims and sometimes non-Muslims. The answer has been set out at length in several places. Here, however, the point is to distinguish between the two kinds of things ascribed to Allah:

If what is ascribed to Him is something that subsists in its own right, or something that inheres in such a self-subsisting entity, it cannot be an attribute of Allah, because an attribute subsists in that which it describes. The entities Allah has created subsist in their own right, and the attributes subsisting in them cannot be attributes of Allah. Ascribing them to Him therefore entails that they are created and owned by Him. They are ascribed to Him because of a particular connection that warrants this ascription, not because they are His attributes.

The Spirit, who is Gabriel, belongs to this category, as do the Kaaba and the she-camel. Wealth belonging to Allah also falls into this category, as do the souls of Adam’s descendants. Examples include His words:

“Then We sent to her Our Spirit, and he appeared to her as a well-proportioned man.”

“When I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit.”

“And purify My House.”

“Allah’s she-camel and her turn to drink!”

“Whatever Allah has granted His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and to the Messenger.”

translated_text:
But if what is ascribed to Him does not subsist in its own right, but can only be an attribute—such as knowledge, power, speech, pleasure, or anger—then this can only be the ascription of an attribute to Him, one that subsists in Him, glorified is He. Thus, when one says:

“I seek Your guidance through Your knowledge, and seek ability through Your power,”

His knowledge is an attribute subsisting in Him, and His power is an attribute subsisting in Him. Likewise, when one says:

“I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath, and in Your pardon from Your punishment,”

His pleasure and wrath subsist in Him, as do His pardon and punishment. Their effects, however—the blessings that reach the servant and the afflictions averted from him—are created, separate from Him, and are not His attributes. The effect may be called by the name of the attribute, as in the authentic hadith:

“Allah says to Paradise: ‘You are My mercy; through you I show mercy to whomever I will among My servants.’”

Here, mercy is a self-subsisting entity and cannot be an attribute of something else. This, then, is the distinction between ascribing something as an attribute and ascribing it as a possession.

When it is said, “The Messiah is the Word of Allah,” this means that he was created through the word, for the Messiah himself is not speech. This is unlike the Quran, which is itself speech. Speech does not subsist in its own right, but only in the speaker. Its ascription to the speaker is therefore the ascription of an attribute to the one it describes, even though the speaker speaks through his power and will. Even if it is called an act in this respect, it is an attribute insofar as it subsists in the speaker.

 هَلْ بَعْضُ كُتُبِ اللَّهِ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ بَعْضٍ - وَكِتَابُ اللَّهِ عِنْدَهُ هُوَ الْقُرْآنُ الْعَرَبِيُّ الْمَخْلُوقُ عِنْدَهُ - فَهَذَا السُّؤَالُ يَتَوَجَّهُ عَلَى قَوْلِهِ فِي الظَّاهِرِ وَأَمَّا فِي نَفْسِ الْأَمْرِ فَكِلَاهُمَا مُمْتَنِعٌ عَلَى قَوْلِهِ لِأَنَّ الْعِبَارَةَ تَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمَعَانِي فَإِنَّ الْمَعَانِيَ الْقَائِمَةَ فِي النَّفْسِ تَدُلُّ عَلَيْهَا الْعِبَارَاتُ وَقَدْ عُلِمَ أَنَّ الْعِبَارَاتِ تَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعَانٍ مُتَنَوِّعَةٍ وَعَلَى أَصْلِهِ لَيْسَ الْمَعْنَى إلَّا وَاحِدًا فَيَمْتَنِعُ بِالضَّرُورَةِ الْعَقْلِيَّةِ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْقُرْآنُ الْعَرَبِيُّ كُلُّهُ وَالتَّوْرَاةُ وَالْإِنْجِيلُ وَسَائِرُ مَا يُضَافُ إلَى اللَّهِ مِنْ الْعِبَارَاتِ إنَّمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنًى وَاحِدٍ لَا يَتَعَدَّدُ وَلَا يَتَبَعَّضُ وَحِينَئِذٍ فَتَبَعُّضُ الْعِبَارَاتِ الدَّالَّةِ عَلَى الْمَعَانِي بِدُونِ تَبَعُّضِ تِلْكَ الْمَعَانِي مُمْتَنِعٌ.
 وَلِهَذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ:
 مُوسَى عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ لَمَّا سَمِعَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ أَسْمَعَهُ كُلَّهُ أَمْ سَمِعَ بَعْضَهُ؟
 إنْ قُلْتُمْ:
 
" كُلَّهُ "
 فَقَدْ عَلِمَ كُلَّ مَا أَخْبَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ وَمَا أَمَرَ بِهِ وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحِ أَنَّ الْخَضِرَ قَالَ لَهُ 
{مَا نَقَصَ عِلْمِي وَعِلْمُك مِنْ عِلْمِ اللَّهِ إلَّا كَمَا نَقَصَ هَذَا الْعُصْفُورُ مِنْ هَذَا الْبَحْرِ}
 وَقَدْ
translated_text:
to him, “Are some parts of Allah’s speech superior to others?” he cannot, on his own premises, answer either yes or no, since he considers it indivisible and does not regard its verbal expression as Allah’s speech.

But suppose “speech” means the verbal expression, or he is asked, “Are some parts of the Quran superior to others?”—meaning by “Quran” the Arabic speech brought down by Gabriel, which he considers created, not spoken by Allah, but composed by Gabriel or someone else. Or suppose he is asked, “Are some of Allah’s scriptures superior to others?”—while Allah’s Book, according to him, is the Arabic Quran, which he considers created. Such a question would appear applicable to his position. In reality, however, both are impossible on his premises, because verbal expressions signify meanings: the meanings subsisting within the self are conveyed by verbal expressions. It is known that verbal expressions signify diverse meanings, whereas his premise allows only a single meaning. It is therefore necessarily impossible, as a matter of reason, for the entire Arabic Quran, the Torah, the Gospel, and all other verbal expressions attributed to Allah to signify only one meaning admitting neither multiplicity nor division. Thus, verbal expressions signifying meanings cannot be divisible unless those meanings are divisible as well.

For this reason, they have been asked: “When Moses, peace be upon him, heard Allah’s speech, did he hear all of it or only part of it?” If you say, “All of it,” then he knew everything Allah has communicated and everything He has commanded. Yet it is authentically reported that al-Khidr said to him:

“My knowledge and yours have diminished Allah’s knowledge only as much as this sparrow has diminished this sea.”

And indeed,

original_text:
قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{قُلْ لَوْ كَانَ الْبَحْرُ مِدَادًا لِكَلِمَاتِ رَبِّي لَنَفِدَ الْبَحْرُ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَنْفَدَ كَلِمَاتُ رَبِّي وَلَوْ جِئْنَا بِمِثْلِهِ مَدَدًا}
 . وَإِنْ قُلْتُمْ 
" سَمِعَ بَعْضَهُ "
 فَقَدْ تَبَعَّضَ وَعِنْدَكُمْ لَا يَتَبَعَّضُ. وَأَيْضًا فَقَدْ فَرَّقَ اللَّهُ بَيْنَ تَكْلِيمِهِ لِمُوسَى عَلَيْهِ الصَّلَاةُ وَالسَّلَامُ وَبَيْنَ إيحَائِهِ إلَى غَيْرِهِ مِنْ النَّبِيِّينَ وَفَرَّقَ بَيْنَ الْإِيحَاءِ وَبَيْنَ التَّكْلِيمِ مِنْ وَرَاءِ حِجَابٍ فَلَوْ كَانَ الْمَعْنَى وَاحِدًا لَكَانَ الْجَمِيعُ إيحَاءً وَلَمْ يَكُنْ هُنَاكَ تَكْلِيمٌ يَتَمَيَّزُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ. وَلَا يَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّبُّ تَعَالَى مُنَادِيًا لِأَحَدِ إذْ الْمَعْنَى الْقَائِمُ بِالنَّفْسِ لَا يَكُونُ نِدَاءً وَقَدْ أَخْبَرَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى بِنِدَائِهِ فِي الْقُرْآنِ فِي عِدَّةِ مَوَاضِعَ.
 وَعَلَى هَذَا فَمَنْ قَالَ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ:
 إنَّ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ لَا يَفْضُلُ بَعْضُهُ بَعْضًا فَحَقِيقَةُ قَوْلِهِ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةَ مُمْتَنِعَةٌ فَلَيْسَ هُنَاكَ أَمْرَانِ حَتَّى يُقَالَ إنَّ أَحَدَهُمَا يَكُونُ مِثْلَ الْآخَرِ أَوْ أَفْضَلَ مِنْهُ. وَالتَّمَاثُلُ وَالتَّفَاضُلُ إنَّمَا يُعْقَلُ بَيْنَ اثْنَيْنِ فَصَاعِدًا. وَهَكَذَا عِنْدَ هَؤُلَاءِ فِي إرَادَتِهِ وَعِلْمِهِ وَسَمْعِهِ وَبَصَرِهِ فَكُلُّ مَنْ جَعَلَ الصِّفَةَ وَاحِدَةً بِالْعَيْنِ امْتَنَعَ - عَلَى قَوْلِهِ -
 أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 هَلْ بَعْضُهَا أَفْضَلُ مِنْ بَعْضٍ أَمْ لَا؟ إذْ لَا بَعْضَ لَهَا عِنْدَهُ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ وَافَقَ هَؤُلَاءِ عَلَى وَحْدَةِ هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ بِالْعَيْنِ وَقَالَ:
 إنَّ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ حُرُوفٌ قَدِيمَةُ الْأَعْيَانِ أَوْ حُرُوفٌ وَأَصْوَاتٌ قَدِيمَةُ الْأَعْيَانِ سَوَاءٌ قَالَ مَعَ ذَلِكَ إنَّهَا أَعْيَانُ الْأَصْوَاتِ الْمَسْمُوعَةِ مِنْ الْقُرَّاءِ أَوْ قَالَ إنَّهَا بَعْضُ الْأَصْوَاتِ الْمَسْمُوعَةِ مِنْ الْقُرَّاءِ. وَإِنْ كَانَ فَسَادُ ذَلِكَ مَعْلُومًا بِالِاضْطِرَارِ،
translated_text:
He, the Exalted, says:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought another like it to replenish it.’”

If you say, “He heard part of it,” then it is divisible, whereas according to you it is indivisible. Moreover, Allah distinguished between His speaking to Moses, blessings and peace be upon him, and His revealing to the other prophets. He also distinguished between revelation and speaking from behind a veil. If the meaning were one and the same, all of this would be revelation, and there would be no distinct speaking beyond that. Nor is it impossible for the Lord Most High to call out to someone, since a meaning subsisting within the self does not constitute a call. Allah Most High has stated in several places in the Quran that He called out.

Accordingly, when any of these people says that no part of Allah’s speech is superior to another, what his position actually entails is that the question itself is impossible: there are not two things such that one could be said to equal the other or be superior to it. Equality and superiority are conceivable only between two or more things. They hold the same position concerning His will, knowledge, hearing, and sight. For anyone who regards an attribute as a single entity, it is impossible—on his own premises—to ask whether some parts of it are superior to others, since he holds that it has no parts.

The same applies to anyone who agrees with them that these attributes are each a single entity, yet says that Allah’s speech consists of letters that are individually beginningless, or of letters and sounds that are individually beginningless—whether he also says that they are the very sounds heard from reciters, or that they are some of the sounds heard from reciters—even though the falsity of this is self-evident,

original_text:
وَقَالَ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَصْوَاتَ غَيْرُ تِلْكَ.
 فَمَنْ قَالَ بِأَنَّ الْكَلَامَ حُرُوفٌ أَوْ حُرُوفٌ وَأَصْوَاتٌ مُقْتَرِنٌ بَعْضُهَا بِبَعْضِ أَزَلًا وَأَبَدًا وَهِيَ مَعَ ذَلِكَ شَيْءٌ وَاحِدٌ فَقَوْلُهُ مَعْلُومُ الْفَسَادِ عِنْدَ جُمْهُورِ الْعُقَلَاءِ كَمَا أَنَّ مَنْ جَعَلَهَا قَوْلًا وَاحِدًا فَقَوْلُهُ مَعْلُومُ الْفَسَادِ عِنْدَ جُمْهُورِ الْعُقَلَاءِ عَلَى كُلِّ تَقْدِيرٍ فَيَمْتَنِعُ مَعَ الْقَوْلِ بِوَحْدَةِ شَيْءٍ أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 هَلْ بَعْضُهُ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ بَعْضٍ أَمْ لَا؟
 وَأَمَّا مَنْ أَثْبَتَ مَا يَتَعَدَّدُ مِنْ الْمَعَانِي وَالْحُرُوفِ أَوْ أَحَدِهِمَا فَهَذَا يُعْقَلُ عَلَى قَوْلِهِ:
 السُّؤَالُ عَنْ التَّمَاثُلِ وَالتَّفَاضُلِ.
 ثُمَّ حِينَئِذٍ يَقَعُ السُّؤَالُ:
 هَلْ يَتَفَاضَلُ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ وَصِفَاتُهُ وَأَسْمَاؤُهُ أَمْ لَا يَقَعُ التَّفَاضُلُ إلَّا فِي الْمَخْلُوقِ؟ .
 وَعَلَى هَذَا فَمَا ذَكَرَهُ ابْنُ بَطَّالٍ فِي شَرْحِ الْبُخَارِيِّ لَمَّا تَكَلَّمَ عَلَى هَذَا الْحَدِيثِ حَيْثُ قَالَ:
 قَالَ الْمُهَلَّبُ - وَحَكَاهُ عَنْ الْأَصِيلِيَّ - وَمَذْهَبِ الْأَشْعَرِيِّ وَأَبِي بَكْرِ بْنِ الطَّيِّبِ وَابْنِ أَبِي زَيْدٍ والدَاوُدي وَأَبِي الْحَسَنِ الْقَابِسِيِّ وَجَمَاعَةِ عُلَمَاءِ السُّنَّةِ أَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ لَا يَفْضُلُ بَعْضُهُ بَعْضًا إذْ كُلُّهُ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَصِفَتُهُ وَهُوَ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ وَلَا يَجُوزُ التَّفَاضُلُ إلَّا فِي الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ هُوَ نَقْلٌ لِأَقْوَالِ هَؤُلَاءِ بِحَسَبِ مَا ظَنَّهُ لَازِمًا لَهُمْ حَيْثُ اعْتَقَدَ أَنَّ التَّفَاضُلَ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا فِي الْمَخْلُوقِ وَالْقُرْآنُ عِنْدَ هَؤُلَاءِ لَيْسَ بِمَخْلُوقِ. لَكِنْ قَدَّمْنَا أَنَّ السَّلَفَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا إنَّهُ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ لَمْ يُنْقَلْ عَنْ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ أَنَّهُ قَالَ لَيْسَ بَعْضُهُ أَفْضَلَ مِنْ بَعْضٍ بَلْ الْمَنْقُولُ عَنْهُمْ
translated_text:
and says that these sounds are distinct from those.

Whoever maintains that speech consists of letters, or letters and sounds, conjoined with one another without beginning or end, yet constituting a single entity, holds a position whose falsity is recognized by the great majority of rational people. Likewise, the position of anyone who regards them as a single utterance is recognized as false by the great majority of rational people. In any event, if something is held to be a single entity, it is impossible to ask whether some of it is superior to the rest.

As for someone who affirms multiplicity in meanings and letters, or in either of them, his position makes the question of equality and superiority intelligible. The question then arises: can there be degrees of superiority within Allah’s speech, attributes, and names, or can such differences exist only among created things?

Accordingly, Ibn Battāl’s account in his commentary on al-Bukhārī, when discussing this hadith, reads:

“Al-Muhallab said—and he related this from al-Asīlī; it is also the position of al-Ash'arī, Abū Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, Ibn Abī Zayd, al-Dāwūdī, Abū al-Hasan al-Qābisī, and a group of Sunni scholars—that no part of the Quran is superior to another, since all of it is the speech of Allah Most High and His attribute, and it is uncreated. Degrees of superiority are possible only among created things.”

This presents these scholars’ views according to what he supposed their positions entailed, since he believed that degrees of superiority could exist only among created things, whereas these scholars held the Quran to be uncreated. Yet we have already explained that none of the early generations who declared it uncreated is reported to have said that no part of it is superior to another. Rather, what is reported from them is

original_text:
خِلَافُ ذَلِكَ. وَأَمَّا نَقْلُ هَذَا الْقَوْلِ عَنْ الْأَشْعَرِيِّ وَمُوَافَقِيهِ فَغَلَطٌ عَلَيْهِمْ؛
 إذْ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ عِنْدَهُمْ لَيْسَ لَهُ كُلٌّ وَلَا بَعْضٌ وَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 هَلْ يَفْضُلُ بَعْضُهُ بَعْضًا أَوْ لَا يَفْضُلُ فَامْتِنَاعِ التَّفَاضُلِ فِيهِ عِنْدَهُ كَامْتِنَاعِ التَّمَاثُلِ وَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُقَالَ إنَّهُ مُتَمَاثِلٌ وَلَا مُتَفَاضِلٌ إذْ ذَلِكَ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا بَيْنَ شَيْئَيْنِ.
 وَلَكِنَّ هَذَا السُّؤَالَ يُتَصَوَّرُ عِنْدَهُ فِي الصِّفَاتِ الْمُتَعَدِّدَةِ كَالْعِلْمِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ فَيُقَالُ:
 أَيُّهَا أَفْضَلُ؟
 فَإِنْ كَانَ قَالَ:
 إنَّ صِفَاتِ الرَّبِّ لَا تَتَفَاضَلُ؛
 لِأَنَّ مُقْتَضَى الْأَفْضَلِ نَقْصُ الْمَفْضُولِ عَنْهُ فَإِنَّمَا يَسْتَقِيمُ هَذَا الْجَوَابُ فِي هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ الْمُتَعَدِّدَةِ لَا فِي نَفْسِ الْكَلَامِ مَعَ أَنَّ هَذَا النَّقْلَ عَنْ الْأَشْعَرِيِّ فِي نَفْيِ تَفَاضُلِ الصِّفَاتِ غَيْرُ مُحَرَّرٍ فَإِنَّ الْأَشْعَرِيَّ لَمْ يَقُلْ:

translated_text:
the opposite. As for attributing this position to al-Ash'arī and those who agree with him, this misrepresents them. In their view, Allah’s speech has neither a whole nor parts, and it is therefore inadmissible to ask whether some of it is superior to the rest. For him, degrees of superiority within it are impossible just as likeness is impossible. It cannot be described as having either mutually alike or mutually superior parts, since such relations require two things.

However, on his view, this question is conceivable with respect to multiple attributes, such as knowledge and power: which is superior? If he did say, “The Lord’s attributes do not differ in excellence, because the superiority of one implies that the other falls short of it,” this answer would apply only to these multiple attributes, not to speech itself. Moreover, this attribution to al-Ash'arī of a denial of degrees of superiority among the attributes has not been properly established. Al-Ash'arī did not say that the attributes do not differ in excellence; rather, attributing this to him is an error. What he does say is that speech admits neither degrees of superiority nor likeness because, in his view, it is one—not for the reason mentioned.

As for the multiple attributes, he explicitly stated that they are not mutually alike. His position is that the Essence is not like the attributes, nor is each attribute like the others. Thus, he does not affirm likeness among the meanings he regards as eternal. How, then, can anything entailing their likeness be asserted on the basis of his principles? If he refrains from applying the term “degrees of superiority,” this is like his refraining from applying the terms “likeness” and “mutual distinctness.” In short, anyone who reports that he denied degrees of superiority and affirmed likeness has erred.

translated_text:
but he may refrain from using the term “degrees of superiority,” just as he refrains from using the term “likeness”—not because he considers the attributes alike. Rather, he denies likeness because there is no multiplicity, and because he does not apply the term “mutual distinctness.” Similar questions arise: Should the attributes be described as different or not? Are they mutually distinct or not? Should each attribute be said to be the Essence itself or other than it? Or should these two negations not be combined, but each be stated separately? Or should none of these expressions be used? These matters are not peculiar to this question—the question of superiority.

There is no doubt that likeness or degrees of superiority can be conceived only where there is multiplicity. The multiplicity of Allah’s names, attributes, and words is the position held by the majority of Muslims, and was the position of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars. It accords with the natural disposition Allah has instilled in His servants. Thus, people speak to one another in accordance with this natural disposition and the revealed law, even though some of them hold other views that contradict both and entail the invalidity of what they themselves say in accordance with them. The Quran and Sunnah indicate in numerous places that Allah’s words are multiple. The Exalted has said:

“Say, ‘If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought its like as a supplement.’”

The Exalted has also said:

“If all the trees on earth were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven more seas, were ink, Allah’s words would not be exhausted.”

translated_text:
many speculative theologians share the majority view that these are multiple, and that those who maintain that He wills everything He wills through a single will merely adopted this view from Ibn Kullāb. Most rational people consider its invalidity self-evident. Indeed, some distinguished scholars of rational inquiry deny that any rational person could hold such a view, because they find it so plainly contrary to reason, unaware that a group of speculative thinkers have maintained it.

Likewise, according to someone who identifies His will itself with both His mercy and His anger, the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

“I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath”

would mean seeking refuge in will itself from will itself. This is impossible, for, in his view, will has no positive attribute by virtue of which refuge could be sought in it in one respect and from it in another. Rather, in his view, will merely has a relation to created beings, and that relation has no real existence. This differs from seeking refuge in Him from Him, for He, glorified be He, possesses diverse attributes: refuge is therefore sought in Him in one respect and from Him in another.

As for anyone who says that He is an essence without attributes, or an absolute existent possessing no positive attribute, such a thing cannot exist in external reality. It can only be conceived in the mind, just as impossibilities can be conceived—let alone be a Lord and Creator of creatures—as has been explained at length in its proper place.

These people were driven to such positions by the pressure that the Jahmiyyah and Muʿtazilah brought to bear on them concerning the attributes. They began saying to them:

translated_text:
He Himself, that is wilful denial of the obvious.”

This was the first argument they put to Imam Ahmad during the ordeal. When al-Muʿtasim told them, “Debate with him,” ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Ishāq said to him, “Abū ʿAbd Allāh, what do you say about the Quran”—or he said, “about Allah’s speech”—meaning, “Is it Allah Himself or other than Him?”

Ahmad replied, “What do you say about Allah’s knowledge? Is it Allah Himself or other than Him?” Ahmad thus countered his argument by invoking Allah’s knowledge, and ʿAbd al-Rahmān fell silent. This illustrates Abū ʿAbd Allāh’s skill in debate—may Allah have mercy on him.

When an innovator has built his doctrine upon a corrupt premise, presenting the truth you hold at the outset will prompt him to dispute it because of the specious argument lodged in his mind. Thus, when an opponent in debate claims to possess the truth, one should begin by dismantling his position. Once he has been defeated and seeks the truth, give it to him. Otherwise, as long as he believes the opposite of the truth, the truth will not enter his heart. It is like a tablet inscribed with falsehood: first erase it, then write the truth upon it.

These people intended to argue in support of their innovation, so Imam Ahmad—may Allah have mercy on him—presented counterarguments and refutations that invalidated it. In his refutation of the Jahmiyyah, Imam Ahmad addressed this argument and explained that revelation does not use the term “other,” either affirmatively or negatively. Accordingly, no binding conclusion follows as to whether it falls within the term “other” in the Lawgiver’s speech or not; thus there is no scriptural proof that it is created.

Furthermore, it is an ambiguous term: “other” may mean something separate from a thing, or it may mean something that is not that thing itself.

Some of them have said: “We say that they are other than the essence, but we do not say that they are other than Allah, because the term ‘essence’ does not include the attributes, whereas the name ‘Allah’ encompasses them.” Accordingly, the correct position—according to Ahl al-Sunnah—is not to say that the attributes are additional to what the name “Allah” denotes. Whoever attributes that statement to them has misrepresented their position.

If it is asked, “Are they additional to the essence or not?” the answer is that the essence as it exists in reality necessarily entails the attributes. The essence cannot exist stripped of its attributes; indeed, no entity exists devoid of all attributes. Moreover, the word dhāt (essence) is the feminine form of dhū (possessor of), and dhū necessarily requires a genitive complement.

This usage arose later. Originally, the word occurred in expressions such as “possessing knowledge,” “possessing power,” and “possessing hearing,” just as Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah and set matters right between you.”

One also says, “Such-and-such a woman possesses wealth” or “possesses beauty.” Then, when they understood that the Lord Himself possesses knowledge, power, hearing, and sight—in refutation of those who denied His attributes—they made the word dhāt definite, so that the definite article took the place of the genitive complement. Thus, wherever the expression “the essence” is used, it means an essence possessing such-and-such. The essence, therefore, can only be an essence possessing knowledge and power

The point is that if al-Ashʿarī or any other affirmer of the attributes who followed the approach of Ibn Kullāb says that the attributes are equivalent to one another, this is something no rational person would say. Two things are equivalent when either can fulfil the function of the other and take its place. Knowledge is not equivalent to power, nor is power equivalent to will. Speech, however, is in his view one single thing, and a single thing cannot admit of degrees of excellence or equivalence.

 إنَّهُ وَاحِدٌ بِالْعَيْنِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ إنَّهُ وَاحِدٌ بِالْعَيْنِ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَجْعَلُهُ مَعَ ذَلِكَ حُرُوفًا أَوْ حُرُوفًا وَأَصْوَاتًا قَدِيمَةَ الْأَعْيَانِ وَيَقُولُ: هُوَ مَعَ ذَلِكَ شَيْءٌ وَاحِدٌ كَمَا يُوجَدُ فِي كَلَامِ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ الَّذِينَ أَخَذُوا عَنْ الْكُلَّابِيَة أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ لَهُ إلَّا إرَادَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ وَعِلْمٌ وَاحِدٌ وَقُدْرَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ وَكَلَامٌ وَاحِدٌ وَأَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ قَدِيمٌ. وَأَخَذُوا عَنْ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ أَنَّهُ مُجَرَّدُ الْحُرُوفِ وَالْأَصْوَاتِ وَالْتَزَمُوا أَنَّ الْحُرُوفَ وَالْأَصْوَاتَ قَدِيمَةُ الْأَعْيَانِ مَعَ أَنَّهَا مُتَرَتِّبَةٌ فِي نَفْسِهَا تَرَتُّبًا ذَاتِيًّا فِي الْوُجُودِ أَزَلِيَّةً لَمْ يَزَلْ بَعْضُهَا مُقَارِنًا لِبَعْضِ وَفَرَّقُوا بَيْنَ ذَاتِ الشَّيْءِ وَبَيْنَ وُجُودِهِ فِي الْخَارِجِ مُوَافَقَةً لِمَنْ يَقُولُ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَكَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْقَائِلِينَ بِقِدَمِهِ وَأَنَّهُ حُرُوفٌ وَأَصْوَاتٌ لَا يَقُولُونَ إنَّهُ شَيْءٌ وَاحِدٌ بَلْ يَجْعَلُونَهُ مُتَعَدِّدًا مَعَ قِدَمِ الْقُرْآنِ وَقِدَمِ أَعْيَانِ الْحُرُوفِ وَالْأَصْوَاتِ.

 أَنَّ الْقَدِيمَ هُوَ مَعْنًى وَاحِدٌ لَا يَتَعَدَّدُ وَلَا يَتَبَعَّضُ كَمَا قَدْ بَيَّنَ حَقِيقَةَ قَوْلِهِمْ. وَهَذَا هُوَ الْقَوْلُ الْمَنْسُوبُ إلَى ابْنِ كُلَّابٍ وَالْأَشْعَرِيِّ. وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ أَوَّلُ مَنْ عُرِفَ أَنَّهُ قَالَهُ فِي الْإِسْلَامِ ابْنُ كُلَّابٍ لَمْ يَسْبِقْهُ إلَيْهِ أَحَدٌ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَلَا التَّابِعِينَ وَلَا غَيْرِهِمْ مِنْ أَئِمَّةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ مَعَ كَثْرَةِ مَا تَكَلَّمَ الصَّحَابَةُ وَالتَّابِعُونَ فِي كَلَامِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَمَعَ أَنَّهُ مِنْ أَعْظَمَ وَأَهَمِّ أُمُورِ الدِّينِ الَّذِي تَتَوَفَّرُ
translated_text:
The second is that it is one, and a single thing cannot admit of degrees of excellence or equivalence. This follows the position of those who say that it is one single entity.

Among those who hold that it is one single entity, some nevertheless regard it as letters, or as letters and sounds, whose individual entities are eternal, while maintaining that it is a single thing. This appears in the statements of some later scholars who adopted from the Kullābiyyah the view that Allah has only one will, one knowledge, one power, and one speech, and that the Quran is eternal. From the Mu'tazilah and others, they adopted the view that it consists solely of letters and sounds. They committed themselves to holding that the individual letters and sounds are eternal, although they have an intrinsic order in existence, and that they have existed from eternity, always coexisting with one another. They distinguished between a thing’s essence and its external existence, agreeing with those among the Mu'tazilah who make this distinction. Many who hold that it is eternal and consists of letters and sounds do not say that it is a single thing. Rather, they regard it as multiple, while maintaining the eternity of the Quran and of the individual letters and sounds.

The other position held by those who say that it is one single entity is that what is eternal is a single meaning admitting neither multiplicity nor division, as has already been explained in setting out the true nature of their position. This is the position attributed to Ibn Kullāb and al-Ash'arī. The first person known to have expressed this position in Islam was Ibn Kullāb. No Companion, Successor, or other leading scholar of the Muslims preceded him in it, despite the extensive discussions of Allah’s speech by the Companions and Successors, and despite its being among the greatest and most important matters of religion, to which are devoted

The Book, the Sunnah, and the reports from the early generations contradict every one of these views. Moreover, the majority of rational people who understand these views agree that their falsity is self-evident to reason. A group of rational people may agree upon a statement whose falsity is self-evident to reason if this results from prior agreement, just as they may conspire to agree upon a lie. Without such agreement, however, this is not possible. Thus, a doctrine that people have adopted from one another—such as the doctrines of the Christians, the Rāfidah, the Jahmiyyah, the Dahriyyah, and others—may contain something whose falsity is self-evident to reason, even though a group of rational people have affirmed it in this manner. But for them to affirm it independently, without prior agreement, does not occur. Most people who unquestioningly adopt false views do not conceive of them fully; a full conception of them would necessarily reveal their falsity. Then, when a view becomes widespread among a group who know of no other view attributed to Ahl al-Sunnah, they assume that it is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah.

Since it is widely known among Muslims that Ahl al-Sunnah do not say that the Quran is created, anyone who sees a group rejecting the claim that the Quran is created comes to suppose that everything that group says on this subject is the position of the early generations and the leading scholars of the Sunnah—and those who said that the Quran is uncreated, but rather subsists in Allah’s essence, and agreed with

the early generations and the leading scholars on this point. When the Jahmiyyah’s inquisition arose—and Imam Ahmad, through whom Allah strengthened and supported the Sunnah, stood firm throughout it—the hallmark of Ahl al-Sunnah became the affirmation that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, and that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter. In common parlance, anyone who denied this was counted among the people of innovation. Consequently, many came to agree with the adherents of the Sunnah and hadith on these matters without understanding their actual position. Rather, they retained certain principles of the Jahmī innovators and sought to reconcile them with the position of Ahl al-Sunnah, just as an adherent of philosophy seeks to reconcile the statements of philosophers who oppose the messengers with what the messengers brought.

Thus, those who affiliate themselves with the Sunnah and affirm that the Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated, came to hold several views:

One is the view of those who say that the Quran is beginningless in its individual existence, that Allah does not speak by His will and power, and that He does not speak one utterance after another. These people, in turn, hold two views. Some say that this beginningless speech is a single meaning eternally inseparable from Allah’s essence, or five meanings.

Others say that it consists instead of letters and sounds, each individually beginningless and eternally inseparable from Allah’s essence.

The third (1) is the view of those who say that, in the Lord’s beginningless eternity, speech was not possible for Him, just as, according to them, action was not possible for Him. This is because speech and action occur only through His will and choice, while they hold that anything occurring through will and choice cannot have existed perpetually.

The view commonly reported from these people is that of those who say:

 لَمْ يَزَلْ مُتَكَلِّمًا لَا يَسْكُتُ بَلْ لَا يَزَالُ مُتَكَلِّمًا بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ. وَهَذَا هُوَ الَّذِي جَعَلَهُ ابْنُ حَامِدٍ الْمَشْهُورَ مِنْ مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَأَصْحَابِهِ مَعَ أَنَّهُ حُكِيَ أَنَّهُ لَا يَخْتَلِفُ قَوْلُ أَحْمَد أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَزَلْ مُتَكَلِّمًا كَيْفَ شَاءَ وَكَمَا شَاءَ. وَالْقَوْلُ الثَّانِي أَنَّهُ يَتَكَلَّمُ إذَا شَاءَ وَيَسْكُتُ إذَا شَاءَ. وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ حَكَاهُ أَبُو بَكْرٍ عَبْدُ الْعَزِيزِ عَنْ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد وَكَذَلِكَ خَرَّجَهُ ابْنُ حَامِدٍ قَوْلًا فِي الْمَذْهَبِ مَعَ ذِكْرِهِ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَخْتَلِفْ مَذْهَبُهُ فِي أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَزَلْ مُتَكَلِّمًا كَيْفَ شَاءَ وَكَمَا شَاءَ وَأَنَّهُ لَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ لَمْ يَزَلْ سَاكِتًا ثُمَّ صَارَ مُتَكَلِّمًا كَمَا يَقُولُهُ الكَرَّامِيَة.
 وَهَذِهِ الْأَقْوَالُ وَتَوَابِعُهَا مَبْسُوطَةٌ فِي مَوْضِعٍ آخَرَ وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا أَنَّ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا:
 
" كَلَامُ اللَّهِ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ "
 تَنَازَعُوا
translated_text:
He came to speak, in the eternity to come, with letters and sounds subsisting in His essence, as several groups maintain, including the Karrāmiyyah. Some people make statements implying that the speech which subsisted in Him successively was nothing but instances of knowledge and volition. Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī inclines toward this in some of his books.

The fifth (1) is the view of those who say: He has always spoken however He wills. This is the position known from the early generations and the leading scholars of the Sunnah, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and the other adherents of hadith and the Sunnah.

Among these scholars, some say: He has always spoken and is never silent; rather, He continually speaks by His will and power. Ibn Hāmid identified this as the well-known position of Ahmad and his followers, although it has been reported that Ahmad’s statements consistently affirm that He has always spoken however He wills and as He wills.

The second view is that He speaks when He wills and is silent when He wills. Abū Bakr ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz reported this view from a group of Ahmad’s followers. Ibn Hāmid likewise inferred it as a position within the school, while stating that Ahmad’s position had never varied concerning His having always spoken however He wills and as He wills, and that He could not have always been silent and then begun to speak, as the Karrāmiyyah maintain.

These views and their implications are discussed at length elsewhere. The point here is that those who said, “Allah’s speech is uncreated,” disagreed

Indeed, even their leading scholars who have written on this subject know, at most, two, three, or four of these views—such as those of the Mu'tazilah, the Kullābiyyah, the Sālimiyyah, and the Karrāmiyyah. They do not know that anyone within Islam has held any other view. One of them may compile a large book on “the doctrines of Muslims” and “religions and sects,” mentioning most of the innovated views on this subject, yet neither knowing nor transmitting the view handed down from the early generations and the leading scholars. Yet the Quran and the Sunnah, together with sound reason, support that view alone. All the others are contradictory positions, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

The point here is that someone may regard, for example, the view of the Mu'tazilah—or the views of the Mu'tazilah and the Karrāmiyyah, or those views together with that of the Kullābiyyah, or those views together with that of the Sālimiyyah—as false doctrines held by the people of innovation. He then believes that the only remaining position that could represent Ahl al-Sunnah is the other view, even though it too is an innovated position contrary to sound reason and authentic transmitted evidence. He derives further conclusions from that view and attributes them to the Sunnah. Then, when he reflects on the texts of the Quran and the Sunnah and the reports from the early generations, he finds that they contradict that view in both its foundations and its implications.

This is what happened to those who denied the superiority of “the Opening of the Book,” “the Verse of the Throne,” and “Say: He is Allah, One” over other portions of the Quran. translated_text:
differences in excellence, equivalence, or multiplicity. As for the assertion that the Lord’s attributes do not differ in excellence—sometimes expressed as “What is beginningless does not admit differences in excellence,” which resembles the assertion of the Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah, and others that “What is beginningless does not admit multiplicity”—this is an ambiguous expression. If “what is beginningless” means the Lord of the worlds, then the Lord of the worlds is indeed one God, without partner. But if it means His attributes, then whoever says that the Lord’s attributes do not admit multiplicity is saying that knowledge is power, power is will, and hearing and sight are knowledge. Some of them may also say that knowledge is speech, while others say that knowledge and power are will. They may then say that the attribute is identical with the one possessing it: knowledge is the one who knows, and power is the one who possesses power.

These assertions have been explicitly made by those philosophers, Jahmiyyah, and others who deny the divine attributes, as I have quoted their actual words elsewhere. These assertions plainly contradict sound reason and authentic transmitted evidence—indeed, they contradict what rational people know self-evidently and what is necessarily known in the religion of Islam and the religion of the messengers—to such an extent that their utter invalidity, both in revelation and in reason, is clear.

These people then interpreted the texts of the Quran and the Sunnah in invalid ways. Some said that describing it as greater, more excellent, and better merely means that it is great in itself. They refused to understand these descriptions as expressing superiority. This position has been attributed to al-Ash'arī, Ibn al-Bāqillānī, and a number of others. Anyone who reflects on the wording of the Quran and the Sunnah will plainly see that it cannot bear this meaning; rather, this is a form of Qarmatian interpretation. For Allah

{أَفْضَلُ الْكَلَامِ بَعْدَ الْقُرْآنِ أَرْبَعٌ - وَهُنَّ مِنْ الْقُرْآنِ - سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَلَا إلَّا إلَّا اللَّهُ وَاَللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ}
translated_text:
Most High says:

“He has sent down the best of speech.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Ubayy, “Do you know which verse that you know from Allah’s Book is the greatest?” He also said, “I shall certainly teach you a surah the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Quran.” There are other examples already mentioned.

Some of them said: Rather, what is meant by His words “better than it” is “better for you”—that is, bringing greater reward or involving less hardship. They said that whatever indicates that some of it is more excellent than the rest does not establish the superiority of the speech itself, but of what relates to it: reciting this passage and acting upon it brings greater reward than reciting and acting upon another.

The response to these people is: What you have mentioned is evidence against you, besides contradicting the text. For the reward for one of two utterances or deeds is greater than that for the other only because it is intrinsically more excellent. This is why the texts speak of the excellence of the utterance or deed itself. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked on more than one occasion, “Which deed is most excellent?” He would answer by declaring one deed superior to another, which necessarily entails its greater reward. As for a greater reward when the two deeds are equal, this is contrary to both revelation and reason.

The same applies to speech. In Sahīh Muslim, Samurah reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The most excellent utterances after the Quran are four—and they are part of the Quran: Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; none has the right to be worshipped but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.”

original_text:
فَأَخْبَرَ أَنَّهَا أَفْضَلُ الْكَلَامِ بَعْدَ الْقُرْآنِ مَعَ كَوْنِهَا مِنْ الْقُرْآنِ فَفَضَّلَ نَفْسَ هَذِهِ الْأَقْوَالِ بَعْدَ الْقُرْآنِ عَلَى سِوَاهَا وَكَذَلِكَ فِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ 
{أَنَّهُ سُئِلَ: أَيُّ الْكَلَامِ أَفْضَلُ؟
 فَقَالَ مَا اصْطَفَى اللَّهُ لِمَلَائِكَتِهِ:
 سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ وَبِحَمْدِهِ}
 . وَفِي الْمُوَطَّأِ وَغَيْرِهِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ 
{أَفْضَلُ مَا قُلْت أَنَا وَالنَّبِيُّونَ مِنْ قَبْلِي: لَا إلَّا إلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ لَهُ الْمُلْكُ وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ}
 فَأَخْبَرَ أَنَّ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ أَفْضَلُ مَا قَالَهُ هُوَ وَالنَّبِيُّونَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِ.

{أَفْضَلُ الذَّكَرِ: لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ.

 وَقَدْ رَوَاهُ ابْنُ أَبِي الدُّنْيَا. وَفِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ 
{الْإِيمَانُ بِضْعٌ وَسِتُّونَ - أَوْ وَسَبْعُونَ - شُعْبَةً أَعْلَاهَا قَوْلُ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ}
 . وَمِثْلُ هَذَا كَثِيرٌ فِي النُّصُوصِ يُفَضِّلُ الْعَمَلَ عَلَى الْعَمَلِ وَالْقَوْلَ عَلَى الْقَوْلِ. وَيُعْلَمُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ فَضْلُ ثَوَابِ أَحَدِهِمَا عَلَى الْآخَرِ. أَمَّا تَفْضِيلُ الثَّوَابِ بِدُونِ تَفْضِيلِ نَفْسِ الْقَوْلِ وَالْعَمَلِ فَلَمْ يَرِدْ بِهِ نَقْلٌ وَلَا يَقْتَضِيهِ عَقْلٌ فَإِنَّهُ إذَا كَانَ الْقَوْلَانِ مُتَمَاثِلَيْنِ مِنْ كُلِّ وَجْهٍ أَوْ الْعَمَلَانِ مُتَمَاثِلَيْنِ مِنْ كُلِّ وَجْهٍ كَانَ جَعَلَ ثَوَابَ أَحَدِهِمَا أَعْظَمَ مِنْ ثَوَابِ الْآخَرِ تَرْجِيحًا لِأَحَدِ الْمُتَمَاثِلَيْنِ عَلَى الْآخَرِ بِلَا مُرَجَّحٍ.
 وَهَذَا أَصْلُ قَوْلِ الْقَدَرِيَّةِ وَالْجَهْمِيَّة الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّ الْقَادِرَ يُرَجِّحُ أَحَدَ مَقْدُورَيْهِ بِلَا مُرَجِّحٍ وَظَنُّوا أَنَّهُمْ بِهَذَا الْأَصْلِ يَنْصُرُونَ الْإِسْلَامَ فَلَا لِلْإِسْلَامِ
translated_text:
Thus he stated that these are the most excellent utterances after the Quran, even though they are themselves part of the Quran. He therefore declared these utterances themselves superior to all others apart from the Quran. Likewise, Sahīh Muslim relates that he was asked:

“Which utterance is most excellent?”

He replied, “What Allah has chosen for His angels: Glory and praise be to Allah.”

Al-Muwatta’ and other works report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The most excellent thing that I and the prophets before me have said is: None has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone, with no partner. His is the dominion, and His is all praise, and He has power over all things.”

He thus stated that these words are the most excellent thing that he and the prophets before him have said.

Sunan Ibn Mājah reports that he said:

“The most excellent remembrance is: None has the right to be worshipped but Allah. And the most excellent supplication is: Praise be to Allah.”

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā also narrated this. In Sahīh al-Bukhārī and Sahīh Muslim, he is reported to have said:

“Faith has sixty-odd—or seventy-odd—branches, the highest of which is saying: None has the right to be worshipped but Allah.”

There are many such examples in the revealed texts, declaring one deed superior to another and one utterance superior to another. From this, we know that the reward for one is greater than that for the other. But a greater reward without any superiority in the utterance or deed itself is neither established by any transmitted text nor warranted by reason. For if two utterances, or two deeds, are identical in every respect, assigning a greater reward to one than to the other would mean favoring one of two identical things over the other without any grounds for preference.

This is the fundamental premise of the Qadariyyah and the Jahmiyyah, who say that one who has power gives preference to one of two things within his power without any determining factor. They imagined that through this premise they were supporting Islam. Yet neither for Islam

 وَأَيْضًا فَفِي الْحَدِيثِ الصَّحِيحِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ فِي الْفَاتِحَةِ:
 
{لَمْ يَنْزِلْ فِي التَّوْرَاةِ وَلَا فِي الْإِنْجِيلِ وَلَا فِي الْقُرْآنِ مِثْلُهَا}
 فَقَدْ صَرَّحَ الرَّسُولُ
translated_text:
did they secure victory, nor did they crush its enemy. Rather, the early generations and leading scholars of the Muslim community assailed them with charges of religious innovation, misguidance, disbelief, and ignorance. Their opponents—the eternalists and others—also assailed them by demonstrating that their position contradicted reason, and used this as a pretext for departing still further from revelation and reason, as happened between the heretics and the religious innovators.

Furthermore, to say:

“One part is no better than another; rather, one brings a greater reward,”

is to reject Allah’s explicit statement, for Allah says:

“We bring one better than it or similar to it.”

How, then, can it be said that no part is better than another? If all are identical in themselves, none can be better than another. To interpret “better” as meaning “greater in reward,” while maintaining that they are identical in themselves, is supported by the wording neither literally nor figuratively. It is therefore impermissible to interpret it in this way. It is entirely unknown for someone to say, “This is better than that,” or “This is superior to that,” when the two things and their attributes are equal in every respect. Rather, using such an expression necessarily implies a difference in excellence, even if only in some attributes.

Suppose, however, that an agent exercising choice assigned to one of two identical things something not assigned to the other, despite their being equal in their attributes in every respect. Such a situation is inconceivable. Even if it were conceivable, one would not say that one is better or superior to the other on account of something that is not an attribute of either at all.

Furthermore, an authentic hadith reports that he said concerning al-Fātiha:

“Nothing like it has been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, or the Quran.”

Thus the Messenger explicitly stated

 إنَّ الْقَادِرَ الْمُرَجِّحَ يُرَجِّحُ بِلَا مُرَجِّحٍ.
 ثُمَّ قَالَتْ الْجَهْمِيَّة:
 وَالْعَبْدُ لَيْسَ بِقَادِرِ فِي الْحَقِيقَةِ فَلَا يُرَجِّحُ شَيْئًا بَلْ اللَّهُ هُوَ الْفَاعِلُ لِفِعْلِهِ وَفِعْلُهُ هُوَ نَفْسُ فِعْلِ الرَّبِّ. وَقَالَتْ
translated_text:
that Allah has revealed nothing like it. Whoever says, “Everything revealed of Allah’s speech is like it in every respect,” has therefore contradicted what the Messenger reported.

Furthermore, His words have already been cited:

“The best of speech.”

Yet if all of Allah’s speech were identical, the Quran would not be better than the Torah and the Gospel. The rulings with which Allah has singled out the Quran have likewise already been discussed.

If it is said:

“We concede that Allah has assigned certain parts of His speech rewards and rulings that others do not share. In our view, however, this is solely by His will, not because that speech possesses an attribute distinguishing it from the rest.”

The reply is:

First, this contradicts the explicit texts of the Quran and Sunnah and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community, as well as contradicting sound reason. Moreover, it rests upon a principle held by the Jahmiyyah and Qadariyyah: that an agent possessing power and exercising choice can give preference to one of two identical things over the other without any determining factor.

Having admitted this possibility, they said:

“The Lord had always been inactive, and in the eternal past it was not possible for Him either to speak or to act. Then speech and action became possible without anything arising that would account for their transition from impossibility to possibility.”

They also said:

“An agent with the power to give preference can do so without any determining factor.”

The Jahmiyyah then said:

“The servant has no real power and therefore gives preference to nothing. Rather, Allah performs the servant’s act, and the servant’s act is itself the Lord’s act.”

 الْعَبْدُ قَادِرٌ تَامُّ الْقُدْرَةِ يُرَجِّحُ أَحَدَ مَقْدُورَيْهِ عَلَى الْآخَرِ بِلَا سَبَبٍ حَادِثٍ وَلَا حَاجَةٍ إلَى أَنْ يُحَدِّثَ اللَّهَ مَا بِهِ يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ فِعْلُ أَحَدِهِمَا؛ بَلْ هُوَ - مَعَ أَنَّ نِسْبَتَهُ إلَى الضِّدَّيْنِ الْإِيمَانُ وَالْكُفْرُ سَوَاءٌ - يُرَجَّحُ أَحَدُهُمَا بِلَا مُرَجِّحٍ لَا مِنْ اللَّهِ وَلَا مِنْ الْعَبْدِ وَلَا يَفْتَقِرُ إلَى إعَانَةِ اللَّهِ وَلَا إلَى أَنْ يَجْعَلَهُ شَائِيًا وَلَا يَجْعَلَهُ يُقِيمُ الصَّلَاةَ وَلَا يَجْعَلَهُ مُسْلِمًا. وَمَعْلُومٌ بِالْعُقُولِ خِلَافُ هَذَا وَاَللَّهُ تَعَالَى يَفْعَلُ مَا يَشَاءُ وَيَحْكُمُ مَا يُرِيدُ وَمَا شَاءَ كَانَ وَمَا لَمْ يُشَاء لَمْ يَكُنْ لَكِنَّ الْمَدْحَ فِي هَذَا الْكَلَامِ مَعْنَاهُ أَنَّهُ مُطْلَقُ الْمَشِيئَةِ لَا مُعَوِّقٌ لَا إذَا أَرَادَ شَيْئًا كَمَا قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{لَا يَقُولَنَّ أَحَدُكُمْ: اللَّهُمَّ اغْفِرْ لِي إنْ شِئْت اللَّهُمَّ ارْحَمْنِي إنْ شِئْت وَلَكِنْ لِيَعْزِمَ الْمَسْأَلَةَ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا مُكْرِهَ لَهُ}

translated_text:
the Qadariyyah:

“The servant possesses complete power and gives preference to one of two possible acts over the other without any newly arising cause, and without any need for Allah to bring about something that determines the performance of one rather than the other. Although he stands in the same relation to the two opposites—faith and disbelief—one is preferred over the other without any determining factor, whether from Allah or from the servant. He needs neither Allah’s help nor for Him to make him willing, make him establish prayer, or make him a Muslim.”

Sound reason establishes the contrary. Allah Most High does whatever He wills and decrees whatever He wishes. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. The praise expressed in these words, however, means that His will is unrestricted: nothing can obstruct Him when He wills something. As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“None of you should say, ‘O Allah, forgive me if You will; O Allah, have mercy on me if You will.’ Rather, let him be firm in his request, for no one can compel Allah.”

He thus explained that Allah acts only by His will. No one can compel Him such that He should be told, “Do it if You will,” nor does He act if He does not will. When He, glorified be He, wills something, He has the power to do it, and nothing can prevent Him.

This does not mean that He acts merely by a will unaccompanied by wisdom. Yet, according to them, He performs acts whose performance and nonperformance are, in relation to Him, alike in every respect. This is no praise; rather, reason recognizes it as a blameworthy attribute. Whoever acts merely because he wishes to act, with no wisdom behind his action and no abstract end that it serves, would be better off not acting. Allah, glorified be He, has condemned in His Book those who attribute this to Him. He Most High said:

“We did not create the heaven and the earth and all that lies between them without purpose. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve. So woe to those who disbelieve because of the Fire!”

He Most High also said:

“Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?”

“Exalted is Allah, the True King! There is no god but Him, Lord of the Noble Throne.”

The Quran commentators explained that futility means performing an act with no wisdom behind it; it is a kind of play.

He also said:

“We did not create the heaven and the earth and all that lies between them in play.”

“Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from what is with Us—if We were to do so.”

And He said:

“Does man think that he will be left unattended?”

The Quran commentators and linguists explained that one left unattended is one who is neglected, neither commanded nor forbidden—as when someone leaves camels unattended and neglected.

He Most High also said:

“It is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth. On the Day He says, ‘Be,’ it will be.”

He Most High said:

“We did not create the heavens and the earth and all that lies between them except in truth. The Hour is surely coming, so pardon graciously.”

“Indeed, your Lord is the All-Knowing Creator.”

He, glorified be He, has made clear the distinction between what He commands and what He forbids, and between His allies whom He praises and honors and His enemies whom He censures and punishes. They are different, and it is not permissible to treat the two alike. He has declared the contrary to be reprehensible and wholly unjustifiable. He Most High said:

“Shall We then treat those who submit to Us like the criminals?”

“What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”

He also said:

“Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption on earth? Or shall We treat the righteous like the wicked?”

He Most High also said:

“Do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds—equal in their life and their death? How evil is their judgment!”

He thus made clear that this judgment is evil in itself; judging them to be equal is not equivalent to recognizing their differing merits.

Then He said:

“Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned, and they will not be wronged.”

He declared that He created creation to recompense every soul for what it has earned, and that He wrongs no one by diminishing any of their good deeds. Rather, as He said:

“They will find all that they did present before them, and your Lord wrongs no one.”

In several places in the Quran, He has declared Himself free of wronging any of His creatures by withholding their reward or burdening them with another’s sin. He Most High said:

“Whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer need fear neither injustice nor deprivation.”

He Most High also said:

“Do not dispute before Me, for I had already given you warning.”

“My word cannot be changed, and I am never unjust to My servants.”

He Most High also said:

“These are some of the accounts of the towns which We relate to you; some are still standing, while others have been mown down.”

“We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. The gods they invoked besides Allah availed them nothing when your Lord’s command came; they only increased them in ruin.”

In the authentic divine hadith, He says:

“O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself and have made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another.”

The Qadariyyah’s claim that His favoring some of His servants over others through His grace and kindness constitutes injustice stems from their ignorance. Likewise, His recompensing them for their deeds, which came to pass

 وَهَذِهِ الْأُمُورُ مَبْسُوطَةٌ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ.
 وَالْمَقْصُودُ:
 هُنَا أَنَّ مَا يَقُولُهُ الْقَدَرِيَّةُ مِنْ الظُّلْمِ وَالْعَدْلِ الَّذِي يَقِيسُونَ بِهِ الرَّبَّ عَلَى عِبَادِهِ مِنْ بِدَعِهِمْ الَّتِي ضَلُّوا بِهَا وَخَالَفُوا بِهَا الْكِتَابَ وَالسُّنَّةَ

For if one person punishes another for his misdeeds and secures redress for the wronged against the wrongdoer, all rational people agree that this is not injustice on his part. Rather, it is praiseworthy, and no one says that the wrongdoer is excused on account of divine decree. So when the Lord of all worlds secures justice for some of His servants against others and recovers the rights of the wronged from their wrongdoers, how could this be injustice on His part on account of divine decree?

Likewise, when a servant puts everything in its proper place, placing the pure with the pure in a place suited to it, and the impure with the impure in a place suited to it, this is justice and wisdom on his part. The same applies when the Lord of all worlds puts everything in its proper place and does not treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption on earth, nor the God-fearing like the wicked, nor Muslims like criminals.

Paradise is pure, and only one who is pure is fit to enter it. Hence, no one enters it until after the settling of claims that cleanses them of impurity, as authentically reported from Abū Sa‘īd, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When the believers have crossed the bridge—that is, the Sirāt stretched across Hell—they will be stopped on a bridge between Paradise and Hell. Redress will then be exacted from some on behalf of others for wrongs committed among them in this world. Once they have been purified and cleansed, they will be permitted to enter Paradise.”

These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that the Qadariyyah’s assertions concerning injustice and justice, by which they draw an analogy between the Lord and His servants, are among the innovations through which they have gone astray and contravened the Book and the Sunnah

and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community. The same applies to those who opposed them by denying the Lord’s wisdom established in His creation and His commands, the mercy He has prescribed for Himself, the injustice He has forbidden Himself, and the causes He has established for created things and prescribed ordinances. These causes are attested by revelation, reason, and sensory experience, and affirmed by the early generations of the Muslim community and the leading scholars of the religion. Thus, Allah Most High says:

“and the water Allah sends down from the sky, giving life thereby to the earth after its death.”

And He says:

“Then We send down water thereby, and with it bring forth every kind of fruit.”

There are other similar passages. These views originated with al-Jahm ibn Safwān, the leader of the extreme determinists. He denied the Lord’s mercy and would go out to people afflicted with leprosy and say, “Does the Most Merciful of the merciful do such a thing?” He meant that there is nothing but a will by which He gives preference to one of two equal possibilities without any reason for preferring it—neither wisdom nor mercy.

This is why those who agreed with his position while professing adherence to the way of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah fall into contradiction. When they discuss the revealed law, they need to follow the approach of the leading scholars of the religion in affirming the merits of the Sharī‘ah: its commands to pursue what serves people’s welfare and benefits them, its prohibitions against what corrupts their affairs and harms them, and the fact that the Messenger sent with it was sent as a mercy. As Allah Most High says:

“We have sent you only as a mercy to all the worlds.”

Allah Most High has described him in His words:

“My mercy encompasses all things. I shall ordain it for those who fear Me and give zakah, and those who believe in Our signs.”

“Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find described in the Torah and the Gospel they possess, who commands them to do what is right and forbids them

from what is wrong, makes lawful for them what is wholesome, and forbids them what is foul.” Thus, He states that the Messenger commands what is right, forbids what is wrong, makes lawful what is wholesome, and prohibits what is foul.

If “right” meant nothing more than what is commanded, and “wrong” meant nothing more than what is prohibited, this would be like saying: “He commands them to do what he commands them, forbids them what he forbids them, makes lawful for them what he makes lawful, and prohibits for them what he prohibits.” Such words convey nothing of benefit, let alone establish his superiority over others. Clearly, anyone who issues a command can be described in this way, and the same is true of every prophet who was sent.

Allah Most High says:

“Because of the wrongdoing of the Jews, We forbade them wholesome things which had been lawful to them.”

This establishes that wholesomeness is a quality of the thing itself, and that Allah may nevertheless prohibit it as a punishment for His servants. Thus, after mentioning what He prohibited for the Children of Israel, Allah Most High says:

“That is how We recompensed them for their transgression, and We are indeed truthful.”

Allah Most High also says:

“They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say, ‘Wholesome things have been made lawful for you.’”

If “wholesome” meant merely what is lawful, these words would convey nothing of benefit. It is therefore clear that wholesomeness and foulness are qualities inherent in things themselves. What is meant is not merely the pleasure derived from eating, for a person may enjoy harmful poisons and things a physician tells him to avoid. Nor does it mean that a particular people, such as the Arabs, find something pleasurable, or that the Arabs are accustomed to it. does not mean that Allah must forbid all believers whatever these people are unaccustomed to, or permit all believers whatever they are accustomed to. How could it, when the Arabs were accustomed to eating blood, carrion, and other things that Allah Most High has forbidden?

An Arab was once asked, “What do you eat?”

He replied, “Everything that crawls or walks, except Umm Hubayn (a small lizard-like creature).”

The questioner said, “Then may Umm Hubayn enjoy being spared!”

Quraysh themselves used to eat foul things that Allah has forbidden, while finding repugnant foods that Allah has not forbidden. The two Sahīh collections relate:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was served spiny-tailed lizard meat, but he withdrew his hand and did not eat. He was asked, ‘Is it forbidden, Messenger of Allah?’ He replied, ‘No, but it is not found in the land of my people, so I find myself averse to it.’”

It is therefore clear that the aversion of Quraysh or others to a particular food does not warrant prohibiting it for believers among all other Arabs and non-Arabs. Moreover, neither the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor any of his Companions prohibited whatever the Arabs disliked or permitted everything the Arabs ate.

Allah Most High says:

“He makes lawful for them what is wholesome and forbids them what is foul.”

This foretells that he would do so. Accordingly, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, permitted wholesome things and prohibited foul things, such as every fanged beast of prey and every bird with talons. These creatures are aggressive and predatory. When people eat them—and food resembles the one who consumes it—their character becomes tinged with the traits of these beasts, namely oppression and aggression. Likewise, he prohibited blood poured forth, because it is where the appetitive and irascible faculties of the soul are concentrated, and an increase in it causes these faculties to run rampant

and blood is Satan’s pathway through the body, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Satan flows through the son of Adam as blood flows.”

For this reason, when Ramadan begins, the devils are chained, for fasting is a shield. The wholesome things he permitted are foods that benefit the mind and character, while foul things are those that harm the mind and character. Likewise, wine is the mother of all evils because it corrupts the mind and character.

Allah has therefore permitted the God-fearing wholesome things that help them worship their Lord—the purpose for which they were created—and forbidden them foul things that hinder them from fulfilling that purpose. Along with consuming these wholesome things, He commanded them to give thanks and forbade them to declare such things unlawful. Whoever consumes them without giving thanks neglects what Allah has commanded and deserves punishment. Whoever declares them unlawful—as monks do—has transgressed Allah’s limits and deserves punishment. Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, eat of the wholesome things We have provided for you, and give thanks to Allah, if it is Him that you worship.”

In an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah is indeed pleased with a servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or takes a drink and praises Him for it.”

Another hadith states:

“The grateful person who eats is like the patient person who fasts.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Then, on that Day, you will surely be questioned about your blessings.”

That is, about giving thanks for them. For He does not permit something and then punish someone for doing it. Rather, He questions the person about the duty He prescribed alongside it and about what He prohibited: whether that person fell short by neglecting a command or committing a forbidden act. As Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, do not forbid the wholesome things

that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”

He thus forbade them to declare wholesome things unlawful. A group of the Companions had resolved to adopt monasticism, so Allah revealed this verse. The two Sahīh collections relate that some Companions made the following statements. One said, “As for me, I will fast without taking a day off.” Another said, “As for me, I will pray all night and never sleep.” Another said, “As for me, I will not approach women.” Another said, “As for me, I will not eat meat.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“What is the matter with men who say such-and-such? Yet I fast and refrain from fasting, pray at night and sleep, marry women, and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me.”

A fuller discussion of these matters belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that Allah has explained, in His Book and through His Messenger, His wisdom in His creation and His commands. For example, He says:

“Do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse. It is indeed an immorality and an evil way.”

He thus explains its prohibition by the fact that it is an immorality independently of the prohibition, and that this is the reason for forbidding it. He also says:

“When they commit an immoral act, they say, ‘We found our fathers doing it, and Allah has commanded us to do it.’ Say, ‘Allah does not command immorality.’”

He thus declares Himself free of this, presenting it as grounds for praising Him and affirming that He is exalted above it. This shows that there are things that cannot be ascribed to Allah as His commands. Things are not all equal in themselves or in His sight. He does not distinguish what is commanded from what is forbidden merely by arbitrary choice. Rather, He assigns commands to what He commands and prohibitions to what He forbids in accordance with the requirements of His wisdom.

I have reflected on most of the statements of the early generations that I have encountered—having researched them extensively and read a great many—to see whether the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness, or any one of them, held the views I have mentioned, which I found in the books of the speculative theologians: the Jahmiyyah, the Qadariyyah, and those who adopted these views from them.

These include the Jahmiyyah’s claim that, of two identical things, Allah commands one and forbids the other without any reason or wisdom; or that, of statements and deeds identical in every respect, Allah makes some more richly rewarded than others without any reason or wisdom. Similar claims include their assertion that all of Allah’s speech is alike, even though the reward for some of it is greater.

I have found nothing in the statements of the early generations that agrees with this. Rather, they explicitly discuss the wisdom and reasons involved, explaining the good qualities in what is commanded that make it fitting to command it, and the bad qualities in what is forbidden that make it fitting to forbid it. They also explain that some statements and deeds are intrinsically superior to others. I have never seen any report from any of them contradicting the scriptural texts that indicate this, finding it problematic, or interpreting it according to his own understanding. Yet they are reported to have found difficulties and ambiguities in many verses and hadiths and to have interpreted them in different ways, some of which may be mistaken, while another interpretation is correct.

Nor have I found them, regarding such statements as Allah’s words:

“Allah has sent down the best statement: a consistent Book wherein is reiteration,”

and the Prophet’s question to Ubayy, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Which verse in the Book of Allah is the greatest?”

and his statement concerning al-Fātihah:

“Nothing like it has been sent down in the Torah, the Gospel, or the Quran,”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asked Ubayy, “Which verse in the Book of Allah is the greatest?” Ubayy answered that it was the Verse of the Throne. He then struck Ubayy on the chest with his hand and said, “May your knowledge bring you joy, Abū al-Mundhir!”

Neither Ubayy nor anyone else found anything problematic in the question of some parts of the Quran being greater than others. Rather, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, attested to the knowledge of someone who recognized the superiority of some parts over others and knew which verse was the most excellent. The same applies to Allah’s words:

“Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten.”

I have not seen them disagree over the interpretation of “with one better than it.”

This verse has two well-known readings. The majority read aw nunsihā (“or cause it to be forgotten”), from ansāhu–yunsīhi, meaning to cause someone to forget. Ibn Kathīr and Abū Amr read aw nansaʾhā (“or defer it”), with a hamzah, from nasaʾahu–yansaʾuhu. The first derives from forgetting, while the second derives from nasaʾa, meaning to defer.

The linguists say: “Nasaʾtuhu nasʾan means ‘I deferred it,’ as does ansaʾtuhu. One says nasaʾtuhu al-bayʿa and ansaʾtuhu, meaning ‘I allowed him to defer payment for the sale.’” Al-Asmaʿī said: “Ansaʾa Allāhu fī ajalihi and nasaʾa fī ajalihi have the same meaning: ‘May Allah prolong his life.’” The expression bayʿ al-nasīʾah (sale on deferred payment) derives from this same root.

Among the sayings of the Arabs is:

“Whoever desires a prolonged life—though there is no prolongation—should eat early, keep his debts light, and have intercourse with women less often.”

As for the first reading, its meaning is clear to most Quran commentators. They say that it refers to what Allah caused to be forgotten of the Quran, as the transmitted reports indicate. For whatever is removed

from the Quran may be withdrawn through divine legislation by being erased from people’s hearts; this is causing it to be forgotten. Allah Most High thus states that whatever He abrogates or causes to be forgotten, He replaces with something better or similar. This demonstrates His bounty and mercy toward His believing servants, for He says immediately before this:

“O you who believe, do not say, ‘Rāʿinā (Attend to us),’ but say, ‘Unzurnā (Look upon us),’ and listen. And for the disbelievers there is a painful punishment.”

“Neither the disbelievers among the People of the Book nor the polytheists wish for any good to be sent down to you from your Lord. But Allah singles out for His mercy whomever He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of immense bounty.”

He thus forbade them to imitate the People of the Book in their disrespect toward the Messenger and what he brought. He explained that, because of their envy, they did not wish Allah to send down to him any of the Book or wisdom. He then described His favor toward the believers: some of the Quran was abrogated, and some was caused to be forgotten—as the transmitted reports indicate. What He, glorified be He, caused to be forgotten belongs to those passages whose rulings and recitation He abrogated. This differs from abrogated passages that are still recited, though their rulings have been abrogated, or passages whose recitation He abrogated but which were not forgotten. Abrogation and causing passages to be forgotten involve a reduction in what He revealed to His servants.

He, glorified be He, therefore explained that there is no diminution in this. Rather, whatever is abrogated or caused to be forgotten, Allah replaces with something better or similar. The believers thus continually enjoy a blessing from Allah that does not diminish but increases: when He brings something better, the blessing increases, and when He brings something similar, the blessing remains. Allah Most High says:

“Or cause it to be forgotten.”

He thus attributes the act of causing it to be forgotten to Himself, for this is not blameworthy, unlike forgetting what must be retained, which is blameworthy.

for this is being made to forget what Allah has withdrawn. Forgetting what He has commanded one to retain, however, is blameworthy. Allah Most High says:

“Thus did Our signs come to you, but you forgot them; and thus will you be forgotten today.”

Although this forgetting includes neglecting to act upon them while retaining them in memory, forgetting the verses altogether, so that their contents are no longer known, entails an even greater neglect of acting upon them. This, therefore, is blameworthy. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith recorded in the Sunan collections:

“Whoever recites the Quran and then forgets it will meet Allah maimed.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, disliked a person attributing forgetfulness to himself. He said in the hadith recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“How bad it is for someone to say, ‘I have forgotten such-and-such a verse!’ Rather, he has been made to forget it. Keep reviewing the Quran, for it escapes from people’s hearts more readily than camels escape their tethers.”

Some interpreters understood “Whatever verse We abrogate” to refer to a verse whose recitation and written text Allah retained while abrogating its ruling, and what He caused to be forgotten to refer to what He withdrew, so that it is no longer recited. Others included in the first category verses whose recitation was abrogated, even if they remained memorized.

The first interpretation is that of Mujāhid and the companions of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd. Scholars have transmitted through sound chains, from Ibn Abī Najīh, that Mujāhid explained “Whatever verse We abrogate” as follows: “We retain its written text and change its ruling.” He said: “This is also the view of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.” “Or cause it to be forgotten” means “We erase it,” for what has been forgotten has not been retained.

Ibn Abī Hātim narrated through his chain of transmission, from ʿIkrimah, that Ibn ʿAbbās said:

“Revelation would sometimes come down to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, at night

and he would forget it during the day. So Allah revealed:

‘Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it.’”

The same was also reported from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Qatādah, and ʿIkrimah.

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās used to recite it as aw tunsihā (“or you forget it”), in the second person—that is, “you forget it, O Muhammad.” He recited Allah’s words, “We will make you recite, and you will not forget,” and His words:

“Remember your Lord when you forget.”

Reports also relate that one of them would memorize passages of the Quran and then forget them. They would mention this to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he would say, “It has been withdrawn.” An example is the sound report transmitted by al-Zuhrī: Abū Umāmah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf told me, in the gathering of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib:

“A man had memorized a surah and rose during the night to recite it, but could not. Another rose to recite it, but could not, and another rose to recite it, but could not. In the morning, they came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. One of them said, ‘Last night I tried to recite such-and-such a surah, but could not.’ Another said, ‘That is the only reason I have come.’ Another said, ‘That is the only reason I have come.’ And another said, ‘The same happened to me, O Messenger of Allah.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘It was abrogated last night.’”

As for the reading “or We defer it,” the word nasʾ means postponement. The early generations held two views concerning this. The first is reported from a group of them. Some have interpreted the first reading in this sense, saying that nunsihā means “We leave it with you,” since nisyān (“forgetting”) can mean leaving something. Al-Azharī said: “Nunsihā means ‘We command that it be left.’ One says ansaytu al-shayʾ.” He cited the verse:

“I have a turn of duty to fulfil;
I shall neither leave it nor bid that it be left.”

That is, “nor command that it be left.” The third view is: “We suspend its application by abrogating it.” The correct view is the middle one.

Ibn Abī Hātim narrated through his chain of transmission from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said:

“ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, addressed us, saying: ‘Allah says, “Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten”—that is, We defer it.’”

Through his well-known chain of transmission, he also reported from Abū al-ʿĀliyah: “‘Whatever verse We abrogate’—so that it is no longer acted upon—‘or cause to be forgotten,’ meaning: We hold it back with Us.” In another wording from Abū al-ʿĀliyah: “We defer it with Us.” From ʿAtāʾ it is reported: “We defer it.”

A third view has also been reported from the early generations, constituting a fourth view here. Its meaning is:

“Whatever verse We abrogate”—that is, what We have sent down to you and do not withdraw—“or cause to be forgotten,” meaning: We defer its revelation and do not send it down. Some have attributed this to Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and ʿAtāʾ. As for
