translated_text:
“Whatever verse We abrogate,” it refers to what has already been revealed of the Quran; the two understood this as referring to transcription. “Or defer it” means: We delay it so that it is not forthcoming—namely, what has not been revealed.

This interpretation, however, is questionable. Ibn Abī Hātim narrated through an established chain of transmission from ʿAtāʾ concerning “Whatever verse We abrogate”: “As for what has been abrogated, it is what was left of the Quran”—turika, “was left” (with the letter kāf). It seems that someone misread this as nazala (“was revealed”), from nuzūl (“revelation”), since the expression “was left” is ambiguous. Thus Ibn Abī Hātim said: “He means that it was left unrevealed to Muhammad.”

Yet this is not what ʿAtāʾ meant. Rather, he meant that it was left written and recited, while its ruling was abrogated, as previously reported from others. What Allah deferred is what He delayed and did not reveal. Saʿīd and ʿAtāʾ were among the most knowledgeable of the Successors; this would not have escaped them.

Ibn ʿĀmir read, “Mā nansakh min āyah” (“Whatever verse We abrogate”). Abū Hātim claimed that he had erred, but that is not so. Some interpreted it in this sense, explaining: “Whatever We transcribe” means “We cause you to transcribe it,” just as one says, “I had him write this.”

Another explanation is that ansakha means “to make something abrogated,” just as qabarahu is used to mean burying someone, whereas aqbarahu means providing him with a grave; and taradahu means banishing someone, whereas atradahu means making him an outcast. This is closer to the reading of the majority.

The correct interpretation of “or defer it” is: We hold it back with Us and do not reveal it. The meaning is: whatever We abrogate of the verses We have revealed, or defer revealing of the verses We have not yet revealed, “We bring one better than it or similar to it.” Just as He provides them with a replacement for what has been withdrawn, He provides them with a replacement for what is awaited and has not yet been revealed, until He sends it down

translated_text:
for wisdom has required that its revelation be delayed. He therefore provides them, at that time, with something like it or better, until the time comes for its revelation. He then reveals it as well, alongside what came before, while what He provided in its place before its revelation is like it or better.

As for what He has revealed to them and has not abrogated, it needs no replacement. Were Allah to bring something better or similar in place of everything He had not abrogated, this would entail an endless succession of revelations. Likewise, if the intended meaning were that He postpones its abrogation until a certain time and then abrogates it, then, as long as it remains with them, it needs no replacement that is like it or better. A replacement is needed only for what they do not have: what they have been made to forget, or what He has delayed revealing and has not yet revealed. Hence, He does not provide a replacement for everything He has not revealed, but rather for what He has deferred, delaying its revelation. For if everything not yet revealed were to have a replacement, this would entail an endless succession of revelations. Rather, whatever was known to be forthcoming, but whose revelation He delayed, remains unavailable to them until it is revealed, just as they lose what was revealed and then abrogated. Thus He, glorified be He, provides a replacement for each of these.

As for what He has revealed and left with them, postponing its abrogation until a certain time, this needs no replacement, since it itself remains.

If this were the intended meaning, then, for every Quranic passage He abrogated, something like it or better would have to be revealed before its abrogation. Then, upon abrogating it, He would bring something better or similar. Every abrogated passage would thus have two replacements: one before its abrogation and another after it. The replacement preceding its abrogation would have no designated time for its revelation to begin, so it would have to be revealed from the very outset. This would entail all of that being revealed at the very beginning of revelation, and this is false

beyond doubt.

If it is said, “The same consequence follows for what He deferred and did not reveal, since it has a replacement, yet there is no appointed time for that replacement to be revealed,” the answer is: What He has deferred revealing, while intending to reveal it, is known, and a replacement like it or better is provided at every stage, for the Quran continued to be revealed. This implies that whatever He deferred revealing must be preceded by the revelation of something like it or better. This is indeed what occurred. Much of the Quran that was revealed earlier and was not abrogated is better than what was revealed later. The Meccan verses, for example, explain Allah’s oneness, prophethood, the Resurrection, and the foundations of the revealed laws—matters superior to the detailed rulings concerning usury, marriage, divorce, and other such matters.

Thus, before revealing what He deferred—such as the verse on usury, which was among the last Quranic passages revealed and has been reported to be the very last, and likewise the verses concerning debt, waiting periods, menstruation, and similar matters—Allah had already revealed something better: verses containing more important rulings and more important foundations.

For this reason, Sūrat al-An‘ām is superior to other surahs, as are Sūrat Yā Sīn and similar surahs containing the foundations of religion upon which all the Messengers agreed—may Allah’s blessings be upon them all. This is also why the surah “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’,” despite its few letters, is equivalent to one-third of the Quran: it contains the affirmation of Allah’s oneness. It is thus clear that the verses concerning Allah’s oneness are superior to others. The Opening of the Book was undoubtedly revealed in Mecca, as indicated by His words

translated_text:
—Exalted is He—:

“And We have certainly given you seven oft-repeated verses and the great Quran.”

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“It is the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Quran that I have been given.”

Sūrat al-Hijr is undoubtedly Meccan. It recounts the words of the polytheists of Mecca and the Prophet’s dealings with them. This indicates that whatever portion of the Quran Allah deferred, postponing its revelation, was preceded by the revelation of something superior to it. The surah “Say, ‘O disbelievers’” is also undoubtedly Meccan, which is the majority view. It has been said that it is Medinan, but this is clearly mistaken.

Likewise, the claim that al-Fātihah was revealed only in Medina is undoubtedly mistaken. Even if we had no sound evidence establishing this, those who held that it was Meccan would possess additional knowledge.

Most scholars hold that the surah “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” is Meccan. The reported occasions of its revelation include a question posed by the polytheists in Mecca and a question posed by disbelievers among the People of the Book—the Jews—in Medina. There is no contradiction here: Allah first revealed it in Mecca, then revealed it again when the Prophet was asked a similar question.

A number of scholars have mentioned this, explaining that a verse or surah may be revealed twice or more. Thus, the various reported occasions of revelation may all be true. What this means is that whenever an occasion arose to which the passage was relevant, Gabriel would descend and recite it to the Prophet, showing him that it contained the answer appropriate to that occasion, even though the Messenger had already memorized it.

translated_text:
One of us may ask about an issue and be reminded of a verse or hadith to show how the text bears upon that issue. Although he has already memorized it, the text is recited to him so that its relevance to the matter in question becomes clear.

It has thus become clear that a substitute is provided for what Allah has deferred revealing, unlike what they already possessed that had not been abrogated, for the latter has no substitute. Even supposing that it would eventually be abrogated, its substitute would not be better than it while it remained in force. Likewise, the substitute for an abrogated passage is better than it. Most of the early generations used the expression “better than it” without qualification, just as it appears in the Quran, and none of them found this problematic.

In al-Wālibī’s commentary, it is explained as: “More beneficial to you and easier for you.” Regarding “We bring one better than it or like it,” Qatādah said: “A verse containing relief, a concession, a command, or a prohibition.” Neither of these two found any difficulty in its being better than the earlier verse. Rather, they explained the nature of its superiority. As discussed above, prescriptive speech varies in excellence according to what is required: when what is required is more beneficial to the person addressed, requiring it is better. Likewise, Allah’s mercy, which precedes His wrath, is better than His wrath. Their statements therefore affirm this superiority rather than deny it.

If it is objected:

“It is established that the Verse of the Throne is the greatest verse in Allah’s Book. Yet it was revealed in Sūrat al-Baqarah—which is unanimously agreed to be Medinan. Its revelation was therefore deferred, although nothing better than it or equal to it had been revealed before it.”

The reply is that there are several answers to this:

First: Allah said:

“We bring one better than it or like it.”

He did not say, “a verse better than it.” Rather, He brings Quranic revelation better than it or like it. Although the Verse of the Throne is the best of all verses, a collection of verses may be better than it. Although Sūrat al-Baqarah is unanimously agreed to be Medinan, and has been described as the first revelation sent down in Medina, this undoubtedly applies only to some of its verses. The prohibition of usury, for instance, was revealed only later.

His words:

“And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah”

were among the last revelations. His words:

“And complete the pilgrimage and the lesser pilgrimage for Allah”

were revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, in 6 AH, by scholarly consensus. Sūrat al-Hashr had been revealed before that, for everyone agrees that it was revealed concerning Banū al-Nadīr. Everyone also agrees that the events involving Banū al-Nadīr preceded al-Hudaybiyyah—indeed, they preceded the Battle of the Trench. It was only the affair of Banū Qurayzah that occurred after the Battle of the Trench: they were the ones whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, besieged immediately after that battle. As for Banū al-Nadīr, he had expelled them before then, by scholarly consensus.

Likewise, Sūrat al-Hadīd is Medinan according to the majority. It has been said to be Meccan, but this is a weak view, because it mentions the hypocrites and the People of the Book, and such passages were revealed only in Medina. Nevertheless, it may have been revealed before much of Sūrat al-Baqarah.

In short, it is possible that the beginning of Sūrat al-Hadīd and the end of Sūrat al-Hashr were revealed before the Verse of the Throne. Sūrat al-An‘ām, Sūrat Yā Sīn, and other surahs were revealed before the Verse of the Throne by unanimous agreement.

translated_text:
Second answer:

It was when Allah Most High revealed the following verse that He promised that, whenever He abrogated a verse or deferred it, He would bring something better than it or like it:

“Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or like it.”

This verse is a conditional statement containing His promise that He will certainly do so, and He is true to His promise. Thus, whatever He abrogates after this verse, or whatever revelation He intends to send down but postpones, He will bring something better than it or like it. As for what He abrogated or deferred before this verse, He had not yet promised at that time to bring something better than it or like it.

This also addresses the question concerning al-Fātihah. There is no doubt that it was revealed after the surah beginning, “Read in the name of your Lord,” yet it is superior to that surah. This establishes that the revelation of a superior passage may be delayed, and that not everything revealed later was preceded by something equal or superior to it. But if the promise concerns what comes after it, this objection does not arise. This is indicated by His words, “Whatever We abrogate”: this imperfect verb in the jussive refers only to the future. The particles governing the jussive—inna and its counterparts—and those governing the subjunctive restrict the verb to future reference.

A third answer may also be offered:

What was revealed at a particular time was better for them then, even if something else was better for them at another time. Accordingly, the superiority of some passages over others would be of two kinds: enduring superiority, such as that of the Verse of the Throne, the Opening of the Book, and “Say: He is Allah, One”; and contingent superiority, whereby one passage is superior at one time and another is superior at another time. This might be said, for example, of the verse giving a person who is not travelling the choice between fasting and breaking the fast while providing compensation, as compared with the verse making fasting obligatory without that choice. This is just as

each prescribed act is superior at its appointed time. Thus, before abrogation, praying towards Jerusalem was superior; after abrogation, praying towards the Kaʿbah is superior.

On this understanding, the verse can indeed be cited as evidence that only the Quran can abrogate the Quran. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and the better-known of the two positions reported from Imam Ahmad. Indeed, he explicitly stated that only a Quranic passage revealed subsequently can abrogate the Quran, and this is the position of the majority of his followers. For Allah has promised that whatever is abrogated must have a replacement equal or superior to it. He has likewise promised this regarding whatever He causes the believers to forget, and whatever He defers whose time for revelation has not yet come. All this indicates that the believer always has either the Quranic passage that is withdrawn or another equal or superior to it. If it were abrogated by the Sunnah without an equal or superior Quranic passage being brought, this would contradict Allah’s promise.

If it is said instead that such a passage comes after its abrogation by the Sunnah, there would be an interval between its abrogation and the provision of its replacement during which no replacement was present. This contradicts the intended meaning of the verse: either the withdrawn passage or one equal or superior to it must be available.

Moreover, His words, “We bring,” do not mean after a period of time. For it is already known that whatever He defers while intending to reveal it will be revealed after a period of time. Thus, when He states that, before revealing what He has deferred, He brings something equal or superior to it, we know that He does not defer it without providing a replacement. If it were permissible for a period to pass without a replacement, it would be more fitting for a passage not yet revealed to be without a replacement than for an abrogated passage.  الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّهُ إذَا كَانَ قَدْ ضَمِنَ لَهُمْ الْإِتْيَانَ بِالْبَدَلِ عَنْ الْمَنْسُوخِ عُلِمَ أَنَّ مَقْصُودَهُ أَنَّهُ لَا يَنْقُصُهُمْ شَيْءٌ مِمَّا أَنْزَلَهُ بَلْ لَا بُدَّ مِنْ مِثْلِ الْمَرْفُوعِ أَوْ خَيْرٍ مِنْهُ وَلَوْ بَقُوا مُدَّةً بِلَا بَدَلٍ لَنَقَصُوا.
 وَأَيْضًا فَإِنَّ هَذَا وَعْدٌ مُعَلَّقٌ بِشَرْطِ وَالْوَعْدُ الْمُعَلَّقُ بِشَرْطِ يَلْزَمُ عَقِبَهُ فَإِنَّهُ مِنْ جِنْسِ الْمُعَاوَضَةِ وَذَلِكَ مِمَّا يَلْزَمُ فِيهِ أَدَاءُ الْعِوَضِ عَلَى الْفَوْرِ إذَا قَبَضَ الْمُعَوَّضَ كَمَا إذَا قَالَ:
 مَا أَلْقَيْت مِنْ مَتَاعِك فِي الْبَحْرِ فَعَلَيَّ بَدَلُهُ وَلَيْسَ هَذَا وَعْدًا مُطْلَقًا كَقَوْلِهِ 
{لَتَدْخُلُنَّ الْمَسْجِدَ الْحَرَامَ}
 .
 وَلِهَذَا يُفَرَّقُ بَيْنَ قَوْلِهِ:
 وَاَللَّهِ لَأُعْطِيَنَّكَ مِائَةً وَبَيْنَ قَوْلِهِ: وَاَللَّهِ لَا آخُذُ مِنْك شَيْئًا إلَّا أَعْطَيْتُك بَدَلَهُ فَإِنَّ هَذَا وَاجِبٌ عَلَى الْفَوْرِ.
translated_text:
the moment it is abrogated is then all the more fitting and appropriate. Moreover, it is known that the Quran was revealed gradually. If He delayed revealing the replacement for an abrogated passage, it would not be recognized as its replacement, nor could it be distinguished from other revelations. His words,

“We bring something better than it or equal to it,”

would then convey no more than was already known even if nothing had been abrogated.

The most that could be said is this: if nothing were abrogated, it would be possible for nothing further to be revealed; but if something were abrogated, its replacement would necessarily come, even after some time. Yet this was something they already believed, for they had become accustomed to the Quran being revealed in response to events, questions and needs. When a verse was abrogated, they would not have thought that nothing would be revealed after it. They would not have thought this even if it had not been abrogated, so how could they think it when it was abrogated?

Second: since He has guaranteed them a replacement for what is abrogated, it is clear that His intent is that they should lose nothing of what He has revealed. Rather, there must be something equal or superior to what has been withdrawn. If they remained for a time without a replacement, they would suffer a loss.

Furthermore, this is a promise contingent upon a condition, and such a promise must be fulfilled immediately after that condition is met. It is akin to an exchange, in which the compensation must be paid immediately upon receipt of what is given in exchange for it. An example is someone saying, “Whatever belongings you throw into the sea, I undertake to replace.” This is not an unconditional promise like His words,

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque.”

For this reason, a distinction is drawn between saying, “By Allah, I will certainly give you a hundred,” and saying, “By Allah, I will not take anything from you without giving you its replacement.” In the latter case, immediate fulfillment is obligatory.

translated_text:
Further evidence for this position is that the Companions and Successors from whom knowledge of abrogating and abrogated passages was transmitted mention only the abrogation of the Quran by the Quran. They do not mention its abrogation without another Quranic passage, by the Sunnah instead. The works on abrogating and abrogated passages that draw upon their teachings contain only this.

Likewise, ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said to a preacher:

“Can you distinguish the abrogating passages from the abrogated passages in the Quran?”

If something other than the Quran could abrogate the Quran, he would have had to mention that as well.

Moreover, those among the speculative theologians and proponents of reasoned opinion who allow the Quran to be abrogated without another Quranic passage rely primarily on the argument that reason contains nothing that renders this impossible. Yet the absence of any rationally discernible impediment does not establish that revealed law allows it. Revelation may impart knowledge through its reports of matters unknown to reason. Likewise, the wisdom of the Lawgiver, as made known through revelation, may disclose what cannot be known through reason alone. Hence, those who considered this rationally possible differed over whether it had actually occurred under revealed law. That being so, the statement in this verse is evidence that such abrogation is precluded by revealed law.

Furthermore, an abrogating text has authority over the abrogated text, determines its status and takes precedence over it. It should therefore be equal or superior to it, as the Quran states. Thus, since the Quran has authority over the Scripture that preceded it—confirming the truth it contains, upholding what it upholds and abrogating what it abrogates—it is superior to it. If the Sunnah could abrogate the Book, it would necessarily be equal or superior to it.

وَالنَّاسُ فِي هَذَا الْمَقَامِ - وَهُوَ مَقَامُ حِكْمَةِ الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ -

translated_text:
Furthermore, no verse of the Quran is known to have been abrogated by anything other than the Quran. The requirement to make bequests to parents and close relatives was abrogated by the verse on inheritance, as the early generations unanimously agreed. Allah Most High says:

“These are the limits set by Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him to Gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever. That is the great triumph.”

“But whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, to abide therein forever, and he will have a humiliating punishment.”

The prescribed inheritance shares are among His limits. This is why He stated this immediately after mentioning those shares. Whoever gives someone entitled to a prescribed share more than his allotted portion has transgressed Allah’s limits by depriving one person of his due and granting another more than his due. Thus, the Quran indicates that this is forbidden, and it is the Quran that abrogates the earlier ruling.

Section:

On this question—the wisdom underlying commands and prohibitions—people fall into three groups.

The Mu'tazilite Qadarīs maintain that acts commanded or forbidden were already good or evil, respectively, before the commands and prohibitions were issued. Commands and prohibitions merely disclose the qualities those acts already possessed; they do not confer goodness or evil upon them. In their view, Allah cannot command or forbid for a wise purpose brought about by the command itself. They therefore denied the possibility of abrogation before one has had the opportunity to perform the act of worship, as in the account of the son who was to be sacrificed, and the abrogation of the fifty prayers enjoined on the Night of the Ascension, reducing them to five. Their rejection of abrogation before the appointed time for worship was also shared by

a group among Ahl al-Sunnah who affirm divine decree, because they assumed that there must be wisdom inherent in the act commanded or forbidden, and that He therefore cannot forbid the very thing He has commanded.

This is the logical implication of the view that abrogation restricts a ruling’s temporal scope, since restricting the scope of wording does not eliminate everything it denotes. Yet they contradicted themselves.

The Jahmī determinists maintain that no wise purpose arises from either the command itself or the act commanded, and that Allah creates nothing for a wise purpose. Rather, sheer will necessitated whatever occurred and the selection of one of two equivalent alternatives without any determining factor. Good deeds are not causes of reward, nor are evil deeds causes of punishment. Neither possesses any quality by virtue of which it is good or evil. Rather, a good deed means nothing more than an act to which a command applies, and an evil deed means nothing more than an act to which a prohibition applies. Thus, it is possible for Him to command anything—even disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience—and to forbid anything—even monotheism, truthfulness, and justice. Were He to do so, it would be just as if He had commanded monotheism, truthfulness, and justice, and forbidden polytheism, lying, and injustice.

This is what some of them say. Others say that anything may be commanded provided it does not preclude recognition of the command, unlike that which does preclude its recognition. In their view, there are no causes in existence. Rather, when one thing is associated with another, whether in creation or in revealed law, it becomes a sign of it. Deeds are therefore nothing but signs, not effective causes.

They also said that commanding those who have not believed to believe means: “I intend to punish you

and your lack of faith is a sign of punishment.” Likewise, His command to believe, addressed to someone He knows will believe, means: “I intend to reward you, and faith is a sign.” Some of these people reject analogy in revealed law and the attribution of legal rulings to underlying causes. Those among them who affirm analogy regard these causes as mere signs. Yet they know that the ruling in the original case is established by the revealed text and consensus, which provide evidence for it. What need, then, is there for the underlying cause? How can that cause conceivably be a sign of the ruling in the original case, when its cause is sought only after the existence of Hell is known to be established? At that point, the sign serves no purpose.

As for the new case, something cannot be its underlying cause unless it is also the underlying cause in the original case. Some of these people deny that legal causes are appropriate to their rulings, saying: “Appropriateness is not a means of identifying legal causes.” These constitute the majority of those who hold this view. Those among their later adherents who accept appropriateness say that revealed law has been observed to take it into account. They thus infer the cause from mere association, not because the Lawgiver prescribed His ruling to secure the benefit sought through it or to avert any harm whatsoever. For, according to them, there is no “in order to” in either His creation or His commands.

Thus Jahm—the leading figure of the determinists—and his followers stand at one extreme, while the Qadariyyah stand at the other. As for the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, the imams of Islam—including the renowned jurists and others—and those who follow their path among scholars of jurisprudence and hadith and theologians discussing the foundations of religion and the principles of jurisprudence, they affirm divine decree, affirm revealed law, and affirm Allah’s wisdom in His creation and His commands—although an individual among them may or may not know that wisdom—

and they affirm the causes He has established and the benefits within His creation and His commands that He has made a mercy to His servants, while acknowledging that He is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything—the deeds of His servants and all else. They affirm that whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass; and that everything that occurs in His creation and His commands is just and wise, whether or not the servant understands how this is so.

The wisdom arising from His commands is of three kinds:

The first is wisdom inherent in the act itself—even if it has not been commanded—as with truthfulness, justice, and similar acts whose benefits accrue to those who perform them, even without a command to do so. Allah commands what is good and forbids corruption.

The second is that what He commands acquires goodness from His command, and what He prohibits acquires badness from His prohibition. Thus wine, which was initially not forbidden, was then prohibited and became foul; and prayer facing the Rock, which had been good, became bad when He prohibited it. For He loves and is pleased with what He commands, and He hates and is displeased with what He prohibits. When He loves a servant and takes him as a friend, He bestows upon him good qualities that give him distinction over those whom He hates and takes as enemies. Likewise, He singles out places and times that He loves and honors—such as the Kaaba and the month of Ramadan—for qualities that distinguish them above others, so that in those times and places there is a measure of His mercy

If it is said: “Wine is the same before and after its prohibition. Does declaring it foul only after its prohibition not amount to making a distinction without a distinguishing reason?”

The reply is: This is not so. Rather, He prohibited it precisely when wisdom called for its prohibition. Something’s being good or bad is not like its being black or white. Rather, it is like its being beneficial or harmful, agreeable or disagreeable, a friend or an enemy, and other such qualities that belong to the thing described but change as circumstances change.

Something may be beneficial at one time and harmful at another. A harmful thing may be left unprohibited when the harm resulting from prohibiting it would be greater—as would have been the case had wine been prohibited at the beginning of Islam. People had become deeply accustomed to it, and their faith had not yet grown strong enough for them to accept its prohibition. Nor had their faith and religious practice become so complete that no deficiency remained except that caused by drinking wine, which hindered them from remembering Allah and from prayer. For this reason, its prohibition came gradually.

Allah first revealed concerning it:

“They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, ‘In them is great sin and benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit.’”

Then, after a group had drunk wine and prayed, and the imam had made a mistake in his recitation, He revealed the verse forbidding prayer while intoxicated. Then Allah revealed the verse prohibiting wine:

And the third category is where the wisdom arises from the command itself, while there is no benefit whatsoever in the act. Rather, the purpose is to test the servant: will he obey or disobey? Once he believes the act to be obligatory and resolves to perform it, the purpose of the command has been achieved, and it is then abrogated. This is what happened to Allah’s intimate friend in the account of the sacrifice. The sacrifice itself offered no benefit, nor was it what the Lord actually sought. Rather, the Lord intended to test Abraham so that he would give obedience to his Lord and love for Him precedence over his love for his son, and no attachment to anything other than Allah would remain in his heart. He loved his son deeply and had asked Allah to grant him that son—yet he was Allah’s intimate friend. Thus, Allah Most High wished to perfect his intimate friendship with Him, so that nothing would remain in his heart to rival his love for his Lord:

“And when they had both submitted and he laid him down upon his forehead, We called to him, ‘O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision.’ Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good. Indeed, this was the clear trial.”

Similar to this is the hadith in Sahīh al-Bukhārī concerning a leper, a bald man, and a blind man: the purpose was to test them, not the act itself.

This category and the preceding one escaped the Mu'tazilah. They did not recognize the wisdom arising from the command itself, or that arising in the commanded act by virtue of its being commanded. They recognized only the first category. As for those who deny wisdom, all these cases are alike to them. They take no account of wisdom, or of a particular act being singled out for a command, or anything else of this kind, as is already known from their fundamental position.

Thus, someone may claim that “Say: He is Allah, One” and al-Fātihah may each be intrinsically equal to all other surahs, and that the Verse of the Throne is equal to all other verses; that they were singled out for greater rewards for their reciters—or al-Fātihah was specifically prescribed for prayer and the like—solely by sheer will, without possessing any quality warranting such distinction. This claim rests on Jahm’s principles concerning creation and command, even though Abū al-Hasan and others agreed with him on it.

The well-known works on the Sunnah containing reports from the early generations mention both positions. They identify this view as that of the Jabriyyah (determinists), who follow Jahm, and include it among the doctrines of the innovating, determinist Qadariyyah. The early generations rejected the position of the Jahmī determinists just as they rejected that of the Mu'tazilite Qadariyyah. This is well known from Sufyān al-Thawrī, al-Awzā'ī, al-Zubaydī, 'Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others. Numerous followers of the imams among the Hanafīs, Mālikīs, Shāfi'īs, Hanbalīs, and the rest of Ahl al-Sunnah have mentioned this in their books. It has been explained at length in its appropriate places, and I have cited the statements of the early generations and the imams concerning it.

We have drawn attention here only to the underlying principle, because many people are unaware of this. They imagine that the position of Ahl al-Sunnah concerning divine decree is none other than what Ahl al-Sunnah themselves regard as the position of Jahm and his determinist followers, or something similar. Likewise, some imagine that the position of Ahl al-Sunnah on questions of religious designations and rulings, and of divine promise and threat, is also the position known among Ahl al-Sunnah as that of Jahm. “‘Gather together so that I may recite one-third of the Quran to you.’ They gathered, and he recited to them: ‘Say: He is Allah, the One.’ He said: ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, it is equivalent to one-third of the Quran.’”

As for the explanation of this, some scholars have said that, in terms of its meanings, the Quran consists of three parts: one-third concerns Allah’s oneness, one-third consists of narratives, and one-third contains commands and prohibitions. “Say: He is Allah, the One” describes the Most Merciful and declares who He is; thus, it encompasses one-third of the Quran.

This is because the Quran is the speech of Allah Most High, and speech is either prescriptive or informative. Prescriptive speech consists of commands, prohibitions, and related matters, such as permission and the like; this constitutes its rulings.

Informative speech conveys information either about the Creator or about creation. Information about the Creator concerns His oneness, including His names and attributes. Information about creation consists of narratives: accounts of what has happened and what will happen. This includes accounts of the prophets, their peoples, and those who denied them, as well as information about Paradise and Hell, reward and punishment.

They said: In this respect, “Say: He is Allah, the One” is equivalent to one-third of the Quran because it affirms Allah’s oneness, which constitutes one-third of the Quran’s meanings.

translated_text:
possible for a person to content himself with it and dispense with the rest of the Quran.

The answer is that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“It is equivalent to one-third of the Quran.”

The word ‘adl (equivalent), pronounced with the vowel a, is used of something of a different kind, as Allah Most High says:

“Or an equivalent amount of fasting.”

Thus, He made fasting equivalent to an expiation, although they are of two different kinds. Undoubtedly, the rewards in Paradise are of various kinds. Everything from which a servant derives benefit and pleasure—food, drink, spouses, and fragrances—is part of that reward, the highest of which is gazing upon the Face of Allah Most High.

The things of this world are all needed because of their different benefits, even though some are equivalent in value to others much greater in physical size. A thousand dinars, for example, are equivalent to a greater bulk of silver, food, clothing, and other things. Someone who possesses that gold thus possesses the equivalent of a thousand dinars’ worth of those things, although this does not enable him to dispense with the other kinds of wealth from which he benefits. This is because the equivalence is in amount, not in kind or quality.

Likewise, although the reward for “Say: He is Allah, the One” equals the reward for one-third of the Quran in amount, it need not be identical to it in kind or quality. The rest of the Quran contains commands, prohibitions, promises, and warnings that people need. They therefore need the rest of the Quran and derive from it benefits for which this surah cannot substitute, even though it is equivalent to one-third of the Quran.

translated_text:

Later scholars have two well-known views on this. Some say that it does not vary in excellence in itself, because it is all Allah’s speech, and Allah’s speech is an attribute of His. They maintain that an attribute of Allah does not admit of degrees of excellence, especially according to the view that it is eternal, since that which is eternal does not admit of such degrees. Likewise, concerning the words of Allah Most High:

“Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or like it,”

they say that “better” refers only to something other than the verse itself, such as the benefit and reward that people receive.

The second view is that some parts of the Quran are superior to others. This is the view of the majority of both earlier and later scholars. For in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said concerning al-Fātihah:

“Nothing like it has been revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, or the Quran.”

He thus denied that anything was like it. How, then, can it be said that the Quran is all equal in excellence? It is also authentically established that he said to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb:

“O Abū al-Mundhir, do you know which verse in Allah’s Book is the greatest?”

He replied: “Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all.”

The Prophet then struck him on the chest with his hand and said to him: “May your knowledge bring you joy, Abū al-Mundhir!”

He thus made clear that this verse is the greatest verse in the Quran, demonstrating that some verses are greater than others.

Furthermore, the Quran is Allah’s speech, and speech derives its nobility from the one who speaks it, whether it conveys information or a command. A statement derives its nobility from the nobility of both the one making it and its subject; a command derives its nobility from the nobility of both the one issuing it and what is commanded. In some passages He commands them to believe and forbids them to associate partners with Him; in others He commands them to record debts in writing and forbids them to engage in usury.

It is well known that what He says about Himself, such as:

“Say, ‘He is Allah, the One,’”

is greater than what He says about His creation, such as:

“May the hands of Abū Lahab perish.”

Likewise, passages in which He commands faith and forbids associating partners with Him are greater than those in which He commands debts to be recorded in writing and forbids usury.

Similarly, a person’s speech shares a common source with respect to the speaker: it is the speech of one speaker. Yet it varies in excellence according to its subject matter. A person’s speech in which he remembers his Lord, enjoins right, and forbids wrong is better than his speech in which he mentions His creation and commands something permissible or forbidden. Those who held the first view erred because they considered only one aspect of speech—the speaker—and disregarded the other—its subject matter. Speech is related to both, and these relationships give rise to differences or equality in excellence.

They said: Whoever attributes differences in excellence merely to greater or lesser reward, without the speech itself being superior, is like someone who considers two deeds equal, yet regards the reward for one as many times that of the other, even though neither deed has any distinguishing merit in itself. translated_text:
common to both, to two equally deserving recipients. His intention is the same in both cases, and neither gift has any merit over the other. How, then, could the reward for one be many times the reward for the other? Rather, differences in reward and punishment indicate differences in the goodness and evil of deeds. This discussion is connected to the question of deeds possessing qualities that make them righteous and good, or corrupt and evil. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The claim that “Allah’s attributes do not vary in excellence,” and similar statements, has no supporting evidence; indeed, it is precisely the point in dispute. Who has established that His attribute of mercy is not superior to His attribute of anger? It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah wrote in a book kept with Him above the Throne: ‘My mercy prevails over My anger’—and in another narration, ‘precedes My anger.’”

The attributes of a being—knowledge, will, power, speech, pleasure, anger, and other attributes—vary in excellence in two ways. First, some attributes are superior to others and more integral to the one who possesses them as a whole. We know that a servant’s possessing knowledge, power, and mercy is better than his possessing their opposites. Allah Most High, however, is not described by their opposites; He is described only by attributes of perfection. To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names, by which He is invoked, and He is invoked only by His Most Beautiful Names. His names encompass His attributes, and some of His names are superior to others

and more integral to the perfection of the One they describe. Hence the wording in the transmitted supplication:

“I ask You by Your mighty and most mighty, great and greatest name.”

And:

“He has indeed called upon Allah by His mighty name, by which, when He is invoked, He answers, and when He is asked, He gives.”

There are other reports of this kind. Thus, differences in excellence among the names and attributes are evident matters.

Second, a single attribute may itself vary in excellence. A command to do one thing may be more perfect than a command to do another. Allah’s pleasure with the prophets is greater than His pleasure with those below them, and His mercy towards them is more perfect than His mercy towards others. Allah’s speaking to some of His servants is more perfect than His speaking to others. The same applies to everything else in this category. Just as His names and attributes are diverse, they also vary in excellence, as indicated by the Quran, the Sunnah, consensus, and reason.

The specious argument of those who deny that they vary in excellence is of the same kind as that of those who deny their multiplicity. This ultimately amounts to denying the attributes, as advocated by the Jahmiyyah because of the composition they allege this would entail. We have explained the invalidity of this at length in its proper place.

He was also asked:

Should someone reciting the Quran recite (Surah al-Ikhlās) once or three times? What is the Sunnah in this regard?

He replied:

When reciting the entire Quran, one should recite this surah only once, as it appears in the written copy. This is what the scholars have stated, so that nothing is added to what is in that copy. But when reciting it on its own or together with part of the Quran, reciting it three times is equivalent to the Quran. And Allah knows best.

Section: Commentary on

“Say: He is Allah, the One;
Allah, the Eternal Refuge.
He neither begets nor was He begotten,
and there is none comparable to Him.”

The early generations offered several explanations of the name al-Samad that might be thought to differ. This is not so; rather, they are all correct.

The two best-known explanations are:

First, al-Samad is the One who has no hollow interior.

Second, He is the Master to whom people turn for their needs. The first is the view of

The second is the view of a group of earlier and later scholars and the majority of linguists. Reports from the early generations are preserved with their chains of transmission in works of Quranic commentary containing such chains, in works on the Sunnah, and elsewhere. We have already recorded many reports on this subject with their chains of transmission.

The explanation of “al-Samad” as the One who has no hollow interior is well known from Ibn Masʿūd, both as his own statement and as a statement attributed to the Prophet. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Hasan al-Basrī, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, al-Dahhāk, al-Suddī, and Qatādah. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib expressed a similar meaning, saying: “He is the One who has no internal contents.” Likewise, Ibn Masʿūd said: “He is the One who has no internal organs.” Al-Shaʿbī similarly said: “He is the One who neither eats nor drinks.” Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī and ʿIkrimah are reported to have said: “He is the One from whom nothing issues.” Maysarah is reported to have said: “He is the Solid One.”

Ibn Qutaybah said: “According to this explanation, it is as though the letter dāl has replaced a tāʾ. The word samt (silence) is related to this.”

I say: There is no substitution here. Rather, this is an instance of al-ishtiqāq al-akbar (the broadest form of derivation). Allah willing, we shall explain the basis of this interpretation in terms of derivation and language.

(الصَّمَدُ)

 وَيُرْوَى هَذَا عَنْ عَلِيٍّ وَعَنْ كَعْبِ الْأَحْبَارِ:
 الَّذِي لَا يُكَافِئُهُ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ أَحَدٌ وَعَنْ السدي أَيْضًا: هُوَ الْمَقْصُودُ إلَيْهِ فِي الرَّغَائِبِ وَالْمُسْتَغَاثِ بِهِ عِنْدَ الْمَصَائِبِ.
 وَعَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ هُوَ الْمُسْتَغْنِي عَنْ كُلِّ أَحَدٍ الْمُحْتَاجُ إلَيْهِ كُلُّ أَحَدٍ وَعَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ جُبَيْرٍ أَيْضًا:
 الْكَامِلُ فِي جَمِيعِ صِفَاتِهِ وَأَفْعَالِهِ. وَعَنْ الرَّبِيعِ الَّذِي لَا تَعْتَرِيهِ الْآفَاتُ. وَعَنْ مُقَاتِلِ بْنِ حَيَّانَ الَّذِي لَا عَيْبَ فِيهِ. وَعَنْ ابْنِ كيسان هُوَ الَّذِي لَا يُوصَفُ بِصِفَتِهِ أَحَدٌ.
 قَالَ أَبُو بَكْرٍ الْأَنْبَارِيُّ:
 لَا خِلَافَ بَيْنِ أَهْلِ اللُّغَةِ أَنَّ الصَّمَدَ السَّيِّدَ الَّذِي لَيْسَ فَوْقَهُ أَحَدٌ الَّذِي يَصْمُدُ إلَيْهِ النَّاسُ فِي حَوَائِجِهِمْ وَأُمُورِهِمْ.
translated_text:
from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, from Abū al-ʿĀliyah, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who reported that the polytheists said to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: ‘Tell us your Lord’s lineage.’ Allah then revealed:

‘Say, He is Allah, One; Allah, the Eternal Refuge,’

through to the end of the surah. He said: ‘Al-Samad is the One who neither begets nor is born; for whatever is born will die, and whatever dies will be inherited from. Allah neither dies nor is inherited from.’”

As for the explanation that He is the Master to whom people turn for their needs, this too is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, both as his own statement and as a statement attributed to the Prophet. It appears in al-Wālibī’s transmission of Ibn ʿAbbās’s commentary. He said: “(Al-Samad) is the Master whose sovereignty is perfect.” This explanation is also well known from Abū Wāʾil, Shaqīq ibn Salamah, who said: “He is the Master whose sovereignty has reached its utmost perfection.”

Abū Ishāq al-Kūfī reported from ʿIkrimah: “Al-Samad is the One above whom there is none.” This is also reported from ʿAlī. Kaʿb al-Ahbār is reported to have said: “The One whom none of His creation can equal.” Al-Suddī is also reported to have said: “He is the One to whom people turn for what they desire, and whose aid they seek when calamities strike.”

Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, is reported to have said: “He is the One who needs no one, while everyone needs Him.” Saʿīd ibn Jubayr is also reported to have said: “The One who is perfect in all His attributes and actions.” Al-Rabīʿ said: “The One whom no afflictions befall.” Muqātil ibn Hayyān said: “The One in whom there is no defect.” Ibn Kaysān said: “He is the One whose qualities cannot be ascribed to anyone else.”

Abū Bakr al-Anbārī said: “There is no disagreement among linguists that al-samad is the master above whom there is none, to whom people turn for their needs and affairs.”

وَقَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ:

translated_text:
Al-Zajjāj said: “He is the One in whom sovereignty reaches its utmost perfection. Everything turns to Him—that is, seeks Him.” Two well-known lines of poetry have been cited in this connection. One is:

“Lo, the herald came early to announce the deaths of Banū Asad’s two finest:
ʿAmr ibn Masʿūd and the chief to whom people turn.”

Another poet said:

“I struck him with my keen-edged sword, then said to him:
‘Take that, Hudhayf, for you are the chief to whom people turn!’”

Some linguists said:

“Al-samad is the master to whom people turn for their needs. The Arabs say samadtu fulānan, asmiduhu—with an i vowel on the m—or asmuduhu—with a u vowel on the m—and samdan—with no vowel on the m—when they mean, ‘I sought him.’ Samad means masmūd (one who is sought), just as qabd means maqbūd (what is taken), and naqd means manqūd (what is undone). A house is called masmūd or musammad when people turn to it for their needs. Tarafah said:

‘If the whole tribe gathers, you will find me
At the summit of the lofty house to which people turn.’”

Al-Jawharī said:

“Samadahu, yasmuduhu, samdan means ‘he sought him.’ Al-samad—with both consonants vowelled—is the master, because people turn to him for their needs. A house is called musammad—with the m doubled—meaning ‘sought out.’”

translated_text:
Al-Khattābī said:

“The soundest interpretation is that He is the Master to whom people turn for their needs, because the word’s derivation supports this. The basic meaning of samad is ‘seeking.’ One says, usmud samda fulān, meaning, ‘Head towards so-and-so.’ Thus, al-Samad is the Master to whom people turn in their affairs and whom they seek for their needs.”

Qatādah said: “Al-Samad is the One who remains after His creation.” Mujāhid and Mu'mar said: “He is the Everlasting.” Al-Khattābī and Abū al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzī classified the interpretations into four: these two and the two mentioned earlier. We shall explain, Allah willing, that His remaining and everlastingness belong to the perfection of His being al-Samad. Murrah al-Hamdānī is reported to have said: “He is the One who neither deteriorates nor perishes.”

He is also reported to have said:

“He is the One who decrees whatever He wills and does whatever He wishes. None can overturn His judgment or repel His decree.”

Ibn 'Atā' said:

“He is the One who transcends coming into being and passing away.”

He also said:

“Al-Samad is the One upon whom no effect appears from what He has brought forth.” He means His words:

“Nor did any weariness touch Us.”

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: “He is the Pre-eternal, without beginning.” Muhammad ibn 'Alī al-Hakīm al-Tirmidhī said: “He is the First without number, the Everlasting without an end, and the One who stands without support.” He also said: “Al-Samad is the One whom eyes cannot perceive, whom thoughts cannot encompass, and whom the farthest regions cannot reach. Everything with Him has its appointed measure.”

It has also been said:

“He is the One exalted above resemblance to those who fashion images.” It has also been said that the name signifies the exclusion of divisibility and composition from His essence. This is the view of many practitioners of speculative theology. It has also been said: “He is the One whose manner of being minds have despaired of discovering.” Likewise, it has been said: “He is the One whose descriptions cannot be comprehended in their true reality

translated_text:
and whose attributes likewise elude comprehension; no tongue can adequately describe Him, nor can any finger point to Him.” It has also been said: “He is the One who has granted His creation no knowledge of Him beyond His name and attribute.”

Al-Junayd is reported to have said:

“He is the One who has given His enemies no way to know Him.”

We shall now mention such statements of the early generations as we have at hand, together with their chains of transmission.

Ibn Abī Hātim related in his Quran commentary:

“My father narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Mūsā ibn Nufay' al-Jurashī narrated to us: 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Īsā—that is, Abū Khalaf al-Khazzāz—narrated to us: Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind narrated to us, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His saying, ‘al-Samad’: he said, ‘Al-Samad is the One to whom all things turn when distress or affliction befalls them.’

Abū Zur'ah narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Tha'labah ibn Sawā' al-Sadūsī narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Sawā' narrated to us: Sa'īd ibn Abī 'Arūbah narrated to us, from Abū Ma'shar, from Ibrāhīm, who said: ‘Al-Samad is the One to whom the servants turn for their needs.’

My father narrated to us: 'Abd al-Rahmān ibn al-Dahhāk narrated to us: Suwayd ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz narrated to us: Sufyān ibn Husayn narrated to us, from al-Hasan, who said: ‘Al-Samad is the Ever-Living, the All-Sustaining, who never passes away.’

My father narrated to us: Nasr ibn 'Alī narrated to us: Yazīd ibn Zuray' narrated to us, from Sa'īd, from Qatādah, from al-Hasan, who said: ‘Al-Samad is the One who remains after His creation.’ This is also Qatādah’s view.

Abū Sa'īd al-Ashajj narrated to us: Ibn Numayr narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Shaqīq, concerning His saying, ‘al-Samad’: he said, ‘The Master whose mastery has attained its utmost perfection.’

(الصَّمَدُ)

(الصَّمَدُ)

 حَدَّثَنَا أَبُو سَعِيدٍ الْأَشَجُّ ثنا أَبُو أَحْمَد ثنا مِنْدَلُ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ عَنْ أَبِي رَوْقٍ عَطِيَّةَ بْنِ الْحَارِثِ عَنْ أَبِي عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ السُّلَمِي عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ مَسْعُودٍ قَالَ:
 
(الصَّمَدُ)
 الَّذِي لَيْسَ لَهُ أَحْشَاءٌ وَرُوِيَ عَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ الْمُسَيِّبِ مِثْلُهُ.
 حَدَّثَنَا أَبِي ثنا مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عُمَرَ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ الرُّومِيُّ ثنا عُبَيْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ سَعِيدٍ قَائِدُ الْأَعْمَشِ عَنْ صَالِحِ بْنِ حَيَّانَ عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ بريدة عَنْ أَبِيهِ قَالَ لَا أَعْلَمُهُ إلَّا قَدْ رَفَعَهُ قَالَ:
 
(الصَّمَدُ)
 الَّذِي لَا جَوْفَ

My father narrated to us: Abū Sālih narrated to us: Mu'āwiyah ibn Sālih narrated to us, from 'Alī ibn Abī Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His saying, ‘al-Samad’: he said, ‘The Master whose mastery is perfect, the Noble One whose nobility is perfect, the Great One whose greatness is perfect, the Forbearing One whose forbearance is perfect, the All-Knowing whose knowledge is perfect, and the All-Wise whose wisdom is perfect. He is perfect in every aspect of nobility and mastery. He is Allah, glorified and exalted is He. This is His attribute, which befits none but Him. He has no equal, and there is nothing like Him. Glory be to Allah, the One, the All-Subduing.’

Kathīr ibn Shihāb al-Madhhijī al-Qazwīnī narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Sa'īd ibn Sābiq narrated to us: Abū Ja'far al-Rāzī narrated to us, from al-Rabī' ibn Anas, concerning His saying, ‘al-Samad’: he said, ‘The One who neither begets nor is begotten.’

Abū Sa'īd al-Ashajj narrated to us: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, from Abū Rajā’, from 'Ikrimah, concerning His saying, ‘al-Samad’: he said, ‘The One from whom nothing has come forth.’

Abū Sa'īd al-Ashajj narrated to us: Abū Ahmad narrated to us: Mindal ibn 'Alī narrated to us, from Abū Rawq 'Atiyyah ibn al-Hārith, from Abū 'Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī, from 'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd, who said, ‘Al-Samad is the One who has no internal organs.’ Something similar was also reported from Sa'īd ibn al-Musayyib.

My father narrated to us: Muhammad ibn 'Umar ibn 'Abd Allāh al-Rūmī narrated to us: 'Ubayd Allāh ibn Sa'īd, al-A'mash’s guide, narrated to us, from Sālih ibn Hayyān, from 'Abd Allāh ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said (the narrator remarked, ‘To the best of my knowledge, he traced it back to the Prophet’): ‘Al-Samad is the One who has no hollow interior

My father narrated to us: Qabīsah narrated to us: Sufyān narrated to us, from Mansūr, from Mujāhid, who said, “Al-Samad is the Solid One, who has no hollow interior.”

My father narrated to us: 'Alī ibn Hāshim ibn Marzūq narrated to us: Hushaym narrated to us, from Ismā'īl ibn Abī Khālid, from al-Sha'bī, who said, “Al-Samad is the One who neither eats food nor drinks.”

My father and Abū Zur'ah narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Manī' narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Maysir—meaning Abū Sa'd al-Saghānī—narrated to us: Abū Ja'far al-Rāzī narrated to us, from al-Rabī' ibn Anas, from Abū al-'Āliyah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, concerning His saying, “al-Samad”: he said, “Al-Samad is the One who neither begets nor is begotten, for everything that begets dies, and everything that dies leaves an inheritance. Allah neither dies nor leaves an inheritance.” Concerning “And there is none comparable to Him,” he said, “He has no likeness or equal, and there is nothing like Him.”

'Alī ibn al-Husayn narrated to us: Mahmūd ibn Khidāsh narrated to us: Abū Sa'd al-Saghānī narrated to us: Abū Ja'far al-Rāzī narrated to us, from al-Rabī' ibn Anas, from Abū al-'Āliyah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b:

“The polytheists said, ‘Tell us your Lord’s lineage,’ so Allah revealed

this surah.”

Abū Zur'ah narrated to us: al-'Abbās ibn al-Walīd narrated to us: Yazīd ibn Zuray' narrated to us, from Sa'īd, from Qatādah, concerning “And there is none comparable to Him.” He said, “None of Allah’s creation is equal to Him.”

'Alī ibn al-Husayn narrated to us: Abū 'Abd Allāh al-Jurashī narrated to us: Abū Khalaf 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Īsā narrated to us: Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind narrated to us, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbās, who said:

“Some Jews came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, including Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and Judayy ibn Akhtab. They said, ‘O Muhammad, describe to us your Lord who sent you.’ So Allah revealed: ‘Say: He is Allah, the One; Allah, al-Samad. He neither begets’—such that a child should issue from Him—‘nor is He begotten’—such that anything should issue from Him.”

Ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī said in his Tafsīr: Ahmad ibn Manī' al-Marwazī and Mahmūd ibn Khidāsh al-Tālaqānī narrated to us. He then related a chain like that of Ibn Abī Hātim, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, concerning the polytheists’ request to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “Tell us your Lord’s lineage.” So Allah revealed: “Say: He is Allah, the One.”

Ibn Humayd narrated to us: Yahyā ibn Wādih narrated to us: al-Husayn narrated to us, from Yazīd, from 'Ikrimah:

“The polytheists said to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘Tell us about the nature of your Lord: what is He, and of what does He consist?’ So Allah revealed this surah.”

He also narrated it from Abū al-'Āliyah and from Jābir ibn 'Abd Allāh: Shurayh narrated to us: Ismā'īl ibn Mujāhid narrated to us, from al-Sha'bī, from Jābir; he then related the report.

He said: It has also been said that this was in response to a question from the Jews. Ibn Humayd narrated to us: Salamah narrated to us: Ibn Ishāq narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Sa'īd,

who said:

“A group of Jews came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘O Muhammad, Allah created all creation; who, then, created Him?’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, became so angry that his complexion changed. Then he lunged at them in anger for his Lord’s sake. Gabriel came to him, calmed him, and said, ‘Restrain yourself, O Muhammad.’ An answer to their question came to him from Allah. He said that Allah says: ‘Say: He is Allah, the One,’ through to the end of the surah. When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited it to them, they said, ‘Describe your Lord to us. What is His form like? What is His upper arm like? What is His forearm like? And what is His arm like?’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, became even angrier than before and lunged at them. Gabriel came to him and repeated his earlier words, bringing him the answer to their question. Allah then revealed: ‘They have not appraised Allah with true appraisal.’”

Al-Hakam ibn Ma'bad narrated in Kitāb al-Radd 'alā al-Jahmiyyah (The Refutation of the Jahmiyyah), saying: 'Abd Allāh ibn Muhammad ibn al-Nu'mān narrated to us: Salamah ibn Shabīb narrated to us: Yahyā ibn 'Abd Allāh narrated to me: Dirār narrated to me, from Abān, from Anas, who said:

“The Jews of Khaybar came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘O Abū al-Qāsim, Allah created the angels from the light of the veil, Adam from dark, altered clay, Iblīs from the flame of fire, heaven from smoke, and the earth from the foam of water. Tell us, then, about your Lord.’”

He said: “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not answer them. Gabriel came to him and said, ‘O Muhammad: “Say: He is Allah, the One; Allah, al-Samad. He neither begets nor is He begotten, and there is none comparable to Him.” He has no veins branching towards Him. Al-Samad is not hollow and does not eat

translated_text:
I say:

Etymology supports both views: that al-Samad is the One who has no cavity, and that He is the Master. It points more clearly to the first, however, for the first meaning underlies the second. In Arabic, the word samad is used of that which has no cavity.

Yahyā ibn Abī Kathīr said: “The angels have no cavities, whereas human beings are hollow.” In the hadith concerning Adam, Iblīs is reported to have said of him: “He is hollow, not solid.” Al-Jawharī said: “Musammad is a variant of musmat, meaning that which has no cavity.” He also said: “Simād is the covering over a bottle’s mouth,” and: “Samad denotes high, solid ground.” Abū al-Najm said:

“It leaves the high ground like the back of a saddle-sore camel.”

The fundamental meaning of this root is gathering together and strength. Thus, one says yasmudu al-māl, meaning “he gathers wealth together.” Likewise, sayyid (master) was originally saywid: the letters yā’ and wāw came together, with the first unvowelled, so the wāw was changed into yā’ and the two were assimilated. Similarly, mayyit (dead) was originally maywit. The root, as found in sawād (blackness) and su’dud (mastery), conveys the sense of gathering together, and black is the color that concentrates the gaze.

Allah Most High has said:

“Noble and chaste.”

Most of the early generations interpreted sayyidan (“noble”) as “forbearing.” This is also reported from al-Hasan, Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr, ‘Ikrimah, ‘Atā’, Abū al-Sha‘thā’, al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas, and Muqātil. Abū Rawq reported from al-Dahhāk that it means “one of good character.” Sālim reported from Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr that it means “the God-fearing.” A man does not become a master over others until he is himself self-possessed and steadfast in character.

translated_text:
‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar said:

“After the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I have seen no one who surpassed Mu‘āwiyah in the qualities of leadership.” He was asked, “Not even Abū Bakr or ‘Umar?” He replied, “Abū Bakr and ‘Umar were better than him, but after the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I have seen no one who surpassed Mu‘āwiyah in the qualities of leadership.”

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “He meant forbearing”—or he said, “generous.” Hence the saying:

“If ever you wish to lead a tribe,
Lead with forbearance, not haste and abuse.”

For this reason, a group of the early generations explained sayyid as one who leads his people in religion. Ibn Zayd said, “It means the noble.” Al-Zajjāj said, “One who surpasses his people in goodness.”

Ibn al-Anbārī said: “Sayyid here means a chief and a leader in goodness.” Ibn ‘Abbās and Mujāhid explained it as “one held in honour by his Lord,” while Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib explained it as “a jurist and scholar.”

It has already been mentioned that they call a bottle’s covering simād. Al-Jawharī said: “The ‘ifās is a piece of leather fitted over the head of a bottle. What goes inside its mouth, however, is the simām. The expression ‘afastu al-qārūrah means: ‘I fastened the covering over the bottle.’”

(I say:

In the authentic hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning lost property, he said:

“Then familiarize yourself with its container and its tie.”

The ‘ifās here means whatever holds the dirhams, such as a cloth in which they are tied. The wikā’ is something like the string used to tie it. This is of the same kind as the covering of a bottle. The words ‘afs, sadd, and samad

 كُلُّ مُمْسِكٍ عَنْ طَعَامٍ أَوْ كَلَامٍ أَوْ سَيْرٍ فَهُوَ صَائِمٌ لِأَنَّ الْإِمْسَاكَ فِيهِ اجْتِمَاعٌ وَالصَّائِمُ لَا يَدْخُلُ جَوْفَهُ شَيْءُ وَيُقَالُ صَامَ الْفَرَسُ إذَا قَامَ فِي غَيْرِ اعْتِلَافٍ.
 قَالَ النَّابِغَةُ:
 خَيْلٌ صِيَامٌ وَخَيْلٌ غَيْرُ صَائِمَةٍ تَحْتَ الْعَجَاجِ وَأُخْرَى تَعْلُكُ اللجما
translated_text:
and jam‘ (gathering) and su’dud (leadership) are similar in meaning: they all convey gathering together and strength. Food is described as ‘afs (astringent), possessing ‘ufūsah (astringency), meaning that it causes contraction. From this comes ‘afs, the gallnuts used to make ink.

Al-Jawharī said:

“It is a later coinage, not part of the speech of the desert Arabs.”

This does not detract from it, for they had no gallnuts to call by this name. Nevertheless, the designation accords with the principles of Arabic speech. The same applies to their calling what is inserted into a bottle’s mouth a simām (stopper), for this root conveys gathering together and sealing.

Al-Jawharī said: A bottle’s simām is its stopper. An asamm stone is hard and solid. An asamm man is one who cannot hear because his hearing is obstructed. A man described as simmah is brave; simmah also means a male snake. The samīm of something is its pure essence, into which nothing has entered to break it apart or weaken it. Thus one says samīm al-harr (the height of the heat), samīm al-bard (the depth of the cold), and “So-and-so is of the pure stock of his people.” A samsām is a sharp, cutting sword that does not bend. The expression sammama, used of travelling or other pursuits, means “he pressed on.” A man described as summ is stout.

Sawm (abstention) is related to this through broader etymological affinity, for sawm means refraining.

Abū ‘Ubaydah said:

“Anyone who refrains from food, speech, or travelling is sā’im.”

This is because refraining involves holding together, and nothing enters the interior of one who is fasting. One says sāma al-faras when a horse stands without feeding.

Al-Nābighah said:

“Some horses stand, others move beneath the dust,
And others champ their bits.”

translated_text:
The same applies to sadd (blocking), sadād (soundness), su’dud (leadership), and sawād (a mass). Likewise, the word samad conveys gathering together, and gathering together entails strength: the more closely something’s parts are joined, without gaps between them, the stronger it is compared with something containing empty spaces.

Thus, firm, elevated ground is called samad because of its strength, cohesion, and compactness. A man described as samad is a leader who is sought out. One may say qasadtuhu, qasadtu lahu, or qasadtu ilayhi, all meaning “I sought him out”; likewise, one may say masmūd, masmūd lahu, or masmūd ilayhi, meaning “one who is sought out.” People seek help with their needs only from someone who can meet them. Only someone who is composed, strong, and steadfast in himself can do this: a noble, generous leader. This contrasts with someone who is anxious and fretful, becoming distracted, agitated, and overwhelmed by the number and burden of their needs. Such a person is not a leader upon whom they can depend and to whom they turn for their needs.

They therefore called a human leader samad because he possesses the quality for which people seek him out to meet their needs. In their language, leadership does not have a merely relational meaning—as nearness and distance do. Rather, it denotes a quality inherent in the leader, on account of which people seek him out. Sayyid (leader) derives from su’dud (leadership) and sawād (a mass). Through broader etymological affinity, this belongs to the same family as sadād, for the Arabs interchange a weak letter and a doubled consonant.

For example, they say taqaddā al-bāzī and taqaddada, both meaning “the hawk swooped down.” A sādd is something that blocks or fills something else, leaving no empty space in it. From this come sidād al-qārūrah (a bottle’s stopper) and sidād al-thaghr (what closes an opening), both pronounced with an i vowel: that which closes the thing in question. {وَعَلَى اللَّهِ قَصْدُ السَّبِيلِ}
 أَيْ السَّبِيلُ الْقَصْدُ وَهُوَ السَّبِيلُ الْعَدْلُ: أَيْ إلَيْهِ تَنْتَهِي السَّبِيلُ الْعَادِلَةُ كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{إنَّ عَلَيْنَا لَلْهُدَى}
 أَيْ الْهُدَى إلَيْنَا
translated_text:
Allah Most High:

“Fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.”

They explained this as “upright and true.” Ibn ‘Abbās explained it as “correct”; Qatādah and Muqātil as “just”; and al-Suddī as “straight.” All these explanations are correct, for sound speech accords with what is right. If it conveys information, it is truthful, corresponding to what it reports without addition or omission. If it gives a command, it commands justice without excess or deficiency. Hence they explain sadād (soundness) in terms of qasd (uprightness), and qasd in terms of justice.

Al-Jawharī said:

“Tasdīd means enabling someone to attain sadād: correctness and uprightness in speech and action. A man is described as musaddad when he acts correctly and uprightly. Musaddad also means ‘straightened’; one says saddada rumhahu, ‘he straightened his spear.’ An affair described as sadīd or asadd is rightly directed. Istadda, said of something, means that it became straight.

“The poet said:

‘I teach him archery every day;
Then, when his arm aimed true, he shot at me.’

“Al-Asma‘ī said: ‘The reading ishtadda [grew strong], with the dotted sh, is of no account.’”

Their explanation of sadd (blocking) in terms of qasd shows that the word qasd carries the sense of gathering together and strength. Qasd means justice, just as it means soundness and correctness: exact correspondence and agreement, without excess or deficiency. This combines completeness with exact correspondence. From this comes the statement of Allah Most High:

“And upon Allah is the direction of the way.”

That is, the way characterized by qasd—the just way. This means that the just way leads to Him, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, upon Us is guidance.”

That is, guidance leads to Us.

translated_text:
This is the soundest interpretation of the two verses. The same applies to His statement, Most High:

“He said, ‘This is a straight path leading to Me.’”

Related to this through intermediate derivation is sidq (truthfulness), whose root letters are the same as those of qasd. This includes truthfulness in speech, because it corresponds to what is reported, as explained concerning sadād (soundness). Sadq, pronounced with a short a, describes a solid spear; it is also said to mean a straight one. Thus, it is straight and solid, with neither defect nor crookedness. A sundūq (box), whose plural is sanādīq, gathers together whatever is placed inside it.

Something that should be understood concerning derivation is that the statement “This is derived from that” has two meanings.

The first is that the two expressions correspond in wording and meaning, regardless of which expression the speakers of the language used first. In this sense, each expression is derived from the other, since what is meant is that they correspond in wording and meaning. This resembles saying, “This water is from that water,” or “This speech is from that speech.” Accordingly, whether one says that the verb is derived from the verbal noun or that the verbal noun is derived from the verb, both statements are correct. This is the sense of derivation supported by morphological evidence.

Minor derivation involves two expressions sharing the same letters in the same order; intermediate derivation involves their sharing the same letters, but not their order; and major derivation involves their sharing some identical letters, while the remaining letters agree in their class rather than their identity—for example, both being guttural letters. Thus, hazara, ʿazzara, and azara all convey strength and firmness. They also share with rā’, zāy, and hā’ the feature that the three are guttural letters.

Accordingly, if it is said that al-Samad means musmat (solid, without a cavity), and that it is derived from it in this sense, this is correct, since dāl is closely related to tā’. For samt means silence: refraining from speech and keeping the mouth closed.

Abū ʿUbayd said: “Musmat means something without a cavity. Asmattuhu means ‘I made it solid.’ A bāb musmat is a door that has been completely shut.”

A musmat horse is one of a single color, with no other color mixed into it. This is also the sense of Ibn ʿAbbās’s statement: “Only pure silk has been forbidden.”

Thus, musmad and musmat correspond through major derivation. The dāl has not changed from a tā’; rather, dāl is stronger, and musmad expresses its meaning more fully than musmat. The stronger the letter, the stronger its meaning, for the language of the Lord displays the utmost precision and harmony. This is why samt means refraining from speech despite

Among these related expressions, none is more complete than those formed from samad. It contains sād, mīm, and dāl, and each of these three letters possesses a distinction over its corresponding letters. The meanings conveyed by such letters are likewise more complete.

Related to these meanings is that of sabr (patience), for patience involves gathering oneself together and exercising restraint. Hence the definition: “Patience is restraining oneself from anguish.” One says sabara (“he was patient”) and sabbartuhu (“I made him patient”). This is also the sense of the Most High’s words:

Likewise, the meaning of “the master, al-Samad” is the opposite of being fretful and withholding. Related to this is subra, a heap of food, because it is gathered and piled together. Subāra means stones, while the sabr of something is its thickness.

“And when good touches him, he is withholding.”

Al-Jawharī said: “Hala‘ (anxiety) is the most extreme form of anguish.” Others said: “In linguistic usage, it means the most intense greed and the worst anguish.” Hence the Prophet’s saying (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“The worst traits in a person are panic-stricken avarice and unnerving cowardice.”

A she-camel is described as halū‘ when she is swift and nimble. A wolf is described as hali‘ bali‘: hali‘ refers to its greed, and bali‘ to its swallowing.

Thus, the explanations given by the early generations encompass these meanings. Ibn ‘Abbās is reported to have said: “It describes someone who is fretful when evil touches him and withholding when good touches him.” He is also reported to have said: “It describes someone who covets what is unlawful for him.” Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr explained it as “avaricious”; ‘Ikrima, “fretful”; Ja‘far, “greedy”; al-Hasan and al-Dahhāk, “stingy”; and Mujāhid, “voracious.” Al-Dahhāk also said: “The halū‘ is someone who is never satisfied.” Muqātil explained it as “constricted in heart,” and ‘Atā’ as “hasty.”

All these meanings are contrary to steadfastness, strength, collectedness, self-restraint, and patience. The Most High has said:

“The building they built will remain a source of doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are torn apart.”

Although this has been interpreted to mean that their hearts split apart and they die, it resembles expressions used in such circumstances: “His heart has split apart,” “My heart has become divided,” “My heart has become scattered,” and “My heart has been torn in different directions.” Hence it is said of fear: “It has scattered his heart.” Conversely, one says: “He is firm of heart,” “His heart is collected,” and “His heart is gathered together.”

 فَهُوَ حَدِيثٌ مَعْلُولٌ قَدَحَ فِيهِ أَئِمَّةُ الْحَدِيثِ كَالْبُخَارِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِ
translated_text:
Section

Allah Most High says:

“Say: He is Allah, One.”
“Allah, the Eternal Refuge.”

He prefixed the definite article al- to Samad (the Eternal Refuge), but not to ahad (One), because no existing being other than Allah Most High is called ahad in an affirmative statement when the word stands alone, without being joined to a following noun in a genitive construction. This differs from negative statements and constructions that function similarly, such as conditions and questions. Thus one says: “Is anyone with you?” and “If anyone comes to me from you, I will honour him.”

Otherwise, it is used only in simple counting: ahad, ithnān (one, two), and ahad ‘ashr (eleven). The first day is called yawm al-ahad (Sunday), for—according to the more correct of the two views—it was on that day that Allah began creating the heavens, the earth, and everything between them, as indicated by the Quran and authentic hadiths.

The Quran states in several places that He created the heavens, the earth, and everything between them in six days. It is established in an authentic hadith, whose authenticity is agreed upon, that Adam was the last creature to be created and that he was created on Friday. Since creation ended on Friday, it follows that it began on Sunday, because the days were six.

As for the hadith narrated by Muslim, which states:

“Allah created the soil on Saturday,”

it is a defective hadith whose authenticity was challenged by leading hadith scholars, including al-Bukhārī and others.

He thus judged this account authentic because he assumed the hadith was authentic, since Muslim had narrated it. Yet there are other instances of this: Muslim narrated hadiths known to contain errors, such as Abū Sufyān’s statement upon accepting Islam: “I wish to marry Umm Habībah to you.” There is no disagreement that the Prophet had married her before Abū Sufyān accepted Islam. Another example is what Muslim narrated through some chains of transmission of the hadith concerning the eclipse prayer: that the Prophet performed it with three or four bowings. The correct account is that he performed it only once, with two bowings. This is why al-Bukhārī included only this account, as did al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal—according to one of the two reports from him—and others.
