that is invalid, for those things are not efficient causes, but merely conditions. Moreover, what proceeds in those cases does not come from a single source, but from two sources; and what proceeds is an accident, not a self-subsisting substance.

It thus becomes clear that the supposed intellectual generation described by these people is among the things furthest removed from generation and emanation. It is even further removed than the claims of the Christians and the Arab polytheists. They have placed His effects on the same footing as an eternal attribute inseparable from His essence, whereas we have already explained that such a thing cannot be said to be generated from Him. Thus, in claiming divinity for the intellects, souls, and stars, they are more deeply steeped in disbelief than either of those groups.

If any among them who profess adherence to revealed religions identify these as al-Malakiyya, their claim that the angels are generated from Allah is worse than the claim of the Arabs and ordinary Christians. The latter affirmed physical generation, which His being al-Samad (the Self-Sufficient) rules out; nevertheless, what they affirmed is conceivable. These others, however, have alleged an intellectual generation that is false in every respect—even more untenable than the Christians’ claim that the Word is generated from the Essence. Rejecting what these people allege therefore takes precedence over rejecting what the others allege.

For something known to be impossible in external reality cannot be conceived as actually existing there, since its existence there is impossible. Rather, one mentally supposes its existence in external reality. This is possible only if it has something analogous to it in some respect, so that one posits something resembling it in external existence. The generation claimed by the Christians, and then by these philosophers, bears less resemblance to generation as we know it than does the generation claimed by some Arab polytheists and ordinary Christians and Jews. This intellectual generation is therefore more impossible than that physical generation. Physical generation is conceivable among self-subsisting entities, whereas intellectual generation is not conceivable among such entities at all.

Moreover, the former affirmed generation from two sources, which is an intelligible form of generation, whereas the latter affirmed generation from a single source. The former affirmed generation through the separation of a part, which is intelligible, whereas the latter affirmed generation without this, which is unintelligible. The former affirmed generation by analogy with the generation of self-subsisting entities from other such entities, whereas the latter affirmed it by analogy with accidents arising from self-subsisting entities. Thus, the former position is evidently closer to what is intelligible, yet it is false, as Allah has explained its falsity and condemned it. The latter position is therefore all the more deserving of rejection as false.

Likewise, if Allah declares someone a disbeliever for affirming a created being that is taken as an intercessor and worshipped besides Allah, then someone who affirms an eternally pre-existent being other than Allah, worshipped and taken as an intercessor, is all the more deserving of being judged a disbeliever. Allah has declared whoever denies the Resurrection a disbeliever even when he maintains that this world came into existence; someone who denies it while maintaining that the world is eternal is therefore greater in disbelief before Allah Most High.

These nations, further removed from Islam, through whom later Muslims have been tested, are worse than the nations through whom the earliest Muslims were tested. This is because the Muslims then were more accomplished and greater in knowledge and religious commitment. When tested by peoples superior to these, the Muslims would overcome them through their superior knowledge and religious commitment. As for these later peoples, although the Muslims fall short of their predecessors, their superiority to these peoples is evident because those peoples are so far removed from Islam.

Yet when religious innovations proliferated among later Muslims, some of these peoples gained ascendancy over them and confused them about their religion. The philosophers’ specious arguments came to seem more formidable to these Muslims than to others, just as fighting the disbelieving Turks seemed more formidable to the people of that age than fighting their predecessors. For they were tested by the swords of those disbelievers and the tongues of those philosophers, while deficiencies in their faith had brought about weakness in knowledge and jihad. The same was true of many Arabs in the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: the two cases are alike.

Further evidence of this is that the pagan Arabs, Jews and Christians affirm that Allah created the heavens and the earth by His will and power. Indeed, they say that He created them in six days. These philosophers, however, hold that He did not bring them into existence after they had not existed, let alone create them in six days. They then mislead Muslims by saying, “The world came into being,” meaning by its origination that it is the effect of an eternal cause. This amounts to saying that it is generated from Allah Most High. Yet this is a notion that has no reality and is unintelligible.

Moreover, the pagan Arabs and the People of the Book acknowledge the angels, although many of them regard angels and devils as a single kind of being: any angel who ceases to obey Allah is cast down and becomes a devil. They deny that Iblīs was the father of the jinn, and that jinn marry, are born, eat and drink. Yet these Christians who deny this, despite their disbelief, are better than these philosophers. For these philosophers recognize no reality to angels beyond the intellects and souls they affirm, or accidents inhering in bodies, such as good powers.

The same applies to the jinn: most of the former peoples affirm their existence, for the Arabs acknowledged the jinn, as do most of the People of the Book. These philosophers, however, do not acknowledge their existence, and regard devils as corrupt powers.

Furthermore, the pagan Arabs, along with the People of the Book, supplicate to Allah and affirm that He hears their supplications and answers them. These philosophers, however, hold that He knows none of the particulars of the world, nor does He hear anyone’s supplication

nor does He answer anyone or bring anything new into existence in the world. In their view, nothing causes events to occur except the movements of the celestial sphere. Supplication, they hold, has an effect because it is the rational soul’s action upon the prime matter of the world. The Sahīh records a hadith narrated by Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ‘The son of Adam has reviled Me, though he ought not to do so, and the son of Adam has denied Me, though he ought not to do so. His reviling Me is his saying that I have taken a son, whereas I am the One, the Self-Sufficient: I have not begotten, nor was I begotten, and none is equal to Me. His denying Me is his saying, “He will not bring me back as He first created me,” yet creating him the first time is no easier for Me than bringing him back.’”

This undoubtedly encompasses the unbelieving Arabs who made both claims, as Allah Most High says:

“Man says, ‘When I am dead, will I really be brought forth alive?’”

And thereafter:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a son.’ You have indeed uttered something monstrous. The heavens almost rupture because of it.”

Allah thus mentions both claims. Yet these texts apply to these philosophers with even greater force, for they deny both the resurrection and the initial creation. They do not affirm that Allah first brought the heavens and the earth into existence, nor that humanity had a beginning, with Adam as the first human.

As for reviling Him by saying that He has taken a son, these philosophers hold that the entire celestial sphere is a necessary consequence of His existence and an effect caused by Him, bound to Him more necessarily than a child is bound to its parent. A parent has choice and power in bringing a child into existence, whereas, according to these philosophers, Allah has neither will nor power concerning the celestial sphere’s necessary dependence upon Him. Indeed, He cannot even prevent it from necessarily proceeding from Him. The generation they affirm is thus more extreme than the generation found among created beings. They do not say that He has taken a son through His power, for He is unable

Even if they call it “cause and effect,” on close examination their position amounts to nothing definite, for their doctrine contains greater contradictions and errors than that of the Christians.

A group of speculative theologians have observed that their doctrine of cause and effect is of the same kind as others’ doctrine of parent and offspring. Their intention was to place both groups in the same category of blameworthiness. Yet this falls far short of the mark: the latter are better than these philosophers. If you closely examine the statements of those among these philosophers who are nearest to Islam, such as Ibn Rushd the grandson, you will find that, at most, they make the Lord a condition for the world’s existence, not the agent who brings it into being.

The same applies to those heretical Sufis who follow their path and claim penetrating understanding, such as Ibn ‘Arabī and Ibn Sab‘īn. Their doctrine really amounts to saying that this world is a necessarily existent, beginningless being, with no maker other than itself. They say, “Existence is one.” What their doctrine really means is that there is no Creator who has created another being. Their statements concerning resurrection, prophethood, and divine oneness are worse than those of the Jews, Christians, and idol-worshippers, for these people permit the worship of every idol in the world; they do not restrict worship to particular idols.

 أَصْلُ الصَّمَدِ الِاجْتِمَاعُ وَمِنْهُ تَصْمِيدُ الْمَالِ وَهَذَا إنَّمَا يُعْقَلُ فِي الْجِسْمِ الْمُجْتَمِعُ وَأَمَّا الْنُّفَاةِ فَقَالُوا: الصَّمَدُ الَّذِي لَا يَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ التَّفَرُّقُ وَالِانْقِسَامُ وَكُلُّ جِسْمٍ فِي الْعَالَمِ يَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ التَّفَرُّقُ وَالِانْقِسَامُ.
 وَقَالُوا أَيْضًا:
 الْأَحَدُ الَّذِي لَا يَقْبَلُ التَّجَزُّؤَ وَالِانْقِسَامَ وَكُلُّ جِسْمٍ فِي الْعَالَمِ يَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ التَّفَرُّقُ وَالتَّجَزُّىءُ وَالِانْقِسَامُ.
 وَقَالُوا:
translated_text:
Section

Sūrat al-Ikhlās has been invoked as evidence by two groups among the proponents of innovated speculative theology: those who say that the Lord Most High is a body, such as some who agreed with Hishām ibn al-Hakam, Muhammad ibn Karrām, and others; and those who deny this and say that He is not a body, among those who agreed with Jahm ibn Safwān, Abū al-Hudhayl al-‘Allāf, and others like them.

The former argued: “He is al-Samad, and al-Samad has no internal cavity. This applies only to solid bodies, which have no internal cavity, such as mountains, rocks, and columns made of stone. Likewise, it has been said: ‘The angels are solid.’ For this reason, it has been said that nothing comes out of Him or enters Him, that He neither eats nor drinks, and so forth. Denying these things is conceivable only with regard to something that is a body.”

They also said: “The root meaning of samad is gathering together, as in the expression tasmīd al-māl (amassing wealth). This can be conceived only in a body formed by aggregation.”

As for those who deny that He is a body, they argued: “Al-Samad is the One for whom separation and division are impossible, whereas every body in the world is capable of separation and division.”

They also said: “Al-Ahad (the One) does not admit of partition or division, whereas every body in the world is capable of separation, partition, and division.”

They further said:

translated_text:
“If you say that He is a body, He would be a composite assembled from indivisible atoms or from matter and form. Whatever is composed and assembled from things other than itself depends upon them. Yet He—glory be to Him—is al-Samad, and al-Samad is the One who has no need of anything besides Himself. Thus, a composite cannot be al-Samad.”

The response is as follows:

The claim that He—glory be to Him—is a composite assembled from parts, and that He admits of partition, division, and separation, is false according to both revelation and reason. This contradicts His being al-Samad, as explained above. This applies whether one means that the parts were separate and then came together, or says that they have always been joined together but can be separated from one another, as with the human body and other bodies. For although a person’s limbs have been joined together from the outset, some can be separated from others. Allah—glory be to Him—is exalted above that.

For this reason, we stated earlier that He possesses the perfection of being al-Samad. Such separation is possible only for something a part of which can perish or cease to exist. Whatever admits of nonexistence and extinction is neither necessarily existent in itself nor eternal and without beginning, for whatever is necessarily eternal cannot cease to exist. The same applies to His attributes, which He has always possessed and which are inseparable from His essence: that which is inseparable cannot cease to exist unless that from which it is inseparable also ceases to exist.

Hence some of the early Muslims said: “Al-Samad is the Everlasting, the One who remains after His creation passes away.” This necessarily follows from His being al-Samad. Were He capable of ceasing to exist, His being al-Samad would not be inseparable from Him; rather, it could cease, so He would no longer be al-Samad; nor

 فَهَذَا مَذْهَبُ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ لَهُمْ بِإِحْسَانِ وَأَئِمَّةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَأَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ وَالْجَمَاعَةِ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الطَّوَائِفِ. وَالْخِلَافُ فِي ذَلِكَ مَشْهُورٌ مَعَ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ
translated_text:
could His being al-Samad cease unless nonexistence were possible for Him, which is impossible. Thus, He necessarily possesses the quality of being al-Samad only if it is inseparable from Him, and this precludes His nonexistence. He does necessarily possess this quality; He did not become al-Samad after not having been so—exalted and holy is He—for that would imply that He had been in separate parts and was then assembled, and that He was something made, brought into existence, and fashioned. These are characteristics of His creatures.

As for the Creator, who is eternal without beginning, it is impossible for Him to be nonexistent, to have been made, or to need anything besides Himself in any respect. None of these things is therefore possible for Him. It follows that He has always been al-Samad and will always remain al-Samad. Thus, it cannot be said that He was in separate parts and then came together, or that He could become separated, or even that anything could come out of Him or enter Him.

This is agreed upon among the various Muslim groups, both those adhering to the Sunnah and those following innovations. Although some ignorant or uninformed individuals may say otherwise, the corrupt imaginings of such people know no bounds. Likewise, no Muslim group maintains that He was begotten or that He begets, although some disbelievers have said this. Indeed, those who profess philosophy and affiliate themselves with Islam have made statements concerning generation and causation that are worse than what those disbelievers said.

As for affirming His attributes, that He will be seen in the Hereafter, that He speaks the Quran and other words, and that His speech is uncreated—this is the position of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, the imams of the Muslims, and Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah across all their groups. The disagreement over this with the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah is well known

and many of the philosophers and the Bātiniyyah. These people say that affirming the attributes entails His being a body; yet He is not a body, so no attributes can be affirmed of Him.

They say: “For attributes, as we can conceive them, are accidents inhering in a body, and an attribute of His cannot be conceived otherwise.”

They say: “Seeing can only be conceived as direct visual observation. Such observation is possible only if what is seen is in a direction, and only a body can be in a direction.”

They say: “Moreover, if speech or anything else inhered in Him, this would necessarily mean that He is a body. Thus, the speech attributed to Him can only be something created and separate from Him.”

These were among the arguments they used in debating Imam Ahmad during the “Inquisition.” Among those who argued that the Quran was created on the grounds of rejecting corporeality was Abū ‘Īsā Muhammad ibn ‘Īsā Burghūth, a pupil of Husayn al-Najjār. He was one of the foremost speculative theologians. Ibn Abī Du’ād had assembled to debate Imam Ahmad as many speculative theologians from Basra, Baghdad, and elsewhere as he could who maintained that the Quran was created.

This position was not exclusive to the Mu‘tazilah, as some people suppose. Many—or indeed most—of those speculative theologians were not Mu‘tazilah. Bishr al-Marīsī was not one of the Mu‘tazilah either. Rather, they included Najjāriyyah, among them Burghūth, and Dirāriyyah. Hafs al-Fard, who debated al-Shāfi‘ī, belonged to the Dirāriyyah, the followers of Dirār ibn ‘Amr. They also included Murji’ah, among them Bishr al-Marīsī. Du’ād was not a Mu‘tazilī; rather, he was a Jahmī who denied the attributes. The Mu‘tazilah also deny the attributes, so the attribute-denying Jahmiyyah are a broader category than the Mu‘tazilah. When Burghūth argued against Ahmad that, if Allah spoke and speech inhered in Him, He would be a body—which is denied of Him—Ahmad and others like him among the early generations knew that these expressions introduced by speculative theologians, such as “body” and others, were denied by some in order to deny what Allah Most High and His Messenger had affirmed, and affirmed by others in order to affirm what Allah and His Messenger had denied.

The first approach is that of the Jahmiyyah, including the Mu‘tazilah and others. They deny that Allah is a body so that Muslims will imagine that their purpose is to declare Him free of imperfection. What they mean, however, is that Allah will not be seen in the Hereafter; that He did not speak the Quran or anything else, but instead created speech in something other than Himself; and that He has no knowledge, power, life, or other attributes inhering in Him.

Imam Ahmad said in the introduction to his Refutation of the Jahmiyyah and the Heretics:

“Praise be to Allah, who, in every interval between messengers, has preserved a remnant of people of knowledge who call those who have gone astray to guidance and patiently endure the harm they inflict. Through Allah’s Book they bring the dead to life, and through His light they give sight to the blind. How many a victim of Satan they have revived, and how many a lost wanderer they have guided! How good their effect upon people, and how evil people’s treatment of them! They defend Allah’s Book against the distortions of extremists, the false claims of the purveyors of falsehood, and the misinterpretations of the ignorant—those who have raised the banners of religious innovation and let loose the reins of discord.

and so they disagree over the Book, oppose the Book, and unite in opposing the Book. They make claims about Allah and speak about Him and His Book without knowledge. They use ambiguous language and deceive the ignorant through the confusion they create. We therefore seek refuge in Allah from the trials caused by those who lead others astray.”

The second approach is that of Hishām and his followers. It is reported that they affirmed of Allah what He has declared Himself free of: imperfections and resemblance to created beings. Imam Ahmad answered them by following the way of the prophets and their followers: holding firmly to the rope of Allah, concerning which Allah said:

“O you who believe, fear Allah as He should be feared, and do not die except as Muslims.”

“And hold firmly, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not become divided.”

He also said:

“Mankind was one community. Then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and as warners, and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between people concerning their differences. None differed over it except those who had been given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual rivalry. Then Allah, by His permission, guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they had differed. And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Alif Lām Mīm Sād.”

“A Book has been sent down to you—so let there be no distress in your heart because of it—that you may warn through it, and as a reminder to the believers.”

“Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow any protectors besides Him. How little you take heed!”

Allah Most High also said:

“If guidance comes to you from Me, then whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer misery.”

“But whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a life of hardship, and We will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection.”

“He will say, ‘My Lord, why have You raised me blind

when I could once see?’”

“He will say, ‘Just as Our signs came to you and you forgot them, so today you will be forgotten.’”

Allah Most High also said:

“O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and leads to the finest outcome.”

Allah Most High also said:

“O you who believe, do not put yourselves ahead of Allah and His Messenger, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.”

“O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another, lest your deeds become worthless without your realizing it.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Have you not seen those who claim to believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you? They wish to seek judgment from false authorities, although they were commanded to reject them. Satan wishes to lead them far astray.”

“When they are told, ‘Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger,’ you see the hypocrites turn resolutely away from you.”

“How will it be when a calamity befalls them because of what their own hands have done, and then they come to you, swearing by Allah, ‘We intended only goodwill and reconciliation’?”

“Those are the ones whose hearts Allah knows. So turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them in words that reach their hearts.”

“We have not sent any messenger except to be obeyed, by Allah’s permission. If, when they wronged themselves, they had come to you and sought Allah’s forgiveness, and the Messenger had sought forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah ever Accepting of repentance, Most Merciful.”

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes and then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided

and submit fully.”

Allah Most High also said:

“And this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow other paths, for they will lead you away from His path.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Indeed, those who have divided their religion and become sects—you have nothing to do with them. Their affair rests only with Allah; then He will inform them of what they used to do.”

Allah Most High also said:

“So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth—the natural disposition upon which Allah created mankind. There is no changing Allah’s creation. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.”

“Turn to Him in repentance, fear Him, establish prayer, and do not be among those who associate partners with Him.”

“Among those who divided their religion and became sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has.”

He also said:

“He has ordained for you the same religion that He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We have revealed to you, and that which We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: uphold the religion and do not become divided over it.”

These texts and others make clear that Allah sent the messengers and revealed the scriptures to distinguish truth from falsehood and clarify the matters over which people differed. They show that people must follow what has been sent down to them from their Lord and refer their disputes to the Quran and the Sunnah; that whoever does not follow this is a hypocrite; that whoever follows the guidance brought by the messengers will neither go astray nor suffer misery; and that whoever turns away from it will be gathered blind, astray, wretched, and subjected to punishment. They also show that Allah and His Messenger have disavowed those who divided their religion.

to the Quran and the Sunnah and followed what had been sent down to them from their Lord. This means examining the matter: whatever we find the Lord has affirmed for Himself in His Book, we affirm; and whatever we find He has denied of Himself, we deny. Every term found in the Quran and the Sunnah in an affirmative statement is affirmed, and every term found in a negative statement is negated.

As for terms that occur neither in the Quran and the Sunnah nor in the words of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, or the other imams of the Muslims—whether in affirmation or negation—and over which people have disputed, these terms are neither affirmed nor denied until their meanings have been investigated. If their meanings belong to what the Lord has affirmed for Himself, they are affirmed; and if they belong to what the Lord has denied of Himself, they are denied.

If we find that a term is used to affirm both truth and falsehood, or to deny both truth and falsehood, or that it is ambiguous and admits both true and false meanings, with its user intending only some of them, yet its unqualified use misleads people or conveys to them both what he intended and what he did not intend, then such terms must not be affirmed or denied without qualification. Examples include the terms “substance,” “body,” “occupying space,” “direction,” and other expressions of this kind. Rarely does anyone use them in affirmation or negation without introducing falsehood into them, even if he intends something true.

The early generations and the imams disapproved of this newly introduced discourse because it includes falsehood, lies, and speaking about Allah without knowledge. of that is forbidden by Allah and His Messenger. The early generations did not disapprove of these expressions merely because they were technical conventions, nor did they disapprove of reasoning from sound evidence brought by the Messenger. Rather, they disapproved of false statements contrary to the Quran and the Sunnah. Whatever contradicts the Quran and the Sunnah is false and cannot be substantiated by either reason or revelation.

Thus, when Abū al-‘Abbās ibn Surayj was asked about Allah’s oneness, he explained the Muslims’ affirmation of His oneness, then said:

“As for the affirmation of Allah’s oneness by the people of falsehood, it consists of delving into substances and accidents. Allah sent the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to reject that.”

He did not mean that the Prophet rejected these two terms, for they had not yet been introduced in his time. Rather, he meant the rejection of the false meanings intended by them. The first to introduce these terms were the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah. Their purpose was to deny Allah’s attributes, or that He can be seen, or that He possesses speech as an attribute. The Jahmiyyah also denied His names.

The first person known to have denied these things was al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham, whom Khālid ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Qasrī sacrificed at Wāsit. He said:

“O people, offer your sacrifices—may Allah accept your sacrifices—for I am sacrificing al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham. He claims that Allah did not take Abraham as a close friend and did not truly speak to Moses. Exalted is Allah, far above what al-Ja‘d says!”

Then he came down and slaughtered him. The statements of the early generations and the imams condemning this speculative theology and its adherents are set out at length elsewhere.

original_text:
وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا:

translated_text:
The point here is that when the people of innovation presented the imams of the Sunnah, such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, with ambiguous terms such as “body,” “substance,” “spatial location,” and the like, they would agree neither to affirm them unconditionally nor to deny them unconditionally. The people of innovation, by contrast, introduced terms and meanings involving either negation or affirmation, and made them the definitive rational foundation that must be believed and built upon. They then examined the Quran and the Sunnah: whatever they could reinterpret to fit their own position, they reinterpreted; otherwise, they said, “These are ambiguous, problematic expressions whose intended meaning we do not know.”

Thus, they made their innovations a definitive foundation and made what the Messenger brought subordinate to it, treating it as problematic whenever it did not accord with that foundation. This is the approach of the Jahmiyyah, the Qadariyyah, and their like, as well as that of the heretics among the esoteric philosophers. All their books follow this method. Recognizing the difference between these two approaches is among the most important means of distinguishing the straight path with which Allah sent His Messenger from the paths that oppose it.

The same principle applies to scholarly questions of jurisprudence, questions concerning the deeds of the heart and their realities, and other matters. Newly introduced terms and meanings, as well as terms and meanings admitting more than one interpretation, have entered all these fields. It is therefore obligatory to make the Book and wisdom that Allah has revealed the foundation in all these matters, then refer people’s statements back to that foundation, and clarify which meanings contained in ambiguous expressions accord with the Quran and the Sunnah and are therefore to be accepted, and which meanings they contain

original_text: الْمُخَالَفَةِ لِلْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ فَتُرَدُّ. وَلِهَذَا كُلُّ طَائِفَةٍ أَنُكِرَ عَلَيْهَا مَا ابْتَدَعَتْ احْتَجَّتْ بِمَا ابْتَدَعَتْهُ الْأُخْرَى كَمَا يُوجَدُ فِي أَلْفَاظِ أَهْل الرَّأْيِ وَالْكَلَامِ وَالتَّصَوُّفِ وَإِنَّمَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُقَالَ فِي بَعْضِ الْآيَاتِ إنَّهُ مُشْكِلٌ وَمُتَشَابِهٌ إذَا ظَنَّ أَنَّهُ يُخَالِفُ غَيْرَهُ مِنْ الْآيَاتِ الْمُحْكَمَةِ الْبَيِّنَةِ فَإِذَا جَاءَتْ نُصُوصٌ بَيِّنَةٌ مُحْكَمَةٌ بِأَمْرِ وجَاءَ نَصٌّ آخَرُ يَظُنُّ أَنَّ ظَاهِرَهُ يُخَالِفُ ذَلِكَ يُقَالُ فِي هَذَا إنَّهُ يَرُدُّ الْمُتَشَابِهَ إلَى الْمُحْكَمِ أَمَّا إذَا نَطَقَ الْكِتَابُ أَوْ السُّنَّةُ بِمَعْنَى وَاحِدٍ لَمْ يَجُزْ أَنْ يُجْعَلَ مَا يُضَادُّ ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى هُوَ الْأَصْلُ وَيَجْعَلَ مَا فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَالسُّنَّةِ مُشْكِلًا مُتَشَابِهًا فَلَا يُقْبَلُ مَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ. نَعَمْ قَدْ يُشْكِلُ عَلَى كَثِيرٍ مِنْ النَّاسِ نُصُوصٌ لَا يَفْهَمُونَهَا فَتَكُونُ مُشْكِلَةً بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَيْهِمْ لِعَجْزِ فَهِمَهُمْ عَنْ مَعَانِيهَا وَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ فِي الْقُرْآنِ مَا يُخَالِفُ صَرِيحَ الْعَقْلِ وَالْحِسِّ إلَّا وَفِي الْقُرْآنِ بَيَانُ مَعْنَاهُ فَإِنَّ الْقُرْآنَ جَعَلَهُ اللَّهُ شِفَاءً لِمَا فِي الصُّدُورِ وَبَيَانًا لِلنَّاسِ فَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ بِخِلَافِ ذَلِكَ؛ لَكِنَّ قَدْ تَخْفَى آثَارُ الرِّسَالَةِ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَمْكِنَةِ وَالْأَزْمِنَةِ حَتَّى لَا يَعْرِفُونَ مَا جَاءَ بِهِ الرَّسُول صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ. إمَّا أَنْ لَا يَعْرِفُوا اللَّفْظَ وَإِمَّا أَنْ يَعْرِفُوا اللَّفْظَ وَلَا يَعْرِفُوا مَعْنَاهُ فَحِينَئِذٍ يَصِيرُونَ فِي جَاهِلِيَّةٍ بِسَبَبِ عَدَمِ نُورِ النُّبُوَّةِ وَمِنْ هَهُنَا يَقَعُ الشِّرْكُ وَتَفْرِيقُ الدِّينِ شِيَعًا كَالْفِتَنِ الَّتِي تُحْدِثُ السَّيْفَ فَالْفِتَنُ الْقَوْلِيَّةُ وَالْعَمَلِيَّةُ
translated_text:
contradict the Quran and the Sunnah and are therefore to be rejected. Thus, whenever a group is challenged over its innovations, it cites another group’s innovations in its own defense, as can be seen in the terminology used by adherents of juristic opinion, speculative theology, and Sufism.

A verse may be described as problematic and ambiguous only when it is thought to conflict with other clear, unambiguous verses. If clear, unambiguous texts establish something, and another text appears whose apparent meaning is thought to contradict it, this is a case in which the ambiguous must be referred back to the unambiguous. But when the Quran or the Sunnah expresses a single meaning, it is impermissible to make the opposite meaning the foundation, then treat what is in the Quran and the Sunnah as problematic and ambiguous, thereby rejecting what they indicate.

Admittedly, many people may find certain texts difficult because they do not understand them. Such texts are problematic relative to those people because their understanding falls short of grasping their meanings. Nothing in the Quran can contradict plain reason or sensory perception without the Quran itself explaining its meaning. Allah has made the Quran a healing for what is in people’s hearts and a clarification for mankind, so it cannot be otherwise.

Yet traces of the prophetic message may become obscure in certain places and times, until people no longer know what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. They may be unfamiliar with its wording, or they may know the wording without understanding its meaning. They then fall into a state of jāhiliyyah (ignorance) because the light of prophethood is absent. From this arise polytheism and the division of religion into sects, as with the strife that leads to armed conflict. Thus, strife in word and deed

هِيَ مِنْ الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ بِسَبَبِ خَفَاءِ نُورِ النُّبُوَّةِ عَنْهُمْ كَمَا قَالَ مَالِكُ بْنُ أَنَسٍ:

 وَلِهَذَا شُبِّهَتْ الْفِتَنُ بِقِطَعِ اللَّيْلِ الْمُظْلِمِ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ أَحْمَد فِي خُطْبَتِهِ:
 الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي جَعَلَ فِي كُلِّ زَمَانٍ فَتْرَةً بَقَايَا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ.
 فَالْهُدَى الْحَاصِلُ لِأَهْلِ الْأَرْضِ إنَّمَا هُوَ مِنْ نُورِ النُّبُوَّةِ كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{فَإِمَّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ مِنِّي هُدًى فَمَنِ اتَّبَعَ هُدَايَ فَلَا يَضِلُّ وَلَا يَشْقَى}
 فَأَهْلُ الْهُدَى وَالْفَلَاحِ: هُمْ الْمُتَّبِعُونَ لِلْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَهُمْ الْمُسْلِمُونَ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ فِي كُلِّ زَمَانٍ وَمَكَانٍ.
 وَأَهْلُ الْعَذَابِ وَالضَّلَالِ:
 هُمْ الْمُكَذِّبُونَ لِلْأَنْبِيَاءِ يَبْقَى أَهْلُ الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يَصِلُ إلَيْهِمْ مَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ الْأَنْبِيَاءُ.
 فَهَؤُلَاءِ فِي ضَلَالٍ وَجَهْلٍ وَشِرْكٍ وَشَرٍّ لَكِنَّ اللَّهَ يَقُولُ:
 
{وَمَا كُنَّا مُعَذِّبِينَ حَتَّى نَبْعَثَ رَسُولًا}
 وَقَالَ: 
{رُسُلًا مُبَشِّرِينَ وَمُنْذِرِينَ لِئَلَّا يَكُونَ لِلنَّاسِ عَلَى اللَّهِ حُجَّةٌ بَعْدَ الرُّسُلِ}
 وَقَالَ: 
{وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ مُهْلِكَ الْقُرَى حَتَّى يَبْعَثَ فِي أُمِّهَا رَسُولًا يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِنَا وَمَا كُنَّا مُهْلِكِي الْقُرَى إلَّا وَأَهْلُهَا ظَالِمُونَ}
 فَهَؤُلَاءِ لَا يُهْلِكُهُمْ اللَّهُ وَيُعَذِّبُهُمْ حَتَّى يُرْسِلَ إلَيْهِمْ رَسُولًا. وَقَدْ رُوِيَتْ آثَارٌ مُتَعَدِّدَةٌ فِي أَنَّ مِنْ لَمْ تَبْلُغْهُ الرِّسَالَةُ فِي الدُّنْيَا فَإِنَّهُ يُبْعَثُ إلَيْهِ رَسُولٌ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ فِي عَرَصَاتِ الْقِيَامَةِ.
translated_text:
is a manifestation of jāhiliyyah because the light of prophethood is obscured from them. As Mālik ibn Anas said:

“When knowledge diminishes, harshness appears; and when transmitted reports diminish, whims prevail.”

This is why tribulations have been likened to stretches of a dark night, and why Ahmad said in his address:

“Praise be to Allah, who has preserved remnants of the people of knowledge in every interval between prophetic missions.”

Whatever guidance the people of the earth possess comes only from the light of prophethood. As Allah Most High says:

“If guidance comes to you from Me, then whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer.”

Those who attain guidance and success are the followers of the prophets: the Muslims and believers in every time and place. Those who suffer punishment and go astray are those who reject the prophets.

There remain those living in jāhiliyyah whom the teachings brought by the prophets have not reached. They are in a state of misguidance, ignorance, polytheism, and evil. Yet Allah says:

“We would never punish until We had sent a messenger.”

And He says:

“Messengers bearing good news and warnings, so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers.”

And He says:

“Your Lord would never destroy the towns until He had sent to their principal town a messenger reciting Our verses to them. Nor would We destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers.”

Thus, Allah does not destroy or punish these people until He sends a messenger to them. Numerous reports have been transmitted stating that those whom the message did not reach in this world will have a messenger sent to them on the Day of Resurrection, on the plains of the Resurrection.

original_text:
وَقَدْ زَعَمَ بَعْضُهُمْ أَنَّ هَذَا يُخَالِفُ دِين الْمُسْلِمِينَ؛
 فَإِنَّ الْآخِرَةَ لَا تَكْلِيفَ فِيهَا وَلَيْسَ كَمَا قَالَ إنَّمَا يَنْقَطِعُ التَّكْلِيفُ إذَا دَخَلُوا دَارَ الْجَزَاءِ الْجَنَّةَ أَوْ النَّارَ وَإِلَّا فَهُمْ فِي قُبُورِهِمْ مُمْتَحَنُونَ وَمَفْتُونُونَ يُقَالُ لِأَحَدِهِمْ:

Some, however, have claimed that this contradicts the religion of the Muslims, on the grounds that there are no religious obligations in the Hereafter. This is not correct. Such obligations cease only when people enter the abode of recompense—Paradise or Hell. Before that, they are tested and tried in their graves. Each person is asked:

“Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your prophet?”

Likewise, on the plains of the Resurrection, it will be said:

“Let every people follow what they used to worship.”

Those who worshipped the sun will follow the sun; those who worshipped the moon will follow the moon; and those who worshipped false deities will follow those false deities. This community will remain, including its hypocrites. Allah will then come to them in a form different from the form in which they saw Him the first time, and He will say, “I am your Lord.” They will reply, “We seek refuge in Allah from you. We shall remain here until our Lord comes to us.” According to another narration, He questions them and makes them steadfast.

This is a test for them: will they follow anyone other than the Lord whom they recognized as Allah, who manifested Himself to them the first time? Allah Most High makes them steadfast during this trial, just as He makes them steadfast during the trial of the grave. When they do not follow Him because He has come in a form other than the one they recognize, He then comes to them in the form they recognize and uncovers a shin. When they see Him, they fall down before Him in prostration, except for anyone who was a hypocrite: he will wish to prostrate but will be unable to do so, his back remaining rigid like a platter.

This meaning is widely transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in several authentic hadiths narrated by Abū Hurayrah and Abū Sa'īd, both recorded in the two Sahīh collections. It is also narrated from Jābir—and Muslim has related it—and from Ibn Mas'ūd and Abū Mūsā, as is well known through the narrations of Ahmad and others. This demonstrates

that trials cease only when they enter the abode of recompense; before that, there is testing and trial.

When people are deprived of the light of prophethood, they fall into the darkness of tribulations. Religious innovations and wickedness arise, and evil spreads among them. As authentically reported, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I asked my Lord for three things. He granted me two and withheld the third. I asked Him not to destroy my community through a widespread famine, and He granted me that. I asked Him not to give an enemy from outside their ranks power to wipe them out, and He granted me that. I asked Him not to turn their violence against one another, but He withheld that from me.”

The word ba’s (violence) is derived from bu’s (misery). Allah Most High says:

“Say: He has the power to send punishment upon you from above you or from beneath your feet, or to divide you into factions and make you taste one another’s violence.”

The two Sahīh collections report concerning the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When the words of Allah Most High were revealed, ‘Say: He has the power to send punishment upon you from above you,’ he said, ‘I seek refuge in Your Face.’ At ‘or from beneath your feet,’ he said, ‘I seek refuge in Your Face.’ At ‘or to divide you into factions and make you taste one another’s violence,’ he said, ‘These two are less severe.’”

This demonstrates that they will inevitably be divided into factions and made to taste one another’s violence, while the Messenger has no part in this state of affairs, and they are then in a state of pre-Islamic ignorance. Mālik narrated through his reliable chain of transmission that ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, used to say: “People have abandoned acting upon this verse,” meaning the words of Allah Most High:

“And if two groups of believers fight, make peace between them.”

When the Muslims fought one another, the duty was to reconcile them, as Allah Most High had commanded. When this was not done, civil strife and a state of pre-Islamic ignorance ensued.

The same applies to disputed questions over which the Muslim community has differed, whether concerning fundamentals or subsidiary matters. Unless these are referred back to Allah and the Messenger, the truth concerning them will not become clear. Instead, those disputing them will lack clear guidance concerning their affairs. If Allah has mercy on them, they will allow one another to hold their respective views without wronging one another. Such was the conduct of the Companions during the caliphates of ‘Umar and ‘Uthmān: they differed over certain questions open to independent scholarly judgment, yet allowed one another to hold their views without transgressing against one another.

If they are not shown mercy, however, blameworthy discord arises among them, and they wrong one another, either through words—such as declaring one another unbelievers or defiantly sinful—or through actions, such as imprisonment, beating, and killing. This is the condition of people of religious innovation and injustice, such as the Khawārij and their like: they wrong the Muslim community and transgress against its members when they dispute with them over certain religious questions.

The same applies to all the other followers of desires: they introduce an innovation and declare anyone who disagrees with them about it an unbeliever, as do the Rāfidah, the Mu‘tazilah, the Jahmiyyah, and others. Those who subjected people to an inquisition over the createdness of the Quran belonged to this category: they introduced an innovation and declared those who disagreed with them about it unbelievers

and deemed it lawful to withhold their rights and punish them.

When some of what Allah sent the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, with remains unknown to people, they are either just or unjust. The just person acts upon whatever teachings of the prophets have reached him and does not wrong others; the unjust person transgresses against others. These people commit injustice while knowing that they are doing so, as Allah Most High says:

“And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided until after the clear evidence had come to them.”

Had they instead followed the justice they knew, they would have allowed one another to hold their respective views. Such is the case with followers of the leading jurists who recognize that they themselves are unable to ascertain the ruling of Allah and His Messenger on those questions. They therefore take their imams as representatives of the Messenger and say, “This is the utmost we are capable of.” The just among them neither wrong others nor transgress against them in word or deed—for example, by claiming that the view of the imam they follow is correct without presenting any evidence, and disparaging someone who disagrees with them even though that person is excused.

Those who subjected Ahmad and others to the inquisition were among these ignorant people. They introduced ambiguous language through which they denied the truth. When they debated Ahmad during the inquisition and mentioned the term “body” and similar expressions, he answered them, saying: “I say as Allah Most High says:

 قَالَ أَبُو زَيْدٍ الْأَنْصَارِيُّ: الْجِسْمُ الْجَسَدُ وَكَذَلِكَ الْجُسْمَانُ وَالْجُثْمَانُ " وَقَالَ الْأَصْمَعِيُّ: الْجِسْمُ وَالْجَسَدُ وَالْجُثْمَانُ الشَّخْصُ وَقَالَ جَمَاعَةٌ جِسْمُ الْإِنْسَانِ يُقَالُ لَهُ الْجُثْمَانُ وَقَدْ جَسُمَ الشَّيْءُ أَيْ عَظُمَ فَهُوَ جَسِيمٌ وَجِسَامٌ وَالْجِسَامُ بِالْكَسْرِ جَمْعُ جَسِيمٍ. قَالَ أَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ تَجَسَّمْت فُلَانًا مِنْ بَيْنِ الْقَوْمِ أَيْ اخْتَرْته كَأَنَّك قَصَدْت جِسْمَهُ.
 كَمَا تَقُولُ:
 تأتيته أَيْ قَصَدْت أَتْيَهُ وَشَخْصَهُ وَأَنْشَدَ أَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ.
 تَجَسَّمْته مِنْ بَيْنِهِنَّ بِمُرْهَفِ وَتَجَسَّمْت الْأَرْضَ إذَا أَخَذْت نَحْوَهَا تُرِيدُهَا وَتَجَسَّمَ مِنْ الْجِسْمِ وَقَالَ ابْنُ السِّكِّيتِ:
 تَجَسَّمْت الْأَمْرَ: أَيْ رَكِبْت أَجْسَمَهُ وَجَسِيمُهُ أَيْ مُعْظَمُهُ قَالَ: وَكَذَلِكَ تَجَسَّمْت الرَّمْلَ وَالْجَبَلَ أَيْ رَكِبْت أَعْظَمَهُ وَالْأَجْسَمُ الْأَضْخَمُ قَالَ عَامِرُ بْنُ الطُّفَيْلِ:
translated_text:
, and if they speak, you listen to their words.” Allah Most High also says:

“And has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature.”

Ibn ʿAbbās said: Saul was the most knowledgeable of the Children of Israel in warfare, and his shoulders, neck, and head towered above other people. The word bastah means amplitude. Ibn Qutaybah said: It comes from saying, “I spread something out,” when it was gathered together and you unfolded and expanded it. Some have said: The reference to his greater bodily size means superior strength, since a person with a larger body is ordinarily stronger. This, then, is the meaning of the word jism (body) in the Arabic language in which the Quran was revealed.

Al-Jawharī said:

Abū Zayd al-Ansārī said: Jism means the body, as do jusmān and juthmān. Al-Asmaʿī said: Jism, jasad, and juthmān mean the person. A number of authorities said that the human body is called juthmān. Jasuma means that something became large; it is then described as jasīm or jisām. Jisām, pronounced with an i vowel, is the plural of jasīm.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: “Tajassamtu fulānan min bayni al-qawm” means “I singled out so-and-so from among the people,” as though you directed yourself toward his body. Similarly, you say, “Taʾattaytuhu,” meaning that you directed yourself toward his person. Abū ʿUbaydah cited the verse:

“I singled him out from among them with a keen blade.”

You say, “Tajassamtu al-ard,” when you head toward a land, intending to reach it. The verb tajassama is derived from jism.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: “Tajassamtu al-amr” means “I undertook its greatest and weightiest part”—that is, its main part. He said: Likewise, “Tajassamtu al-ramla wa-al-jabal” means “I climbed the largest part of the sand and the mountain.” Al-ajsam means the most massive. ʿĀmir ibn al-Tufayl said:

translated_text:
“The clan of ʿĀmir knows full well
that ours is the greatest summit.”

This, then, is what “body” means in the Arabic language. In this sense, neither air, nor the breath exhaled by a person, nor the spirit breathed into him is called a body. It is known that Allah, glorified be He, is unlike any of these—whether the human body or anything else. Thus, none of the characteristics peculiar to created beings may be ascribed to Allah Most High, nor may He be given names denoting attributes peculiar to created beings. It is therefore impermissible to describe Him as a body, whether using the term jism or jasad.

For the practitioners of speculative theology, however, “body” has a broader meaning. They differ greatly over its meaning, both in their rational conceptions and in their conventional terminology. They say that anything that can be pointed to by a sensory gesture is a body. Beyond this, however, they disagree. Many of them say that anything of this kind is composed of indivisible atoms.

Some of them then say that a body consists, at minimum, of a single atom, provided that it is joined to another. Others say that the minimum is two atoms or more; others, four or more; others, six; others, eight; others, sixteen; and others, thirty-two. These are the views of those who hold that all bodies are composed of indivisible atoms. Others among the philosophers say that all bodies are composed of prime matter

translated_text:
and form, not of indivisible atoms.

Many practitioners of speculative theology, as well as others, say that bodies are composed neither of the one nor of the other—neither of this nor of that. This is the view of the Hishāmiyyah, the Kullābiyyah, the Dirāriyyah, and other major schools, which subscribe neither to the theory of indivisible atoms nor to that of matter and form. Others claim that the Muslims unanimously affirm the existence of indivisible atoms. Thus, Abū al-Ma‘ālī and others said:

“The Muslims agree that the division and subdivision of bodies reaches a limit at which they become indivisible atoms.”

Yet he himself doubted this, as did Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī and Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Rāzī. It is well known that none of the leading authorities of the Muslims held this view: neither the Companions, nor those who followed them in righteousness, nor any of the scholars renowned among the Muslims. The first to advance this view within Islam were a group from among the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah. This is among the speculative theology that the early generations condemned and criticized. However, since the person reporting this consensus knew the fundamentals of religion only through books of speculative theology, and found only people who held this view, he believed it to represent the consensus of the Muslims.

The theory of indivisible atoms is false, and the theory of prime matter and form is false. These doctrines have been discussed at length elsewhere.

 إنَّ الْهَوَاءَ مِثْلُ الْمَاءِ
translated_text:
Others said:

“A body is that which subsists in itself. Everything that subsists in itself is a body, and every body subsists in itself and can be pointed to.”

They differed over whether bodies are alike, holding two well-known views.

With this understood, whoever says that He is a body, meaning that He is composed of parts, makes a false claim. The same applies if he means that He resembles any created being. Both revelation and reason establish that nothing is like Allah in any of His attributes. Whoever affirms that Allah has a likeness in any of His attributes is therefore in error, as is anyone who says that He is a body in this sense.

Likewise, whoever says that He is not a body, meaning that He will not be seen in the Hereafter; that He does not speak the Quran or any other speech; that knowledge, power, and other attributes do not subsist in Him; that hands are not raised to Him in supplication; that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was not taken up to Him; that good words do not ascend to Him; and that the angels and the Spirit do not ascend to Him—such a person’s claim is false.

Similarly, anyone who denies what Allah and His Messenger have affirmed, saying that it amounts to attributing corporeality, makes a false denial, and his describing it as attributing corporeality is misleading. If he means that this is called a body in ordinary language, his claim is false. If he means that this entails being a body composed of indivisible atoms or of matter and form, or that it entails being a body and that all bodies are alike, he should be told:

or that animal bodies are like iron and mountains. How, then, could they agree with you that the Lord Most High would resemble His creation if they affirmed for Him what the Book and Sunnah affirm for Him? Allah Most High has denied likeness between certain created beings, although both are bodies, as when He says:

‘If you turn away, He will replace you with another people, who will not be like you.’

Yet both are human. How, then, can anyone say that if the Lord of the heavens possesses knowledge and power, He must resemble His creation? Nothing is like Allah Most High—not in His essence, His attributes, or His actions.”

The crux of the matter is that, in this denier’s view, being a body necessarily entails resembling all other bodies and being composed of indivisible atoms or of matter and form. Most rational people disagree with him about this necessary connection. Both sides agree that this necessary connection does not obtain, which is the point to be established.

Once they agree that Allah is free of the imperfection denied of Him by revelation and reason, their remaining debate concerns whether a body, as technically defined, necessarily entails this objectionable consequence. This is a rational inquiry, like the debate over whether accidents persist or not. The religion of the Muslims has not been made dependent upon this rational inquiry. Indeed, neither the Book nor the Sunnah nor any report from the early generations uses the term “body” concerning Allah Most High, either to deny or to affirm it.

No one, therefore, may introduce an ambiguous term admitting different meanings, which revelation has not used, and make the religion of the Muslims depend upon it—even if he uses it in its Arabic sense. How much more so if

If he believes that bodies are alike and that nothing is like Allah—that He, glorified be He, has no namesake, no equal, and no rival—then these Quranic expressions convey this meaning without ambiguity or dispute. If, however, he believes that bodies are not alike and that whatever can be seen and possesses attributes is a body, then he must affirm what Allah and His Messenger have affirmed of His knowledge, power, and all His other attributes.

As Allah says:

“They encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.”

And He says:

“Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of Power, the Firm.”

And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said in the hadith concerning the prayer for guidance:

“O Allah, I seek Your guidance through Your knowledge, and I ask You to enable me through Your power.”

And he said in another hadith:

“O Allah, by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation.”

He should also say what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You will see your Lord with your own eyes on the Day of Resurrection, just as you see the sun and the moon, without hindrance in seeing Him.”

Thus, he likened the act of seeing to the act of seeing, although what is seen is not like what is seen. These, then, are the expressions used in the Book and Sunnah to convey this sound meaning, without ambiguity or dispute among Ahl al-Sunnah, who follow the Book, the Sunnah, and the statements of the Companions.

The great majority of speculative theologians have been inconsistent on the question of whether bodies are alike and whether they are composed of indivisible atoms. Many of them adopt one position at one time and another at another time. Most of this stems from ambiguous expressions and meanings that are difficult to distinguish. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here, however, is that even if a person came to understand that bodies are neither alike nor composite in either of the two ways, he would not be entitled to introduce into the religion of Islam the novel statement, “Allah is a body,” and argue for the sound meaning indicated by the Book and Sunnah. Rather, it is sufficient for him to affirm that meaning in scriptural terms. Likewise, even if he came to understand that bodies are alike and that a body is composite, he would not be entitled to introduce a denial using this designation and argue for the meaning he had come to believe through his own reasoning. Rather, that meaning, known through revelation and reason, can be expressed in language free of ambiguity and confusion.

Many of those who say that a body (jism) is composed of atoms claim that this is also its meaning in the Arabic language, because the Arabs say, “This is more massive (ajsam) than that,” meaning that it has more parts than the other. They also say, “This is massive (jasīm),” meaning that it has many parts.

 وَهَذِهِ تخليطة فِي اللَّفْظِ وَإِنْ كُنَّا لَا نُكَفِّرُهُ إذَا لَمْ يَثْبُتْ خَصَائِصُ الْجِسْمِ مِنْ التَّرْكِيبِ وَالتَّأْلِيفِ وَقَدْ نَازَعَهُمْ بَعْضُهُمْ فِي قَوْلِهِمْ هَذَا أَجْسَمُ مِنْ هَذَا وَقَالُوا: لَيْسَ هَذَا اللَّفْظُ مِنْ لُغَةِ الْعَرَبِ كَمَا يُحْكَى عَنْ أَبِي زَيْدٍ فَيُقَالُ لَهُ: لَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ الْعَرَبَ تَقُولُ هَذَا جَسِيمٌ أَيْ عَظِيمُ الْجُثَّةِ. وَهَذَا أَجْسَمُ مِنْ هَذَا أَيْ أَعْظَمُ جُثَّةً لَكِنَّ كَوْنَ الْعَرَبِ تَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ لِكَثْرَةِ الْأَجْزَاءِ الَّتِي هِيَ الْجَوَاهِرُ الْفَرْدَةُ إنَّمَا يَكُونُ إذَا كَانَ أَهْلُ اللُّغَةِ قَاطِبَةً يَعْتَقِدُونَ أَنَّ الْجِسْمَ مُرَكَّبٌ مِنْ الْجَوَاهِرِ الْفَرْدَةِ وَالْجَوْهَرُ الْفَرْدُ هُوَ شَيْءٌ قَدْ بَلَغَ مِنْ الصِّغَرِ وَالْحَقَارَةِ إلَى أَنَّهُ لَا يَتَمَيَّزُ يَمِينُهُ مِنْ يَسَارِهِ. وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ أَكْثَرَ الْعُقَلَاءِ مِنْ بَنِي آدَمَ لَا يَتَصَوَّرُ الْجَوْهَرَ الْفَرْدَ وَاَلَّذِينَ يَتَصَوَّرُونَهُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ لَا يُثْبِتُونَهُ وَاَلَّذِينَ أَثْبَتُوهُ إنَّمَا يُثْبِتُونَهُ بِطُرُقٍ خَفِيَّةٍ طَوِيلَةٍ بَعِيدَةٍ فَيَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ يَكُونَ اللَّفْظُ الشَّائِعُ فِي اللُّغَةِ الَّتِي يَنْطِقُ بِهَا خَوَاصُّهَا وَعَوَامُّهَا أَرَادُوا بِهِ هَذَا. وَقَدْ عُلِمَ بِالِاضْطِرَارِ أَنَّ أَحَدًا مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ لَهُمْ
translated_text:
He said:
“The comparative form af‘al indicates a greater degree of the quality denoted by the word. Thus, saying, ‘This person is more learned and more forbearing,’ indicates superiority in the qualities denoted by knowledge and forbearance. Since they use ajsam (‘more massive’) for something with more parts, this shows that by ‘body’ they mean something composite. Whoever speaks of a body that is not composite has therefore departed from Arabic usage.”

They said:
“This is a confusion in terminology, although we do not declare him an unbeliever so long as he does not affirm the defining characteristics of a body, namely composition and combination.”

Some disputed their use of the expression, “This is more massive than that,” saying that this expression is not part of the Arabic language, as is reported of Abū Zayd. The response is: There is no doubt that the Arabs say, “This is jasīm,” meaning large in bulk, and, “This is ajsam than that,” meaning greater in bulk. However, the claim that the Arabs understand this to be due to a greater number of parts—namely, indivisible atoms—would hold only if all speakers of the language believed that a body is composed of indivisible atoms. An indivisible atom is something so minute and slight that its right side cannot be distinguished from its left.

It is well known that most rational human beings do not form a conception of an indivisible atom. Of those who do, most do not affirm its existence, while those who affirm it do so only through subtle, lengthy, and far-fetched arguments. It is therefore impossible that this should be what they intended by a word in common use in their language, spoken by learned and ordinary people alike. translated_text:
in righteousness ever affirmed the existence of an indivisible atom or said anything indicating that he accepted its existence. Nor did the Arabs before them, the other peoples who retained their innate disposition, or the followers of the Messengers. How, then, can it be claimed that they used the word “body” only for something composite, assembled from parts?

If you were to say to any Arab, “In your view, the sun, moon, and sky—or mountains, air, animals, or plants—are composed of tiny parts, each of which is indivisible,” he would not conceive of this notion without considerable effort. Then, once he had conceived of it, he might reject it on the basis of his innate disposition, saying: “How can anything exist in which one side cannot be distinguished from another?”

Most rational people, among the various Muslim groups and others, deny the existence of indivisible atoms. The jurists all deny it, as do the scholars of hadith and the practitioners of Sufism. Thus, the jurists agree that one body can be transformed into another, as when excrement becomes ash or a pig becomes salt. They then debate whether, through this transformation, the substance becomes pure or not.

According to those who affirm indivisible atoms, however, entities themselves do not undergo transformation. Rather, the very same atoms present in the first substance remain in the second; only their composition differs. Hence, those later jurists who speak of “composition” in relation to water and similar things are those who have adopted this notion of composition from the speculative theologians. Such a jurist says: “Water differs from other things only in its composition.”

Likewise, those who affirm indivisible atoms hold that we have never witnessed Allah Most High bringing into existence any atoms or self-subsisting entities, and that all that He creates of animals, plants, minerals, fruits, and rain

and clouds and other things amounts merely to gathering atoms together, separating them, and changing their attributes from one state to another—not to His bringing into existence any self-subsisting atoms or bodies. Most rational people reject this view and say that it contradicts sensory experience, reason, and revelation. Still less, then, can the word “body” in Arabic necessarily imply this meaning.

Furthermore, “body” may mean thickness itself, which is an accident inhering in something else; or it may mean the thick object, which subsists in itself. Thus we say, “This cloth has body,” meaning thickness. His words,

“and increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature,”

may be cited in support of this, since He pairs “body” with “knowledge,” which is a verbal noun. We would then say that the meaning is that He increased his size, making his body larger than those of others. Thus, “body” would mean size itself, rather than the thing possessing that size.

Likewise, His words, Most High,

“their bodies impress you,”

may mean their forms, which inhere in their bodies—just as you might say, “His attractiveness, beauty, complexion, and radiance impressed me.” The intended meaning may therefore be an attribute of bodies, or it may be the bodies themselves.

When they say, “This one is more corpulent than that one,” they mean that it is thicker and larger. As for their intending thereby that this size and thickness result from a greater number of parts, it is known with certainty that this never occurred to speakers of the language, except those who acquired it from adherents of the newly introduced speculative theology who held this belief.  الْجِسْمُ هُوَ الْمُؤَلَّفُ الْمُرَكَّبُ وَاعْتَقَدَ أَنَّ الْأَجْسَامَ مُرَكَّبَةٌ مِنْ الْجَوَاهِرِ الْفَرْدَةِ فَقَدْ ادَّعَى مَعْنًى عَقْلِيًّا يُنَازِعُهُ فِيهِ أَكْثَرُ الْعُقَلَاءِ مِنْ بَنِي آدَمَ وَلَمْ يُنْقَلْ عَنْ أَحَدٍ مِنْ السَّلَفِ أَنَّهُ وَافَقَهُ عَلَيْهِ وَأَنَّهُ جَعَلَ لَفْظَ الْجِسْمِ فِي اصْطِلَاحِهِ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنًى لَا يَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّفْظُ فِي اللُّغَةِ فَقَدْ غَيَّرَ مَعْنَى اللَّفْظِ فِي اللُّغَةِ وَادَّعَى مَعْنًى عَقْلِيًّا فِيهِ نِزَاعٌ طَوِيلٌ وَلَيْسَ مَعَهُ مِنْ الشَّرْعِ مَا يُوَافِقُ مَا ادَّعَاهُ مِنْ مَعْنَى اللَّفْظِ وَلَا مَا ادَّعَاهُ مِنْ الْمَعْنَى الْعَقْلِيِّ فَاللُّغَةُ لَا تَدُلُّ عَلَى مَا قَالَ وَالشَّرْعُ لَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَا قَالَ وَالْعَقْلُ لَمْ يَدُلَّ عَلَى مُسَمَّيَاتِ الْأَلْفَاظِ وَإِنَّمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمَعْنَى الْمُجَرَّدِ وَذَلِكَ فِيهِ نِزَاعٌ طَوِيلٌ وَنَحْنُ نَعْلَمُ بِالِاضْطِرَارِ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى الَّذِي وَجَبَ نَفْيُهُ عَنْ اللَّهِ لَا يَحْتَاجُ نَفْيُهُ إلَى مَا أَحْدَثَهُ هَذَا مِنْ دَلَالَةِ اللَّفْظِ وَلَا مَا ادَّعَاهُ مِنْ الْمَعْنَى الْعَقْلِيِّ بَلْ الَّذِينَ جَعَلُوا هَذَا عُمْدَتَهُمْ فِي تَنْزِيهِ الرَّبِّ عَلَى نَفْيِ مُسَمَّى الْجِسْمِ لَا يُمْكِنُهُمْ أَنْ يُنَزِّهُوهُ عَنْ شَيْءٍ مِنْ النَّقَائِصِ أَلْبَتَّةَ فَإِنَّهُمْ إذَا قَالُوا: هَذَا مِنْ صِفَاتِ الْأَجْسَامِ فَكُلُّ مَا أَثْبَتُوهُ هُوَ أَيْضًا مِنْ صِفَاتِ الْأَجْسَامِ مِثْلُ كَوْنِهِ حَيًّا عَلِيمًا قَدِيرًا بَلْ كَوْنِهِ مَوْجُودًا قَائِمًا بِنَفْسِهِ فَإِنَّهُمْ لَا يَعْرِفُونَ هَذَا فِي الشَّاهِدِ
translated_text:
known to have been expressed in Islam, either in these terms or in substance, until the final years of Umayyad rule, when Jahm ibn Safwān and al-Ja‘d ibn Dirham appeared. It then appeared among the Mu‘tazilah.

It has thus become clear that anyone who says, “A body is something assembled and composite,” and believes that bodies are composed of indivisible atoms has asserted a rational proposition disputed by most rational people. Nor has it been reported that anyone among the early Muslim generations agreed with him. In his technical usage, he has also assigned the word “body” a meaning that it does not convey in the language. He has thus changed the word’s linguistic meaning and asserted a rational proposition over which there is extensive disagreement. Nothing in revelation supports either his claim about the word’s meaning or his rational proposition. Language does not support what he says, nor does revelation. Reason, meanwhile, does not establish what words denote; it establishes only abstract meanings, and the meaning in question is extensively disputed.

We know necessarily that denying of Allah the meaning that must be denied of Him requires neither this newly devised interpretation of the word nor the rational proposition asserted. Indeed, those who make this their principal basis for declaring the Lord transcendent, by denying of Him what the term “body” denotes, cannot declare Him free of any imperfection whatsoever. For if they say, “This is an attribute of bodies,” everything they affirm is likewise an attribute of bodies: His being living, knowing, and powerful, and even His existing and subsisting in Himself. For they do not know of this in the observable world

translated_text:
except in a body. Thus, if an opponent says, “Concerning what you deny, I say the same as they say concerning what you affirm,” they have no answer.

They hold two views on whether the Lord’s entitlement to the attributes of perfection, as they understand them, is known through consensus alone or through reason as well. Those who say that this is not known through reason, such as Abū al-Ma‘ālī, al-Rāzī, and others, are left with no rational proof by which to declare the Lord free of many imperfections. This is assuming that one denies only what must be denied of Allah, such as imperfections—for the Lord must be declared free of them—and denies that He resembles created beings. Just as the Lord must be declared free of every imperfection and defect, He must also be declared above any created being resembling Him in any of the attributes of perfection established for Him.

These two principles encompass all that must be denied of Allah to affirm His transcendence. “Say: He is Allah, One” indicates both. His description as “One,” together with His words,

“And there is none comparable to Him,”

negates likeness and partnership. His description as “the Eternal Refuge” encompasses all the attributes of perfection. Imperfections of every kind are therefore denied of Allah Most High. Everything peculiar to created beings is among the imperfections of which the Lord must be declared free. This is unlike attributes ascribed to the Lord and also ascribed to the servant in a manner befitting him, such as knowledge, power, mercy, and the like. These are not imperfections. Rather, whichever of these attributes are established for Allah belong to Him in a manner that no created being comes close to, let alone equals. Indeed, even what Allah has created in

translated_text:
Paradise—food, drink, and clothing—does not resemble what He has created in this world, even though they share the same names and both are created.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: “Nothing in this world corresponds to what is in Paradise except in name.” Allah has told us that Paradise contains milk, wine, honey, water, silk, gold, and silver. Yet those realities are unlike their counterparts here, although both are created. The Creator, exalted is He, is therefore even further removed from resembling created beings than one created being is from resembling another.

Allah has called Himself All-Knowing, Forbearing, Compassionate, Merciful, All-Hearing, All-Seeing, Almighty, King, Compeller, Supremely Great, Giver of Security, Magnificent, Generous, Self-Sufficient, Appreciative, Most Great, Preserver, Witness, Truth, Disposer of Affairs, and Protector. He has also called some of His creatures by these names. He has described the human being as hearing and seeing, and His Prophet as compassionate and merciful. He has called some of His servants kings, others grateful, others great, and others forbearing and knowledgeable, and has likewise applied the other names mentioned to created beings. Yet it is known that no created being bearing these names resembles the Creator, majestic is His glory, in any respect whatsoever.

The same applies to the dispute over the terms “occupying space,” “direction,” and the like. Some people say: “He occupies space and is in a direction.” Others say: “He neither occupies space nor is in a direction.” Still others say: “He is in a direction but does not occupy space.” The term “that which occupies space” encompasses both a body and an indivisible atom. that which occupies space, or it may refer to an indivisible atom. Some philosophers claim to establish the existence of self-subsisting substances that do not occupy space.

Later speculative theologians, such as al-Shahrastānī, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others, say that nothing in reason renders this impossible. Hence, someone who follows their approach—and establishes the temporal origination of the world solely through the temporal origination of bodies—says that, assuming intellectual substances exist, this proof contains nothing that establishes their temporal origination. Consequently, some who combined speculative theology with philosophy adopted the view that intellectual substances are eternal, whereas bodies come into being, and that the cause necessitating the latter’s coming into being is the arising of one of the soul’s conceptions. Some prominent authors held this view.

So too did al-Urmawī, the author of al-Lubāb, who answered the philosophers’ specious argument for perpetual agency, which entails that anything coming into being must have a cause. He answered it with the dazzling reply he took from al-Rāzī’s discussion in al-Matālib al-ʿĀliya. Al-Rāzī had given this answer, although in al-Matālib al-ʿĀliya he mixes the philosophers’ discourse with that of the speculative theologians and is bewildered over the question of temporal origination and eternity.

This answer is among the most unsound answers. For one may ask: What necessitates the continual arising of those conceptions? Moreover, according to them, the soul must be connected to a body, making the existence of a soul without a body impossible.

Moreover, the intellectual substances posited by the philosophers exist only in the mind, not in external reality. Most speculative theologians, however, say that their nonexistence is self-evident to reason. This has been discussed at length elsewhere, where it was explained that the intellectual substances whose existence the philosophers claim to establish—namely, the intellects, soul, matter, and form—have no reality outside the mind. Rather, they are intelligible objects within the mind, which the intellect abstracts from particular things, just as it abstracts the universals shared among different kinds, such as universal animality and universal humanity. Universals are universal only in the mind, not in concrete reality.

Some of these philosophers suppose that universals exist as universals in external reality, and that there are universal essences accompanying concrete particulars, distinct from the particular existing things themselves. Likewise, some posit universals separate from concrete particulars, which they call “Platonic Forms.”

Some also posit duration abstracted from moving things and motion, and an abstract void that neither occupies space nor inheres in anything that occupies space. They also posit matter abstracted from all forms. In their terminology, matter means a substrate. Thus, silver is said to be the matter of a ring or a dirham, and wood the matter of a chair—that is, the substrate in which this form is fashioned. This crafted form is an accident among accidents. Such a thing is merely conceived in the mind, just as one conceives extension abstracted from everything extended, number abstracted from everything numbered, and magnitude abstracted from everything possessing magnitude. All these are things posited in the mind, with no existence in external reality. Even speculative thinkers who habitually defend the philosophers have acknowledged this, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Thus, once the intellectual substances posited by these philosophers are fully understood, clear reason establishes that they do not exist in external reality. As for the angels about whom Allah has informed us, these philosophers—the followers of Aristotle—know nothing of them and neither affirm nor deny their existence. Likewise, they know nothing of prophethood and neither affirm nor deny it. Only their later representatives, such as Ibn Sīnā and others like him, discussed these matters. They sought to reconcile prophethood with philosophy, engaging in obfuscation and deception.

Likewise, the “first cause” they posit for this world is merely a final cause: the celestial sphere moves in order to resemble it. Its moving the celestial sphere is akin to a leader’s moving a follower who wishes to resemble his leader and follow his example. In their terminology, the word “deity” means the leader who is followed and whom others seek to resemble. According to them, therefore, the celestial sphere moves in order to resemble the deity. Hence, they held that “the highest philosophy” and “the first wisdom” consist solely in resembling the deity to the extent of one’s ability. and elsewhere revolves entirely around this. At times, he likens its moving the celestial sphere to the beloved’s moving the lover. Yet in this case, the lover may be moved by love for the beloved himself or by some benefit he obtains from him. According to them, the celestial sphere’s movement is not like this. Rather, it moves to resemble the first cause. Thus, it loves that cause—that is, it loves to resemble it; it neither desires to worship it nor desires anything obtained from it.

Aristotle likens this to the way laws move their followers: those who follow a legal code act according to its provisions and take it as their model. By a legal code, they mean the comprehensive system of governance for cities devised by people of sound judgment and intellect for their worldly welfare, so that they do not wrong one another and their worldly affairs do not fall into disorder. Those among them who know of prophethood suppose that the laws brought by the prophets are of the same kind as their own legal codes, and that their purpose is worldly welfare through the establishment of a just legal code.

For this reason, Ibn Sīnā and others like him held prophethood to be necessary, considering it indispensable for establishing this legal code. Since practical philosophy, in their view, comprises ethics, household management, and politics, they classified the acts of worship, religious laws, and rulings brought by the messengers as belonging to these same branches of practical philosophy.

These people do not know Allah; indeed, they are far more removed from knowing Him than the unbelievers among the Jews and Christians. Aristotle, the First Teacher, was among those most profoundly ignorant of the Lord of all worlds. They do, however, possess a good knowledge of natural matters.
