As for His angels, prophets, books, and messengers, and the Hereafter, they know nothing of these whatsoever, nor did they discuss them, whether to deny or affirm them. Only their later thinkers who embraced religious faiths discussed these matters.

The ancient Greeks, however, were polytheists, among those most deeply steeped in polytheism and sorcery. They worshipped celestial bodies and idols, and this is why they devoted such attention to astronomy and the study of celestial bodies: they sought to worship them. They built temples for them, and the last of their kings was Ptolemy, the author of the Almagest.

When the Romans embraced Christianity, the religion of the Messiah—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—came and abolished the polytheism they had practised. Hence, those who altered the religion of the Messiah devised a religion combining the religion of the monotheists with that of the polytheists. The latter had worshipped the sun, moon, and celestial bodies, praying and prostrating to them. Then Constantine, the Christian king, and his followers introduced the practice of praying towards the east, replacing prostration to the sun with prostration in its direction.

Those earlier people had worshipped three-dimensional idols that cast shadows. The Christians then depicted images of saints in churches, replacing freestanding, three-dimensional images that cast shadows with images painted on walls and ceilings.

Aristotle was the minister of Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian—so called after Macedonia, the island of these Greek philosophers known as the Peripatetics. Today it lies in ruins or has been submerged by water. Alexander is the one from whom Christians and Jews reckon their Roman chronology, and he lived about three hundred years before the Messiah. Those who venerate these philosophers suppose that Aristotle was the minister of Dhū al-Qarnayn mentioned in the Quran, seeking thereby to enhance his standing. This is ignorance, for Dhū al-Qarnayn lived long before this Alexander. Dhū al-Qarnayn built the barrier against Gog and Magog, whereas this Macedonian went to Persia and never reached China, let alone the barrier.

As for the angels of whom Allah and His Messenger have told us, only Allah Most High knows their number; they are not ten or nine. They are servants of Allah, living beings endowed with speech, who descend to earth and ascend to heaven. They act only with their Lord’s permission, as Allah has told us concerning them:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a son.’ Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honoured servants.”

“They do not precede Him in speech, and they act at His command.”

“He knows what is before them and what is behind them. They intercede only for those whom He approves, and they tremble in fear of Him.”

And He Most High says:

“How many angels there are in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing, except after Allah gives permission for whom He wills and approves.”

Nevertheless, the theologians are more correct overall in rational questions concerning divine matters and universals, just as they are closer to the revealed teachings than the philosophers. For the philosophers’ discourse on divine matters and rational universals is exceedingly deficient and contains much confusion. They speak well only about sensible, natural matters and the universal principles governing them; their discourse on these subjects is generally sound.

As for the unseen matters reported by the prophets, the rational universals encompassing everything that exists, and the correct classification of all existing things, they have no knowledge of these whatsoever. Such knowledge is possible only for someone whose knowledge encompasses the various kinds of existing things. Yet they know only sensible things and some of their necessary implications, and this amounts to knowledge of very little indeed of what exists. For the things human beings do not witness far surpass those they witness in magnitude and attributes.

Consequently, when these people, who have learned what the philosophers know, hear the prophets’ reports about the angels, the Throne, the Kursī, Paradise, and Hell—while supposing that nothing exists beyond what they and the philosophers know—they become bewildered and reinterpret the prophets’ words to fit what they know, although there is no evidence for this, nor do they have, for this

translated_text:
denial, any knowledge; for absence of knowledge is not knowledge of absence. Their denial is like a physician’s denial of the jinn because nothing in the practice of medicine establishes their existence. Yet nothing in medical knowledge disproves their existence either. Likewise, you find someone who has mastered a branch of knowledge and thereby distinguished himself from ordinary people who do not know it, yet continues, out of ignorance, to deny whatever he does not know. Human beings go astray more through what they reject and deny without knowledge than through what they affirm and believe.

Allah Most High says:

“Rather, they have denied what they do not fully comprehend and whose fulfillment has not yet come to them.”

This is because human beings generally possess sound senses and reason, so when they affirm something and believe it, it is true. For this reason, mass-transmitted reports are accepted from people of every kind: they report what they have seen and heard, and a vast multitude will not all be mistaken about such matters or deliberately lie about them. Once it is known that they have neither colluded over their report nor derived it from one another—as doctrines and opinions are passed down from earlier to later generations—and that the matter is not one about which people ordinarily err, their truthfulness is known with certainty. A person reporting something either deliberately lies or makes a mistake, and both possibilities are ruled out in mass-transmitted reports. The opposite holds for what people deny and reject: most, or many, of them deny what they do not know and reject what they do not fully comprehend.

When someone of this kind hears them mention the angels, he supposes that they are the intellects and souls posited by the philosophers, or the forces within bodies. Likewise, he imagines that the jinn and devils are accidents inhering in souls, since this is the extent of his knowledge. He also accepts what Ibn Sīnā and others like him maintain: that extraordinary phenomena in this world are caused by celestial, natural, or psychic powers. He places the prophets’ miracles in the category of psychic powers, regarding them as belonging to the same kind as sorcery, except that the sorcerer intends evil whereas the prophet intends good.

All this stems from ignorance of the universal principles encompassing existing things and their kinds, and from ignorance of what the Messenger brought. Their knowledge of the universal sciences and metaphysics extends no further than what the ancient philosophers knew, together with additions received from certain speculative theologians or adherents of religious faith.

For this reason, the discussions of metaphysics and universal principles by later philosophers, such as Ibn Sīnā and others like him, were superior to those of their predecessors. This also explains why Greek philosophy became congenial to heretical innovators among the adherents of religious faiths: it contained an admixture of religious teaching. Thus the heretical Banū ‘Ubayd embraced it, taking the Intellect and the Soul from these polytheistic Sabian philosophers, and Light and Darkness from the Magians. translated_text:
a path on which, they claimed, they combined religious teaching with philosophy. Yet they are heretics who do not belong to the seventy-two sects. Both groups have been discussed at length elsewhere. They are mentioned here only because the adherents of innovated speculative theology—through their ignorance of what the early Muslim generations and the leading scholars of the Sunnah knew from the Quran, the Sunnah, and the reports of the Companions, and through the false theological arguments into which they have fallen—have become the means by which these philosophers introduce false notions into Islam. Through them, error and deviation arise to an extent that cannot be detailed here. When the Jahmiyyah instituted their inquisition and called people to submit to it, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal was flogged in the year 220 AH, that period marked the beginnings of the Qarmatians, the esotericist heretics. Thus religious innovations became a gateway to heresy, just as sins are a herald of disbelief. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The purpose here is to discuss the terms “occupying space” and “direction.” These philosophically inclined speculative theologians came to disagree about the angels: do they occupy space or not?

is commonly attributed to the Peripatetics. Rather, they maintained that there was no proof ruling out a greater number. Seeing that prophetic revelations had spoken of the multitude of angels, they sought to establish their multitude through a philosophical method, as did Abū al-Barakāt, author of al-Mu'tabar, and al-Rāzī in al-Matālib al-'Āliyah, among others.

As for the speculative theologians, they say that every contingent thing, everything that has come into being, or every created thing either occupies space or subsists in something that occupies space. Many of them say that every existent either occupies space or subsists in something that occupies space, and that no existent can be conceived otherwise. Various groups engaged in speculative theology and rational inquiry have maintained this.

When philosophically inclined thinkers such as Ibn Sīnā and his followers, al-Shahrastānī, al-Rāzī, and others sought to establish the existence of something that is not of this kind, their principal support was their affirmation of universals, such as shared humanity and shared animality. Since these are universals only in the mind, their opponents did not dispute this with them. Rather, they disputed their affirmation of something existing outside the mind, subsisting in itself, yet entirely imperceptible to the senses—indeed, something that cannot even be conceived.

They said to them: “What is intellectually apprehended is in the intellect. But whatever exists and subsists in itself must be capable of being perceived by the senses, even if we do not perceive it in this world, just as we do not perceive the jinn, the angels, and other such beings. It must therefore be perceptible to beings other than ourselves, such as the angels and jinn, and be perceived after death, or in the Hereafter, or

translated_text:
be perceived in this world by some people but not others, such as the prophets who saw the angels and heard their speech.”

This approach—that everything subsisting in itself can be seen—is the one followed by leading rational thinkers such as Ibn Kullāb and others. Ibn al-Zāghūnī and others also followed it.

As for the claim that every existent can be seen or perceived through all five senses, as maintained by al-Ashʿarī and those who agree with him, such as al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, Abū al-Maʿālī, and others, this approach is rejected by the overwhelming majority of rational thinkers. Indeed, they say that its invalidity is self-evident once it is fully understood, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

The same applies to their dispute concerning the human spirit, which departs from a person at death according to the majority, who hold that it is an entity subsisting in itself, neither an accident of the body, such as life and the like, nor a part of the body, such as the air exhaled from it. Many speculative theologians, however, have claimed that it is an accident subsisting in the body or one of its parts. Yet this contradicts the Quran, the Sunnah, the consensus of the early and later generations, the position of the overwhelming majority of rational thinkers among all nations, and rational proofs. This is one of the points the philosophers have used to assert their superiority over many speculative theologians.

Al-Qādī Abū Bakr said that most speculative theologians hold that the spirit is one of the accidents

translated_text:
and this is our position, provided that by “spirit” he does not mean the soul. For he said:

“The spirit present in the body is of two kinds: one is the life subsisting in it, and the other is breath. Breath is air that spreads through it.”

What is meant by breath is the particles of air released through the pores and expelled in breathing. This is the view of al-Isfarāyīnī and others. Ibn Fūrak said that it is what flows through the cavities of the organs. Abū al-Maʿālī disagreed with them—and rightly so—saying:

“The spirit consists of subtle bodies interwoven with perceptible bodies. Allah has established the customary order whereby bodies remain alive so long as these subtle bodies remain interwoven with them. When they separate from them, death follows life, in accordance with that continuing customary order.”

The position of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, the rest of the early generations of the Muslim community, and the leading scholars of the Sunnah is that the spirit is an entity subsisting in itself, which departs from the body and experiences bliss or punishment. It is neither the body nor any part of it, such as the breath mentioned above.

Since Imam Ahmad explicitly affirmed this, as did other imams, his followers did not disagree on this point. Some of them, however, such as al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, claimed that it is a body and that it is the air moving back and forth through the body’s passages, in agreement with one of the two meanings mentioned by Ibn al-Bāqillānī. Since these views were among the weakest, many people used them to gain the upper hand over their proponents.

original_text:
وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا أَنَّ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا:
 إنَّهَا عَيْنٌ قَائِمَةٌ بِنَفْسِهَا غَيْرُ الْبَدَنِ وَأَجْزَائِهِ وَأَعْرَاضِهِ تَنَازَعُوا: هَلْ هِيَ جِسْمٌ مُتَحَيِّزٌ؟ عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ كَتَنَازُعِهِمْ فِي الْمَلَائِكَةِ.
 فالمتكلمون مِنْهُمْ يَقُولُونَ:
 جِسْمٌ والمتفلسفة يَقُولُونَ: جَوْهَرٌ عَقْلِيٌّ لَيْسَ بِجِسْمِ وَقَدْ أَشَرْنَا فِيمَا تَقَدَّمَ إلَى أَنَّ مَا تُسَمِّيهِ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةُ جَوَاهِرَ عَقْلِيَّةً لَا تُوجَدُ إلَّا فِي الذِّهْنِ وَأَصْلُ تَسْمِيَتِهِمْ الْمُجَرَّدَاتِ وَالْمُفَارِقَاتِ هُوَ مَأْخُوذٌ مِنْ نَفْسِ الْإِنْسَانِ فَإِنَّهَا لَمَّا كَانَتْ تُفَارِقُ بَدَنَهُ بِالْمَوْتِ وَتَتَجَرَّدُ عَنْهُ سَمَّوْهَا مُفَارِقَةً مُجَرَّدَةً ثُمَّ أَثْبَتُوا مَا أَثْبَتُوهُ مِنْ الْعُقُولِ وَالنُّفُوسِ وَسَمَّوْهَا مُفَارِقَاتٍ وَمُجَرَّدَاتٍ بِنَاءً عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَهُمْ يُرِيدُونَ بِالْمُفَارِقِ لِلْمَادَّةِ مَا لَا يَكُونُ جِسْمًا وَلَا قَائِمًا بِجِسْمِ لَكِنَّ النَّفْسَ مُتَعَلِّقَةٌ بِالْجِسْمِ تَعَلُّقَ التَّدْبِيرِ وَالْعَقْلِ وَلَا تَعَلُّقَ لَهُ بِالْأَجْسَامِ أَصْلًا وَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ جَمَاهِيرَ الْعُقَلَاءَ عَلَى إثْبَاتِ الْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ الْبَدَنِ وَالرُّوحِ الَّتِي تُفَارِقُ وَالْجُمْهُورُ يُسَمُّونَ ذَلِكَ رُوحًا وَهَذَا جِسْمًا لَكِنَّ لَفْظَ الْجِسْمِ فِي اللُّغَةِ لَيْسَ هُوَ الْجِسْمَ فِي اصْطِلَاحِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ بَلْ الْجِسْمُ هُوَ الْجَسَدُ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ وَهُوَ الْجِسْمُ الْغَلِيظُ أَوْ غِلَظُهُ وَالرُّوحُ لَيْسَتْ مِثْلَ الْبَدَنِ فِي الْغِلَظِ وَالْكَثَافَةِ وَلِذَلِكَ لَا تُسَمَّى جِسْمًا فَمَنْ جَعَلَ الْمَلَائِكَةَ وَالْأَرْوَاحَ وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ لَيْسَتْ أَجْسَامًا بِالْمَعْنَى اللُّغَوِيِّ فَقَدْ أَصَابَ فِي ذَلِكَ وَرَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ أَوْلَى أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ جِسْمًا فَإِنَّهُ مِنْ الْمَشْهُورِ فِي اللُّغَةِ الْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ الْأَرْوَاحِ وَالْأَجْسَامِ.
translated_text:
The point here is that those who hold that the spirit is an entity subsisting in itself, distinct from the body, its parts, and its accidents, disagreed over whether it is a body occupying space. They held two views, just as they disagreed concerning the angels. The speculative theologians among them say that it is a body, whereas the philosophers say that it is an intellectual substance, not a body.

We have already indicated that what the philosophers call intellectual substances exist only in the mind. Their designation of entities as “abstract” and “separate” originally derives from the human soul: since it separates from the body at death and becomes detached from it, they called it “separate” and “abstract.” They then posited the intellects and souls they affirm, calling them “separate” and “abstract” entities on that basis. By something “separate from matter,” they mean something that is neither a body nor subsists in a body. The soul, however, is connected to the body through governing it, whereas the intellect has no connection whatsoever with bodies.

There is no doubt that the vast majority of rational people affirm a distinction between the body and the spirit that departs from it. People generally call the latter a spirit and the former a body. Yet the word “body” in ordinary Arabic does not have the same meaning as “body” in the technical terminology of the speculative theologians. Rather, as explained earlier, it means the bodily frame: the dense body, or its bulk. The spirit does not resemble the body in bulk and density, and is therefore not called a body.

Thus, whoever holds that angels, spirits, and the like are not bodies in the ordinary linguistic sense is correct in this. The Lord of all worlds is all the more entitled not to be described as a body, for the distinction between spirits and bodies is well established in ordinary language.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا أَهْلُ الِاصْطِلَاح مِنْ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ والمتفلسفة فَيَجْعَلُونَ مُسَمَّى الْجِسْمِ أَعَمَّ مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَهُوَ مَا أَمْكَنَتْ الْإِشَارَةُ الْحِسِّيَّةُ إلَيْهِ وَمَا قِيلَ إنَّهُ هُنَا وَهُنَاكَ وَمَا قَبِلَ الْأَبْعَادَ الثَّلَاثَةَ وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ الْمُتَحَيِّزُ فِي اصْطِلَاحِ هَؤُلَاءِ هُوَ الْجِسْمُ وَيَدْخُلُ فِيهِ الْجَوْهَرُ الْفَرْدُ عِنْدَ مَنْ أَثْبَتَهُ وَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ مَعْنَى الْجِسْمِ فِي اللُّغَةِ وَأَمَّا الْمُتَحَيِّزُ فَقَدْ قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَمَنْ يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ إلَّا مُتَحَرِّفًا لِقِتَالٍ أَوْ مُتَحَيِّزًا إلَى فِئَةٍ فَقَدْ بَاءَ بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ}
 .
 وَقَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ:
 الْحَوْزُ الْجَمْعُ وَكُلُّ مَنْ ضَمٍّ إلَى نَفْسِهِ شَيْئًا فَقَدْ حَازَهُ حَوْزًا وَحِيَازَةً وَاحْتَازَهُ أَيْضًا وَالْحَوْزُ وَالْحَيِّزُ السُّوقُ اللَّيِّنُ وَقَدْ حَازَ الْإِبِلَ يَحُوزُهَا وَيَحِيزُهَا وَحَوَّزَ الْإِبِلَ سَاقَهَا إلَى الْمَاءِ وَقَالَ الْأَصْمَعِيُّ: إذَا كَانَتْ الْإِبِلُ بَعِيدَةَ الْمَرْعَى عَنْ الْمَاءِ فَأَوَّلُ لَيْلَةٍ تُوَجِّهُهَا إلَى الْمَاءِ لَيْلَةُ الْحَوْزِ وَتَحَوَّزَتْ الْحَيَّةُ وَتَحَيَّزَتْ تَلَوَّتْ.
 يُقَالُ مَا لَك تَتَحَوَّزُ تَحَوُّزَ الْحَيَّةِ وَتَتَحَيَّزُ تَحَيُّزَ الْحَيَّةِ قَالَ سِيبَوَيْهِ هُوَ تَفَعُّلٌ مِنْ حُزْت الشَّيْءَ قَالَ الْقَطَامِيُّ:
 تَحَيَّزَ مِنِّي خَشْيَةَ أَنْ أُضِيفَهَا كَمَا انْحَازَتْ الْأَفْعَى مَخَافَةَ ضَارِبِ يَقُولُ تَتَنَحَّى عَنِّي هَذِهِ الْعَجُوزُ وَتَتَأَخَّرُ خَشْيَةَ أَنْ أَنْزِلَ عَلَيْهَا ضَيْفًا.
translated_text:
As for the speculative theologians and philosophers who employ technical terminology, they give “body” a broader meaning: anything that can be indicated through the senses, described as being here or there, or admit of three dimensions, and the like.

Likewise, in their terminology, “that which occupies space” means a body, and includes the indivisible atom according to those who affirm its existence. The linguistic meaning of “body” has already been explained. As for *mutahayyiz*, Allah Most High says:

“And whoever turns his back to them that day—unless maneuvering for battle or joining another company—has indeed incurred Allah’s wrath.”

Al-Jawharī said:

“*Al-hawz* means gathering. Anyone who takes something into his possession is said to have *hāzahu*, with the verbal nouns *hawz* and *hiyāzah*; *ihtāzahu* is also used. *Al-hawz* and *al-hayyiz* mean gentle driving. One says *hāza al-ibila*, with the present-tense forms *yahūzuhā* and *yahīzuhā*, meaning that he drove the camels. *Hawwaza al-ibila* means that he drove the camels to water. Al-Asma‘ī said: ‘When the camels graze far from water, the first night on which you direct them towards water is called the night of *al-hawz*.’ *Tahawwazat al-hayyah* and *tahayyazat* mean that the snake writhed.

“One says: ‘Why do you writhe like a snake?’ This is expressed both as *tatahawwazu tahawwuza al-hayyah* and *tatahayyazu tahayyuza al-hayyah*. Sībawayh said: ‘It follows the pattern *tafa‘‘ul*, from *huztu al-shay’a*—I gathered the thing.’ Al-Qatāmī said:

She drew away from me, fearing I would be her guest,
As a viper withdraws, fearing one who would strike.

“He means: this old woman moves away from me and draws back, fearing that I will stay with her as a guest.

original_text:
وَالْحَيِّزُ مَا انْضَمَّ إلَى الدَّارِ مِنْ مَرَافِقِهَا وَكُلُّ نَاحِيَةٍ حَيِّزٌ وَأَصْلُهُ مِنْ الْوَاوِ وَالْحَيِّزُ تَخْفِيفُ الْحَيِّزِ مِثْلُ هَيْنٍ وَهَيِّنٌ وَلَيْنٍ وَلَيِّنٍ وَالْجَمْعُ أحياز وَالْحَوْزَةُ النَّاحِيَةُ وَانْحَازَ عَنْهُ انعدل وَانْحَازَ الْقَوْمُ تَرَكُوا مَرْكَزَهُمْ إلَى آخَرَ يُقَالُ لِلْأَوْلِيَاءِ انْحَازُوا عَنْ الْعَدُوِّ وَحَاصُوا وَالْأَعْدَاءُ انْهَزَمُوا وَوَلَّوْا مُدْبِرِينَ وَتَحَاوَزَ الْفَرِيقَانِ فِي الْحَرْبِ انْحَازَ كُلُّ فَرِيقٍ عَنْ الْآخَرِ. فَهَذَا الْمَذْكُورُ عَنْ أَهْلِ اللُّغَةِ فِي هَذَا اللَّفْظِ وَمَادَّتِهِ يَقْتَضِي أَنَّ التَّحَيُّزَ وَالِانْحِيَازَ وَالتَّحَوُّزَ وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ يَتَضَمَّنُ عُدُولًا مِنْ مَحَلٍّ إلَى مَحَلٍّ وَهَذَا أَخَصُّ مِنْ كَوْنِهِ يَحُوزُهُ أَمْرٌ مَوْجُودٌ فَهُمْ يُرَاعُونَ فِي مَعْنَى الْحَوْزِ ذَهَابَهُ مِنْ جِهَةٍ إلَى جِهَةٍ؛
 وَلِهَذَا يَقُولُونَ:
 حُزْت الْمَالَ وَحُزْت الْإِبِلَ وَذَلِكَ يَتَضَمَّنُ نَقْلَهُ مِنْ جِهَةٍ إلَى جِهَةٍ فَالشَّيْءُ الْمُسْتَقِرُّ فِي مَوْضِعِهِ كَالْجَبَلِ وَالشَّمْسِ وَالْقَمَرِ لَا يُسَمُّونَهُ مُتَحَيِّزًا وَأَعَمُّ مِنْ هَذَا أَنْ يُرَادَ بِالْمُتَحَيِّزِ مَا يُحِيطُ بِهِ حَيِّزٌ مَوْجُودٌ فَيُسَمَّى كُلُّ مَا أَحَاطَ بِهِ غَيْرُهُ أَنَّهُ مُتَحَيِّزٌ وَعَلَى هَذَا فَمَا بَيْنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ مُتَحَيِّزٌ؛ بَلْ مَا فِي الْعَالَمِ مُتَحَيِّزٌ إلَّا سَطْحَ الْعَالَمِ الَّذِي لَا يُحِيطُ بِهِ شَيْءٌ فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ لَيْسَ بِمُتَحَيِّزِ وَكَذَلِكَ الْعَالَمُ جُمْلَةً لَيْسَ بِمُتَحَيِّزٍ بِهَذَا الِاعْتِبَارِ فَإِنَّهُ لَيْسَ فِي عَالَمٍ آخَرَ أَحَاطَ بِهِ والمتكلمون يُرِيدُونَ بِالْمُتَحَيِّزِ مَا هُوَ أَعَمُّ مِنْ هَذَا وَالْحَيِّزُ عِنْدَهُمْ أَعَمُّ مِنْ الْمَكَانِ فَالْعَالَمُ كُلُّهُ فِي حَيِّزٍ وَلَيْسَ هُوَ فِي مَكَانٍ
translated_text:
Al-hayyiz denotes the appurtenances adjoining a house, and every distinct area is a hayyiz. Its root originally contains the letter wāw (w). Hayz is a shortened pronunciation of hayyiz, just as hayn is of hayyin (‘easy’), and layn of layyin (‘soft’). Its plural is ahyāz. Al-hawzah means an area. Inhāza ‘anhu means ‘he turned aside from it.’ When people are said to have inhāzū, they have left their position for another. Of one’s allies, one says that they ‘withdrew from the enemy’ or ‘turned aside’; of enemies, that they ‘were routed’ and ‘turned their backs in flight.’ When two parties in battle are said to have tahāwazā, each has withdrawn from the other.”

These statements by the lexicographers concerning this word and its root imply that tahayyuz, inhiyāz, tahawwuz, and similar expressions involve moving from one location to another. This is narrower than merely being contained by something that exists. Thus, in the meaning of hawz, they take into account movement from one quarter to another. Hence they say, “Huztu al-māl” (I gathered the wealth into my possession) and “Huztu al-ibil” (I drove the camels together). This involves moving them from one quarter to another. They therefore do not call something fixed in its position—such as a mountain, the sun, or the moon—mutahayyiz, “occupying space.”

A broader sense is to understand “occupying space” as being surrounded by an actually existing spatial region. Anything surrounded by something else would then be described as occupying space. On this understanding, whatever lies between heaven and earth occupies space. Indeed, everything in the universe occupies space except the universe’s surface, which nothing surrounds: that does not occupy space. Likewise, the universe as a whole does not occupy space in this sense, since it is not within another universe surrounding it.

The speculative theologians, however, intend something broader by “occupying space.” For them, a spatial region is broader than a place: the entire universe is in a spatial region, but it is not in a place.

original_text:
وَالْمُتَحَيِّزُ عِنْدَهُمْ لَا يُعْتَبَرُ فِيهِ أَنَّهُ يَحُوزُهُ غَيْرُهُ وَلَا يَكُونُ لَهُ حَيِّزٌ وُجُودِيٌّ بَلْ كُلَّمَا أُشِيرَ إلَيْهِ وَامْتَازَ مِنْهُ شَيْءٌ عَنْ شَيْءٍ فَهُوَ مُتَحَيِّزٌ عِنْدَهُمْ.
 ثُمَّ هُمْ مُخْتَلِفُونَ بَعْدَ هَذَا فِي الْمُتَحَيِّزِ:
 هَلْ هُوَ مُرَكَّبٌ مِنْ الْجَوَاهِرِ الْمُنْفَرِدَةِ أَوْ مِنْ الْمَادَّةِ وَالصُّورَةِ؟ أَوْ هُوَ غَيْرُ مُرَكَّبٍ لَا مِنْ هَذَا وَلَا مِنْ هَذَا؟ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ نِزَاعُهُمْ فِي الْجِسْمِ.
 فَالْجِسْمُ عِنْدَهُمْ مُتَحَيِّزٌ وَلَا يَخْرُجُ عَنْهُ شَيْءٌ إلَّا الْجَوْهَرُ الْفَرْدُ عِنْدَ مَنْ أَثْبَتَهُ وَهَؤُلَاءِ يَعْتَقِدُ كَثِيرٌ مِنْهُمْ أَوْ أَكْثَرُهُمْ أَنَّ كُلَّ مُتَحَيِّزٍ فَهُوَ مُرَكَّبٌ أَيْ يَقْبَلُ الِانْقِسَامَ إلَى جُزْءٍ لَا يَتَجَزَّأُ بَلْ يَظُنُّ بَعْضُهُمْ أَنَّ هَذَا إجْمَاعُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَأَكْثَرُهُمْ يَقُولُونَ الْمُتَحَيِّزَاتُ مُتَمَاثِلَةً فِي الْحَدِّ وَالْحَقِيقَةِ وَمَنْ كَانَ مَعْنَى الْمُتَحَيِّزِ عِنْدَهُ هَذَا فَعَلَيْهِ أَنْ يُنَزِّهَ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى أَنْ يَكُونَ مُتَحَيِّزًا بِهَذَا الِاعْتِبَارِ وَإِذَا قَالَ:
 الْمَلَائِكَةُ مُتَحَيِّزُونَ بِهَذَا الِاعْتِبَارِ أَوْ الرُّوحُ مُتَحَيِّزَةٌ بِهَذَا الِاعْتِبَارِ نَازَعَهُ فِي ذَلِكَ جُمْهُورُ الْعُقَلَاءِ مِنْ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَغَيْرِهِمْ؛
 بَلْ لَا يُعْرَفُ أَحَدٌ مِنْ سَلَفِ الْأُمَّةِ وَأَئِمَّتِهَا يَقُولُ:
 إنَّ الْمَلَائِكَةَ مُتَحَيِّزَةٌ بِهَذَا الِاعْتِبَارِ وَلَا قَالُوا لَفْظًا يَدُلُّ عَلَى هَذَا الْمَعْنَى وَكَذَلِكَ رُوحُ بَنِي آدَمَ الَّتِي تُفَارِقُهُ بِالْمَوْتِ لَمْ يَقُلْ أَحَدٌ مِنْ السَّلَفِ إنَّهَا مُتَحَيِّزَةٌ بِهَذَا الِاعْتِبَارِ وَلَا قَالَ فِيهَا لَفْظًا يَدُلُّ عَلَى هَذَا الْمَعْنَى فَإِذَا كَانَ إثْبَاتُ هَذَا التَّحَيُّزِ لِلْمَلَائِكَةِ وَالرُّوحِ بِدْعَةً فِي الشَّرْعِ وَبَاطِلًا فِي الْعَقْلِ فَلَأَنْ يَكُونَ ذَلِكَ بِدْعَةً وَبَاطِلًا فِي رَبِّ
translated_text:
and, in their view, something that occupies space need not be contained by anything else, nor need it have an actually existing spatial region. Rather, anything that can be pointed to and has distinguishable parts occupies space according to them.

They then disagree about what occupies space: is it composed of indivisible atoms, or of matter and form? Or is it composed of neither? Their disagreement concerning bodies has already been discussed.

In their view, a body occupies space, and nothing that occupies space falls outside the category of body except the indivisible atom, according to those who affirm its existence. Many or most of these thinkers believe that everything occupying space is composite—that is, it admits division into indivisible parts. Some even imagine that this is the consensus of the Muslims. Most of them maintain that things occupying space are identical in definition and essential reality.

Anyone who understands spatial occupation in this sense must declare Allah Most High free of occupying space in this sense. If he says, “The angels occupy space in this sense,” or, “The soul occupies space in this sense,” the majority of rational people, Muslims and others, dispute his claim. Indeed, no one among the early generations of the Muslim community or its leading scholars is known to have said that the angels occupy space in this sense, nor did they use any expression conveying this meaning. Likewise, none of the early generations said that the human soul, which departs from a person at death, occupies space in this sense, nor did anyone use an expression conveying this meaning concerning it.

If, then, ascribing this kind of spatial occupation to the angels and the soul is an innovation in religion and rationally false, then it must likewise be an innovation and a falsehood when ascribed to the Lord of

the worlds, all the more so. From this it becomes clear that most of what the philosophers and these speculative theologians say about human souls and the angels is false. What, then, of what they say about the Lord of the worlds?

Thus, the books that set out the positions of these two groups on these great questions—concerning the Lord of the worlds, His angels, human souls, the Hereafter, and prophethood—contain no position that accords with reason and revelation. They know neither what the early generations and the leading scholars said on these matters nor what the Quran and Sunnah indicate. Bewilderment therefore prevails even among their most accomplished thinkers: when they reach the end of their inquiry, they have attained no knowledge, because the statements of both groups that they have examined contain falsehood on both sides.

For this reason, Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said near the end of his life:

“I have reflected on the methods of speculative theology and the approaches of philosophy, and I have not found them to heal the ailing or quench thirst. I have found the most direct path to be the way of the Quran. Read, concerning affirmation:

‘To Him ascends good speech, and righteous work raises it.’

‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.’

And read, concerning negation:

‘There is nothing like Him.’

‘They do not encompass Him in knowledge.’

Whoever undergoes what I have undergone will come to know what I know.”

As for someone who believes that what occupies space is whatever is distinct from something else and stands apart from it, and that it is not

مِنْ شَرْطِهِ أَنْ يَكُونَ مُرَكَّبًا مِنْ الْأَجْزَاءِ الْمُنْفَرِدَةِ وَلَا أَنَّهُ يَقْبَلُ التَّفْرِيقَ وَالتَّقْسِيمَ.
 فَإِذَا قَالَ:
 إنَّ الرَّبَّ مُتَحَيِّزٌ بِهَذَا الْمَعْنَى أَيْ أَنَّهُ بَائِنٌ عَنْ مَخْلُوقَاتِهِ فَقَدْ أَرَادَ مَعْنًى صَحِيحًا لَكِنَّ إطْلَاقَ هَذِهِ الْعِبَارَةِ بِدْعَةٌ وَفِيهَا تَلْبِيسٌ فَإِنَّ هَذَا الَّذِي أَرَادَهُ لَيْسَ مَعْنَى الْمُتَحَيِّزِ فِي اللُّغَةِ وَهُوَ اصْطِلَاحٌ لَهُ وَلِطَائِفَتِهِ وَفِي الْمَعْنَى الْمُصْطَلَحِ نِزَاعٌ بَيْنَ الْعُقَلَاءِ فَصَارَ يَحْتَمِلُ مَعْنًى فَاسِدًا يَجِبُ تَنْزِيهُ الرَّبِّ عَنْهُ وَلَيْسَ لِلْإِنْسَانِ أَنْ يُطْلِقَ لَفْظًا يَدُلُّ عِنْدَ غَيْرِهِ عَلَى مَعْنًى فَاسِدٍ وَيُفْهَمَ ذَلِكَ الْغَيْرَ ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى الْفَاسِدَ مِنْ غَيْرِ بَيَان مُرَادِهِ؛
 بَلْ هَؤُلَاءِ الْمُتَكَلِّمُونَ الَّذِينَ أَرَادُوا بِالْمُتَحَيِّزِ مَا كَانَ مُؤَلَّفًا مِنْ أَجْزَاءٍ لَا تَقْبَلُ الْقِسْمَةَ وَهُوَ مَا كَانَ قَابِلًا لِلْقِسْمَةِ إذَا قَالُوا إنَّ كُلَّ مُمْكِنٍ أَوْ كُلَّ مُحْدَثٍ أَوْ كُلَّ مَخْلُوقٍ فَهُوَ:
 إمَّا مُتَحَيِّزٌ وَإِمَّا قَائِمٌ بِمُتَحَيِّزٍ كَانَ جَمَاهِيرُ الْعُقَلَاءِ يُخَالِفُونَهُمْ فِي هَذَا التَّقْسِيمِ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ أَحَدٌ مِنْ أَئِمَّةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ لَا مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَلَا مِنْ التَّابِعِينَ لَهُمْ بِإِحْسَانٍ إلَى يَوْمِ الدِّينِ وَلَا سَائِرِ أَئِمَّةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ مُوَافِقًا لَهُمْ عَلَى هَذَا التَّقْسِيمِ فَكَيْفَ إذَا قَالَ مَنْ قَالَ مِنْهُمْ: كُلُّ مَوْجُودٍ فَهُوَ إمَّا مُتَحَيِّزٌ وَإِمَّا قَائِمٌ بِمُتَحَيِّزِ وَأَرَادَ بِالْمُتَحَيِّزِ مَا أَرَادَهُ هَؤُلَاءِ فَإِنَّ قَوْلَهُ حِينَئِذٍ يَكُونُ أَبْعَدَ عَنْ الشَّرْعِ وَالْعَقْلِ مِنْ قَوْلِ أُولَئِكَ وَلِهَذَا طَالَبَهُمْ مُتَأَخِّرُوهُمْ بِالدَّلِيلِ عَلَى هَذَا الْحَصْرِ. وَلَيْسَ خَطَأُ هَؤُلَاءِ مِنْ جِهَةِ مَا أَثْبَتَهُ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةُ مِنْ الْجَوَاهِرِ الْعَقْلِيَّةِ فَإِنَّ تِلْكَ قَدْ عُلِمَ بُطْلَانُهَا بِصَرِيحِ الْعَقْلِ أَيْضًا.
translated_text:
a requirement that it be composed of discrete parts or admit of separation and division: if he says, “The Lord occupies space in this sense,” meaning that He is distinct from His creatures, he intends a sound meaning. Using this expression, however, is an innovation and introduces confusion, for the meaning he intends is not the linguistic meaning of “occupying space”; rather, it is a technical usage adopted by him and his group. Rational thinkers dispute this technical meaning, so the expression can convey a false meaning from which the Lord must be declared free. A person may not use an expression that conveys a false meaning to someone else, thereby leading that person to understand that false meaning, without explaining what he intends.

Indeed, consider these speculative theologians who mean by “that which occupies space” something composed of indivisible parts—that is, something that admits of division. When they say, “Every contingent being, or every originated being, or every created being, is either something that occupies space or something subsisting in what occupies space,” the great majority of rational thinkers disagree with this classification. No leading Muslim scholar has agreed with them on this classification: neither the Companions, nor those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment, nor any other leading Muslim scholars.

How much more so, then, when one of them says, “Everything that exists either occupies space or subsists in something that occupies space,” intending by “that which occupies space” what these theologians intend! His statement is then further removed from revelation and reason than theirs. This is why their later thinkers demanded that they provide proof that these are the only possibilities. The error of these theologians is not on account of the intelligible substances posited by the philosophers, for the falsity of those has likewise been established by clear reason.

original_text: وَمَا يَقُولُهُ هَؤُلَاءِ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةُ فِي النَّفْسِ النَّاطِقَةِ مِنْ أَنَّهَا لَا يُشَارُ إلَيْهَا وَلَا تُوصَفُ بِحَرَكَةِ وَلَا سُكُونٍ وَلَا صُعُودٍ وَلَا نُزُولٍ وَلَيْسَتْ دَاخِلَ الْعَالَمِ وَلَا خَارِجَهُ هُوَ أَيْضًا كَلَامٌ أَبْطَلُ مِنْ كَلَامِ أُولَئِكَ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ عِنْدَ جَمَاهِيرِ الْعُقَلَاءِ وَلَا سِيَّمَا مَنْ يَقُولُ مِنْهُمْ - كَابْنِ سِينَا وَأَمْثَالِهِ - إنَّهَا لَا تَعْرِفُ شَيْئًا مِنْ الْأُمُورِ الْجُزْئِيَّةِ وَإِنَّمَا تَعْرِفُ الْأُمُورَ الْكُلِّيَّةَ؛ فَإِنَّ هَذَا مُكَابَرَةٌ ظَاهِرَةٌ فَإِنَّهَا تَعْرِفُ بَدَنَهَا وَتَعْرِفُ كُلَّ مَا تَرَاهُ بِالْبَدَنِ وَتَشُمُّهُ وَتَسْمَعُهُ وَتَذُوقُهُ وَتَقْصِدُهُ وَتَأْمُرُ بِهِ وَتُحِبُّهُ وَتَكْرَهُهُ إلَى غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا تَتَصَرَّفُ فِيهِ بِعِلْمِهَا وَعَمَلِهَا فَكَيْفَ يُقَالُ إنَّهَا لَا تَعْرِفُ الْأُمُورَ الْمُعَيَّنَةَ وَإِنَّمَا تَعْرِفُ أُمُورًا كُلِّيَّةً وَكَذَلِكَ قَوْلُهُمْ إنَّ تَعَلُّقَهَا بِالْبَدَنِ لَيْسَ إلَّا مُجَرَّدَ تَعَلُّقِ التَّدْبِيرِ وَالتَّصْرِيفِ كَتَدْبِيرِ الْمَلِكِ لِمَمْلَكَتِهِ مِنْ أَفْسَدِ الْكَلَامِ فَإِنَّ الْمَلِكَ يُدَبِّرُ أَمْرَ مَمْلَكَتِهِ فَيَأْمُرُ وَيُنْهِي وَلَكِنْ لَا يَصْرِفُهُمْ هُوَ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ إنْ لَمْ يَتَحَرَّكُوا هُمْ بِإِرَادَتِهِمْ وَقُدْرَتِهِمْ وَالْمَلِكُ لَا يَلْتَذُّ بِلَذَّةِ أَحَدِهِمْ وَلَا يَتَأَلَّمُ بِتَأَلُّمِهِ وَلَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ الرُّوحَ وَالْبَدَنَ بَلْ قَدْ جَعَلَ اللَّهُ بَيْنَهُمَا مِنْ الِاتِّحَادِ والائتلاف مَا لَا يُعْرَفُ لَهُ نَظِيرٌ يُقَاسُ بِهِ وَلَكِنَّ دُخُولَ الرُّوحِ فِيهِ لَيْسَ هُوَ مُمَاثِلًا لِدُخُولِ شَيْءٍ مِنْ الْأَجْسَامِ الْمَشْهُودَةِ فَلَيْسَ دُخُولُهَا فِيهِ كَدُخُولِ الْمَاءِ وَنَحْوِهِ مِنْ الْمَائِعَاتِ فِي الْأَوْعِيَةِ فَإِنَّ هَذِهِ إنَّمَا تَلَاقِي السَّطْحَ الدَّاخِلَ مِنْ الْأَوْعِيَةِ لَا بُطُونَهَا وَلَا ظُهُورَهَا وَإِنَّمَا يُلَاقِي
translated_text:
And what these philosophers say about the rational soul—that it cannot be pointed to, cannot be described as moving or being at rest, ascending or descending, and is neither within the world nor outside it—is likewise, in the judgment of the great majority of rational thinkers, even more false than what those speculative theologians say. This applies especially to the claim made by some of them—such as Ibn Sīnā and his like—that it knows nothing of particulars, but knows only universals. This is a blatant denial of the obvious: the soul knows its own body and knows everything it sees, smells, hears, and tastes through the body, as well as what it seeks, commands, loves, and hates, and everything else with which it engages through its knowledge and action. How, then, can it be said that it does not know particular things, but knows only universals?

Likewise, their claim that its connection to the body is merely one of governance and direction, like a king’s governance of his kingdom, is utterly unsound. A king manages the affairs of his kingdom, issuing commands and prohibitions, but he cannot direct his subjects by his own will and power unless they themselves act by their own will and power. Nor does the king experience the pleasure that any one of them experiences, or suffer the pain that he suffers. The relationship between the soul and the body is not like this. Rather, Allah has established between them such union and harmony that no known counterpart can serve as an analogy.

Yet the soul’s entry into the body does not resemble the entry of any observable physical body into another. Its entry into the body is not like that of water and similar liquids into vessels. Likewise, its entry into the body is not like the entry of food and drink into the body of someone who consumes them: these pass through known channels and undergo transformation, among their other properties. Nor does the soul flow through the body as blood does, for blood is present in some parts of the body but not others.

In short, none of the proposed analogies involves every part of one thing being connected with the other, as is the case with the soul and the body. Nevertheless, the soul is within the body and has entered it. It leaves the body at death and is drawn out gradually, emerging from it little by little. It does not leave it as a king leaves the city he governs. Because people have witnessed nothing comparable to the soul, they find it difficult to express its true nature.

This should alert them to the fact that they do not know the true nature of the Lord of all worlds, nor have they conceived how He is—glorified and exalted is He—and that the attributes ascribed to Him are as befits Him, majestic is His glory. For the soul, which is itself one of His servants, is described as ascending when a person sleeps and prostrating beneath the Throne, while still remaining in that person’s body, without having left it altogether. In sleep, a person senses the activities of his soul—activities that affect his body.

Thus, the ascent attributed to the soul does not resemble the ascent of observable things. When these ascend to a place, they leave their former place entirely, and their movement

Thus, when His Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—describes the Lord, glorified is He, as descending to the lowest heaven every night, drawing near to the pilgrims on the afternoon of Arafah, speaking to Moses on the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree, and rising towards heaven while it was smoke, saying to it and to the earth, “Come willingly or unwillingly,” to which they replied, “We come willingly”—it does not follow that these actions are of the same kind as the descent we observe in visible entities, such that one could say that they necessarily entail vacating one place and occupying another.

The soul’s descent and ascent do not entail this, so how much less would this follow in the case of the Lord of all worlds? Likewise, the angels have an ascent and descent of this kind.

It is therefore impermissible to deny any of the names and attributes that Allah and His Messenger have affirmed, or to liken them to the attributes of created beings. This is particularly clear in the case of created beings we do not observe: the names and attributes established for them are not like those of the creatures we do observe. How much more, then, does this apply to the Lord of all worlds, who is far further removed from resembling any created being than one created being is from resembling another? Every created being bears a greater resemblance to another created being unlike itself than the Creator bears to any created being. Glorified and exalted is He, far above what the wrongdoers say.

What we have pointed out helps make clear that the classifications of existing things presented by the author of al-Muhassil and others like him, according to the views of the philosophers and speculative theologians, are all incomplete. Each of these two groups falls short of its predecessors.

As for the speculative theologians, their classifications do not follow the approach indicated by the Quran and Sunnah and followed by the early generations of the Muslim community. Likewise, these philosophers who follow Aristotle did not follow the approach of the great philosophers of antiquity. Those earlier philosophers held that this world came into being. They maintained that above this world there is another world, which they described in some of the same terms the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—used to describe Paradise. They also affirmed bodily resurrection, as can be found in the statements of Socrates, Thales, and other leading philosophers. It has been reported that Aristotle was the first among them to maintain that the world has no beginning.

translated_text:
and expressed it in those terms as a stipulated usage—a convention adopted by him and those who share his doctrine. This is neither the usage of the Arabic language in which the Quran was revealed nor that of any other people. He then makes that meaning the intended sense of such names as “the One and Only,” “the Self-Sufficient,” and “the One,” and similar names found in the Quran and Sunnah. He regards his denial of meanings affirmed by Allah and His Messenger as part of perfecting tawhīd (monotheism).

“Tawhīd” is a revered term: the Messengers brought it, and the revealed Books taught it. When he treats the denial of those meanings as part of tawhīd, anyone unaware that his intended meaning differs from that of the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—supposes that he professes the tawhīd brought by the Messengers. He calls his group “the monotheists,” as do the Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah, and those who agree with them in denying any of the divine attributes. They call this tawhīd, call their group “the monotheists,” and call their discipline “the science of tawhīd.” Likewise, the Mu'tazilah and those who agree with them call the denial of divine decree “justice,” and call themselves “the advocates of justice” and “the people of justice.”

Innovations of this kind are exceedingly numerous: expressions from the Quran and Sunnah are used to convey meanings contrary to what Allah and His Messenger intended by those expressions. Those who hold such views did not originally receive them from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—but rather from specious arguments that occurred to them and from their own leaders. They make their expression of these views in the language of the Quran and Sunnah an argument and a mainstay for their position, so as to appear to be following the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—rather than opposing him. Many of them do not realize

translated_text:
that what they have stated contradicts the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, they suppose that the meaning they intend is the very meaning intended by the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his Companions. Muslims therefore need two things:

The first is to know what Allah and His Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—intended by the expressions used in the Quran and Sunnah. This requires knowing the language in which the Quran was revealed and what the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and the other Muslim scholars said about the meanings of those expressions. When the Messenger addressed them through the Quran and Sunnah, he explained what he intended by those expressions. The Companions’ knowledge of the Quran’s meanings was more complete than their memorization of its wording, and they transmitted those meanings to the succeeding generation more extensively than they transmitted its wording. As for the general meanings that all Muslims need—such as the meaning of tawhīd, of “the One” and “the One and Only,” of faith and Islam, and the like—all the Companions knew what Allah and His Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—wanted them to know. Yet only a few of them memorized the entire Quran, although every part of it was memorized by a number of them sufficient for mass transmission.

The Quran is filled with descriptions of Allah as the One and Only and the One, with statements that your God is One, that there is no god but Allah, and the like. The Companions must therefore have understood this, for knowing it is the foundation of religion. It was the first thing to which the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—called people, and it was the first

thing for which he fought them, and the first thing he instructed his envoys to command people to do. Reports transmitted from him through numerous independent chains establish that the first thing he called people to was to say, “There is no god but Allah.” When he commanded jihad after the Hijrah, he said:

“I have been commanded to fight the people until they bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah.”

The two Sahīh collections relate that when he sent Mu‘ādh to Yemen, he told him:

“You are going to a people from among the People of the Book. Let the first thing you call them to be the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah. If they obey you in this, inform them that Allah Most High has prescribed for them five prayers each day and night. If they obey you in this, inform them that Allah Most High has prescribed for them charity to be taken from their wealthy and given to their poor. If they obey you in this, beware of taking their most prized possessions, and beware of the supplication of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and Allah.”

Thus he told Mu‘ādh: “Let the first thing you call them to be monotheism.” Yet they were People of the Book—they were Jews, for Jews were numerous in Yemen. This instruction to Mu‘ādh accords with the words of Allah Most High:

“When the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every lookout. But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then let them go their way.”

And in the other verse:

“But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then they are your brothers in religion.”

This also accords with the words of Allah Most High:

“They were commanded only to worship Allah, devoting their religion sincerely to Him, upright in faith, to establish prayer, and to give zakat. That is the upright religion.”

The two Sahīh collections also report from him—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

 يَجْتَنِبُ الْمُتَكَلِّمُ فِي الْفِقْهِ هَذَيْنِ الْأَصْلَيْنِ الْمُجْمَلِ وَالْقِيَاسِ وَهَذِهِ الطَّرِيقُ يَشْتَرِكُ فِيهَا جَمِيعُ أَهْلُ الْبِدَعِ الْكِبَارِ وَالصِّغَارِ
translated_text:
that he said:

“Faith has sixty-odd or seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road. Modesty is a branch of faith.”

The point is that knowing what the Messenger brought and what he intended by the wording of the Quran and hadith is the foundation of knowledge, faith, happiness, and salvation. Next comes knowing what people have said on these matters, so that one can distinguish meanings consistent with the Messenger’s teaching from those that contradict it.

Terms are of two kinds: those found in the speech of Allah and His Messenger, and those not found in their speech. One should understand the meaning of the first kind and make that meaning the foundation, then ascertain what people mean by the second kind and assess it against the first.

This is the way of those who follow guidance and the Sunnah. Those who follow misguidance and innovation take the opposite approach: they make the terms they have introduced, and their meanings, the foundation, subordinating what Allah and His Messenger have said to their own formulations. Through reinterpretation and distortion, they force the revealed words to conform to their own meanings. They say, “We interpret the Quran through reason and language.” What they mean is that they adopt a meaning on the basis of their own reasoning and opinion, then interpret the Quran accordingly, using whatever interpretations and explanations they can devise, which involve displacing words from their proper meanings. Hence Imam Ahmad said: “Most of people’s errors arise from reinterpretation and analogical reasoning.”

He also said: “Anyone speaking on jurisprudence should avoid these two foundations: ambiguous formulations and analogical reasoning.” This approach is shared by all proponents of innovation, great and small.

 إنَّ الرَّسُولَ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمْ يُبَيِّنْ وَلَمْ يُفَهِّمْ؛ بَلْ وَلَمْ يَقْصِدْ ذَلِكَ. وَهُمْ مُتَنَازِعُونَ هَلْ كَانَ يَعْلَمُ الْأُمُورَ عَلَى مَا هِيَ عَلَيْهِ؟

translated_text:
for this is the way of the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, and those philosophers and heretical Bātiniyyah who engage in reinterpretation.

The most adept philosophers, however, say:

“The sole purpose of the Messenger’s discourse—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is to evoke in the minds of the masses ideas that serve their worldly interests, even if these do not correspond to the truth.”

They say:

“The Messenger’s purpose—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is not to explain the truth and make it known, but to evoke in their minds ideas for them to believe.”

They regard the distinctive characteristic of prophethood as the power to evoke such imaginative representations. Thus, they say that the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—neither explained the truth nor enabled people to understand it; indeed, he did not even intend to do so. They disagree, however, over whether he knew things as they really are, holding two views.

Some say that he knew them but could not explain them. Those who hold this view may regard the Messenger as superior to the philosopher. Others say that he did not know them, or was not adept in knowing them, and that he knew only practical matters. These regard the philosopher as more perfect than the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—because practical matters are more perfect than theoretical ones.

Thus, these people regard the reports conveyed by Allah and by the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—as containing nothing but imaginative representations. The others say that he did not intend to evoke imaginative representations, but rather intended a meaning that could be understood through reinterpretation.

Many Jahmī speculative theologians agree with those philosophers that he could not openly declare the truth concerning divine oneness, and therefore addressed the masses in terms that would evoke images in their minds, as when they say: “Had he said:

translated_text:
‘Your Lord is neither within the world nor outside it; He cannot be pointed to; He is not above the world, nor such-and-such, nor such-and-such,’ their hearts would have recoiled from him, and they would have said, ‘This is something unknown.’” They say: “He therefore addressed them in terms of corporeality to establish for them a Lord whom they could worship, even though he knew that attributing corporeality to Allah was false.”

This is said by groups of prominent, well-known jurists of later times who supposed that the position of those who deny the divine attributes was correct, and therefore needed to explain away the Messenger’s affirmation of them—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Such statements can be found in the writings of more than one of them.

At other times, they say: “The Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—refrained from explaining the truth only so that they would strive to discover it without his making it known to them, and strive to reinterpret his words, thereby earning greater rewards for doing so.” This refers to their efforts in rational speculation and reinterpretation. They do not say that he intended thereby to instil falsehood in the minds of ordinary people, as those philosophers maintain.

This is the position of most speculative theologians who deny the divine attributes among the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, and those who follow their path—even Ibn ‘Aqīl and others like him. The first view, however, is found in the writings of Abū Hāmid, Ibn Rushd the grandson, and others like them.

It was only to preserve this principle that Abū Hāmid condemned reinterpretation toward the end of his life and composed Iljām al-‘awāmm ‘an ‘ilm al-kalām (Restraining the Common People from Speculative Theology). For he considered that the welfare of the masses could be secured only by leaving the apparent meanings as they stood, even though he himself held the view expressed in his books al-Madnūn bihā: that negation is what is true in reality.

Thus, they did not regard clarification and guidance as the purpose of his address, although Allah described His Book and His Prophet in these terms, saying:

“Guidance for the God-fearing.”

And He said:

“This is a clear explanation for mankind.”

And He said:

“We have sent it down as an Arabic Quran so that you may understand.”

And He said:

“The Messenger’s duty is only to convey the message clearly.”

And He said:

“A Book We have sent down to you so that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light.”

There are many similar passages. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“I have left you upon a clear path, whose night is like its day. No one will deviate from it after me except one who is doomed.”

Allah Most High said:

“This is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow other paths, lest they lead you away from His path.”

And He said:

“There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book.”

“Through it Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the paths of peace, brings them out of darkness into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path.”

And He said:

“You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was, but We made it a light by which We guide whomever We will of Our servants. And you indeed guide to a straight path.”

And He said:

“Those who believe in him, honour him, support him, and follow the light sent down with him—it is they who will prosper.”

Then there is a third group, which has become numerous among later people who affiliate themselves with the Sunnah. They make statements implying that the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—did not know the meanings of what was revealed to him of the Quran, such as the verses concerning the divine attributes. Indeed, their position also necessarily implies that he would relate hadiths concerning the divine attributes without knowing their meanings. and those who followed them in righteousness—that a full stop should be made at His words,

“And none knows its interpretation except Allah”—

they agreed with the early generations, and rightly so. But they assumed that “interpretation” (ta’wīl) meant the meaning and explanation of the wording, or the technical interpretation frequently mentioned by many later scholars of jurisprudence and legal theory: shifting a term from its more likely meaning to a less likely one on the basis of accompanying evidence. They had heard the statements of both groups, so this became what the word “interpretation” meant to them.

When they heard Allah Most High’s words,

“And none knows its interpretation except Allah,”

they assumed that “interpretation” in the Quran meant what it meant in the discourse of these scholars. This necessarily implied that no one knows the meaning of these texts except Allah: neither Gabriel nor Muhammad nor anyone else. Indeed, according to their position, each of the two messengers recites the noblest passages of the Quran—its statements about Allah, His names and His attributes—without knowing their meaning at all. Furthermore, many of them condemn and reject the interpretations offered by the people of innovation, such as the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah and others. This is good.

Yet they may say, “These texts are to be taken at face value, and none knows their interpretation except Allah.” If by “at face value” they mean the meanings apparent from them, this contradicts their assertion that these texts have an interpretation contrary to their apparent meaning, known only to Allah. If, however, they mean merely their wording, their statement amounts to saying that the speaker utters these words, but they have an inner meaning contrary to their apparent meaning: this is their interpretation, and none knows it except Allah. Sometimes a text is explained in a way consistent with its apparent meaning, and it becomes clear that this is not interpretation in the third sense. Yet they reject this and dislike reflecting on the texts and examining their meanings—I mean the texts whose interpretation, they say, is known only to Allah.

Their approach to these texts then depends on their beliefs. If they are Qadariyyah, they say: “The texts affirming that the servant acts are unambiguous, while the texts affirming that Allah Most High creates the acts of His servants, or wills everything that occurs, are ambiguous texts whose interpretation none knows except Allah”—if they are among those who do not reinterpret them. For most groups include those who reinterpret whatever conflicts with their position and those who do not.

If they are among those who affirm the divine attributes they claim to know through reason, but not the attributes known through revealed reports—as was the case with many later Kullābiyyah, such as Abū al-Maʿālī towards the end of his life and Ibn ʿAqīl in much of his discourse—they say of the texts containing attributes that, according to them, cannot be known through reason: “These are ambiguous texts whose interpretation none knows except Allah.” Many of them have two positions and adopt two different stances: sometimes they reinterpret the texts and deem such interpretation obligatory or permissible; at other times they prohibit it. As for those heretical Bātinīs and their philosophers who advocate reinterpretation, they reinterpret everything the messengers taught concerning belief in Allah and the Last Day. They then reinterpret the expressions used, as is well known from the interpretations of the Bātinī Qarmatians.

Abū Hāmid, in al-Ihyā’, mentioned the position of these philosophers who advocate reinterpretation. He said that they had gone to excess in reinterpretation, while the Hanbalīs had been excessively rigid. He also attributed to Ahmad ibn Hanbal statements that Ahmad never made, for he did not know what Ahmad or the other early generations had said on this subject, nor what the Quran and hadith teach concerning it. He had heard views ascribed to the Hanbalīs which were held by some of them, as well as by some Mālikīs, Shāfiʿīs, and others, concerning letters, sound, and certain attributes.

Examples include their claims that the sounds heard from Quran reciters are eternal and beginningless; that the successive letters are each individually beginningless; and that He descends to the lowest heaven, leaving the Throne vacant of Him, so that some created things are above Him and others below Him—along with other objectionable claims.

There is no group without some members who make statements that are manifestly unsound. These are the statements remembered by those who are averse to them and used to vilify them, even though most members of those groups reject and repudiate such statements. Nevertheless, among adherents of hadith generally, whether Hanbalīs or others, errors in affirming attributes are more common than among speculative theologians. Conversely, errors in negation are more common among speculative theologians than among adherents of hadith. For hadith came to affirm the attributes and contains none of the forms of negation peculiar to speculative theologians. The speculative theology inherited from the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah is founded upon negation that contradicts the explicit teachings of the Quran and hadith—indeed, sound reason as well. Yet they claim that reason establishes this negation. Other groups of speculative theologians have opposed them and gone further in affirmation, such as the Hishāmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and others. Nevertheless, negation predominates in the innovated speculative theology condemned by the early generations.

Those Hanbalīs and others who identify with the Sunnah and make the term “reinterpretation” encompass both categories appeal to statements they find from the leading scholars concerning ambiguous texts. One example is Ahmad’s statement, as reported by Hanbal: “Neither a ‘how’ nor a meaning.” They supposed that he meant that we do not know their meaning. Yet Ahmad’s statements explicitly show otherwise in several places. He explained that he rejects only the reinterpretations of the Jahmiyyah and others like them, whose interpretations of the Quran depart from its proper interpretation. He composed his book, Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah, concerning the ambiguous passages of the Quran that they rejected and interpreted contrary to their proper meaning. Thus he condemned their reinterpretation of the Quran

some said: “The realization of the punishment with which they were threatened.” Ta’wīl is what a matter ultimately comes to. Al-Dahhāk explained: “It means the eventual outcome of the punishment that Allah promised in the Quran would come to pass.” Ta’wīl is what a matter ultimately comes to.

Al-Tha‘labī said: “Its explanation.” This is untenable.

Al-Zajjāj said: “They had no knowledge of its ta’wīl.” Joseph the truthful, peace be upon him, said:

“O my father, this is the fulfillment of my earlier dream.”

He thus identified his parents’ actual prostration before him as the fulfillment of his dream.

Earlier, he had said:

“No food will come to you as your provision without my telling you its interpretation before it comes to you.”

That is, before its fulfillment comes to you. The meaning is: no food will come to you as your provision in a dream—for one of them had said:

“I saw myself pressing grapes for wine,” and the other said, “I saw myself carrying bread on my head”—

“without my telling you its interpretation” in waking life, “before it comes to you,” namely, the food. This is the view of most Quran commentators, and it is correct.

Some said: “No food will come to you as provision—that is, food you are given to eat and consume—without my telling you its interpretation: its description and varieties, what food you ate, how much you ate, and when you ate.” They said: “This is what diviners and soothsayers do.” He replied: “I am no soothsayer. This knowledge is only part of what my Lord teaches me.”

This view is untenable, for he said:

“Without my telling you its interpretation.”

One of them had said:

“I saw myself pressing grapes for wine,” and the other said, “I saw myself carrying bread on my head, from which birds were eating. Tell us its interpretation.”

Thus, they asked him to interpret what they had seen, and he told them its interpretation. The interpretation was not of food in

waking life, nor does the Quran say that he told them what provisions they would receive while awake. How, then, could he make the unrestricted statement:

“No food will come to you as your provision”?

Only Allah can provide such comprehensive information. The prophets relate some such matters, but not all of them. Moreover, describing food and its quantity is not its interpretation. Furthermore, Allah only stated that He had taught him the interpretation of dreams. Jacob, peace be upon him, said:

“Thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of dreams.”

Joseph, peace be upon him, said:

“My Lord, You have granted me a share of sovereignty and taught me the interpretation of dreams.”

He also said:

“This is the fulfillment of my earlier dream.”

When the king had his dream, the man who remembered after some time said to him:

“I will tell you its interpretation, so send me.”

The king had said:

“O eminent ones, explain my dream to me, if you can interpret dreams.”

“They said, ‘A confused jumble of dreams, and we have no knowledge of the interpretation of dreams.’”

Here the word ta’wīl occurs in several places, always with the same meaning.

Allah Most High also said:

“If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and best in outcome.”

Mujāhid and Qatādah explained this as “recompense and reward.” Al-Suddī, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjāj explained it as “the eventual outcome.” Another explanation reported from Ibn Zayd is “confirmation,” as in His words:

“This is the fulfillment of my earlier dream.”

All these explanations are correct and convey the same meaning. This is the interpretation given by

Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī says:

“Scholars have differed over whether tafsīr and ta’wīl have the same meaning or different meanings. Some whose inclination is toward Arabic language studies held that they mean the same thing. This is the view of the majority of the early Quranic commentators. Others, whose inclination is toward jurisprudence, held that they differ. They said: Tafsīr brings something out of obscurity into clarity, whereas ta’wīl shifts speech from its ordinary sense to a meaning whose establishment requires evidence, without which the apparent meaning of the wording would not be abandoned. It is derived from the expression āla al-shay’u ilā kadhā, meaning that something came to such-and-such a state.”

These scholars mention only the first and second meanings of ta’wīl; they do not mention its meaning in the language of the Quran. It has already been established that ta’wīl in the Quran is the actual reality to which the speech ultimately refers, even when that accords with the meaning apparent from the wording. Indeed, nowhere in the Quran is the term ta’wīl known to signify something contrary to what the wording indicates, unlike the convention of later scholars.

Speech is of two kinds: directive and informative. Directive speech comprises commands, prohibitions, and permissions. The ta’wīl of a command or prohibition is the actual performance of what is commanded or the actual abandonment of what is forbidden.

Thus, in the Sahīh, ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say while bowing and prostrating: ‘Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You.

O Allah, forgive me.’ He was putting the Quran into practice.” These words were thus the ta’wīl of His saying:

“Then glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness.”

Ibn ‘Uyaynah said: “The Sunnah is the ta’wīl of commands and prohibitions.” When discussing the disagreement between jurists and linguists concerning “the Prophet’s prohibition of ishtimāl al-sammā’ (a manner of wrapping oneself in a garment),” Abū ‘Ubayd said: “The jurists are more knowledgeable about ta’wīl.”

He means that they are more knowledgeable about the ta’wīl of what Allah has commanded and forbidden: they recognize the actual, concrete actions He has commanded and the prohibited actions He has forbidden. The explanation of His speech is not itself what exists in external reality; rather, it clarifies His speech, expounds it, and reveals its meaning. Thus, tafsīr belongs to the realm of speech: speech is explained through other speech that clarifies it. Ta’wīl, however, consists in doing what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden; it does not belong to the realm of speech.

The second kind is informative speech, such as the Lord’s statements about Himself—exalted is He—concerning His names and attributes, and His statements about the promises and warnings He has mentioned to His servants. This is the ta’wīl mentioned in His words:

“We have certainly brought them a Book which We explained in detail with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for people who believe.”

“Are they waiting for anything but its fulfilment? On the Day its fulfilment comes, those who had forgotten it before will say, ‘The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth.’”

This is like their words:

“Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth.”

Similarly, He says:

“Proceed to that which you used to deny.”

And He says:

“They say, ‘When will this promise come to pass, if you are truthful?’”

“Say, ‘Knowledge of it is with Allah alone, and I am only a clear warner.’”

“But when they see it close at hand, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed, and it will be said, ‘This is what you were calling for.’”

There are many similar passages in the Quran. Likewise, He says:

“Or do they say, ‘He has fabricated it’? Say, ‘Then produce a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.’”

“Rather, they have denied that which they have not fully grasped in knowledge and whose fulfilment has not yet come to them.”

What they were promised in the Quran has not yet come to them, but it will. Tafsīr is full knowledge of it, whereas ta’wīl is the very thing they were promised, when it comes to them. They denied the Quran without fully grasping it in knowledge, and before its ta’wīl had come to them. Yet people may fully grasp it in knowledge before its ta’wīl comes to them. The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, fully grasps what Allah has revealed to him, even though its ta’wīl has not yet come.

A hadith relates that when the verse beginning with His words, “Say, ‘He has the power to send punishment upon you from above you,’” was revealed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “It will surely come to pass, but its ta’wīl has not yet come.”

Allah Most High says:

“Your people have denied it, though it is the truth. Say, ‘I am not a guardian over you.’”

Muqātil said: “Every announcement Allah makes has a time and place in which it comes to pass, without fail or delay.”

Al-Hasan said:
“Every deed has its recompense. Whoever does a good deed will be rewarded for it in Paradise, and whoever does an evil deed will be repaid for it in Hell. And you will come to know.”

Al-Hasan’s meaning is that deeds are subject to promises of reward and threats of punishment. These promises and threats constitute the announcement that has its appointed fulfilment. He thus explained the meaning; he did not mean that the recompense itself is the announcement itself.

Concerning “Every announcement has its appointed fulfilment,” al-Suddī said: “That is, an appointed time that I have promised you. It will come to you, and then you will recognize it.”

Concerning “Every announcement has its appointed fulfilment,” ‘Atā’ said: “His punishment is deferred so that he may commit his sin.” Once he commits his sin, He punishes him. That is, He does not inflict the threatened punishment until the person commits the sin for which He threatened him.

Another example is the statement of many of the early generations concerning certain verses: “The ta’wīl of this verse has already passed, while the ta’wīl of that verse has not yet come.” For instance, Abū al-Ashhab related from al-Hasan, and al-Rabī‘ from Abū al-‘Āliyah, that the following verse was recited to Ibn Mas‘ūd:

“O you who believe, attend to yourselves”—to the end of the verse.

Ibn Mas‘ūd said:
“This is not the time for its application. Proclaim it as long as it is accepted from you; but when it is rejected, attend to yourselves.”

Then he said: “The Quran was revealed when it was revealed. Some of its verses concern matters whose ta’wīl had already passed before they were revealed. Some had their ta’wīl during the lifetime of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; some had their ta’wīl shortly after the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; some will have their ta’wīl after today; some will have their ta’wīl at the end of time; and some will have their ta’wīl on the Day of Resurrection—those that mention the Reckoning, Paradise and Hell. So, as long as

your hearts and inclinations remain united, you are not divided into factions, and you do not suffer violence at one another’s hands, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. But when hearts and inclinations differ, you are divided into factions, and you suffer violence at one another’s hands, let each person attend to himself. At that point, the ta’wīl of this verse will have arrived.”

In these words, Ibn Mas‘ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned both the ta’wīl of a command and the ta’wīl of a report. The verse,

“Attend to yourselves,”

is a command, whereas what is mentioned concerning the Reckoning and the Resurrection is a report. It has become clear that the ta’wīl of a report is the actual occurrence of what is reported, while the ta’wīl of a command is carrying out what is commanded. Thus, a verse whose ta’wīl preceded its revelation belongs to the category of reports: something happens, and Allah then mentions it, as He mentioned what the polytheists said to the Messenger and their denial of his truthfulness. Although its ta’wīl has already occurred, it remains a lesson, and its meaning holds true in analogous cases. An example is Ibn Mas‘ūd’s statement, “Five have already come to pass.” Another is Allah’s statement:

“The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split.”

these things and their counterparts in this world there is a similarity in wording and meaning. Nevertheless, their reality differs from that of their worldly counterparts, and we do not know that reality in this world. Allah Most High says:

“No soul knows what joy is kept hidden for them as a reward for what they used to do.”

And in an authentic hadith:

“Allah Most High says: ‘I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever conceived.’”

These things that Allah has promised His believing servants, which no soul knows, belong to the ta’wīl known only to Allah. Likewise, none but Allah knows the time of the Hour and its signs. Nor does anyone but Allah know how the Reckoning, the Bridge, the Balance, the Cistern, reward and punishment will actually be. For this has not yet been created for the angels to know it, nor does it have a counterpart identical in every respect through which it could be known. Thus, it belongs to the ta’wīl of the ambiguous passages that none but Allah knows.

Likewise, regarding what the Lord has told us about Himself—such as His rising over His Throne, His hearing, His sight, His speech and so forth—none but Allah knows how these are. This is what Rabī‘ah ibn Abī ‘Abd al-Rahmān and Mālik ibn Anas stated, and the other scholars have accepted their words. When the question was put, “‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne’—how did He rise over it?” he replied:

“The rising over is known; how it is, is unknown. Belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation.”

This is Mālik’s wording. He stated that the rising over is known, which concerns the explanation of the wording, and that how it is remains unknown. This is the manner of being whose knowledge Allah has reserved for Himself.
