translated_text:
Likewise, the other early scholars, such as Ibn al-Mājishūn, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, explain that people do not know the manner of being of what Allah has told them about Himself. This manner of being is the ta’wīl known only to Allah. As for the meaning itself that Allah has explained, people understand it, each according to their capacity. They understand the meaning of hearing and the meaning of sight, and that these are distinct concepts. They also understand the difference between these and “the All-Knowing” and “the All-Powerful,” even though they do not know how His hearing and sight are. Indeed, they have a general understanding of the soul within them, yet do not know its manner of being. Likewise, they understand the meaning of rising over the Throne, and that it entails the Lord’s being above His Throne and His elevation over it, as the early scholars before them explained. This is the known meaning of the expression; linguistically, it admits no other meaning, as has been explained at length elsewhere. This is why Mālik said:

“The rising over is known.”

Anyone who says, “Isti wā’ has several meanings,” has spoken without making the necessary distinctions. For people say simply istawā, without attaching a preposition, and this has a particular meaning. They also use istawā with ‘alā (“over”), which has a particular meaning; with ilā (“toward”), which has a particular meaning; and with ma‘a (“with”), which has a particular meaning. Its meanings thus vary according to the words attached to it. As for istawā ‘alā something, it has only one meaning in the Quran and in established Arabic usage. Allah Most High says:

“Then strengthened it, so that it grew stout and stood upright on its stalks.”

And He says:

“And it came to rest on Mount Jūdī.”

And He says:

“So that you may settle upon their backs, then remember your Lord’s blessing when you have settled upon them.”

And He says:

“Then, when you have settled, you

and those with you, aboard the ship.”

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was brought a mount to ride. When he placed his foot in the stirrup, he said, ‘In the name of Allah.’ When he had settled on its back, he said, ‘Praise be to Allah.’”

Ibn ‘Umar said: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited the pilgrimage invocation for Hajj when he had settled on his camel.”

This meaning entails two things: being above that upon which one has settled, and also being upright. They do not describe someone leaning over something as having settled upon it. This also includes the account of al-Khalīl ibn Ahmad saying, “Straighten yourselves.”

The verse:

“Then Bishr rose over Iraq,
Without a sword or blood being shed,”

belongs to this same category. The person meant is Bishr ibn Marwān, and his rising over Iraq means taking his place upon its royal throne. The poet did not mean merely gaining mastery over it, but Bishr’s taking his place over it. Otherwise, ‘Abd al-Malik, who was the caliph, would also have risen over Iraq and the rest of the Islamic realm; ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb would have risen over Iraq, Khurāsān, Syria, Egypt, and all the other lands he conquered; and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have risen over Yemen and the other lands he conquered.

Yet it is well known that their speech contains no instance of using “rising over” in any of these cases. Rather, it was said of someone who personally took his place over a land, for he takes his place upon his royal throne, just as one says, “So-and-so sat upon the throne,” or, “He seated himself upon the royal seat.” This also includes His saying:

“And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them. She has been given of all things, and she has a magnificent throne.”

And the claim of al-Zamakhsharī and others that “‘He rose over something’ means ‘he possessed it’” is a bare assertion, unsupported by any example from Arab speech. Even if such usage were conceded, this meaning would still be invalid when applied to Allah’s rising over the Throne. For He has stated that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne. He has also stated that the Throne existed before the creation of the heavens and the earth, as both the Quran and the Sunnah indicate. Thus, from the moment He created the Throne, He owned it and held dominion over it. How, then, could His rising over it have occurred after the creation of the heavens and the earth?

Moreover, He owns everything and holds dominion over it, so the Throne would not be singled out for His rising over it. This is not like singling it out in connection with His lordship when He says:

“Lord of the Magnificent Throne.”

The Throne may be singled out because of its magnificence, but the same expression may also be applied to all other created things. Thus, one may say, “Lord of the Throne and Lord of all things.” Rising over, however, applies specifically to the Throne. It is therefore not said, “He rose over the Throne and over all things.” Nor has any Muslim used this expression with reference to all things, nor is such usage found in the Quran or the Sunnah. By contrast, the expression of lordship is used both specifically of the Throne and generally of all things. The same applies to creation and similar expressions that admit both specific and general application, as in His words, exalted is He:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created—created man from a clinging substance.”

Rising over is therefore an expression specific to the Throne; it is not applied to anything else, either specifically or generally. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The purpose here is simply to demonstrate the correctness of the statement of the early generations:

“What ‘rising over’ means is known.”

translated_text:
unlike those who assign this expression ten-odd meanings, as mentioned by Ibn ‘Arabī al-Ma‘āfirī.

This is clarified by the circumstances in which this verse was revealed: the arrival of the Christians of Najrān and their debate with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning the Messiah, as related by Quran commentators and biographers. It is widely known—indeed, established by mass transmission—that the Christians of Najrān came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he challenged them to the mutual invocation of Allah’s curse mentioned in Surah Āl ‘Imrān. They agreed to pay the jizyah but did not accept that challenge. The opening of Āl ‘Imrān was revealed because of these events; hence most of it concerns the Messiah.

They relate that these Christians cited such Quranic expressions as “that We” and “We” as evidence that there are three gods. Thus they followed what was ambiguous and abandoned the Quran’s unambiguous declaration that God is One:

“Seeking discord and seeking an interpretation of it.”

Their purpose was to cause discord—that is, to lead hearts into disbelief—and to seek the ultimate reality signified by the expressions “Indeed, We” and “We.” Only Allah knows the ultimate reality denoted by these expressions, for they are used only of a single individual who has helpers, whether these are his partners or servants whom he owns.

This is why these expressions admit ambiguity. Someone who has partners says, “We have done such-and-such, and We indeed do such-and-such.” This is impossible in the case of Allah Most High. Someone who has servants whom he owns and subjects who obey him—such as a king—says, “We have done such-and-such,” meaning, “I

have done this through those under my rule and in my possession.” Everything other than Allah is created by Him and belongs to Him. He, glorified is He, governs the affairs of the world Himself and through His angels, who are His messengers in His creation and command. In this respect, He is the One most entitled to say “Indeed, We” and “We,” for no one besides Him possesses absolute sovereignty or issues commands that are obeyed completely. He therefore deserves to say “Indeed, We” and “We.” Kings bear some resemblance to this, so there is another respect in which these expressions are ambiguous. Yet nothing resembles Allah in the unique prerogative attributed to Him in this regard.

Knowing the ultimate reality of this means knowing His angels, their attributes and ranks, and how He governs the affairs of heaven and earth through them. Allah Most High has said:

“None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him.”

Thus, only He knows the ultimate reality of these ambiguous expressions. Even if we know their explanation and meaning, we do not know the ultimate reality to which they refer in actual existence.

This is unlike His words:

“Allah is the One who created.”

This is an unambiguous verse containing no ambiguity, for this name belongs exclusively to Allah. It is not like “Indeed, We” and “We,” which are used by someone who has partners or helpers whom he needs. Allah Most High is far above either of these, as He has said:

“Say, ‘Call upon those whom you claim to be gods besides Allah. They possess not an atom’s weight in the heavens or on earth, nor do they have any share in either, nor does He have any helper among them.’”

And He has said:

“And say, ‘All praise is for Allah, who has never taken a son, who has no partner in His sovereignty, and who needs no protector out of weakness.’ And proclaim His greatness.”

The meaning intended by these expressions when applied to created beings cannot have any counterpart established for Allah. This is why they are ambiguous.

The same applies to His words:

“Then He rose over the Throne.”

For He has also said:

“And it came to rest on Mount Jūdī.”

And He has said:

“Then it stands firm upon its stalks.”

And He has said:

“Then, when you and those with you have boarded the Ark.”

And He has said:

“So that you may settle upon their backs.”

All these instances of istiwāʾ (being established upon something) entail the dependence of what is above upon what is beneath it: were that which supports it absent, it would fall. Allah Most High, however, has no need of the Throne or anything else. Rather, He, glorified is He, bears the Throne and its bearers by His power. It has been reported that they were only able to bear the Throne when He commanded them to say: “There is no power nor strength except through Allah.”

Thus, the term istiwāʾ is ambiguous: when applied to created beings, it entails meanings from which Allah is utterly free. We know its meaning—elevation and evenness—but we do not know the manner unique to the Lord, whereby He is established above the Throne without any need of it. Rather, the Throne needs Him, and everything depends upon Him in every respect. Among existing things, we have never known anything to be established upon something else while having no need of it, with that which is beneath it instead depending upon what is above it. It is therefore ambiguous in this respect.

The two expressions and their meanings have an element in common, as well as a distinguishing element intended in each case. We do not know the distinguishing reality unique to the Lord. Thus, we know it in one respect and do not know it in another. The latter is its ultimate reality, while the former is its explanation.

The same applies to what Allah has told us about the food, drink, and clothing in Paradise, such as milk, honey, wine, and water. We know of no milk except that produced by livestock

 . فَهَذَا الْمُشْتَبِهُ عَلَى بَعْضِ النَّاسِ يُمْكِنُ الْآخَرِينَ أَنْ يَعْرِفُوا الْحَقَّ فِيهِ وَيُبَيِّنُوا الْفَرْقَ بَيْنَ الْمُشْتَبِهَيْنِ وَهَذَا هُوَ الَّذِي أَرَادَهُ مَنْ جَعَلَ الرَّاسِخِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ التَّأْوِيلَ فَإِنَّهُ جَعَلَ الْمُشْتَبِهَاتِ فِي الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ هَذَا الْبَابِ الَّذِي يَشْتَبِهُ عَلَى بَعْضِ النَّاسِ دُونَ بَعْضٍ وَيَكُونُ بَيْنَهُمَا مِنْ الْفُرُوقِ الْمَانِعَةِ لِلتَّشَابُهِ مَا يَعْرِفُهُ بَعْضُ النَّاسِ وَهَذَا الْمَعْنَى صَحِيحٌ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَا يُنْكَرُ وَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ الرَّاسِخِينَ فِي الْعِلْمِ يَعْلَمُونَ مَا اشْتَبَهَ عَلَى غَيْرِهِمْ وَقَدْ يَكُونُ هَذَا قِرَاءَةً فِي الْآيَةِ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ أَنَّهُ يَكُونُ فِيهَا قِرَاءَتَانِ؛ لَكِنَّ لَفْظَ التَّأْوِيلِ عَلَى هَذَا يُرَادُ بِهِ التَّفْسِيرُ وَوَجْهُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ تَأْوِيلَهُ مِنْ حَيْثُ الْجُمْلَةِ كَمَا يَعْلَمُونَ تَأْوِيلَ الْمُحْكَمِ فَيَعْرِفُونَ الْحِسَابَ وَالْمِيزَانَ وَالصِّرَاطَ وَالثَّوَابَ وَالْعِقَابَ وَغَيْرَ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا أَخْبَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ وَرَسُولُهُ مَعْرِفَةً مُجْمَلَةً فَيَكُونُونَ عَالِمِينَ بِالتَّأْوِيلِ وَهُوَ مَا يَقَعُ فِي الْخَارِجِ عَلَى هَذَا الْوَجْهِ
translated_text:
with falsehood, as in the words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) in the hadith:

“What is lawful is clear, and what is unlawful is clear. Between them are doubtful matters whose status many people do not know.”

This indicates that some people do know their status. They are therefore not doubtful to everyone, but only to some people. This differs from that whose ta’wīl (interpretation) is known only to Allah, for all people share in not knowing its ta’wīl. Related to this is what is reported from the Messiah (peace be upon him), who said:

“Matters are of three kinds: those that are clearly right, so follow them; those that are clearly wrong, so avoid them; and those that are unclear to you, so leave them to whoever knows them.”

Thus, when something is unclear to some people, others may know the truth concerning it and explain the distinction between the two things being confused. This is what those who hold that people firmly grounded in knowledge know the ta’wīl intended: they regarded the ambiguous passages of the Quran as belonging to this category—things that are unclear to some people but not to others. There are distinctions between the two things that prevent their being confused, and some people recognize these distinctions. This understanding is sound in itself and cannot be denied. Undoubtedly, those firmly grounded in knowledge understand what is unclear to others.

This may be one reading of the verse, as discussed earlier concerning its admitting two readings. On this reading, however, the term ta’wīl means explanation. The reason is that they know its ta’wīl in general terms, just as they know the ta’wīl of the clear passages. Thus, they have a general knowledge of the Reckoning, the Balance, the Bridge, reward, punishment, and the other things about which Allah and His Messenger have informed us. They therefore know the ta’wīl—what takes place in external reality—in this general sense

وَعَلَى قِرَاءَةِ النَّفْيِ هَلْ يُقَالُ أَيْضًا:
 إنَّ الْمُحْكَمَ لَهُ تَأْوِيلٌ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ تَفْصِيلَهُ؟
 فَإِنَّ قَوْلَهُ:
 وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَ مَا تَشَابَهَ مِنْهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ لَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ غَيْرَهُ يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَ الْمُحْكَمِ بَلْ قَدْ يُقَالُ: إنَّ مِنْ الْمُحْكَمِ أَيْضًا مَا لَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَإِنَّمَا خَصَّ الْمُتَشَابِهَ بِالذِّكْرِ لِأَنَّ أُولَئِكَ طَلَبُوا عِلْمَ تَأْوِيلِهِ أَوْ يُقَالُ بَلْ الْمُحْكَمُ يَعْلَمُونَ تَأْوِيلَهُ لَكِنْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ وَقْتَ تَأْوِيلِهِ وَمَكَانَهُ وَصِفَتَهُ.
 وَقَدْ قَالَ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ السَّلَفِ:
 إنَّ الْمُحْكَمَ مَا يُعْمَلُ بِهِ وَالْمُتَشَابِهَ مَا يُؤْمَنُ بِهِ وَلَا يُعْمَلُ بِهِ كَمَا يَجِيءُ فِي كَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْآثَارِ وَنَعْمَلُ بِمُحْكَمِهِ،
 وَنُؤْمِنُ بِمُتَشَابِهِهِ وَكَمَا جَاءَ عَنْ ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ وَغَيْرِهِ فِي قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى:
 
{الَّذِينَ آتَيْنَاهُمُ الْكِتَابَ يَتْلُونَهُ حَقَّ تِلَاوَتِهِ}
 قَالَ يُحَلِّلُونَ حَلَالَهُ وَيُحَرِّمُونَ حَرَامَهُ وَيَعْمَلُونَ بِمُحْكَمِهِ وَيُؤْمِنُونَ بِمُتَشَابِهِهِ. وَكَلَامُ السَّلَفِ فِي ذَلِكَ يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ التَّشَابُهَ أَمْرٌ إضَافِيٌّ فَقَدْ يَشْتَبِهُ عَلَى هَذَا مَا لَا يَشْتَبِهُ عَلَى هَذَا فَعَلَى كُلِّ أَحَدٍ أَنْ يَعْمَلَ بِمَا اسْتَبَانَ لَهُ وَيَكِلَ مَا اشْتَبَهَ عَلَيْهِ إلَى اللَّهِ. كَقَوْلِ أبي بْنِ كَعْبٍ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ - فِي الْحَدِيثِ الَّذِي رَوَاهُ
translated_text:
but they do not know it in detail, for they do not know how it is or what its true reality is, since it is unlike what they have known and witnessed in this world. Accordingly, it is valid to say that they know its ta’wīl, meaning that they understand its explanation; and it is also valid to say that they do not know its ta’wīl. Both readings are true.

On the reading that denies them this knowledge, may it also be said that the clear passages have a ta’wīl whose details they do not know? For His words, “None but Allah knows the ta’wīl of its ambiguous passages,” do not indicate that anyone other than Him knows the ta’wīl of the clear passages. Rather, it may be said that some clear passages, too, have a ta’wīl known only to Allah, and that the ambiguous passages were specifically mentioned only because those people sought knowledge of their ta’wīl. Alternatively, it may be said that they do know the ta’wīl of the clear passages, but do not know the time, place, or manner of its realization.

Many of the early generations said: “The clear passages are those to be acted upon, while the ambiguous passages are those to be believed in but not acted upon.” Thus, many transmitted reports state: “We act upon its clear passages and believe in its ambiguous passages.” Likewise, Ibn Mas‘ūd and others are reported to have said concerning the words of the Most High:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture recite it as it should be recited.”

He said: “They regard as lawful what it declares lawful, regard as unlawful what it declares unlawful, act upon its clear passages, and believe in its ambiguous passages.”

The statements of the early generations on this subject indicate that ambiguity is relative: something may be unclear to one person but not to another. Everyone must therefore act upon what has become clear to them and entrust to Allah what remains unclear to them, as in the words of Ubayy ibn Ka‘b (may Allah be pleased with him) in the report narrated by

الثَّوْرِيُّ عَنْ مُغِيرَةَ - وَلَيْسَ بِشَيْءِ -

{فَيَنْسَخُ اللَّهُ مَا يُلْقِي الشَّيْطَانُ ثُمَّ يُحْكِمُ اللَّهُ آيَاتِهِ}

translated_text:
al-Thawrī from Mughīra—of no weight—from Abū al-‘Āliya, who said:

Ubayy ibn Ka‘b was asked, “Give me counsel.” He replied: “Take the Book of Allah as your guide, and accept it as judge and arbiter. It is what His Messenger appointed as his successor among you: an intercessor whose intercession is heeded and a witness above suspicion. It contains accounts of what preceded you, accounts of what is among you, mention of what preceded you, and mention of what is in your midst.”

Sufyān also narrated from a man whom he named, from Ibn Abzā, from Ubayy, who said: “Act upon whatever becomes clear to you; whatever remains unclear to you, believe in it and entrust it to the One who knows it.”

Some of them said that the ambiguous passages are those that have been abrogated, while others included all declarative passages. Thus, Qatāda, al-Rabī‘, al-Dahhāk, and al-Suddī are reported to have said: “The clear passages are the abrogating passages, which are acted upon; the ambiguous passages are the abrogated passages, which are believed in but not acted upon.” The same appears in al-‘Awfī’s transmission of the commentary of Ibn ‘Abbās.

As for al-Wālibī’s transmission of the commentary of Ibn ‘Abbās, it states: “The clear passages of the Quran are its abrogating passages, its declarations of what is lawful and unlawful, its prescribed limits and obligations, and whatever is to be believed in and acted upon. The ambiguous passages are its abrogated passages, its earlier and later passages, its parables and oaths, and whatever is to be believed in but not acted upon.”

The first view is, and Allah knows best, derived from His words:

“Allah abolishes what Satan casts, then Allah makes His verses firm.”

Here He contrasts what is abolished with what is made firm. Yet He, glorified be He, meant only the abolition of what Satan had cast, not the abrogation of what He Himself had revealed. They nevertheless classified abrogated passages in general as ambiguous because they resemble other passages in recitation and composition

 الْمُحْكَمُ مَا فِيهِ مِنْ الْحَلَالِ وَالْحَرَامِ وَمَا سِوَى ذَلِكَ مُتَشَابِهٌ يُصَدِّقُ بَعْضُهُ بَعْضًا.
 فَعَلَى هَذَا الْقَوْلِ يَكُونُ الْمُتَشَابِهُ هُوَ الْمَذْكُورَ فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{كِتَابًا مُتَشَابِهًا مَثَانِيَ}
 .

 إنَّ الْعُلَمَاءَ يَعْلَمُونَ تَأْوِيلَهُ؛ لَكِنَّ تَفْسِيرَ الْمُتَشَابِهِ بِهَذَا مَعَ أَنَّ كُلَّ الْقُرْآنِ مُتَشَابِهٌ وَهُنَا خَصَّ الْبَعْضَ بِهِ فَيُسْتَدَلُّ بِهِ عَلَى ضَعْفِ هَذَا الْقَوْلِ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ قَوْلُهُ:
 
{فَيَتَّبِعُونَ مَا تَشَابَهَ مِنْهُ ابْتِغَاءَ الْفِتْنَةِ}
 لَوْ أُرِيدَ بِالْمُتَشَابِهِ
translated_text:
and in being Allah’s speech, Quran, and miraculous, as well as in other respects, although their meaning has been abrogated. Those who classify as ambiguous everything that is not acted upon—abrogated passages, oaths, and parables—do so because these are ambiguous, and people have not been commanded to know their details. Rather, general belief in them suffices, unlike passages that are acted upon, which require detailed knowledge.

This explains what is incumbent upon the entire community: they must know in detail what is to be acted upon so that they may act upon it. As for matters of which they have been informed, they are not obliged to have knowledge of them; rather, they must believe in them. Although knowledge of these matters may be commendable or a communal obligation, it is not an individual obligation, unlike knowledge of what must be acted upon. Every person must therefore know in detail the actions required of him, but is not required to have detailed knowledge of matters that do not require action.

It has been reported from Mujāhid and ‘Ikrima:

“The clear passages are those concerning what is lawful and unlawful; everything else is ambiguous, its parts confirming one another.”

According to this view, the ambiguous passages are what is mentioned in His words:

“a Book, consistent within itself, with recurring themes.”

What is lawful, however, differs from what is unlawful. This accords with Mujāhid’s view that scholars know its interpretation. Yet explaining “ambiguous” in this way, when the entire Quran is mutually consistent, whereas here He applies the description only to part of it, provides evidence of the weakness of this view.

Likewise, regarding His words:

“They follow what is ambiguous in it, seeking discord,”

This means that the clear wording can refer to only one thing in external reality. Ambiguous wording, however, admits several interpretations, although Allah intends only one of them, and the context of the verse indicates the intended meaning. Thus, those firmly grounded in knowledge know what is intended by the ambiguous passages just as they know what is intended by the clear passages. Yet the interpretation itself—in the sense of the actual reality, the timing of events, and the like—is something they do not know from either kind of passage.

It has also been said that the Christians of Najrān cited His words “a word from Allah” and “a spirit from Him” as evidence. The expression “the word of Allah” may refer to speech or to what is created through speech. Likewise, “from” in “a spirit from Him” may indicate origin or a partitive relationship. If the choice is between saying that the Messenger did not know the meaning of the Quran’s ambiguous passages and saying that those firmly grounded in knowledge do know it, this affirmation is better than that negation. For the many proofs from the Quran, the Sunnah, and the statements of the early generations indicate that the entire Quran can be known, understood, and reflected upon. This must be held with certainty. There is, however, no conclusive indication that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know the explanation of its ambiguous passages. Indeed, many of the early generations said that they knew their interpretation, including Mujāhid—with his eminent standing—al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas, and Muhammad ibn Ja‘far ibn al-Zubayr. They also transmitted this from Ibn ‘Abbās, reporting that he said:

“I am among those firmly grounded in knowledge who know its interpretation.”

translated_text:
Ahmad’s remarks in his refutation of the heretics and the Jahmiyyah concerning the ambiguous passages of the Quran about which they entertained doubts and which they misinterpreted, together with his statement that the Jahmiyyah interpreted three ambiguous verses, followed by his explanation of their meaning, demonstrate that, in his view, scholars know the meaning of the ambiguous passages. What is blameworthy is interpreting them incorrectly. Explaining them in accordance with their meaning, however, is praiseworthy, not blameworthy. This implies that, in his view, those firmly grounded in knowledge know the correct interpretation of the ambiguous passages—what the early generations called explanation.

Thus, neither Ahmad nor anyone else among the early generations said that the Quran contains verses whose meaning neither the Messenger nor anyone else knows, but whose wording they recite without understanding it. This position was adopted by many of Ahl al-Sunnah, including Ibn Qutaybah, Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī, and others.

Ibn Qutaybah was among those affiliated with Ahmad and Ishāq who championed the well-known doctrines of the Sunnah. He wrote numerous works on this subject. The author of An Account of the Merits of the Scholars of Hadith said of him:

“He was one of the most distinguished imams, scholars, and men of virtue, the finest among them in composition and the best in organizing his material. He wrote approximately three hundred works and inclined towards the teachings of Ahmad and Ishāq. He was a contemporary of Ibrāhīm al-Harbī and Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī. The people of the Maghrib held him in great esteem and would say: ‘Anyone who considers it permissible to disparage Ibn Qutaybah is suspected of heresy.’ They would also say: ‘There is no good in a house that contains none of his writings.’”

I say:

And it is said that he is to Ahl al-Sunnah what al-Jāhiz is to the Mu‘tazilah: he is the spokesman for the Sunnah, just as al-Jāhiz is the spokesman for the Mu‘tazilah.

The other view has also been transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās, as well as from other Companions and a group of the Successors. Those holding this view cited no explicit statement from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in support of their position. It therefore became a disputed question, to be referred back to Allah and the Messenger. The proponents of that view argued that Allah linked seeking discord with seeking its interpretation, and that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, censured those who pursue ambiguous passages, saying:

“When you see those who follow its ambiguous passages, beware of them.”

For this reason, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—beat Subaygh ibn ‘Isl when he questioned him about the ambiguous passages. They also argued that Allah said:

“And those firmly grounded in knowledge say”.

If “and” coordinated one noun phrase with another, rather than introducing a new sentence linked to the preceding one, He would have said: “and they say”.

The other side answered this by pointing to Allah’s words:

“For the poor emigrants who were driven out of their homes and possessions, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure”.

Then He said:

“And those who had settled in the city and embraced the faith before them love those who emigrate to them and do not find…”—to the end of the verse.

Then He said:

“And those who came after them say, ‘Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith.’”

{وَمَا يَذَّكَّرُ إلَّا أُولُو الْأَلْبَابِ}
 وَهَذَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ هُنَا تَذَكُّرًا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ أُولُو الْأَلْبَابِ فَإِنْ كَانَ مَا ثَمَّ إلَّا الْإِيمَانُ بِأَلْفَاظٍ فَلَا يُذَكِّرُ لِمَا يَدُلُّهُمْ عَلَى مَا أُرِيدَ بِالْمُتَشَابِهِ.

translated_text:
knowledge say, ‘We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.’”

They said: Moreover, if the intent were merely to describe them as having faith, He would not have singled out those firmly grounded in knowledge, but would have said: “And the believers say, ‘We believe in it.’” Every believer is obliged to believe in it. Since He specifically mentioned those firmly grounded in knowledge, it is clear that they were distinguished by knowing its interpretation. They knew it because they possessed knowledge, and believed in it because they had faith. Their belief in it, accompanied by knowledge, was thus a more perfect attribute. Immediately afterward, He said:

“None take heed except people of understanding.”

This indicates that there is a taking of heed here that is particular to people of understanding. If nothing more were involved than believing in words, there would be no taking heed of what shows them the intended meaning of the ambiguous passages.

A parallel to this is His statement in the other verse:

“But those among them who are firmly grounded in knowledge, and the believers, believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you.”

When He described them as firmly grounded in knowledge and as believing, He mentioned the believers alongside them. Had mere belief been intended here, He would have said: “And those firmly grounded in knowledge and the believers say, ‘We believe in it.’” This is just as, in that other verse, He mentioned both groups together when His purpose was simply to state their belief.

They said: As for the censure, it applies only to those who pursue the ambiguous passages, seeking discord and seeking their interpretation. This describes people with corrupt intentions who wish to discredit the Quran. They seek out only its ambiguous passages in order to corrupt hearts, thereby putting them to trial through it, and they seek its interpretation. translated_text:
for the sake of causing discord. Likewise, ʿUmar beat Sabīgh ibn ʿAsal because his purpose in asking about the ambiguous passages was to stir up discord. This resembles someone who raises questions and objections about another person’s words, asking, “What was meant by such-and-such?” His aim is to cast doubt on those words and discredit them, not to discover the truth. These are the people whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, meant when he said:

“When you see those who pursue its ambiguous passages…”

Thus, “pursue” means that they seek out and deliberately focus on the ambiguous passages rather than the clear ones, just as someone pursuing something deliberately seeks it out. This is the conduct of someone intent on causing discord. But someone who asks about the meaning of an ambiguous passage in order to understand it and dispel doubts that have arisen—while knowing and following the clear passages, believing in the ambiguous passages, and having no intention of causing discord—is not censured by Allah.

This is also what the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, used to say. An example is the well-known report narrated by Ibrāhīm ibn Yaʿqūb al-Jūzajānī and also mentioned by al-Talamankī:

Yazīd ibn ʿAbd Rabbih narrated to us: Baqiyyah narrated to us: ʿUtbah ibn Abī Hakīm narrated to us: ʿImārah ibn Rāshid al-Kinānī narrated to me, from Ziyād, from Muʿādh ibn Jabal, who said:

“Two kinds of men read the Quran. One reads it with personal desires and an ulterior motive, combing through it as one searches a head for lice, hoping to find something with which to turn against people. Such people are the worst members of their community; Allah blinds them to the paths of guidance.

“The other reads it without personal desires or an ulterior motive, combing through it as one searches a head for lice. Whatever becomes clear to him, he acts upon; whatever remains unclear, he entrusts to Allah. He will surely gain an understanding of it such as no people have ever attained. Even if one of them were to wait twenty years, Allah would surely send him someone to explain the verse that puzzled him, or enable him to understand it for himself.”

translated_text:
Baqiyyah said, “Ibn ʿUyaynah called me as a witness to this report of ʿUtbah.”

Thus, Muʿādh censures those who pursue ambiguous passages with the intention of causing discord. As for those whose purpose is understanding, he states that Allah will surely grant them, through understanding the ambiguous passages, an insight such as no people have ever attained.

They said: The evidence for this is that whenever a Companion encountered a difficulty concerning a verse or hadith, he would ask about it. Thus, ʿUmar asked the Prophet, “Did you not tell us that we would come to the House and circumambulate it?” ʿUmar also asked him, “Why do we shorten the prayer when we are now safe?”

When Allah’s words were revealed:

“and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing,”

they found this distressing and said, “Which of us has not wronged himself?” Then he explained it to them. Likewise, when His words were revealed:

“Whether you reveal what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it,”

they found this distressing until he explained the wisdom behind it to them.

When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Whoever is subjected to a detailed examination of his account will be punished,” ʿĀʾishah asked, “Did Allah not say, ‘He will receive an easy reckoning’?” He replied, “That refers only to the presentation of one’s deeds.”

They said: The consensus of the early generations also supports what we have stated, for they explained the entire Quran. Mujāhid said, “I went through the Quran with Ibn ʿAbbās from beginning to end, stopping him at every verse and asking him about it.”

 لَا تَدَبَّرُوا الْمُتَشَابِهَ وَالتَّدَبُّرُ بِدُونِ الْفَهْمِ مُمْتَنِعٌ وَلَوْ كَانَ مِنْ الْقُرْآنِ مَا لَا يُتَدَبَّرُ لَمْ يُعْرَفْ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَمْ يُمَيِّزْ الْمُتَشَابِهَ بِحَدٍّ ظَاهِرٍ حَتَّى يُجْتَنَبَ تَدَبُّرُهُ. وَهَذَا أَيْضًا مِمَّا يَحْتَجُّونَ بِهِ وَيَقُولُونَ الْمُتَشَابِهُ أَمْرٌ نِسْبِيٌّ إضَافِيٌّ فَقَدْ يَشْتَبِهُ عَلَى هَذَا مَا لَا يَشْتَبِهُ عَلَى غَيْرِهِ قَالُوا؛

 وَلِأَنَّ مِنْ الْعَظِيمِ أَنْ يُقَالَ: إنَّ اللَّهَ أَنْزَلَ عَلَى نَبِيِّهِ كَلَامًا لَمْ يَكُنْ يَفْهَمُ مَعْنَاهُ لَا هُوَ وَلَا جِبْرِيلُ بَلْ وَعَلَى قَوْلِ هَؤُلَاءِ كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يُحَدِّثُ بِأَحَادِيثِ الصِّفَاتِ وَالْقَدَرِ وَالْمَعَادِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا هُوَ نَظِيرُ مُتَشَابِهِ الْقُرْآنِ عِنْدَهُمْ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ يَعْرِفُ مَعْنَى مَا يَقُولُهُ وَهَذَا لَا يُظَنُّ بِأَقَلِّ النَّاسِ.
translated_text:
they had learned the knowledge and practice contained in them. They said, ‘Thus we learned the Quran, knowledge, and practice together.’”

The explanations given by the Quranic commentators among the Companions and Successors cover the entire Quran, except for passages that some of them may find difficult and concerning which they therefore withhold judgment—not because no one knows their meaning, but because they themselves do not know it.

Moreover, Allah has commanded reflection upon the Quran without qualification. He has not excepted any part of it from such reflection, nor has He said, “Do not reflect upon the ambiguous passages.” Reflection without understanding is impossible. If there were any part of the Quran upon which one should not reflect, it would be impossible to identify it, for Allah has not distinguished the ambiguous passages by a clear criterion that would allow people to avoid reflecting upon them. This, too, is among their arguments. They say that ambiguity is relative: what is unclear to one person may not be unclear to another.

They said: Allah has also declared that the Quran is clarification, guidance, healing, and light, without excluding any part of it from this description. Yet none of this is possible without understanding its meaning.

They said: Furthermore, it is a grave matter to say that Allah revealed to His Prophet words whose meaning neither he nor Gabriel understood. Indeed, according to these people, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would relate hadiths concerning the divine attributes, divine decree, resurrection, and similar matters—which they regard as comparable to the ambiguous passages of the Quran—without knowing the meaning of what he was saying. Yet such a thing would not be presumed of even the lowliest person.

translated_text:
Moreover, the purpose of speech is to convey understanding. If that is not its purpose, it is futile and vain. Allah Most High has declared Himself far above doing anything vain or futile. How, then, could He utter vain and futile words, sending down speech to His creation without intending them to understand it? This is among the strongest arguments of those who reject the faith.

Furthermore, there is not a verse in the Quran whose meaning the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness have not discussed and explained. If it is said, “But they may disagree about some of this,” the answer is: “They may likewise disagree about verses containing commands and prohibitions.” Yet Muslims agree that those firmly grounded in knowledge know the meanings of verses containing commands and prohibitions.

This also demonstrates that those firmly grounded in knowledge know the explanation of the ambiguous passages. For ambiguity may occur in verses containing commands and prohibitions just as it may occur in verses conveying information. Scholars agree that those firmly grounded in knowledge understand the former; the same therefore applies to the latter. According to those who deny this, however, none but Allah knows the meaning of the ambiguous passages—not an angel, a messenger, or a scholar. This contradicts the consensus of Muslims concerning ambiguous passages containing commands and prohibitions.

Moreover, the term “interpretation” applies to clear passages just as it applies to ambiguous ones, as the Quran, the Sunnah, and the statements of the Companions demonstrate. Since they know the meaning of the clear passages, they likewise know the meaning of the ambiguous ones. What distinction do the ambiguous passages possess that Allah alone should know their meaning? The clear passages are superior to them, yet He has explained their meaning to His servants. What distinction, then, do the ambiguous passages possess that Allah should reserve knowledge of their meaning for Himself? As for matters whose knowledge Allah has reserved for Himself, such as the time of the Hour, He has not sent down concerning them

The dispute concerns only speech that He has sent down, described as guidance, clarification, and healing, and commanded people to reflect upon. Yet it is then claimed that some of it has a meaning known only to Allah, although neither Allah nor His Messenger has identified that portion whose meaning no one knows. They had argued from His words “Indeed, We” and “We,” and from His description of Jesus as “a word” from Him and “a spirit” from Him. Muslims agree that the meaning of these expressions is known. How, then, can it be said that neither the angels, nor the prophets, nor any of the early generations knows the meaning of the ambiguous passages? These are part of Allah’s speech, which He sent down to us and commanded us to reflect upon and understand, describing it as clarification, guidance, healing, and light. The sole purpose of speech is to convey its meanings; were meaning not intended, it would not be permissible to utter words devoid of meaning.

Al-Hasan said:

“Allah has not sent down any verse without loving that people should know what it was revealed about and what was meant by it.”

 وَبِالْجُمْلَةِ:
 فَالدَّلَائِلُ الْكَثِيرَةُ تُوجِبُ الْقَطْعَ بِبُطْلَانِ قَوْلِ مَنْ يَقُولُ: إنَّ فِي الْقُرْآنِ آيَاتٌ لَا يَعْلَمُ مَعْنَاهَا الرَّسُولُ وَلَا غَيْرُهُ.
translated_text:
Second, it has been said that they made this statement when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, first arrived in Medina. Yet the opening of Surah Āl ʿImrān was revealed only later, when the delegation from Najrān arrived, as established by widespread, mass-transmitted reports. It was in this surah that Hajj was prescribed, and it was prescribed only in the ninth or tenth year after the Hijrah—not at the outset of the Hijrah, as all Muslims agree.

Third, the letters of the alphabet and a letter’s indication of how long this community will endure are not part of that interpretation of the Quran whose knowledge Allah has reserved for Himself. Either one says that this is not something Allah intended by His speech—in which case one cannot say that He alone knows it; rather, the claim that the letters indicate it is false—or one says that they do indicate it, in which case some people have understood what they indicate. Thus, people have come to know it. What is false is to claim both that the Quran indicates this and that no one knows it.

Furthermore, if the Messenger did not understand the matters of knowledge that Allah conveyed in the Quran, this would provide the heretics with one of their strongest grounds for attacking him. It would support their claim that he either did not understand these matters or understood them but did not explain them. Indeed, this position entails that he did not know them, since whatever Allah alone knows is known neither to the Prophet nor to anyone else.

In short, the abundant evidence establishes with certainty the falsity of the claim that the Quran contains verses whose meaning neither the Messenger nor anyone else knows.

original_text:
نَعَمْ قَدْ يَكُونُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ آيَاتٌ لَا يَعْلَمُ مَعْنَاهَا كَثِيرٌ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ فَضْلًا عَنْ غَيْرِهِمْ وَلَيْسَ ذَلِكَ فِي آيَةٍ مُعَيَّنَةٍ بَلْ قَدْ يُشْكِلُ عَلَى هَذَا مَا يَعْرِفُهُ هَذَا وَذَلِكَ تَارَةً يَكُونُ لِغَرَابَةِ اللَّفْظِ وَتَارَةً لِاشْتِبَاهِ الْمَعْنَى بِغَيْرِهِ وَتَارَةً لِشُبْهَةٍ فِي نَفْسِ الْإِنْسَانِ تَمْنَعُهُ مِنْ مَعْرِفَةِ الْحَقِّ وَتَارَةً لِعَدَمِ التَّدَبُّرِ التَّامِّ وَتَارَةً لِغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَسْبَابِ فَيَجِبُ الْقَطْعُ بِأَنَّ قَوْلَهُ:
 
{وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَالرَّاسِخُونَ فِي الْعِلْمِ يَقُولُونَ آمَنَّا بِهِ}
 .
 أَنَّ الصَّوَابَ قَوْلُ مَنْ يَجْعَلُهُ مَعْطُوفًا وَيَجْعَلُ الْوَاوَ لِعَطْفِ مُفْرَدٍ عَلَى مُفْرَدٍ أَوْ يَكُونُ كِلَا الْقَوْلَيْنِ حَقًّا وَهِيَ قِرَاءَتَانِ وَالتَّأْوِيلُ الْمَنْفِيُّ غَيْرُ التَّأْوِيلِ الْمُثْبَتِ وَإِنْ كَانَ الصَّوَابُ هُوَ قَوْلُ مَنْ يَجْعَلُهَا وَاوَ اسْتِئْنَافٍ فَيَكُونُ التَّأْوِيلُ الْمَنْفِيُّ عِلْمُهُ عَنْ غَيْرِ اللَّهِ هُوَ الْكَيْفِيَّاتُ الَّتِي لَا يَعْلَمُهَا غَيْرُهُ وَهَذَا فِيهِ نَظَرٌ وَابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ جَاءَ عَنْهُ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 أَنَا مِنْ الرَّاسِخِينَ الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ تَأْوِيلَهُ وَجَاءَ عَنْهُ أَنَّ الرَّاسِخِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ تَأْوِيلَهُ.
 وَجَاءَ عَنْهُ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 التَّفْسِيرُ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَوْجُهٍ: تَفْسِيرٌ تَعْرِفُهُ الْعَرَبُ مِنْ كَلَامِهَا " وَتَفْسِيرٌ لَا يُعْذَرُ أَحَدٌ بِجَهَالَتِهِ وَتَفْسِيرٌ يَعْلَمُهُ الْعُلَمَاءُ وَتَفْسِيرٌ لَا يَعْلَمُهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ مَنْ ادَّعَى عِلْمَهُ فَهُوَ كَاذِبٌ. وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ يَجْمَعُ الْقَوْلَيْنِ وَيُبَيِّنُ أَنَّ الْعُلَمَاءَ يَعْلَمُونَ مِنْ تَفْسِيرِهِ مَا لَا يَعْلَمُهُ غَيْرُهُمْ وَأَنَّ فِيهِ مَا لَا يَعْلَمُهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ فَأَمَّا مَنْ جَعَلَ الصَّوَابَ قَوْلَ مَنْ جَعَلَ الْوَقْفَ عِنْدَ قَوْلِهِ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَجَعَلَ التَّأْوِيلَ بِمَعْنَى التَّفْسِيرِ فَهَذَا خَطَأٌ قَطْعًا.
translated_text:
Certainly, the Quran may contain verses whose meanings are unknown to many scholars, let alone others. This is not tied to any particular verse; rather, one person may find obscure what another understands. Sometimes this is because the wording is unfamiliar; sometimes because its meaning is confused with another; sometimes because a misconception within a person prevents him from recognizing the truth; sometimes because he has not reflected deeply enough; and sometimes for other reasons. It must therefore be affirmed with certainty that, regarding His words:

“No one knows its interpretation except Allah and those firmly grounded in knowledge. They say, ‘We believe in it.’”

the correct view is that “those firmly grounded in knowledge” is conjoined to “Allah,” with “and” coordinating one noun phrase with another. Or both views may be correct, corresponding to two readings, with “interpretation” referring to one thing when knowledge of it is denied and another when such knowledge is affirmed. If, however, the correct view is that “and” begins a new sentence, then the interpretation whose knowledge is denied to anyone other than Allah must refer to the modalities that He alone knows. This, however, is open to question.

It is reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said, “I am among those firmly grounded in knowledge who know its interpretation.” It is also reported from him that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know its interpretation. And it is reported that he said:

“Explanation of the Quran is of four kinds: an explanation that the Arabs understand through their own language; an explanation that no one is excused for not knowing; an explanation known to scholars; and an explanation known only to Allah—whoever claims to know it is a liar.”

This statement reconciles the two views. It shows that scholars know aspects of its explanation that others do not, and that it contains matters known only to Allah. But anyone who holds that the correct view is to pause at His words “except Allah,” while taking ‘interpretation’ to mean explanation, is unquestionably mistaken.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا التَّأْوِيلُ بِالْمَعْنَى الثَّالِثِ وَهُوَ صَرْفُ اللَّفْظِ عَنْ الِاحْتِمَالِ الرَّاجِحِ إلَى الِاحْتِمَالِ الْمَرْجُوحِ فَهَذَا الِاصْطِلَاحُ لَمْ يَكُنْ بَعْدُ عُرِفَ فِي عَهْدِ الصَّحَابَةِ بَلْ وَلَا التَّابِعِينَ بَلْ وَلَا الْأَئِمَّةِ الْأَرْبِعَةِ وَلَا كَانَ التَّكَلُّمُ بِهَذَا الِاصْطِلَاحِ مَعْرُوفًا فِي الْقُرُونِ الثَّلَاثَةِ بَلْ وَلَا عَلِمْت أَحَدًا مِنْهُمْ خَصَّ لَفْظَ التَّأْوِيلِ بِهَذَا وَلَكِنْ لَمَّا صَارَ تَخْصِيصُ لَفْظِ التَّأْوِيلِ بِهَذَا شَائِعًا فِي عُرْفِ كَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ فَظَنُّوا أَنَّ التَّأْوِيلَ فِي الْآيَةِ هَذَا مَعْنَاهُ صَارُوا يَعْتَقِدُونَ أَنَّ لِمُتَشَابِهِ الْقُرْآنِ مَعَانِيَ تُخَالِفُ مَا يُفْهَمُ مِنْهُ وَفَرَّقُوا دَيْنَهُمْ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ وَصَارُوا شِيَعًا وَالْمُتَشَابِهُ الْمَذْكُورُ الَّذِي كَانَ سَبَبَ نُزُولِ الْآيَةِ لَا يَدُلُّ ظَاهِرُهُ عَلَى مَعْنًى فَاسِدٍ وَإِنَّمَا الْخَطَأُ فِي فَهْمِ السَّامِعِ.
 نَعَمْ قَدْ يُقَالُ:
 إنَّ مُجَرَّدَ هَذَا الْخِطَابِ لَا يُبَيِّنُ كَمَالَ الْمَطْلُوبِ وَلَكِنْ فَرْقٌ بَيْنَ عَدَمِ دِلَالَتِهِ عَلَى الْمَطْلُوبِ وَبَيْنَ دِلَالَتِهِ عَلَى نَقِيضِ الْمَطْلُوبِ. فَهَذَا الثَّانِي هُوَ الْمَنْفِيُّ؛ بَلْ وَلَيْسَ فِي الْقُرْآنِ مَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْبَاطِلِ أَلْبَتَّةَ كَمَا قَدْ بُسِطَ فِي مَوْضِعِهِ. وَلَكِنْ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ النَّاسِ يَزْعُمُ أَنَّ لِظَاهِرِ الْآيَةِ مَعْنًى إمَّا مَعْنًى يَعْتَقِدُهُ وَإِمَّا مَعْنًى بَاطِلًا فَيَحْتَاجُ إلَى تَأْوِيلِهِ وَيَكُونُ مَا قَالَهُ بَاطِلًا لَا تَدُلُّ الْآيَةُ عَلَى مُعْتَقَدِهِ وَلَا عَلَى الْمَعْنَى الْبَاطِلِ وَهَذَا كَثِيرٌ جِدًّا وَهَؤُلَاءِ هُمْ الَّذِينَ يَجْعَلُونَ الْقُرْآنَ كَثِيرًا مَا يَحْتَاجُ إلَى التَّأْوِيلِ الْمُحْدَثِ وَهُوَ صَرْفُ اللَّفْظِ عَنْ مَدْلُولِهِ إلَى خِلَافِ مَدْلُولِهِ.
translated_text:
As for interpretation in its third sense—diverting an expression from its more likely meaning to a less likely one—this technical usage was not yet known in the time of the Companions, nor even among the Successors or the four imams. Nor was this terminology current during the first three generations. Indeed, I know of none of them who restricted the word “interpretation” to this meaning. However, when this restricted usage became widespread among many later scholars, they assumed that this was what “interpretation” meant in the verse. They consequently came to believe that the ambiguous passages of the Quran had meanings contrary to what is understood from them. Thereafter, they divided their religion and split into sects. Yet the ambiguous passages in question, which occasioned the revelation of the verse, do not outwardly indicate any unsound meaning; rather, the error lies in the hearer’s understanding.

Admittedly, it may be said that this wording alone does not fully explain what is intended. But there is a difference between its not indicating the intended meaning and its indicating the opposite of that meaning. It is the latter that is denied. Indeed, nothing in the Quran indicates falsehood at all, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Yet many people claim that the apparent wording of a verse conveys a particular meaning—either a meaning they themselves believe, or a false meaning that therefore requires reinterpretation. Their claim is false: the verse indicates neither their belief nor that false meaning. This is exceedingly common. These are the people who hold that the Quran frequently requires interpretation in its newly introduced sense: diverting an expression from what it signifies to something contrary to what it signifies.

original_text:
وَمِمَّا يَحْتَجُّ بِهِ مَنْ قَالَ الرَّاسِخُونَ فِي الْعِلْمِ يَعْلَمُونَ التَّأْوِيلَ:
 مَا ثَبَتَ فِي صَحِيحِ الْبُخَارِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِ - 
{عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ: أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ دَعَا لَهُ وَقَالَ: اللَّهُمَّ فَقِّهْهُ فِي الدِّينِ وَعَلِّمْهُ التَّأْوِيلَ}
 فَقَدْ دَعَا لَهُ بِعِلْمِ التَّأْوِيلِ مُطْلَقًا وَابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ فَسَّرَ الْقُرْآنَ كُلَّهُ قَالَ مُجَاهِدٌ: عَرَضْت الْمُصْحَفَ عَلَى ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ مِنْ أَوَّلِهِ إلَى آخِرِهِ أَقِفُهُ عِنْدَ كُلِّ آيَةٍ وَأَسْأَلُهُ عَنْهَا وَكَانَ يَقُولُ: أَنَا مِنْ الرَّاسِخِينَ فِي الْعِلْمِ الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ تَأْوِيلَهُ. وَأَيْضًا فَالنُّقُولُ مُتَوَاتِرَةٌ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ أَنَّهُ تَكَلَّمَ فِي جَمِيعِ مَعَانِي الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ الْأَمْرِ وَالْخَبَرِ فَلَهُ مِنْ الْكَلَامِ فِي الْأَسْمَاءِ وَالصِّفَاتِ وَالْوَعْدِ وَالْوَعِيدِ وَالْقَصَصِ وَمِنْ الْكَلَامِ فِي الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ وَالْأَحْكَامِ مَا يُبَيِّنُ أَنَّهُ كَانَ يَتَكَلَّمُ فِي جَمِيعِ مَعَانِي الْقُرْآنِ. وَأَيْضًا قَدْ قَالَ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ مَا مِنْ آيَةٍ فِي كِتَابِ اللَّهِ إلَّا وَأَنَا أَعْلَمُ فِي مَاذَا أُنْزِلَتْ. وَأَيْضًا فَإِنَّهُمْ مُتَّفِقُونَ عَلَى أَنَّ آيَاتِ الْأَحْكَامِ يُعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلُهَا وَهِيَ نَحْوُ خَمْسمِائَةِ آيَةٍ وَسَائِرُ الْقُرْآنِ خَبَرٌ عَنْ اللَّهِ وَأَسْمَائِهِ وَصِفَاتِهِ أَوْ عَنْ الْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَالْجَنَّةِ وَالنَّارِ أَوْ عَنْ الْقَصَصِ وَعَاقِبَةِ أَهْلِ الْإِيمَانِ وَعَاقِبَةِ أَهْلِ الْكُفْرِ فَإِنْ كَانَ هَذَا هُوَ الْمُتَشَابِهَ الَّذِي لَا يَعْلَمُ مَعْنَاهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ
translated_text:
Among the evidence cited by those who maintain that those firmly grounded in knowledge know the interpretation is the report established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere, from Ibn ‘Abbās:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, supplicated for him, saying: ‘O Allah, grant him understanding of the religion and teach him interpretation.’”

Thus, he prayed for him to have knowledge of interpretation without qualification. Ibn ‘Abbās explained the entire Quran. Mujāhid said: “I went through the Quran with Ibn ‘Abbās from beginning to end, stopping him at every verse and asking him about it.” Ibn ‘Abbās used to say: “I am among those firmly grounded in knowledge who know its interpretation.”

Moreover, reports transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, through numerous independent chains establish that he discussed all the meanings of the Quran, both its commands and its accounts. His discussions of Allah’s names and attributes, promises of reward and warnings of punishment, and narratives, as well as his discussions of commands, prohibitions, and rulings, demonstrate that he addressed all the meanings of the Quran.

Ibn Mas‘ūd also said: “There is no verse in the Book of Allah but that I know what it was revealed about.”

Furthermore, they agree that the interpretation of the verses concerning rulings is known; these number some five hundred verses. The rest of the Quran speaks of Allah and His names and attributes; of the Last Day, Paradise, and Hell; or of narratives and the ultimate fate of the believers and the disbelievers. If this constitutes the ambiguous portion whose meaning is known only to Allah,

then no one knows the meaning of most of the Quran—neither the Messenger nor anyone in the community. Clearly, this is a blatant denial of the obvious.

Moreover, it is well known that understanding the interpretation of dreams is more difficult than understanding the interpretation of spoken accounts. The way a dream points to its interpretation is subtle and obscure, beyond the grasp of most people, unlike the way words indicate their meaning. If Allah has taught His servants to interpret what they see in dreams, then all the more would He teach them the interpretation of the clear Arabic speech He reveals to His prophets. Jacob said to Joseph:

“Thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of dreams.”

Joseph said:

“My Lord, You have granted me authority and taught me the interpretation of dreams.”

He also said:

“No food will come to you as your provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it reaches you.”

Furthermore, Allah has censured the disbelievers, saying:

“Or do they say, ‘He has fabricated it’? Say, ‘Then produce a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.’”

“Rather, they have denied what they do not fully comprehend, and whose fulfilment has not yet come to them.”

He also said:

“And on the Day We gather from every nation a company of those who denied Our signs, they will be kept in order.”

“Until, when they arrive, He will say, ‘Did you deny My signs without fully comprehending them? Or what was it that you were doing?’”

This is a censure of anyone who denies what he does not fully comprehend.

Thus, among the differing views people have expressed concerning the explanation and interpretation of the Quran, no one may accept one view rather than another without knowledge, nor reject any of them without fully comprehending it. This is possible only if he knows the true meaning intended by the verse, thereby knowing that whatever contradicts it is false, and so rejecting the falsehood he fully comprehends. But if he does not know its meaning and does not fully comprehend any of these views, he may not reject any of them, even though some of these contradictory views are certainly false. On that basis, someone who denies the Quran would be no different from someone who rejects contradictory views, and someone who denies the truth would be no different from someone who rejects falsehood. The falsity of a necessary consequence demonstrates the falsity of the premise that entails it.

Moreover, if he proceeds on his belief that only Allah knows the meanings of verses conveying information, he must reject the claims of everyone who cites such a Quranic verse as evidence for any matter concerning belief in Allah and the Last Day, as well as everyone who explains such verses. The same consequence necessarily follows regarding the hadiths of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

If he says, “The ambiguous passages comprise only some of those conveying information,” he must provide a clear distinction between Quranic verses whose meanings can be known and those whose meanings cannot be known—not by an angel brought near to Allah, nor a prophet sent by Him, nor any of the Companions, nor anyone else. Yet it is well known that no one can provide a dividing criterion between passages whose meanings some people can know and those whose meanings no one can know. translated_text:
whose meaning no one can know. This is an independent proof concerning this question.

Moreover, His statements,

“They have not fully comprehended it,”

and,

“Did you deny My signs without fully comprehending them?”

reproach them for their lack of comprehension together with their denial. If everyone were equally unable to comprehend the ambiguous passages, there would be no point in reproaching them for this particular failing; the reproach would concern their denial alone. It would be tantamount to saying, “Did you deny what you have not fully comprehended, when none but Allah can fully comprehend it?” Yet someone who denies what Allah alone knows has more excuse than someone who denies what people can know. Thus, if those firmly grounded in knowledge did not fully comprehend these signs, omitting this description would make the reproach stronger than including it.

This becomes clear from another consideration, which also constitutes evidence concerning this question: Allah reproaches those who deviate for their ignorance and evil intent. They pursue the ambiguous passages, seeking their interpretation, although none knows their interpretation except those firmly grounded in knowledge—and they are not among them. They seek discord, not knowledge and truth. This resembles His statement, exalted is He:

“Had Allah known any good in them, He would have made them hear. But even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away in aversion.”

Here, “He would have made them hear” means enabling them to understand the Quran. That is, had Allah known that they had good intentions and were receptive to the truth, He would have enabled them to understand the Quran. Yet even if He had enabled them to understand it, they would have turned away from faith and acceptance of the truth because of their evil intent. Thus, they are ignorant and wrongdoing. Likewise, those whose hearts are inclined to deviation are

" كَانَ رُسُوخُهُمْ فِي الْعِلْمِ أَنْ آمَنُوا بِمُحْكَمِهِ وَبِمُتَشَابِهِهِ وَلَا يَعْلَمُونَهُ "
translated_text:
blamed for their evil intent while seeking knowledge for which they are not qualified. The fact that these people are reproached for seeking such knowledge and denied it does not mean that blame attaches to someone whose intention is good and whom Allah has made firmly grounded in knowledge.

If it is objected:

Most of the early generations held that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know the interpretation, as did most scholars of language. This is reported from Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUrwah, Qatādah, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, al-Farrāʾ, Abū ʿUbayd, Thaʿlab, and Ibn al-Anbārī. Ibn al-Anbārī said: In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, it is: “Its interpretation is with Allah alone; and those firmly grounded in knowledge.” In the reading of Ubayy and Ibn ʿAbbās, it is: “And those firmly grounded in knowledge say.”

He said: Allah has revealed in His Book matters whose knowledge He has reserved exclusively for Himself, as in His statement, exalted is He:

“Say: Its knowledge is with Allah alone.”

And His statement:

“And many generations in between.”

Thus, He revealed the unambiguous passages so that the believer might believe in them and attain felicity, while the disbeliever might reject them and suffer misery. Ibn al-Anbārī said: The person who transmitted the other opinion from Mujāhid was Ibn Abī Najīh, and his transmission of Quranic commentary from Mujāhid is not sound.

The response is:

The claim that most of the early generations held this view is made without knowledge. It is not established that any of the Companions said that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know the interpretation of the ambiguous passages. Ibn Abī Mulaykah reported from ʿĀʾishah that she said:

“Their firmness in knowledge lay in believing in its unambiguous and ambiguous passages, though they did not understand it.”

Yet al-Bukhārī narrated the Prophetic hadith on this subject through Ibn Abī Mulaykah, from al-Qāsim, from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, without this addition. Nor did Ibn Abī Mulaykah mention hearing this addition from al-Qāsim. Rather, what is established from the Companions is that those firmly grounded in knowledge understand the ambiguous passages, as shown by the previously mentioned report of Muʿādh ibn Jabal on this subject. Similar reports are also transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and others. The readings attributed to Ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb have no known chain of transmission by which they could serve as evidence. What is well known from Ibn Masʿūd is that he used to say:

“There is no verse in Allah’s Book without my knowing what it was revealed about and what was intended by it.”

Abū ʿAbd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī said:

“Those who taught us the Quran—ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, and others—told us that whenever they learned ten verses from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, they would not proceed beyond them until they understood the knowledge and practice they contained.”

This is widely known and has been transmitted from scholars of hadith and Quranic commentary generally. It has a known chain of transmission, unlike the readings attributed to those two Companions. Likewise, Ibn ʿAbbās is known to have said: “I am among those firmly grounded in knowledge who know its interpretation.” It is also authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed that he be granted knowledge of the interpretation of the Book. How, then, could he not know its interpretation?

Moreover, ʿAbd Allāh’s reading, “Its interpretation is with Allah alone,” does not contradict this view, for only Allah can bring about its actual fulfillment. As He, exalted is He, says:

“Are they waiting for anything but its fulfillment? On the Day its fulfillment comes”

And He says:

“Rather, they have denied what they have not fully grasped, and whose fulfillment has not yet come to them.”

It is widely reported from the early scholars generally that promises and warnings belong to the ambiguous passages. Their interpretation is the actual fulfillment of what has been promised, and that rests with Allah: none but He can bring it about. The Quran does not say, “Knowledge of its interpretation is with Allah alone,” as it says concerning the Hour:

“They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive? Say, ‘Knowledge of it is only with my Lord. None but He will reveal it at its appointed time. It weighs heavily upon the heavens and the earth. It will come upon you only suddenly.’ They ask you as though you were well informed about it. Say, ‘Knowledge of it is only with Allah, but most people do not know.’”

“Say, ‘I have no power to benefit or harm myself, except as Allah wills. Had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much good, and no harm would have touched me.’”

Likewise, when Pharaoh said to Moses:

“What, then, of the former generations?”

“He said, ‘Knowledge of them is with my Lord, in a record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets.’”

Thus, if Ibn Mas‘ūd’s reading excluded those firmly grounded in knowledge from possessing this knowledge, it would have read, “Knowledge of its interpretation is with Allah alone,” rather than, “Its interpretation is with Allah alone.” The latter is indisputably true.

As for the other reading attributed to Ubayy and Ibn ‘Abbās, statements contradicting it have been transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās. The disciple most closely associated with him in Quranic commentary was Mujāhid, whose commentary most leading scholars rely upon, including al-Thawrī, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and al-Bukhārī. Al-Thawrī said, “If a Quranic commentary reaches you from Mujāhid, that is sufficient for you.” Most of the commentary al-Shāfi‘ī transmits in his books comes through Ibn ‘Uyaynah, from Ibn Abī Najīh, from Mujāhid. commentary. The claim that Ibn Abī Najīh’s transmission from Mujāhid is not authentic is answered as follows:

The commentary transmitted by Ibn Abī Najīh from Mujāhid is among the most authentic Quranic commentaries. Indeed, no commentary available to Quranic scholars surpasses it in authenticity; others may, at most, equal it. Moreover, it is corroborated by Mujāhid’s statement: “I went through the Quran with Ibn ‘Abbās, stopping him at every verse and asking him about it.”

Furthermore, Ubayy ibn Ka‘b (may Allah be pleased with him) was known to explain the ambiguous passages of the Quran. For example, he explained Allah’s words:

“Then We sent to her Our Spirit,”

and His words:

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth,”

and:

“And when your Lord took,”

as well as other passages. These explanations are well known through chains of transmission from him and are more firmly established than this reading, for which no chain of transmission is known. He would also answer questions about ambiguous meanings in the Quran, as when ‘Umar questioned him; he was also asked about the Night of Decree.

As for his statement, “Allah revealed what is stated in general terms so that the believer might believe in it,” the response is: This is true. But does the Quran, the Sunnah, or any statement of the early scholars say that the prophets, angels, and Companions do not understand that general wording? Or do the scholars agree that the meaning of what is stated in general terms in the Quran is understood, and that what remains unspecified in it is recognized? Such is the example given concerning the time of the Hour. All Muslims understand the meaning of Allah’s words concerning the Hour: that it will certainly come, and that Allah alone knows its time and has disclosed it to no one. in response to the questioner—who appeared to be an unknown Bedouin and asked him about the Hour, ‘When will the Hour be?’—‘The one questioned about it knows no more than the questioner.’” He did not say that no one understands the words revealed concerning it. Rather, such a claim contradicts the consensus of Muslims, indeed of all rational people. Allah’s statements concerning the Hour and its signs are clear and intelligible, and their meaning is understood. The same applies to His words:

“And many generations in between.”

The intended meaning of these words is known: Allah created many generations whose number none but He knows. As He says:

“And none knows the forces of your Lord except Him.”

What in any of this indicates that no one—neither the angels, nor the prophets, nor the Companions, nor anyone else—understands the meaning of what Allah has told us concerning faith in Allah and the Last Day?

As for what was related from ‘Urwah, it is known from reports transmitted through him that he did not interpret most verses of the Quran, apart from a few whose explanations he related from ‘Ā’ishah. Clearly, if ‘Urwah did not know the interpretation, it does not follow that others did not know it, such as the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the scholars among the Companions, including Ibn Mas‘ūd, Ubayy ibn Ka‘b, Ibn ‘Abbās, and others.

As for the linguists who say that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know the meaning of the ambiguous passages, they contradict themselves in this. All of them discuss the interpretation of everything in the Quran and elaborate extensively on it, to the point that every one of them has advanced interpretations without precedent, which are erroneous. It is well known that much of their explanation of the ambiguous passages is correct, while some of it is mistaken. For this reason, most authors of Quranic commentaries cite his views, since they are authentically transmitted from him. Yet the entire Quran—both its clear and its ambiguous passages—is explained in it.

What made the statement that none but Allah knows the interpretation of the ambiguous passages widespread among Ahl al-Sunnah was the emergence of false interpretations advanced by the people of innovation, such as the Jahmiyyah and the Qadariyyah among the Mu‘tazilah and others. They began interpreting the Quran according to their own unsound opinions. This is a well-known approach among the people of innovation: they explain the Quran according to their own rational judgments and linguistic interpretations. Thus, the Quranic commentaries of the Mu‘tazilah are filled with interpretations of the texts affirming the divine attributes and decree that depart from what Allah and His Messenger intended. It was these corrupt interpretations that the early generations and the leading scholars condemned, as Imam Ahmad stated in his refutation of the heretics and the Jahmiyyah concerning the ambiguous passages of the Quran about which they entertained doubts and which they interpreted contrary to their true meaning. This, then, is the kind of interpretation that the early generations and the leading scholars condemned.

After them came people who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah without a thorough knowledge of it or of what contradicts it. They supposed that none but Allah knows the meaning of the ambiguous passages. They also assumed that “interpretation” bore the meaning assigned to it in the terminology of later scholars: diverting an expression from its more likely meaning to a less likely one. Thus, in one place they assert and defend the view that, as for the ambiguous passages, no one knows

their meaning except Allah. Yet they contradict themselves in several ways.

First, they say that the texts are to be understood according to their apparent meanings, and they do not go beyond those meanings. Accordingly, they reject every interpretation that conflicts with the apparent meaning and affirm that meaning. At the same time, however, they say that the text has an interpretation known only to Allah, while “interpretation,” as they understand it, contradicts the apparent meaning. How, then, can it have an interpretation contrary to its apparent meaning when they have already affirmed that apparent meaning? Their opponents in debate challenged them on this point; indeed, Ibn ‘Aqīl challenged his own teacher, the judge Abū Ya‘lā, over it.

Another contradiction is that we find that whenever any of these people are confronted with a text that contradicts their position, whether on a fundamental or a subsidiary question, they invariably interpret it in strained, contrived ways that amount to distorting words from their proper places—the same sort of interpretations that the Jahmiyyah and Qadariyyah give to texts that contradict their views. How can this be reconciled with their statement, “None but Allah Most High knows the meanings of the ambiguous texts”?

Consider what you find in their books of their debates with the Mu‘tazilah concerning the divine attributes, the Quran, and divine decree. When the Mu‘tazilah support their own position by citing verses that contradict these people’s position, such as His words:

“And Allah does not love corruption.”

“And He does not approve of disbelief for His servants.”

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

“No vision can encompass Him.”

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

“And when your Lord said to the angels”

and similar verses, observe how they interpret these texts in ways that are mostly unsound

Consider Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the imam of Ahl al-Sunnah, who remained steadfast during the inquisition and became a standard by which Muslims distinguish adherents of the Sunnah from adherents of innovation. When he composed his book, “Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah,” concerning the ambiguous passages of the Quran about which they expressed doubts and which they misinterpreted, he discussed their meanings verse by verse. These were the passages pursued by those who deviated, seeking discord and seeking their interpretation. He clarified and explained their meanings to expose the unsoundness of those deviant interpretations.

He established through rational and scriptural proofs that Allah can be seen, that the Quran is uncreated, and that Allah is above the Throne. He refuted the rational and scriptural arguments advanced by those who denied these matters, and clarified the meanings of the verses he himself called ambiguous, explaining them verse by verse.

Likewise, when they debated him and cited scriptural texts against him, he explained them verse by verse and hadith by hadith, exposing the unsoundness of the interpretations given by those who deviated and clarifying their meanings himself. Ahmad did not say that none but Allah understands the meanings of these verses and hadiths, nor did anyone say this to him. Rather, all the groups agree that their meanings can be known; they disagree only over what is intended, just as they disagree over verses containing commands and prohibitions.

Similarly, Ahmad would explain the ambiguous verses and hadiths cited as evidence by those who deviated among the Khawārij

 وَلَكِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ يَعْتَرِفُونَ بِأَنَّهُمْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ التَّأْوِيلَ وَإِنَّمَا غَايَتُهُمْ أَنْ يَقُولُوا:
 ظَاهِرُ هَذِهِ الْآيَةِ غَيْرُ مُرَادٍ وَلَكِنْ يُحْتَمَلُ أَنْ يُرَادَ كَذَا وَأَنْ يُرَادَ كَذَا وَلَوْ تَأَوَّلَهَا الْوَاحِدُ مِنْهُمْ بِتَأْوِيلٍ مُعَيَّنٍ فَهُوَ لَا يَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ
translated_text:
and others, such as the Prophet’s saying:

“No adulterer commits adultery while he is a believer; no thief steals while he is a believer; and no drinker drinks wine while he is a believer,”

and similar reports.

He refuted the positions of the Murjiʾah and Jahmiyyah, as well as those of the Khawārij and Muʿtazilah. All these groups cite ambiguous texts to support their positions. Yet no one, whether from Ahl al-Sunnah or from these groups, ever said concerning the texts he himself cited, or those his opponent cited against him: “These are verses and hadiths whose meanings no human being knows, so refrain from citing them as evidence.”

Imam Ahmad rejected the approach of the people of innovation who explain the Quran according to their own opinions and interpretations, without drawing upon the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or the statements of the Companions and the Successors. The Companions conveyed the meanings of the Quran to the Successors just as they conveyed its wording; they transmitted the one just as they transmitted the other. The people of innovation, however, interpret the texts in ways that contradict what Allah and His Messenger intended, claiming that this is the interpretation known to those firmly grounded in knowledge. Their claim is false, especially in the case of the interpretations of the heretical Qarmatians and Bātiniyyah. The same applies to the adherents of newly introduced speculative theology among the Jahmiyyah, Qadariyyah, and others.

These latter, however, acknowledge that they do not know the interpretation. The most they can say is: “The apparent meaning of this verse is not intended, but such-and-such may be intended, or such-and-such.” Even if one of them assigns it a particular interpretation, he does not know that it is

translated_text:
neither understand nor reason, in numerous passages of His Book. Those who follow religious innovations contrary to the Quran and Sunnah claim knowledge, insight, and thorough understanding, yet they are among the most ignorant of matters known through revelation and reason. They devise vague, ambiguous terms encompassing both truth and falsehood, then treat these as clear, foundational principles. Any texts of the Quran and Sunnah that conflict with them they classify as ambiguous texts whose meaning, in their view, Allah alone knows. Their interpretations based on possible meanings are of no avail. Thus they turn conclusive proofs into specious arguments, and specious arguments into conclusive proofs, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Judge Abū Ya‘lā reported that Imam Ahmad said:

“A clear text stands on its own and requires no explanation; an ambiguous text requires explanation.”

Imam Ahmad also stated this in one report. Al-Shāfi‘ī said:

“A clear text admits of only one interpretation; an ambiguous text admits of several interpretations.”

Imam Ahmad likewise said this. Ibn al-Anbārī also said:

“A clear text admits of only one interpretation; an ambiguous text is open to competing interpretations.”

The response, then, is that the entire Muslim community, its earlier and later generations alike, discusses meanings of the Quran that admit of multiple interpretations. Indeed, those who champion the view that people firmly grounded in knowledge do not know the meaning of ambiguous texts are themselves among those who discuss it most extensively.

translated_text:
And the imams, such as al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and those before them, all discuss texts that admit of several meanings, giving preference to some meanings over others on the basis of evidence, in all foundational and subsidiary questions of knowledge. No Muslim scholar is known to have said of a text cited as evidence in a particular issue: “No one knows what this means, so it cannot be used as evidence.” Were anyone to say this, the same could be said in reply to him. If, in the well-known disputes among the imams, someone claims that the text he cites is clear and its meaning known, whereas the other text is ambiguous and no one knows its meaning, his claim can be met with an identical counterclaim.

This differs from our saying: “Some texts have a plain, clear, evident meaning, admitting of only one interpretation and leaving no room for uncertainty; others contain obscurity and ambiguity, but those firmly grounded in knowledge know their meaning.” This is a sound explanation. On this understanding, disagreement over ambiguous texts indicates that the meaning of all of them can be known. Whoever maintains that their meaning can be known sets out his evidence for this. Moreover, what the earlier and later generations have said about ambiguous texts indicates that the meaning of all of them can be known.

As for those who say that ambiguous texts are the abrogated texts, the meaning of an abrogated text is known. This view is reported from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Suddī, and others. Yet Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Qatāda are the very people reported as saying that those firmly grounded in knowledge do not know its interpretation. It is known with certainty, by the consensus of Muslims, that those firmly grounded in knowledge know both the meaning of an abrogated text and that it has been abrogated. Thus, this report from them contradicts the other report and shows that the latter is false, if the former is true; otherwise, the two reports conflict
