The point here is that the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness never built a mosque over the grave of a prophet or a righteous man, nor made it a shrine or a place of visitation. Nor did they build mosques at sites associated with the prophets, such as a place where a prophet had stopped, prayed, or done something of that kind. They did not deliberately build mosques on account of places associated with the prophets and the righteous.

The majority of them did not deliberately seek to pray at a place that the Messenger had not specifically chosen for prayer, but where he had merely stopped or happened to pray. Indeed, their leading figures, such as ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb and others, forbade deliberately seeking to pray at a place where the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had prayed incidentally, without specifically choosing it.

It is reported only of Ibn ‘Umar that he would take care to travel where the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had travelled, stop where he had stopped, and pray where he had prayed, even when the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had not specifically chosen that spot for that action, but had merely happened to do it there. Ibn ‘Umar—may Allah be pleased with him and his father—was a righteous man, deeply committed to following the Prophet, and he regarded this as part of following him. His father and the other Companions—the Rightly Guided Caliphs ‘Uthmān and ‘Alī, the remaining members of the Ten, and others such as Ibn Mas‘ūd, Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal, and Ubayy ibn Ka‘b—did not do what Ibn ‘Umar did. The majority’s view is more correct.

This is because following his example means doing what he did, in the manner in which he did it, because he did it. If he deliberately chose a particular place for prayer and worship, then deliberately choosing that place for prayer and worship constitutes following his example. But if he did not deliberately choose that spot, then deliberately seeking it out constitutes departing from his example, not following it.

An example of the former is his deliberately stopping for remembrance of Allah and supplication at ‘Arafah, Muzdalifah, and between the two stoning pillars: deliberately seeking out those places constitutes following his example. Likewise, when he circumambulated the Ka‘bah and prayed two units of prayer behind the Station of Abraham, doing the same constitutes following his example. Similarly, when he ascended al-Safā and al-Marwah to remember Allah and supplicate, deliberately doing so constitutes following his example.

Salamah ibn al-Akwa‘ used to make a point of praying beside the pillar. He said, “Because I saw the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—make a point of praying beside it.” Since he saw him deliberately choose that spot for prayer, deliberately choosing it for prayer constituted following his example.

Likewise:

“When ‘Itbān ibn Mālik wished to establish a mosque after becoming blind, he sent word to the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—saying, ‘I would like you to come and pray in my home, so that I may make that spot a place of prayer.’ In another version, he said, ‘Come and designate a place of prayer for me.’ The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—came, accompanied by those of his Companions who wished to come. In another version: ‘The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and Abū Bakr al-Siddīq came to me when the morning was well advanced. The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—asked permission to enter, and I gave him permission. He entered the house and, before sitting down, said, “Where in your house would you like me to pray?” I pointed to a corner of the house. The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—stood to pray, and we stood behind him. He prayed two units of prayer and then concluded with the salutation of peace.’” The hadith continues.

For he intended to build a mosque and wanted the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to be the first to pray in it, and to build it on the spot where he prayed. The purpose, then, was to build the mosque, and he wanted the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to pray where he would build it. The prayer was intended for the sake of the mosque; building the mosque was not intended merely because he had happened to pray there. This was a place where the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—deliberately prayed so that it would become a mosque. Deliberately choosing to pray there therefore constituted following his example, unlike choosing a place where he merely happened to pray without deliberately selecting it.

Likewise, deliberately choosing Mondays and Thursdays for fasting constitutes following his example, because he deliberately fasted on those two days. He said in an authentic hadith:

“The gates of Paradise are opened every Thursday and Monday, and every servant who associates nothing with Allah is forgiven, except a man between whom and his brother there is enmity. It is then said, ‘Let these two wait until they are reconciled.’”

Likewise, deliberately visiting the mosque of Qubā’ constitutes following his example. It is established in the two Sahīh collections that he used to visit Qubā’ every Saturday, sometimes riding and sometimes walking.

This was because Allah had revealed to him:

“A mosque founded on piety from the very first day is more worthy for you to stand in prayer in.”

His mosque had the greatest claim to this description. It is also established in an authentic report:

“He was asked about the mosque founded on piety and said, ‘It is this mosque of mine.’”

He meant that his mosque fulfilled this description more completely than the mosque of Qubā’. The mosque of Qubā’ was also founded on piety, and it was on its account that the verse was revealed. Hence Allah said:

“In it are men who love

to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.”

Besides performing ablution and ritual bathing, the people of Qubā’ used water to cleanse themselves after relieving themselves. They had learned this from their Jewish neighbours; the Arabs had not practised it. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace—therefore wished to prevent anyone from supposing that the mosque founded on piety was that mosque alone, to the exclusion of his own. He explained that his mosque had a greater claim to being the mosque founded on piety. Thus, His words:

“A mosque founded on piety”

include both his mosque and the mosque of Qubā’, as well as every mosque founded on piety, unlike mosques built to cause harm. For this reason, the early Muslims disliked praying in mosques resembling the latter and considered an older mosque superior to a newer one. An older mosque is less likely to have been built to cause harm than a newer one, concerning which such fears may arise. A mosque’s antiquity is one of its praiseworthy qualities. Hence Allah said:

“Then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House.”

And He said:

“Indeed, the first House established for mankind was the one at Bakkah.”

Its antiquity also implies that more worship has been performed there, which further increases its merit. For this reason, apart from the mosque of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace—the early scholars of Medina and elsewhere did not recommend deliberately visiting any of the mosques or visitation sites in and around Medina except the mosque of Qubā’. This was because it was the only particular mosque that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—deliberately went out to visit. There were many mosques in Medina, with each tribe of the Ansār having its own mosque, but there is no special merit in choosing to visit any one of them rather than others like it. The mosque of Qubā’ is different, for it was the first mosque built in Medina

without exception. The Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—deliberately went there, and it is authentically reported that he said:

“Whoever performs ablution in his home, then comes to the mosque of Qubā’ intending only to pray there, will receive a reward equivalent to an ʿumrah.”

Nevertheless, one should not undertake a journey specifically to visit it. Rather, someone already in Medina may go there, without setting out on a journey specifically for that purpose. Such journeys should instead be undertaken to the three mosques, for he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Do not undertake a journey except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, al-Aqsā Mosque, and this mosque of mine.”

Thus, according to the four imams and others, anyone who vows to travel to the mosque of Qubā’ should not fulfil that vow. This differs from the Sacred Mosque: they agree that a vow to travel there must be fulfilled. The same applies to the mosque in Medina and the mosque in Jerusalem, according to the more correct of their two positions. This is the position of Mālik and Ahmad, and one of al-Shāfiʿī’s two positions. According to his other position, which is also that of Abū Hanīfah, fulfilling such a vow is not obligatory, though it is permissible and recommended. For his governing principle is that a vow makes something obligatory only if it is already obligatory under Islamic law. Most scholars, however, hold that every act of obedience to Allah becomes obligatory through a vow, as is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, where ʿĀ’ishah reports that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey Allah, let him not disobey Him.”

translated_text:
this is prescribed for all deceased Muslims, just as it is recommended to greet them with peace, supplicate for them, and seek forgiveness for them.

Visiting graves for this purpose is recommended, whether they are the graves of prophets, righteous people, or others. When Abd Allāh ibn Umar entered the mosque, he would say:

“Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. Peace be upon you, O Abū Bakr. Peace be upon you, O my father.”

Then he would leave.

As for visiting the graves of prophets and righteous people to ask them to fulfil one’s needs, invoke them, adjure Allah by them, or out of a belief that supplication or prayer at their graves is better than in mosques and homes, this is misguidance, associating partners with Allah, and religious innovation, by agreement of the leading Muslim scholars. None of the Companions used to do this. Nor, after greeting the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—would they remain standing to supplicate for themselves. For this reason, Mālik and other scholars disapproved of this and said that it was among the innovations not practised by the early generations.

The four imams and others among the early generations agreed that anyone wishing to supplicate should face the direction of prayer, not the grave of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. When greeting him, however, most of them said that one should face the grave. This was the position of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad. Abū Hanīfah said that one should instead face the direction of prayer in this case too, with the grave to one’s left. Another view is that one should instead turn one’s back to the direction of prayer.

Further illustrating this principle is the fact that when the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and Abū Bakr emigrated, they went to the cave on Mount Thawr, which was not on their route

translated_text:
to Medina, for it lies in the direction of Yemen, whereas Medina lies in the direction of Syria. Rather, they hid there for three days so that the polytheists would lose track of them and not know where they had gone. The polytheists were pursuing them and had offered, for each of them, a reward equivalent to his blood money to anyone who brought him in. They sought to prevent the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—from reaching his Companions in Medina and from leaving Mecca. Indeed, when they failed to kill him, they sought to confine him in Mecca. Had he taken the road immediately, they would have caught up with him. It was for this reason that he remained in the cave for three days. Thus, if someone travelling from Mecca to Medina wished to go to the cave and then return, this would not be recommended; rather, it would be disliked.

During the emigration, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—took the coastal route, which is long and circuitous. On his ‘umrah pilgrimages and his Hajj, however, he took the middle route, which is a shorter way to Mecca. He took the coastal route during the emigration because it was less likely to be where the polytheists would look for him. The middle route was a shorter way to Medina, so they would suppose that he had taken it. Similarly, when he intended to undertake a military expedition, he would conceal his destination by indicating another.

After dividing the spoils of Hunayn at al-Ji‘rānah, he—may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace—performed ‘umrah from there. When the polytheists barred him from Mecca, he left the state of ihrām at al-Hudaybiyyah, having entered ihrām for ‘umrah at Dhū al-Hulayfah, the designated point for entering ihrām for those coming from Medina. When he performed ‘Umrat al-Qadiyyah the following year, he again began his ‘umrah at Dhū al-Hulayfah. He did not enter the Kaaba during any of his ‘umrah pilgrimages or his Hajj; he entered it only in the year of the conquest. There were images depicted inside it, and he did not enter it until

those images had been erased. He then prayed two rak‘ahs inside it. On the day of the conquest, he prayed eight rak‘ahs in the forenoon, as Umm Hāni’ reported. He did not deliberately pray in the forenoon except for a particular reason: for example, when returning from a journey, he would enter the mosque and pray two rak‘ahs there; or when sleep or illness prevented him from offering his night prayers, he would pray twelve rak‘ahs during the day. He normally prayed eleven rak‘ahs at night, but he prayed twelve—an even number—because the time for Witr had passed. For he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Maghrib is the odd-numbered prayer of the day, so make your night prayer odd-numbered.”

He also said:

“Make Witr the last of your prayers at night.”

And he said:

“The night prayer is offered two rak‘ahs at a time. When you fear that dawn is approaching, offer a single rak‘ah as Witr.”

It is reported from the early generations that, if they slept through Witr, they would offer it before the Fajr prayer and would not delay it until after that prayer. In the two Sahīh collections, ‘Ā’ishah—may Allah be pleased with her—is reported to have said:

“The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—never offered the voluntary forenoon prayer, but I certainly do offer it. He would sometimes refrain from a deed he loved to perform for fear that people would practise it and it would then be made obligatory upon them.”

It is also established in the Sahīh that “he advised Abū Hurayrah and Abū al-Dardā’ to offer two rak‘ahs of the forenoon prayer.” There are other hadiths concerning this prayer. However, some scholars regarded the eight rak‘ahs he offered on the day of the conquest as the forenoon prayer.

translated_text:
the conquest. They recommended that, upon the conquest of a city, the imam should offer eight rak‘ahs in gratitude to Allah, calling this the prayer of conquest. They argued that following the Prophet’s example requires considering his intention. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—did not intend to offer this prayer because of the time of day. Had that been his intention, he would have offered it every day, or on most days, just as he offered the two rak‘ahs before Fajr every day. Likewise, he would offer two rak‘ahs after Zuhr and two or four before it. When he missed the two rak‘ahs after Zuhr, he made them up after ‘Asr.

When he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his Companions slept through Fajr during the Khaybar campaign, they offered two rak‘ahs after sunrise, followed by another two. No one has said that offering this prayer at that time is a regular Sunnah, because they offered it only to make up the prayer they had slept through. When he missed ‘Asr on one of the days of the Battle of the Trench, he offered it after sunset. It is also reported that he missed Zuhr, so he offered Zuhr, then ‘Asr, then Maghrib. No one has said that it is recommended to offer eleven rak‘ahs between Maghrib and ‘Ishā’, because these were missed prayers being made up. Indeed, no one has even reported that he singled out the interval between Maghrib and ‘Ishā’ for prayer.

As for the words of Allah Most High:

“Rising at night”

Most scholars understand this to mean rising after sleep, not the early part of the night. This is the correct view, because this was how the Prophet—may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace—used to pray. Reports from him to this effect have been transmitted through so many independent chains that their authenticity is beyond doubt: he would rise to pray after sleeping; he did not offer his night prayer between Maghrib and ‘Ishā’.

Likewise, he ate whatever food was available and wore the clothing available in his city, Taybah, whether produced there or brought there from Yemen and elsewhere, because that was what Allah had made readily available to him. His food was dates, his bread was barley bread, and his fruits were fresh dates, watermelons, and cucumbers. He wore Yemeni garments because these foods and clothes were the most readily available in his land, not because of anything particular to them. Thus, someone living in another land, whose people subsist on wheat and dhura (a cereal grain), whose fruits are grapes, pomegranates, and the like, and whose clothing is silk woven outside Yemen, would not be following the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—by deliberately going to great lengths to obtain food, fruit, and clothing unavailable in his own land and difficult for its people to procure, even if what he sought was dried dates, fresh dates, or barley bread.

It is therefore clear that following the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—necessarily requires consideration of purpose and intention:

“Actions are judged only by intentions, and each person shall have only what he intended.”

It is thus clear that the position held by the majority of the Companions and their leading figures is the correct one. Even so, Ibn Umar—may Allah be pleased with him and his father—only deliberately sought to pray in places where the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had prayed. He did not seek out the places where the Prophet had stopped or stayed in order to pray there. It also shows that touching and kissing the Station of Abraham are not part of the Sunnah. If this applies to the Kaaba itself and the Station of Abraham beside it, then it is well known that all mosques are less sacred than the Kaaba, and that Abraham’s stations in Greater Syria and elsewhere, and all the other stations of the prophets, are inferior to the Station concerning which Allah said:

“Take the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer.”

It follows that the other stations are not to be deliberately sought out for prayer, just as pilgrimage is not to be made to other shrines, nor are they to be rubbed. No part of the prophets’ stations, the mosques, the Rock, or anything else is to be kissed. Nothing on the face of the earth is to be kissed except the Black Stone.

translated_text:
Moreover, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace—did not pray in any mosque in Mecca other than the Sacred Mosque, nor did he visit any places for worship except the ritual sites: Minā, Muzdalifah, and ‘Arafah. For this reason, the leading scholars held that it is not recommended to seek out any mosque in Mecca for prayer other than the Sacred Mosque, nor to single out any place for visitation other than the ritual sites visited by the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. If this applies to the sites associated with them, what then of graves, when the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—cursed those who took them as places of worship and declared that they would be the worst of creation before Allah on the Day of Resurrection?

Islam teaches that no place should be deliberately sought out for prayer unless it is a mosque. Thus, the pilgrimage sites other than the Sacred Mosque are visited for the pilgrimage rites, not for prayer. Accordingly, ‘Arafah is not a place designated for prayer. Rather, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace—prayed the noon and afternoon prayers on the Day of ‘Arafah at ‘Uranah. He delivered a sermon there, then prayed, and afterwards went to ‘Arafāt, where he stood. Likewise, Allah is remembered and supplicated at ‘Arafāt, on Quzah at Muzdalifah, at al-Safā and al-Marwah, between the stoning pillars, and during the stoning; these places are not deliberately sought out for prayer.

Apart from mosques and the pilgrimage sites, no place is to be deliberately sought out for prayer, remembrance of Allah, or supplication. Rather, a Muslim prays wherever he happens to be when prayer falls due, except where prayer is forbidden, and remembers Allah and supplicates Him wherever it is convenient, without intending to single out a particular place for that purpose. If he sets aside a place for this, such as a shrine, he is forbidden to do so, just as prayer in a cemetery is forbidden, except for what a person does when greeting the deceased, by way of

supplicating for him and for the Muslims, as one does in the funeral prayer. Visiting a believer’s grave is akin to offering his funeral prayer: the actions performed in each are of the same nature, and the supplications serve the same purpose.

A similar example is the Helpers’ pledge of allegiance to the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—on the night of al-‘Aqabah, in the valley behind Jamrat al-‘Aqabah. This was a low-lying place near Minā that concealed those within it. The seventy Helpers had come on pilgrimage with their polytheist people; people had continued to make the pilgrimage to Mecca both before and after Islam. They therefore came with their people to Minā for the pilgrimage, then went to that place at night because it was nearby and offered concealment, not because it possessed any special merit. They did not seek it out for any virtue particular to that spot.

For this reason, when the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his Companions performed the pilgrimage, they neither went there nor visited it. A mosque has been built there, but it is a later construction. Every mosque in Mecca and its surroundings other than the Sacred Mosque is likewise a later construction. Even Minā itself had no purpose-built mosque during the time of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, he said:

“Minā is a camping ground for whoever arrives first.”

The Muslims thus camped there, and he would lead them in prayer both in Minā and elsewhere, as did his successors after him. The pilgrims gather in greater numbers at Minā than elsewhere, since they stay there for four days. translated_text:
the prayers at Minā, ‘Arafah, and Muzdalifah, and combine the noon and afternoon prayers at ‘Arafah and the sunset and night prayers at Muzdalifah. All the pilgrims, whether residents of Mecca or otherwise, prayed behind them. They all shortened their prayers at the pilgrimage sites, and all combined their prayers at ‘Arafah and Muzdalifah.

Scholars have differed over whether the people of Mecca and others in similar circumstances may shorten or combine their prayers. Some held that they may neither shorten nor combine them; this is the view of some followers of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad. Others held that they may combine but not shorten them; this is the view of Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad, and those who agreed with him among his own followers and those of al-Shāfi‘ī. Still others held that they may both combine and shorten them; this was the view of Mālik, Ibn ‘Uyaynah, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, some followers of Ahmad, and others.

This last view is undoubtedly correct, for it is unquestionably what the people of Mecca did when praying behind the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Neither the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—nor Abū Bakr nor ‘Umar ever said at Minā, ‘Arafah, or Muzdalifah: “People of Mecca, complete your prayers, for we are travelers.” It is, however, established that ‘Umar said this within Mecca itself. Likewise, the Sunan collections report that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said this within Mecca itself during the campaign of the Conquest.

This is among the strongest proofs that shortening the prayers is prescribed for every traveler, even if his journey is only a barīd, for ‘Arafah is one barīd—four parasangs—from Mecca. Eid. Nor did he lead them in Friday prayer during his travels by delivering a sermon and then praying two rak‘ahs. Rather, when traveling, he prayed two rak‘ahs on Fridays just as he did on other days. Likewise, when he led them in the noon and afternoon prayers at ‘Arafah, he prayed two rak‘ahs for each, as on other days. No one has reported that he recited aloud on Fridays while traveling, whether at ‘Arafah or elsewhere, or that he delivered a Friday sermon during his travels anywhere other than ‘Arafah.

It is thus clear that the correct position is that held by the early generations of the Muslim community and the great majority of its scholars, including the four imams and others: that a traveler does not perform Friday prayer or other prayers. Most of them also hold that he does not perform the Eid prayer. This is the view of Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, and Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him. This, too, is correct, for the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his successors performed the Eid prayer only when resident, not while traveling.

The Eid prayer was performed only in one place, with the imam, who would lead the people out to the open ground and pray there. All the Muslims would pray the Eid prayer behind him, just as they prayed Friday prayer. No Muslim would perform the Eid prayer in his tribal mosque or his home, just as they did not perform Friday prayer in the tribal mosques.

Nor, during the time of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his successors, did any of them perform an Eid prayer in Mecca on the Day of Sacrifice. Rather, their Eid was at Minā after their departure from al-Mash‘ar al-Harām (the Sacred Monument). towns would pray and then slaughter their sacrifices. When the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—departed from Minā, he stopped at al-Muhassab. His Companions differed over whether stopping there was a sunnah because they differed over his intention: had he deliberately chosen to stop there, or had he stopped there because it made his departure easier? This shows that they took intentions into account when following his example.

When he performed the compensatory ‘umrah, Mecca was still under the polytheists’ control and had not yet been conquered. The polytheists had said, “People weakened by the fever of Yathrib are coming to you.” They sat behind Qu‘ayqi‘ān, the hill of al-Marwah, watching them. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—therefore instructed his Companions to jog for three circuits of the circumambulation so that the polytheists would see their stamina and strength. It is also reported that he prayed for those who did so. They did not jog between the two corners, because the polytheists could not see them on that side. Thus, the purpose of jogging at that time was akin to the purpose of jihad.

Some of the earlier scholars therefore thought that it was not a pilgrimage rite, since it had been done for a particular purpose that no longer applied. Yet the following is established:

“It is reported in the Sahīh that when the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his Companions performed Hajj, they jogged from the Black Stone back to the Black Stone, thus extending their jogging to the stretch between the two corners.”

This went beyond what they had done during the compensatory ‘umrah. They did this during the Farewell Pilgrimage, when there was general security, for only believers performed Hajj with him. This demonstrated that jogging had become part of the sunnah of Hajj. It was initially done for a purpose connected with jihad, then prescribed as a pilgrimage rite, as is related concerning Hagar’s running, the stoning of the pillars, and the slaughter of the ram:

 أَنَا أَسْتَحِبُّ الطَّوَافَ بِالصَّخْرَةِ سَبْعًا كَمَا يُطَافُ بِالْكَعْبَةِ أَوْ أَسْتَحِبُّ أَنْ أَتَّخِذَ مِنْ مَقَامِ مُوسَى وَعِيسَى مُصَلًّى كَمَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُتَّخَذَ مِنْ مَقَامِ إبْرَاهِيمَ مُصَلًّى وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ ذَلِكَ لِأَنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى يَخْتَصُّ مَا يَخْتَصُّهُ مِنْ الْأَعْيَانِ وَالْأَفْعَال بِأَحْكَامٍ تَخُصُّهُ يَمْتَنِعُ مَعَهَا قِيَاسُ غَيْرِهِ عَلَيْهِ إمَّا لِمَعْنًى يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ لَا يُوجَدُ بِغَيْرِهِ عَلَى قَوْلِ أَكْثَرِ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ وَإِمَّا لِمَحْضِ تَخْصِيصِ الْمَشِيئَةِ عَلَى قَوْلِ بَعْضِهِمْ كَمَا خَصَّ الْكَعْبَةَ بِأَنْ يُحَجَّ إلَيْهَا وَيُطَافَ بِهَا وَكَمَا خَصَّ عَرَفَاتٍ بِالْوُقُوفِ بِهَا وَكَمَا خَصَّ مِنًى بِرَمْيِ الْجِمَارِ بِهَا وَكَمَا خَصَّ الْأَشْهُرَ الْحُرُمَ بِتَحْرِيمِهَا وَكَمَا خَصَّ شَهْرَ رَمَضَانَ بِصِيَامِهِ وَقِيَامِهِ إلَى أَمْثَالِ ذَلِكَ.
 وَإِبْرَاهِيمُ وَمُحَمَّدٌ كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا خَلِيلُ اللَّهِ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي الصِّحَاحِ مِنْ غَيْرِ وَجْهٍ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{إنَّ اللَّهَ اتَّخَذَنِي خَلِيلًا كَمَا اتَّخَذَ إبْرَاهِيمَ خَلِيلًا}
 وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحِ: 
{أَنَّ رَجُلًا قَالَ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَا خَيْرَ الْبَرِيَّةِ قَالَ: ذَاكَ إبْرَاهِيمُ}
 . فَإِبْرَاهِيمُ أَفْضَلُ الْخَلْقِ بَعْدَ مُحَمَّدٍ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
 وَقَوْلُهُ:
 
" ذَاكَ إبْرَاهِيمُ "
 تَوَاضُعٌ مِنْهُ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي الصَّحِيحِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: 
{أَنَا سَيِّدُ وَلَدِ آدَمَ وَلَا فَخْرَ آدَمَ فَمَنْ دُونَهُ تَحْتَ لِوَائِي يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وَلَا فَخْرَ}
 إلَى غَيْرِ
translated_text:
that it was initially done for a particular purpose, then Allah prescribed it as a rite and an act of worship. But this applies only when Allah has prescribed and commanded it. No one may prescribe what Allah has not prescribed. For example, if someone were to say, “I consider it recommended to circumambulate the Rock seven times, just as the Ka‘bah is circumambulated,” or, “I consider it recommended to take the stations of Moses and Jesus as places of prayer, just as Allah commanded that the station of Abraham be taken as a place of prayer,” or something similar, he would have no right to do so. For Allah Most High singles out particular things and actions for rulings peculiar to them, which preclude extending those rulings to anything else by analogy. According to most scholars, this is because of a distinctive quality not found elsewhere; according to some, it is simply because His will has singled them out. Thus, He singled out the Ka‘bah for pilgrimage and circumambulation, ‘Arafāt for standing there, Minā for stoning the pillars there, the sacred months for their sanctity, and Ramadan for fasting and night prayer, along with other such examples.

Abraham and Muhammad are each an intimate friend of Allah. It is established through several chains of transmission in the authentic hadith collections that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Allah has taken me as an intimate friend, just as He took Abraham as an intimate friend.”

It is also established in the Sahīh:

“A man said to the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—‘O best of creation!’ He replied, ‘That is Abraham.’”

Thus, Abraham is the best of creation after Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

His words, “That is Abraham,” were an expression of humility, for it is established from him—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in the Sahīh that he said:

“I am the leader of the descendants of Adam, and I say this without boasting. Adam and all who came after him will be beneath my banner on the Day of Resurrection, and I say this without boasting.”

This is among other

texts which make clear that he is the best of creation and the most honoured by his Lord. Abraham is the leader of whom Allah said:

“I will make you a leader for the people.”

He is the model—the example to be followed—of whom Allah said:

“Indeed, Abraham was an exemplary leader, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining toward truth.”

It was to him that Allah assigned the site of the House and commanded him to proclaim the pilgrimage to it among the people. Allah declared the Sanctuary sacred through him, and He made Ishmael a prophet alongside him. Ishmael was the one who was to be sacrificed: he offered himself to Allah and patiently endured the trial, as we have demonstrated elsewhere with abundant evidence. His mother, Hagar, was the one who obeyed Allah and His Messenger Abraham by remaining with her son in that uninhabited valley, as Allah’s intimate friend said:

“Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley near Your sacred House.”

Abraham and his family possessed a degree of love for Allah, worship of Him, faith in Him, and obedience to Him unmatched by others. Allah therefore singled them out by granting His House, which they built for Him, distinctive qualities found nowhere else. He also made certain deeds of theirs an example for people and acts of worship in which they follow them.

There is no doubt that Allah prescribed for Abraham the ritual passage between Safā and Marwah, the stoning of the pillars, and the standing at ‘Arafāt after the events involving Hagar and Ishmael, the account of the sacrifice, and the other events that took place—just as He prescribed for Muhammad a brisk gait during circumambulation—when He commanded him to proclaim the pilgrimage to the House among the people. Pilgrimage is founded upon humility and submission to Allah. For this reason, it is specifically called nusk; linguistically, “nusk” means worship.

قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ:
 النُّسُكُ الْعِبَادَةُ وَالنَّاسِكُ الْعَابِدُ وَقَدْ نَسَكَ وَتَنَسَّكَ أَيْ تَعَبَّدَ وَنَسُكَ بِالضَّمِّ أَيْ صَارَ نَاسِكًا ثُمَّ خُصَّ الْحَجُّ بِاسْمِ النُّسُكِ لِأَنَّهُ أَدْخَلُ فِي الْعِبَادَةِ وَالذُّلِّ لِلَّهِ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ وَلِهَذَا كَانَ فِيهِ مِنْ الْأَفْعَالِ مَا لَا يُقْصَدُ فِيهِ إلَّا مُجَرَّدُ الذُّلِّ لِلَّهِ وَالْعِبَادَةِ لَهُ كَالسَّعْيِ وَرَمْيِ الْجِمَارِ. قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{إنَّمَا جُعِلَ رَمْيُ الْجِمَارِ وَالسَّعْيُ بَيْنَ الصَّفَا والمروة لِإِقَامَةِ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ}
 رَوَاهُ التِّرْمِذِيُّ وَخَصَّ بِذَلِكَ الذَّبْحِ الْفِدَاءَ أَيْضًا دُونَ مُطْلَقِ الذَّبْحِ؛ لِأَنَّ إرَاقَةَ الدَّمِ لِلَّهِ أَبْلَغُ فِي الْخُضُوعِ وَالْعِبَادَةِ لَهُ وَلِهَذَا كَانَ مَنْ كَانَ قَبْلَنَا لَا يَأْكُلُونَ الْقُرْبَانَ؛
 بَلْ تَأْتِي نَارٌ مِنْ السَّمَاءِ فَتَأْكُلُهُ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{الَّذِينَ قَالُوا إنَّ اللَّهَ عَهِدَ إلَيْنَا أَلَّا نُؤْمِنَ لِرَسُولٍ حَتَّى يَأْتِيَنَا بِقُرْبَانٍ تَأْكُلُهُ النَّارُ قُلْ قَدْ جَاءَكُمْ رُسُلٌ مِنْ قَبْلِي بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ وَبِالَّذِي قُلْتُمْ فَلِمَ قَتَلْتُمُوهُمْ إنْ كُنْتُمْ صَادِقِينَ}
 . وَكَذَلِكَ كَانُوا إذَا غَنِمُوا غَنِيمَةً جَمَعُوهَا ثُمَّ جَاءَتْ النَّارُ فَأَكَلَتْهَا لِيَكُونَ قِتَالُهُمْ مَحْضًا لِلَّهِ لَا لِلْمَغْنَمِ وَيَكُونَ ذَبْحُهُمْ عِبَادَةً مَحْضَةً لِلَّهِ لَا لِأَجْلِ أَكْلِهِمْ وَأُمَّةُ مُحَمَّدٍ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَسَّعَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ لِكَمَالِ يَقِينِهِمْ وَإِخْلَاصِهِمْ وَأَنَّهُمْ يُقَاتِلُونَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوْ أَكَلُوا الْمَغْنَمَ وَيَذْبَحُونَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوْ أَكَلُوا الْقُرْبَانَ وَلِهَذَا كَانَ عُبَّادُ الشَّيَاطِينِ وَالْأَصْنَامِ يَذْبَحُونَ لَهَا الذَّبَائِحَ أَيْضًا فَالذَّبْحُ لِلْمَعْبُودِ غَايَةُ الذُّلِّ وَالْخُضُوعِ لَهُ. وَلِهَذَا لَمْ يَجُزْ الذَّبْحُ لِغَيْرِ اللَّهِ وَلَا أَنْ يُسَمَّى غَيْرُ اللَّهِ عَلَى الذَّبَائِحِ
translated_text:
Al-Jawharī said:

“Nusk means worship, and a nāsik is a worshipper. Nasaka and tanassaka mean ‘to worship’; nasuka, with the vowel u, means ‘to become a worshipper.’”

Pilgrimage was then singled out by the designation nusk because it involves worship and humility before Allah more fully than other acts. Hence it includes actions whose sole purpose is humility before Allah and worship of Him, such as the ritual passage between Safā and Marwah and the stoning of the pillars. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The stoning of the pillars and the ritual passage between Safā and Marwah were instituted only to establish the remembrance of Allah.”

This was narrated by al-Tirmidhī. Slaughter offered as a sacrificial ransom is likewise singled out by this designation, unlike slaughter in general, because shedding blood for Allah expresses greater submission and worship of Him. For this reason, those before us did not eat their sacrificial offerings; rather, a fire would descend from heaven and consume them. Thus Allah Most High said:

“Those who said, ‘Allah has commanded us not to believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering consumed by fire.’ Say, ‘Messengers before me came to you with clear proofs and with what you speak of. Why, then, did you kill them, if you are truthful?’”

Likewise, whenever they acquired spoils of war, they would gather them together, and fire would come and consume them. This was so that their fighting would be purely for Allah, not for spoils, and their slaughter would be purely an act of worship for Allah, not for their own consumption. Allah granted greater latitude to the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because of their perfect certainty and sincerity, and because they fight for Allah even if they partake of the spoils, and slaughter for Allah even if they eat of the offering.

For this reason, worshippers of devils and idols would likewise slaughter animals for them. Slaughtering for the object of one’s worship is the utmost expression of humility and submission to it. Hence it is not permissible to slaughter for anyone other than Allah, nor to invoke any name other than Allah’s over the animals being slaughtered.

And He, glorified be He, has forbidden what is slaughtered on altars—that is, what is slaughtered for other than Allah—as well as anything over which a name other than Allah’s is pronounced, even if it is intended for meat rather than as a sacrificial offering. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, cursed whoever slaughtered for other than Allah and forbade slaughtering animals for the jinn; people used to slaughter animals for them. Indeed, Allah has forbidden, without qualification, anything over which His name has not been mentioned, as the Quran and Sunnah indicate in numerous places.

Allah Most High said:

“So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.”

That is, sacrifice to your Lord, as Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, said:

“Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

He and Ishmael also said, as they raised the foundations of the House:

“Our Lord, accept this from us. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.”

“Our Lord, make us both submissive to You, and from our descendants a community submissive to You, and show us our rites.”

The rites here encompass all the rites of pilgrimage. Allah Most High said:

“For every community We have appointed rites which they perform.”

Allah Most High also said:

“And for every community We have appointed sacrificial rites, so that they may mention Allah’s name over the livestock He has provided for them.”

And He said:

“Neither their meat nor their blood reaches Allah, but your piety reaches Him.”

Likewise, Allah Most High said:

“And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah—this stems from the piety of hearts.”

The purpose, then, is for hearts to be pious towards Allah: to worship Him alone, to the exclusion of all else, in utter servitude to Him. Such servitude entails the utmost love, humility and sincerity. This is the religion of Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend. All of this makes clear that the worship of the heart is the foundation, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, there is a piece of flesh in the body: if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Truly, it is the heart.”

وَالنِّيَّةُ وَالْقَصْدُ هُمَا عَمَلُ الْقَلْبِ فَلَا بُدَّ فِي الْمُتَابَعَةِ لِلرَّسُولِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِنْ اعْتِبَارِ النِّيَّةِ وَالْقَصْدِ. وَمِنْ هَذَا الْبَابِ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمَّا احْتَجَمَ وَأَمَرَ بِالْحِجَامَةِ.
 وَقَالَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ الصَّحِيحِ:
 
{شِفَاءُ أُمَّتِي فِي شَرْطَةِ مِحْجَمٍ أَوْ شَرْبَةِ عَسَلٍ أَوْ كَيَّةٍ بِنَارِ وَمَا أُحِبُّ أَنْ أَكْتَوِيَ}
 كَانَ مَعْلُومًا أَنَّ الْمَقْصُودَ بِالْحِجَامَةِ إخْرَاجُ الدَّمِ الزَّائِدِ الَّذِي يَضُرُّ الْبَدَنَ فَهَذَا هُوَ الْمَقْصُودُ وَخَصَّ الْحِجَامَةَ لِأَنَّ الْبِلَادَ الْحَارَّةَ يَخْرُجُ الدَّمُ فِيهَا إلَى سَطْحِ الْبَدَنِ فَيَخْرُجُ بِالْحِجَامَةِ فَلِهَذَا كَانَتْ الْحِجَامَةُ فِي الْحِجَازِ وَنَحْوِهِ مِنْ الْبِلَادِ الْحَارَّةِ يَحْصُلُ بِهَا مَقْصُودُ اسْتِفْرَاغِ الدَّمِ وَأَمَّا الْبِلَادُ الْبَارِدَةُ فَالدَّمُ يَغُورُ فِيهَا إلَى الْعُرُوقِ فَيَحْتَاجُونَ إلَى قَطْعِ الْعُرُوقِ بِالْفِصَادِ وَهَذَا أَمْرٌ مَعْرُوفٌ بِالْحِسِّ وَالتَّجْرِبَةِ فَإِنَّهُ فِي زَمَانِ الْبَرْدِ تَسْخَنُ الْأَجْوَافُ وَتَبْرُدُ الظَّوَاهِرُ لِأَنَّ شَبِيهَ الشَّيْءِ مُنْجَذِبٌ إلَيْهِ فَإِذَا بَرَدَ الْهَوَاءُ بَرَدَ مَا يُلَاقِيهِ مِنْ الْأَبْدَانِ وَالْأَرْضِ فَيَهْرُبُ الْحَرُّ الَّذِي فِيهَا مِنْ الْبَرْدِ الْمُضَادِّ لَهُ إلَى الْأَجْوَافِ فَيَسْخَنُ بَاطِنُ الْأَرْضِ. وَأَجْوَافُ الْحَيَوَانِ وَيَأْوِي الْحَيَوَانُ إلَى الْأَكْنَانِ الدَّافِئَةِ. وَلِقُوَّةِ الْحَرَارَةِ فِي بَاطِنِ الْإِنْسَانِ يَأْكُلُ فِي الشِّتَاءِ وَفِي الْبِلَادِ الْبَارِدَةِ أَكْثَرَ مِمَّا يَأْكُلُ فِي الصَّيْفِ وَفِي الْبِلَادِ الْحَارَّةِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْحَرَارَةَ تَطْبُخُ الطَّعَامَ وَتُصَرِّفُهُ وَيَكُونُ الْمَاءُ النَّابِعُ فِي الشِّتَاءِ سُخْنًا لِسُخُونَةِ جَوْفِ الْأَرْضِ وَالدَّمُ سُخْنٌ فَيَكُونُ فِي جَوْفِ الْعُرُوقِ لَا فِي سَطْحِ الْجِلْدِ فَلَوْ احْتَجَمَ لَمْ يَنْفَعْهُ ذَلِكَ بَلْ قَدْ يَضُرُّهُ وَفِي الصَّيْفِ
translated_text:
Intention and purpose are acts of the heart, so following the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, necessarily requires taking intention and purpose into account. An illustration of this is that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, underwent cupping and instructed others to do so, saying in an authentic hadith:

“Healing for my community lies in an incision made with a cupping blade, a draught of honey, or cauterization with fire; but I do not like to undergo cauterization.”

It was understood that the purpose of cupping was to remove excess blood that harms the body. This, then, was the intended aim. He singled out cupping because, in hot countries, blood moves towards the surface of the body and can therefore be drawn out by cupping. Thus, in the Hijāz and similar hot countries, cupping achieves the intended evacuation of blood. In cold countries, however, blood retreats deeper into the veins, so people need to have their veins opened through bloodletting.

This is something known through observation and experience. In cold weather, the internal cavities grow warm while the outer surfaces grow cold, for like is drawn to like. When the air grows cold, the parts of bodies and the earth that come into contact with it grow cold. The heat within them then retreats from the opposing cold into their interiors, warming the interior of the earth and the internal cavities of animals. Animals seek refuge in warm shelters. Because of the strength of the heat inside the human body, people eat more in winter and in cold countries than they do in summer and in hot countries, since heat cooks and processes food. Spring water is warm in winter because the earth’s interior is warm. Blood, too, is warm, so it remains deep within the veins rather than at the surface of the skin. If a person were to undergo cupping, it would therefore not benefit him and might even harm him. In summer

Similarly, when Jewish and Christian unbelievers wear distinctive clothing in yellow or blue, wearing it is prohibited because it involves imitating them, although without that association it would not be considered reprehensible. For this reason, Ahmad and others disapproved of wearing black when doing so involved imitating those who commit injustice or assist in it. They also disapproved of selling it to anyone who would use wearing it to facilitate injustice. When, however, it entails no harm, it is not prohibited. If he did not pay it, he would wrong the Muslims by depriving them of their entitlement from the land. They did not disapprove of selling it because it was an endowment. Selling an endowment is prohibited only because doing so nullifies the endowment; hence it may neither be sold, given away, nor inherited. Land subject to kharāj, however, passes to the heir by scholarly consensus, and it may be given as a gift. The recipient or purchaser takes the seller’s place and pays the kharāj previously due from him. Selling it does not harm those entitled to the kharāj, unlike selling an endowment.

Many jurists have mistakenly supposed that they disapproved of selling such land because it was an endowment. Their confusion arose because they encountered reports expressing disapproval of its sale and knew that ʿUmar had set it aside as property held for the Muslim community, never distributing it. Since this was effectively an endowment, they supposed that this was why selling it was considered reprehensible. They did not examine the matter carefully enough to see that this sale is not of the kind prohibited in the case of an endowment. The land’s revenue goes to those entitled to it on precisely the same basis before and after the sale. It is unlike a house which, once sold, ceases to benefit the endowment’s beneficiaries and becomes the purchaser’s property.

More astonishing still is that some of these jurists said: “The sale of Mecca’s residential properties was disapproved of only because it had been conquered by force and had likewise not been distributed.” Yet they themselves, along with everyone else, maintained that residential properties may be sold in territory conquered by force whose land was set aside as property held for the Muslim community.  كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَالْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ الَّذِي جَعَلْنَاهُ لِلنَّاسِ سَوَاءً الْعَاكِفُ فِيهِ وَالْبَادِي}
 وَهَذِهِ هِيَ الْعِلَّةُ الَّتِي اخْتَصَّتْ بِهَا مَكَّةُ دُونَ سَائِرِ الْأَمْصَارِ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ أَوْجَبَ حَجَّهَا عَلَى جَمِيعِ النَّاسِ وَشَرَعَ اعْتِمَارَهَا دَائِمًا فَجَعَلَهَا مُشْتَرِكَةً بَيْنَ جَمِيعِ عِبَادِهِ.
 كَمَا قَالَ:
 
{سَوَاءً الْعَاكِفُ فِيهِ وَالْبَادِي}
 وَلِهَذَا كَانَتْ مِنًى وَغَيْرُهَا مِنْ الْمَشَاعِرِ مَنْ سَبَقَ إلَى مَكَانٍ فَهُوَ أَحَقُّ بِهِ حَتَّى يَنْتَقِلَ عَنْهُ كَالْمَسَاجِدِ وَمَكَّةُ نَفْسُهَا مَنْ سَبَقَ إلَى مَكَانٍ فَهُوَ أَحَقُّ بِهِ وَالْإِنْسَانُ أَحَقُّ بِمَسْكَنِهِ مَا دَامَ مُحْتَاجًا إلَيْهِ وَمَا اسْتَغْنَى عَنْهُ مِنْ الْمَنَافِعِ فَعَلَيْهِ بَذْلُهُ بِلَا عِوَضٍ لِغَيْرِهِ مِنْ الْحَجِيجِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ. وَلِهَذَا كَانَتْ الْأَقْوَالُ فِي إجَارَةِ دُورِهَا وَبَيْعِ رِبَاعِهَا ثَلَاثَةً.
 قِيلَ:
 لَا يَجُوزُ لَا هَذَا وَلَا هَذَا.
 وَقِيلَ:
 يَجُوزُ الْأَمْرَانِ.
translated_text:
Mecca’s land had been set aside for the Muslims and subjected to kharāj, that would not have prohibited the sale of its residential properties. How, then, could this apply to Mecca when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, left its houses and farmland in the hands of their owners as before, neither distributing the land nor imposing kharāj on it?

This is why some held that it had been conquered by treaty. Yet there is no doubt that it was conquered by force, as the authentic, mass-transmitted hadiths establish. However, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, set all its inhabitants free: he killed only those who fought him, took none of their offspring captive, and seized none of their property as spoils. Hence they were called “those set free.” Ahmad and others among the early generations based their explanation on its having been conquered by force together with its being shared by the Muslims, as Allah Most High says:

“And the Sacred Mosque, which We have made for all people, residents and visitors alike.”

This is the distinguishing consideration that applies to Mecca alone, unlike other cities. Allah has made pilgrimage to it obligatory upon all people and prescribed performing umrah there at all times, thus making it shared by all His servants. As He says:

“Residents and visitors alike.”

For this reason, at Minā and the other pilgrimage sites, whoever first occupies a place has the greater right to it until he leaves, just as in mosques. In Mecca itself, too, whoever first occupies a place has the greater right to it. A person has the greater right to his dwelling for as long as he needs it, but whatever use of it is surplus to his needs he must make available free of charge to others, whether pilgrims or not.

Accordingly, there are three opinions concerning renting out its houses and selling its residential properties. One holds that neither is permissible; another holds that both are permissible.

original_text:
وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّهُ يَجُوزُ بَيْعُ رِبَاعِهَا وَلَا يَجُوزُ إجَارَتُهَا وَعَلَى هَذَا تَدُلُّ الْآثَارُ الْمَنْقُولَةُ فِي ذَلِكَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَعَنْ الصَّحَابَةِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ فَإِنَّ الصَّحَابَةَ كَانُوا يَتَبَايَعُونَ دُورَهَا وَالدُّورُ تُورَثُ وَتُوهَبُ وَإِذَا كَانَتْ تُورَثُ وَتُوهَبُ جَازَ أَنْ تُبَاعَ بِخِلَافِ الْوَقْفِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يُبَاعُ وَلَا يُورَثُ وَلَا يُوهَبُ. وَكَذَلِكَ أُمُّ الْوَلَدِ مَنْ لَمْ يُجَوِّزْ بَيْعَهَا لَمْ يُجَوِّزْ هِبَتَهَا وَلَا أَنْ تُوَرَّثَ وَأَمَّا إجَارَتُهَا فَقَدْ كَانَتْ تُدْعَى السَّوَائِبُ - عَلَى عَهْدِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَأَبِي بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا مَنْ احْتَاجَ سَكَنَ وَمَنْ اسْتَغْنَى أَسْكَنَ؛
 لِأَنَّ الْمُسْلِمِينَ كُلَّهُمْ مُحْتَاجُونَ إلَى الْمَنَافِعِ فَصَارَتْ كَمَنَافِعِ الْأَسْوَاقِ وَالْمَسَاجِدِ وَالطُّرُقَاتِ الَّتِي يَحْتَاجُ إلَيْهَا الْمُسْلِمُونَ فَمَنْ سَبَقَ إلَى شَيْءٍ مِنْهَا فَهُوَ أَحَقُّ بِهِ وَمَا اسْتَغْنَى عَنْهُ أَخَذَهُ غَيْرُهُ بِلَا عِوَضٍ وَكَذَلِكَ الْمُبَاحَاتُ الَّتِي يَشْتَرِكُ فِيهَا النَّاسُ وَيَكُونُ الْمُشْتَرِي لَهَا اسْتَفَادَ بِذَلِكَ أَنَّهُ أَحَقُّ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ مَا دَامَ مُحْتَاجًا وَإِذَا بَاعَهَا الْإِنْسَانُ قَطَعَ اخْتِصَاصَهُ بِهَا وَتَوْرِيثَهُ إيَّاهَا وَغَيْرَ ذَلِكَ مِنْ تَصَرُّفَاتِهِ وَلِهَذَا لَهُ أَنْ لَا يَبْذُلَهُ إلَّا بِعِوَضِ وَالنَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مَنَّ عَلَى أَهْلِ مَكَّةَ فَإِنَّ الْأَسِيرَ يَجُوزُ الْمَنُّ عَلَيْهِ لِلْمَصْلَحَةِ وَأَعْطَاهُمْ مَعَ ذَلِكَ ذَرَارِيَّهُمْ وَأَمْوَالَهُمْ كَمَا مَنَّ عَلَى هَوَازِنَ لَمَّا جَاءُوا مُسْلِمِينَ بِإِحْدَى الطَّائِفَتَيْنِ:
 السَّبْيُ أَوْ الْمَالُ فَاخْتَارُوا السَّبْيَ فَأَعْطَاهُمْ السَّبْيَ وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ بَعْدَ الْقِسْمَةِ
translated_text:
The correct view, however, is that its residential properties may be sold but may not be rented out. This is what the reports transmitted on this matter from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, indicate. The Companions used to buy and sell its houses, and these houses could be inherited and given as gifts. Whatever may be inherited and given as a gift may also be sold, unlike an endowed property, which may neither be sold, inherited, nor given away. Likewise, those who prohibit selling an umm al-walad—a slave woman who has borne her master a child—also prohibit giving her away or passing her on by inheritance.

As for renting out these houses, they were known as al-sawā’ib (houses freely available for lodging) during the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Whoever needed accommodation lived in them, and whoever had no need of them accommodated others. This is because all Muslims need their use. They thus resemble markets, mosques, and roads, whose use Muslims need: whoever first occupies a place has the greater right to it, while whatever he no longer needs may be used by someone else without payment. The same applies to resources freely available for everyone’s use.

What the purchaser of such a house acquires through his purchase is priority over others for as long as he needs it. When a person sells it, he relinquishes his exclusive right to it, his right to pass it on by inheritance, and his other rights of disposal. He may therefore refuse to relinquish it except in return for compensation.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, granted clemency to the people of Mecca, for a captive may be released without ransom when this serves a legitimate interest. He also left them their offspring and property, just as, when Hawāzin came to him as Muslims, he graciously granted them one of the two categories: the captives or the property. They chose the captives, so he gave them the captives. This was after the distribution of the spoils

original_text:
فَعَوَّضَ عَنْ نَصِيبِهِ مَنْ لَمْ يَرْضَ بِأَخْذِهِ مِنْهُمْ وَكَانَ قَدْ قَسَّمَ الْمَالَ فَلَمْ يَرُدَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ وَقُرَيْشٌ لَمْ تُحَارِبْهُ كَمَا حَارَبَتْهُ هَوَازِنُ وَهُوَ إنَّمَا مَنَّ عَلَى مَنْ لَمْ يُقَاتِلْهُ مِنْهُمْ كَمَا قَالَ:
 
{مَنْ أَغْلَقَ بَابَهُ فَهُوَ آمِنٌ وَمَنْ أَلْقَى سِلَاحَهُ فَهُوَ آمِنٌ وَمَنْ دَخَلَ الْمَسْجِدَ فَهُوَ آمِنٌ}
 . فَلَمَّا كَفَّ جُمْهُورُهُمْ عَنْ قِتَالِهِ وَعَرَفَ أَنَّهُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ أَطْلَقَهُمْ وَلَمْ يَغْنَمْ أَمْوَالَهُمْ وَلَا حَرِيمَهُمْ وَلَمْ يَضْرِبْ الرِّقَّ لَا عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا عَلَى أَوْلَادِهِمْ بَلْ سَمَّاهُمْ الطُّلَقَاءَ مِنْ قُرَيْشٍ بِخِلَافِ ثَقِيفٍ فَإِنَّهُمْ سُمُّوا الْعُتَقَاءَ فَإِنَّهُ أَعْتَقَ أَوْلَادَهُمْ بَعْدَ الِاسْتِرْقَاقِ وَالْقِسْمَةِ وَكَانَ فِي هَذَا مَا دَلَّ عَلَى أَنَّ الْإِمَامَ يَفْعَلُ بِالْأَمْوَالِ وَالرِّجَالِ وَالْعَقَارِ وَالْمَنْقُولِ مَا هُوَ أَصْلَحُ فَإِنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَتَحَ خَيْبَرَ فَقَسَّمَهَا بَيْنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَسَبَى بَعْضَ نِسَائِهَا وَأَقَرَّ سَائِرَهُمْ مَعَ ذَرَارِيِّهِمْ حَتَّى أَجْلَوْا بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ فَلَمْ يَسْتَرِقَّهُمْ وَمَكَّةُ فَتَحَهَا عَنْوَةً وَلَمْ يُقَسِّمْهَا لِأَجْلِ الْمَصْلَحَةِ.
وقد تَنَازَعَ الْعُلَمَاءُ فِي الْأَرْضِ إذَا فُتِحَتْ عَنْوَةً هَلْ يَجِبُ قَسْمُهَا كَخَيْبَرِ لِأَنَّهَا مَغْنَمٌ أَوْ تَصِيرُ فَيْئًا كَمَا دَلَّتْ عَلَيْهِ سُورَةُ الْحَشْرِ وَلَيْسَتْ الْأَرْضُ مِنْ الْمَغْنَمِ أَوْ يُخَيَّرُ الْإِمَامُ فِيمَا بَيْنَ هَذَا وَهَذَا عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَقْوَالٍ وَأَكْثَرُ الْعُلَمَاءِ عَلَى التَّخْيِيرِ وَهُوَ الصَّحِيحُ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَأَحْمَد فِي الْمَشْهُورِ عَنْهُ وَغَيْرِهِمَا.
translated_text:
and he compensated anyone who was unwilling to relinquish his share. He had already distributed the property, so he did not return it to them. Quraysh had not fought him as Hawāzin had, and he granted clemency only to those among them who did not fight him, as he said:

“Whoever closes his door is safe; whoever lays down his weapons is safe; and whoever enters the mosque is safe.”

When most of them refrained from fighting him, and he knew that they were Muslims, he released them. He did not seize their property as spoils or take their families captive, nor did he enslave them or their children. Rather, he called them “the released men of Quraysh,” unlike Thaqīf, who were called “the emancipated,” for he freed their children after they had been enslaved and distributed.

This indicates that the ruler should deal with property and men, immovable and movable possessions, in whatever way best serves the public interest. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conquered Khaybar and divided it among the Muslims. He took some of its women captive but allowed the remaining inhabitants and their offspring to stay until they were later expelled; he did not enslave them. He conquered Mecca by force but did not divide it up, in the public interest.

Scholars have differed over land conquered by force, holding three opinions: must it be divided, as Khaybar was, because it constitutes spoils of war? Does it instead become fay’ (property held for the Muslim community), as indicated by Surah al-Hashr, with land not being included among the spoils of war? Or may the ruler choose between these two courses? Most scholars hold that the ruler has this choice, and this is the correct view. It is the position of Abū Hanīfa, of Ahmad according to the well-known report from him, and of others.

original_text:
وَلَوْ فَتَحَ الْإِمَامُ بَلَدًا وَغَلَبَ عَلَى ظَنِّهِ أَنَّ أَهْلَهُ يُسْلِمُونَ وَيُجَاهِدُونَ جَازَ أَنْ يَمُنَّ عَلَيْهِمْ بِأَنْفُسِهِمْ وَأَمْوَالِهِمْ وَأَوْلَادِهِمْ كَمَا فَعَلَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِأَهْلِ مَكَّةَ فَإِنَّهُمْ أَسْلَمُوا كُلُّهُمْ بِلَا خِلَافٍ بِخِلَافِ أَهْلِ خَيْبَرَ فَإِنَّهُ لَمْ يُسْلِمْ مِنْهُمْ أَحَدٌ فَأُولَئِكَ قَسَمَ أَرْضَهُمْ لِأَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا كُفَّارًا مُصِرِّينَ عَلَى الْكُفْرِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ تَرَكَهَا لَهُمْ لِأَنَّهُمْ كُلَّهُمْ صَارُوا مُسْلِمِينَ وَالْمَقْصُودُ بِالْجِهَادِ أَنْ تَكُونَ كَلِمَةُ اللَّهِ هِيَ الْعُلْيَا وَأَنْ يَكُونَ الدِّينُ كُلُّهُ لِلَّهِ وَقَدْ كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يُعْطِي الْمُؤَلَّفَةَ قُلُوبُهُمْ لِيَتَأَلَّفَهُمْ عَلَى الْإِسْلَامِ فَكَيْفَ لَا يَتَأَلَّفُهُمْ بِإِبْقَاءِ دِيَارِهِمْ وَأَمْوَالِهِمْ.
 وَهُمْ لَمَّا حَضَرُوا مَعَهُ حنينا أَعْطَاهُمْ مِنْ غَنَائِمِ حنين مَا تَأْلَفُهُمْ بِهِ حَتَّى عَتَبَ بَعْضُ الْأَنْصَارِ كَمَا فِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ:
 {أَنَّ نَاسًا مِنْ الْأَنْصَارِ قَالُوا يَوْمَ حنين حِينَ أَفَاءَ اللَّهُ عَلَى رَسُولِهِ مِنْ أَمْوَالِ هَوَازِنَ مَا أَفَاءَ فَطَفِقَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يُعْطِي رِجَالًا مِنْ قُرَيْشٍ الْمِائَةَ مِنْ الْإِبِلِ.
 فَقَالُوا:
 يَغْفِرُ اللَّهُ لِرَسُولِ اللَّهِ يُعْطِي قُرَيْشًا وَيَتْرُكُنَا وَسُيُوفُنَا تَقْطُرُ مِنْ دِمَائِهِمْ -
 قَالَ أَنَسٌ:
 فَحُدِّثَ ذَلِكَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِنْ قَوْلِهِمْ فَأَرْسَلَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إلَى الْأَنْصَارِ فَجَمَعَهُمْ فِي قُبَّةٍ مِنْ أُدْمٍ فَلَمَّا اجْتَمَعُوا جَاءَهُمْ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَقَالَ: مَا حَدِيثٌ بَلَغَنِي عَنْكُمْ؟
 فَقَالَ لَهُ فُقَهَاءُ الْأَنْصَارِ:
 أَمَّا ذَوُو رَأْينَا يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ فَلَمْ يَقُولُوا شَيْئًا وَأَمَّا أُنَاسٌ مِنَّا حَدِيثَةٌ
translated_text:
If the ruler were to conquer a town and consider it most likely that its people would embrace Islam and fight in jihad, he would be permitted to grant them clemency, leaving them their freedom, property, and children, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did with the people of Mecca. They all embraced Islam, without dispute, unlike the people of Khaybar, none of whom embraced Islam. He therefore divided the land of the latter because they were unbelievers who persisted in unbelief, whereas he left the former their land because they had all become Muslims. The purpose of jihad is for Allah’s word to be supreme and for religion to be entirely for Allah. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to give gifts to those whose hearts he sought to win over to Islam. How, then, would he not win them over by allowing them to retain their homes and property?

When they accompanied him at Hunayn, he gave them enough of its spoils to win their hearts, to the point that some of the Ansār expressed displeasure, as related in the two Sahīh collections on the authority of Anas ibn Mālik:

He said, ‘After me, you will encounter severe favoritism, so remain patient until you meet Allah and His Messenger, for I shall be at the Cistern.’

“‘If the people followed a valley or a mountain pass, and the Ansār followed another valley or mountain pass, I would follow the valley and mountain pass of the Ansār. All this was generosity and giving intended to bring people to Islam, which is the purpose of jihad.

There are two views concerning the source of what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, gave from the spoils of Khaybar to those whose hearts were to be won over: the first is that it came from the fifth; the second is that it came from the spoils as a whole. The latter is the stronger view.

What he gave them was a considerable amount that the fifth could not have covered. Whoever says that these gifts came from one-fifth of the fifth has not understood what happened. None of the early scholars said this. This is so notwithstanding his statement:

“I am entitled to nothing of what Allah has granted you except the fifth, and that fifth is returned to you.”

This was because those whose hearts were to be won over were members of the army, and he gave them preferential allocations in the public interest, just as he gave them preferential allocations from the fay’ revenues in the public interest.

This demonstrates that the ruler may distribute the spoils of war according to his independent judgment, just as he distributes the fay’ revenues according to his independent judgment, provided he is a just ruler who distributes them with knowledge and justice. Distributing the spoils among those who took them is not like dividing an inheritance among the heirs or distributing zakat among its eight categories of recipients. Hence, he said concerning zakat:

“Allah did not leave its distribution to a prophet or anyone else, but assigned it to eight categories. If you belong to one of those categories, I will give you.”

It is thus clear that the property Allah grants from the unbelievers is different in this respect. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, allotted shares from Khaybar to the people of the ship who arrived with Ja‘far, although he allotted nothing to anyone else who had been absent from it. He also allotted shares from the spoils of Badr to Talhah, al-Zubayr, and ‘Uthmān

Fighting was not undertaken for the sake of spoils. War spoils are therefore not like freely available resources acquired jointly by a group through gathering grass, collecting firewood, or hunting. The purpose of those activities is to acquire wealth, unlike fighting that yields spoils. Indeed, whoever fights for wealth is not striving in Allah’s cause. For this reason, spoils were not made lawful for those before us, but were made lawful for us to help advance the interests of the religion.

Spoils were thus made lawful for the benefit of the religion and its people. Anyone who benefits those fighting in jihad by helping them complete their undertaking is counted among them, even if he is not present. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Muslims are one united body. A pledge of protection given by even the least of them is binding upon them all, and those who go out on expeditions share their spoils with those who remain behind.”

Those who go out on expeditions do so only with the support of those who remain behind. Those who assist the fighters in jihad are therefore themselves counted among them. A fuller discussion of these matters belongs elsewhere.

translated_text:
act of worship is part of the Sunnah. But if he happened to pray there without deliberately choosing the place, deliberately seeking it out for worship is not part of the Sunnah. For this reason, most of the Companions did not seek to imitate him in this regard. Even Ibn ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, despite his fondness for imitating the outward form of the Prophet’s actions, only sought to pray where the Prophet had prayed, not at every place where he had stopped. Accordingly, Ahmad ibn Hanbal permitted this on a limited scale, as Ibn ‘Umar had done. But he, may Allah be pleased with him, prohibited doing it extensively, because it leads to the harmful practice of turning sites associated with the prophets into places of worship—the places known as shrines.

The mosques and shrines introduced into Islam over graves and at such sites are religious innovations introduced by people who did not understand the law of Islam or what Allah sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to establish: complete monotheism, devotion sincerely dedicated to Allah alone, and the closing of the avenues to associating partners with Allah that Satan opens for the children of Adam.

Thus, those furthest removed from monotheism, sincere devotion to Allah alone, and knowledge of the religion of Islam are found to show the greatest veneration for places where partners are associated with Allah. Those knowledgeable about the Sunnah and hadith of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are more faithful to monotheism and sincere devotion to Allah alone, whereas those ignorant of these are closer to associating partners with Allah and to religious innovations.

This is therefore found among the Rāfidah more than among others, because they are more ignorant than others and more given to associating partners with Allah and to religious innovations. Hence they venerate shrines more than others do and do more than others to ruin mosques. As for the mosques, they do not pray in them

translated_text:
for Friday prayer or in congregation; if they pray in them at all, they do so only individually. As for shrines, they venerate them more than mosques, to the point that they may regard visiting them as preferable to performing Hajj to Allah’s Sacred House, calling such visits “the greater pilgrimage.” Ibn al-Mufīd, one of their scholars, wrote a book entitled “The Rites of Pilgrimage to Shrines,” in which he included falsehoods and statements unlike those found among any other group. Although other groups also have some degree of associating partners with Allah, falsehood, and religious innovation, these are more prevalent among them.

The more closely a person follows Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the more fully he affirms Allah’s oneness and devotes his religion sincerely to Him. As he departs from following him, his religion diminishes accordingly. If he strays far from him, forms of associating partners with Allah and religious innovation appear in him that do not appear in those who follow the Messenger more closely.

It is worship in mosques that Allah has commanded in His Book and the Sunnah of His Messenger; worship in them constitutes maintaining them. The Exalted says:

“And who is more unjust than one who prevents Allah’s name from being mentioned in His mosques?”

He did not say, “Allah’s shrines.” The Exalted also says:

“Say, ‘My Lord has commanded justice. Direct your faces toward Him at every mosque, and call upon Him, devoting your religion sincerely to Him.’”

He did not say, “at every shrine.” Those devoted to shrines do not devote their religion sincerely to Allah; rather, they engage in a degree of associating partners with Him. The Exalted says:

“It is not for those who associate partners with Allah to maintain Allah’s mosques while bearing witness against themselves to their disbelief. Their deeds have come to nothing, and they will remain in the Fire forever.”

“Only those who believe in Allah and the Last Day maintain Allah’s mosques

and establish prayer”—and so on through the verses.

Al-Tirmidhī reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If you see a man regularly attending the mosque, bear witness to his faith.” Then he recited this verse.

What is meant by maintaining mosques is maintaining them through worship within them, such as prayer and devotional retreat. A city is described as thriving when it is inhabited, and as desolate when no one lives there. The same usage occurs in the Exalted’s words:

“Do you consider providing water for pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque equal to the deeds of one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in Allah’s cause? They are not equal in Allah’s sight.”

As for the actual construction of mosques, they may be built by the righteous or the wicked, by Muslims or disbelievers. This is called building, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise.”

Allah Most High thus made clear that those who associate partners with Him have no right to maintain Allah’s mosques while bearing witness against themselves to their disbelief. He also made clear that only those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakah, and fear none but Allah maintain them. This describes those who affirm Allah’s oneness and devote their religion sincerely to Him: they fear none but Allah, place their hopes in none but Him, seek help from none but Him, and invoke none but Him.

Those devoted to shrines, however, fear others besides Allah, place their hopes in others, and invoke others. He, glorified is He, did not say, “Only those … maintain Allah’s shrines.” Shrines are not houses of Allah; rather, they are houses where partners are associated with Him. Thus there is no verse in the Quran praising shrines, nor anything from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning

this in any hadith. Allah mentioned it only in His account of those before us, who built a mosque over the grave of the Companions of the Cave. These were among those whom Allah forbade us to imitate, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“Those before you used to take graves as places of worship. Beware! Do not take graves as places of worship, for I forbid you to do so.”

In this hadith he condemned those devoted to shrines, as he did in the other authentic hadiths, saying:

“May Allah curse the Jews and Christians: they took the graves of their prophets as places of worship.” He was warning against what they had done.

He also said:

“When a righteous man among them died, they would build a mosque over his grave and make those images within it. They will be the worst of creation before Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

Moreover, many—or most—of their shrines are based on falsehood, for associating partners with Allah is frequently linked with lying in the Book of Allah. Allah Most High says:

“And avoid false speech, devoting yourselves to Allah alone, associating no partners with Him.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“False testimony is equivalent to associating partners with Allah.” He said this three times.

Such is the shrine built in Cairo over the head of al-Husayn. This is a false claim, by the agreement of the scholars: al-Husayn’s head was never brought there at all. Its origins lie in Ascalon, and it has been said that the head was that of a monk. Al-Husayn’s head was not in Ascalon; this was only introduced toward the end of the rule of the heretical Banū ʿUbayd. Likewise, the shrine of ʿAlī—may Allah be pleased with him—was only established during the rule of Banū

translated_text:
Buwayh. Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh, known as Mutayyan, the hadith master, and others said that it is actually the grave of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba, may Allah be pleased with him. ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, was buried in the governor’s palace in Kufa; Muʿāwiya was buried in the governor’s palace in Damascus; and ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs was buried in the governor’s palace in Egypt. This was for fear that, if they were buried in open cemeteries, the renegade Khārijites would exhume their bodies. The Khārijites had pledged to kill all three: Ibn Muljam killed ʿAlī, and his accomplice wounded Muʿāwiya. As for ʿAmr, he had appointed a man named Khārija to take his place, and the Khārijite killed him instead. The killer said:

“I intended to kill ʿAmr, but Allah willed that it be Khārija.”

This became a proverb. The point is that this shrine was only established under the rule of the heretics—the rule of Banū ʿUbayd.

There was much ignorance and misguidance among them, and they gave extensive support to heretics and to people of innovation among the Muʿtazila and the Rāfida. Consequently, Islam was severely weakened during their time, and the Christians entered Syria. Banū ʿUbayd were heretics and hypocrites who had no interest in believing in Allah and His Messenger or in waging jihad in Allah’s cause. Rather, their aims were disbelief, associating partners with Allah, and opposing Islam as far as they could. All their followers were people of innovation and misguidance. Thus, during their rule, the Christians seized most of Syria. Then Allah raised up Sunni rulers such as Nūr al-Dīn, Salāh al-Dīn and his brothers, together with their followers. They reconquered the Muslim lands and waged jihad against the disbelievers and hypocrites.

translated_text:
And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade prayer at sunrise and sunset because the polytheists prostrate to the sun at those times, and Satan accompanies it. Although a Muslim praying does not intend to prostrate to the sun, the prohibition serves to block the means to polytheism, lest he imitate the polytheists in practices peculiar to them and thereby be led into polytheism. Hence, he forbade deliberately choosing these two times for prayer. This is Ibn ʿUmar’s wording in the two Sahīh collections. Deliberately setting out to pray at these times is therefore forbidden.

However, if an occasion arises for which prayer is prescribed—such as the prayer upon entering a mosque, the eclipse prayer, prostration upon recitation, the two units of prayer following circumambulation, or repeating a prayer with the local imam—there is a well-known disagreement among the scholars concerning these acts. The stronger view is that they are permissible and recommended, for they are good deeds involving no evil, and their opportunity is lost if they are left undone. The prohibition concerns deliberately setting out to pray at that time, because this resembles the disbelievers’ deliberate prostration at that time. When a prayer has no particular occasion, a person has chosen to perform it at that time, even if he did not choose the time for its own sake. By contrast, a prayer prompted by a particular occasion is performed because of that occasion; the time has no bearing on it whatsoever.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also issued a general prohibition against praying in graveyards, saying:

“The whole earth is a place of prayer, except graveyards and bathhouses.”

This was narrated by the compilers of the Sunan collections. It has been transmitted both with a connected chain to the Prophet and as a direct attribution to him by a Successor. The hadith masters have judged the connected version to be correct. Bathhouses are a refuge for devils, while prayer in graveyards was forbidden

because it involves imitating those who take graves as places of worship, even though the person praying may not intend to pray there because of any special merit of that spot, but may simply happen to do so.

Nevertheless, this involves resembling those who do intend that, so he forbade it. Likewise, he forbade prayer without a particular occasion at sunrise and sunset, even when a person does not seek any special merit in that time, because it involves resembling those who do seek special merit in it—namely, the polytheists. His prohibition of prayer at those times is thus like his prohibition of prayer in that place.

The polytheism that has led most of the children of Adam astray originated in, and found its greatest expression in, the worship of human beings and statues fashioned in their likeness. The polytheists were accustomed to gods who begot and were born, who inherited and were inherited from, and who were made of one thing or another. They therefore asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about the God he worshipped: “What is He made of? Is He made of this or that? From whom did He inherit the world, and to whom will He bequeath it?”

So Allah Most High said:

“Say: He is Allah, the One;
Allah, the Eternal Refuge.
He neither begets nor is born,
nor is there anyone equivalent to Him.”

In the hadith of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, it says: “For no one is born but will die, and no one inherits but will be inherited from.”

That is to say, all those worshipped besides Allah have been born, such as the Messiah, Uzayr and other righteous people, along with their images, and the likes of the Pharaohs who claimed divinity. Such a being is born and will die. Even if he inherited his possessions from someone else, when he dies someone else will inherit from him. But Allah, glorified is He, is Ever-Living: He does not die, nor is He inherited from. Glorified and exalted is He. Allah knows best, and may Allah bless Muhammad.

Surah al-Falaq (Daybreak)

Shaykh al-Islām, champion of the Sunnah and suppressor of innovation, Taqī al-Dīn Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may the Lord benefit us through his knowledge—also said the following, among the writings he composed in the Citadel:

Section: On the words,

“Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak.”

Allah Most High says:

“The Cleaver of grain and fruit stones.”

And He Most High says:

“The Cleaver of daybreak, who has made the night for rest.”

Falaq (splitting open) is a verbal noun used in a passive sense, just as qabd (seizing) can mean “that which is seized.” Thus, everything the Lord has split open is falaq. Al-Hasan said: “Falaq is everything that splits open to reveal something, such as daybreak, grain, and fruit stones.”

Al-Zajjāj said: “If you reflect on creation, it will become clear to you that most of it comes into being through splitting open
